case_title: Prakash Chandra Kapoor & Anr. vs Vijay Kumar Iyer, Liquidator of Bharati Defence and Infrastructure Limited & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Edelweiss Asset Reconstruction Company Limited is the Financial Creditor. Bharati Defence and Infrastructure Limited is the Corporate Debtor. Prakash Chandra Kapoor & Anr are Erstwhile Directors. PGI GmbH is a prospective scheme applicant. Vijay Kumar Iyer is the Liquidator. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Edelweiss acquired aggregate debt of Rs.6248.84 Crores in 2014. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default amount is Rs.6248.84 Crores (exact default date not specified). 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Section 7 was admitted on 06.06.2017. Liquidation was ordered on 14.01.2019. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The liquidator invited EOIs for a 'going concern' sale. Multiple applicants submitted proposals but failed to deposit the required Earnest Money Deposit (EMD). Consequently, the liquidator sought to sell assets. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: After NCLT ordered liquidation on 14.01.2019, the liquidator filed IA 3702 of 2019 for directions on the sale of assets. On 18.12.2020, NCLT allowed the application to proceed with liquidation/asset sale due to non-compliance by bidders. Appellants appealed to NCLAT to prevent piecemeal sale and insist on a going concern sale.
legal_issues: Whether the Adjudicating Authority was justified in directing the sale of the Corporate Debtor's assets in parcels instead of granting further time to attempt a sale as a going concern to ensure beneficial liquidation.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Procedural timelines for the liquidation process are directory, and extensions can be granted in exceptional circumstances to maximize asset value and preserve employment. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 35(1)(e) of the IBC mandates carrying on the business for 'beneficial liquidation', which overrides directory timelines under Regulation 47. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Despite previous failures by bidders to deposit EMDs, ongoing interest from global bidders and the need to protect employment justified an extraordinary final opportunity. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Invoking inherent powers under Rule 11 of NCLAT Rules, the bench ruled it just and expedient to grant a final extension for a going concern sale subject to strict EMD compliance.
operative_order: The NCLAT disposed of the appeals by granting a final six-week extension to the Liquidator to attempt the sale of the Corporate Debtor as a going concern. Prospective buyers were directed to deposit the required EMD within two weeks.
summary: Edelweiss initiated CIRP against Bharati Defence, which eventually resulted in a liquidation order. Due to prospective buyers' failure to deposit EMDs, the NCLT authorized the liquidator to proceed with asset sales. The erstwhile directors, workmen union, and PGI Global appealed to the NCLAT, arguing for a 'going concern' sale to preserve 850 jobs and maximize value. The NCLAT held that liquidation timelines are directory and, emphasizing 'beneficial liquidation' under Section 35(1)(e) of the IBC, granted a final six-week extension to execute a going concern sale provided EMDs are deposited within two weeks.

case_title: Bishal Jaiswal vs Asset Reconstruction Company (India) Ltd. & Anr.
appeal_number: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 385 of 2020 with Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 903 of 2021
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Bishal Jaiswal is the Appellant/Director of the Corporate Debtor. Asset Reconstruction Company (India) Ltd. is the Financial Creditor/Respondent No. 1. Corporate Power Limited is the Corporate Debtor. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: The Corporate Debtor availed loan facilities from a consortium of lenders aggregating to INR 2175 crores for phase-I and INR 2387 crores for phase-II of a thermal power plant project. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: The account was classified as NPA on July 31, 2013. The outstanding default amount claimed was INR 5997,80,02,973. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Loan recall notice was issued on March 27, 2015. SARFAESI notice was issued and physical possession taken on June 1, 2016. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The Financial Creditor relied on the Corporate Debtor's balance sheets for FYs ending March 31, 2015, 2016, and 2017, which recorded the 'Rupee Term Loans from Banks and Financial Institutions' under 'Secured Loans'. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The Financial Creditor filed a Section 7 petition on December 26, 2018, which NCLT admitted on February 19, 2020. Following a Supreme Court remand to NCLAT to assess the balance sheets for limitation extension, NCLAT heard the appeal along with a subsequent appeal against an October 8, 2021 NCLT order directing liquidation.
legal_issues: Whether the entries in the balance sheets for the years 2015, 2016, and 2017 contain an unequivocal acknowledgement of debt under Section 18 of the Limitation Act, 1963, thereby extending the limitation period for a Section 7 IBC application.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An acknowledgement of liability in a corporate debtor's balance sheet extends the period of limitation under Section 18 of the Limitation Act, even if accompanied by a claim for damages or set-off. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Explanation (a) to Section 18 of the Limitation Act clarifies that an acknowledgement is valid even if coupled with a refusal to pay or a claim to set-off. Furthermore, procedural rules allow supplementary affidavits and additional documents to be considered without formally amending the Form-1 application. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal scrutinized the balance sheets and notes, determining that the Corporate Debtor's caveat regarding impending damage claims against the banks did not negate the express admission of the 'Secured Loans' liability. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The continuous acknowledgment of debt in the balance sheets signed in 2015, 2016, and 2017 provided fresh periods of limitation from the NPA date of 2013, rendering the 2018 Section 7 application legally within time.
operative_order: The NCLAT dismissed both appeals, upholding the NCLT's admission of the Section 7 application and the subsequent order directing the liquidation of the Corporate Debtor.
summary: The Financial Creditor (ARCIL) filed a Section 7 application under the IBC against Corporate Power Limited in 2018, based on a default that occurred when the account became an NPA in 2013. The Corporate Debtor's director appealed, arguing the petition was barred by limitation. Following a Supreme Court remand, the NCLAT examined whether the Corporate Debtor's balance sheets for FY 2015-2017 constituted an acknowledgement of debt under Section 18 of the Limitation Act. The Tribunal held that despite caveats stating an intent to claim damages from the banks, the balance sheets unequivocally acknowledged the debt. The NCLAT concluded the petition was within time and upheld both the CIRP admission and subsequent liquidation orders, dismissing the appeals.

case_title: B. Prashanth Hegde vs State Bank Of India & Anr
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: State Bank of India and consortium banks are the Financial Creditors. Metal Closures Pvt. Ltd. is the Corporate Debtor. B. Prashanth Hegde is the Suspended Managing Director/Appellant. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: A consortium of banks granted term loans and working capital credit facilities to the Corporate Debtor from 2007 onwards. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: The total credit exposure of the consortium aggregated to Rs. 160.25 crores. Dates of NPA were initially in 2010 but shifted to 2014 (SBI on 28.5.2014) due to failed restructuring. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Possession notices under SARFAESI Section 13(2) were issued in February and September 2015. The Section 7 application was filed on 25.04.2018. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: SBI relied on balance sheets for FY 2013-14 and 2014-15 signed on 30.09.2015, the CD's reply to the 13(2) notice dated 13.11.2015, and a DRT counterclaim dated 09.08.2018 to prove acknowledgment of debt. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT admitted the Section 7 petition on 14.12.2018. NCLAT previously allowed the appeal, but the Supreme Court remanded it in April 2021 to allow SBI to amend pleadings regarding limitation.
legal_issues: Whether the Section 7 application was barred by limitation or if the entries in the balance sheets and replies constituted valid acknowledgments of debt under Section 18 of the Limitation Act, 1963.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Written acknowledgments of liability in balance sheets or formal replies extend the period of limitation under Section 18 of the Limitation Act for initiating CIRP. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 18(1) read with Article 137 of the Limitation Act provides a fresh three-year limitation period starting from the date a debt is acknowledged in writing. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal found that balance sheets signed on 30.09.2015 contained clear and implicit acknowledgments of the debts without qualifying caveats, validating the limitation extension. Furthermore, unadjudicated counterclaims or criminal FIRs do not negate the debt's existence or the limitation extension. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Since the acknowledgments occurred within three years of the default (2014), the fresh limitation period ran until September 2018, making the April 2018 Section 7 application well within time.
operative_order: The NCLAT dismissed the appeal, upholding the NCLT's admission order dated 14.12.2018 and directing that the CIRP against the Corporate Debtor continue.
summary: State Bank of India initiated CIRP against Metal Closures Pvt. Ltd., which was admitted by the NCLT. The suspended MD appealed, arguing the debt was time-barred as the default occurred in 2010, and cited pending DRT counterclaims and criminal FIRs against bank officials. Following a Supreme Court remand, the NCLAT evaluated the amended pleadings. It held that the Corporate Debtor's balance sheets signed in September 2015 and its replies to SARFAESI notices constituted valid acknowledgments of debt under Section 18 of the Limitation Act, providing a fresh limitation period. Consequently, the April 2018 Section 7 application was within time, and the appeal was dismissed.

case_title: Kushan Mitra vs Amit Goel & Anr.
appeal_number: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 128 of 2021 & I.A. 2340 of 2021 and 2413 of 2021
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Kushan Mitra (Suspended Shareholder/Director) is the Appellant. Amit Goel is the Financial Creditor/Respondent No. 1. CMYK Printech Limited is the Corporate Debtor. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Amit Goel was allotted 26,00,566 shares on a preferential basis in lieu of an outstanding loan and prior expenses, treated as share application money of Rs. 1.56 Crores. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: The Corporate Debtor subsequently passed a Board Resolution on 10.05.2019 revoking the allotment and declaring it void ab initio, but defaulted on refunding the share application money of Rs. 1,56,03,396/-. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Shares were allotted in August-September 2018 and revoked on 10.05.2019. Amit Goel filed a Section 7 petition on 08.10.2020. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Form PAS-3 and PAS-4, along with Board Resolutions dated 01.08.2018, 25.08.2018, 11.09.2018, and 10.05.2019, evidenced the allotment and its subsequent revocation without a refund. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Amit Goel filed a Section 7 application which was admitted by NCLT on 19.01.2021. The Appellant challenged this admission at the NCLAT, arguing that un-allotted share application money does not qualify as a financial debt.
legal_issues: Whether Share Application Money, in the event of non-allotment or revocation of shares, transforms into a 'Loan/Debt' carrying statutory interest under Section 42(6) of the Companies Act, 2013, thereby qualifying as a 'Financial Debt' under Section 5(8) of the IBC.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Unrefunded share application money for which shares are not allotted statutorily accrues interest and assumes the character of a deposit or loan, qualifying as a financial debt. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 42(6) of the Companies Act, 2013 mandates that if shares are not allotted within 60 days, the application money must be refunded within 15 days, failing which it attracts 12% interest. This statutory interest satisfies the 'consideration for time value of money' requirement under Section 5(8) of the IBC. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal held that since the allotment was revoked and the money was not refunded, by operation of law, the unrefunded amount assumed the character of a loan with interest, despite pending criminal complaints or internal company disputes. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The failure to refund the share application money constituted a default of a financial debt, justifying the admission of the Section 7 petition and the dismissal of the appeal.
operative_order: The NCLAT dismissed the appeal, upholding the NCLT's admission order, and also dismissed the intervention applications as non-maintainable with no order as to costs.
summary: Amit Goel filed a Section 7 IBC application against CMYK Printech Limited after the company revoked his preferential share allotment but failed to refund his share application money of Rs. 1.56 Crores. The NCLT admitted the application, which was appealed by Kushan Mitra, a suspended director. The Appellant argued that share application money is not a 'financial debt'. The NCLAT held that under Section 42(6) of the Companies Act, 2013, unrefunded share application money statutorily attracts 12% interest, thereby satisfying the 'time value of money' requirement of Section 5(8) of the IBC. The appeal was dismissed, and the CIRP admission was upheld.

case_title: R.K. Industries (Unit-II) LLP vs HR Commercials Pvt. Ltd. & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: R.K. Industries (Unit-II) LLP is the Appellant and anchor bidder. ABG Shipyard Limited is the Corporate Debtor, and Sundaresh Bhat is its Liquidator. Welspun Steel Resources Pvt. Ltd (WSRPL) is Respondent No. 7 and a composite bidder. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: The liquidation and sale of composite assets of ABG Shipyard Limited, including Dahej materials and land. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: The reserve price for composite assets dropped from Rs. 1480 crores to Rs. 1104 crores across failed e-auctions. The Appellant's anchor bid was Rs. 431 crores for Dahej assets, while WSRPL offered Rs. 650-675 crores for composite assets. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Liquidation was ordered on 25.04.2019. The second Swiss Challenge Process started on 22.03.2021. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: After five failed e-auctions, the Liquidator initiated a second Swiss Challenge Process for piecemeal assets where the Appellant became the anchor bidder. Subsequently, WSRPL submitted a composite offer of Rs. 675 crores, prompting the Stakeholders Consultation Committee to recommend cancelling the piecemeal sale for a composite private sale. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The Adjudicating Authority (NCLT) via order dated 16.08.2021 permitted the cancellation of the second Swiss Challenge Process and directed the Liquidator to proceed with the composite sale. The Appellant challenged this order.
legal_issues: Whether a liquidator, in consultation with the Stakeholders Consultation Committee, can legally cancel an ongoing Swiss Challenge Process to pursue a composite private sale for value maximization, and whether such cancellation was arbitrary or malafide.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An authority or liquidator has the power to cancel or modify a tender or auction process if the bid documents permit it, provided the decision is transparent, fair, and free from arbitrariness or favoritism to maximize asset value. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 35(2) of the IBC and Regulation 8 of the Liquidation Regulations empower the liquidator to consult stakeholders. While such consultation is not binding, it is valuable and desirable for maximizing the liquidation value. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal evaluated the liquidator's reliance on the SCC's recommendation and the anchor bid document's clauses, concluding that the shift to a composite private sale was driven by value maximization and timeliness, not favoritism. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The liquidator validly exercised discretion to cancel the Swiss Challenge Process; however, the new composite private sale must be conducted with adequate open notice to all prospective buyers to ensure transparency and maximize value.
operative_order: The NCLAT disposed of the appeal by partially modifying the impugned order, upholding the cancellation of the second Swiss Challenge Process but directing that the new private sale process be undertaken with open notice to all prospective buyers to ensure transparency.
summary: During the liquidation of ABG Shipyard, the Liquidator initiated a second Swiss Challenge Process for piecemeal asset sales, selecting the Appellant as the anchor bidder. Before completion, WSRPL made a higher composite offer for the assets. With the Stakeholders Consultation Committee's approval, the NCLT allowed the Liquidator to cancel the Swiss Challenge and pursue a composite private sale. The Appellant challenged the cancellation as arbitrary. The NCLAT upheld the cancellation, validating the Liquidator's power to modify the sale for value maximization, but partially modified the order to require that the new private sale include open notice to all prospective buyers.

case_title: Arrow Engineering Ltd vs Golden Tobacco Limited
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Arrow Engineering Ltd is the Appellant and Financial Creditor. Golden Tobacco Limited is the Respondent and Corporate Debtor. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: The Appellant provided financial and marketing assistance to develop the Corporate Debtor's 8 acres of land in Vile Parle, Mumbai. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: The default amount claimed was Rs. 41.75 Crores with 18% interest, with the date of default cited as 12.07.2017. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The Section 7 application was filed on 24.06.2020. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The Corporate Debtor acknowledged receipt of Rs. 40.75 Crores in MoU letters dated 10.10.2011 and 01.02.2012, and in its Balance Sheets for the years 2014-15 to 2018-19, which also noted a refund with interest if decided by BIFR. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The NCLT Ahmedabad dismissed the Section 7 application on 25.01.2021, ruling the transaction was a business sharing arrangement and time-barred, which the Appellant appealed.
legal_issues: Whether the advance for real estate development constituted a financial debt, and whether acknowledgments in balance sheets extend the limitation period under Section 18 of the Limitation Act, 1963.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An advance for a development project with terms for repayment with interest upon termination is a financial debt, and recording this debt in balance sheets provides a fresh period of limitation. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 5(8)(f) of the IBC covers amounts raised under transactions having the commercial effect of a borrowing, and Section 18 of the Limitation Act is attracted by acknowledgments in balance sheets mandatorily maintained under the Companies Act. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal reviewed the MoU terms and continuous balance sheet entries from 2014-15 to 2018-19, finding they unequivocally proved a subsisting financial debt rather than a mere joint venture. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The debt was a valid financial debt, and the balance sheet entries extended the limitation period, making the 2020 Section 7 application legally maintainable.
operative_order: The NCLAT allowed the appeal, set aside the NCLT's judgment dated 25.01.2021, and directed the Adjudicating Authority to pass consequential orders including a moratorium within one month.
summary: Arrow Engineering Ltd advanced Rs. 40.75 Crores to Golden Tobacco Limited for developing land in Mumbai. Following disputes, Arrow filed a Section 7 IBC application, which the NCLT rejected as a time-barred business arrangement. On appeal, the NCLAT found that the MoU explicitly promised repayment with interest if the arrangement was terminated, qualifying it as a financial debt. Furthermore, continuous acknowledgments of the advance in the Corporate Debtor's balance sheets from 2014 to 2019 provided a fresh limitation period under Section 18 of the Limitation Act. The NCLAT thus allowed the appeal and directed the NCLT to pass admission orders.

case_title: Axis Bank Limited vs Value Infracon India Private Limited & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Axis Bank Limited is the Appellant/Applicant. Value Infracon India Private Limited is the Corporate Debtor. Value Infra Buyers Association is the Resolution Applicant. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Axis Bank sanctioned housing loans to 44 home buyers/allottees who purchased units in the Corporate Debtor's project. A tripartite agreement was signed between the homebuyers, the bank, and the Corporate Debtor. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Axis Bank filed a claim for Rs. 15,76,14,801/-, which the RP rejected. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The Section 7 application against the Corporate Debtor was admitted on 04.05.2018, and Axis Bank filed its claim on 20.09.2018. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Axis Bank obtained ex-parte recovery certificates from DRT against homebuyers and the Corporate Debtor but had not registered a charge under Section 77 of the Companies Act, 2013. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The NCLT rejected Axis Bank's application to be treated as a secured financial creditor, holding it was only a creditor to the homebuyers, not the Corporate Debtor.
legal_issues: Whether a bank that advances housing loans to homebuyers of a Corporate Debtor can be considered a 'Financial Creditor' of the Corporate Debtor under the IBC.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Banks advancing loans to homebuyers are creditors of the homebuyers, not the Corporate Debtor, and cannot be treated as 'Financial Creditors' of the Corporate Debtor in the CoC. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 5(8)(f) of the IBC recognizes homebuyers as financial creditors regardless of whether they self-finance or borrow, but this does not extend financial creditor status to their financiers. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal noted that the liability to repay the loan rested on individual homebuyers, and the bank failed to register any charge on the Corporate Debtor's assets under Section 77 of the Companies Act, 2013. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: A tripartite agreement does not change the character of the loan; the bank's recourse is against the allottees, and it cannot claim secured financial creditor status against the Corporate Debtor.
operative_order: The NCLAT dismissed the appeal, finding no reasons to interfere with the Adjudicating Authority's order, and disposed of the related I.As without costs.
summary: Axis Bank advanced housing loans to homebuyers investing in Value Infracon's real estate project. When the developer faced CIRP, Axis Bank sought 'Secured Financial Creditor' status based on tripartite agreements and DRT recovery certificates. The NCLT rejected the claim, and Axis Bank appealed. The NCLAT dismissed the appeal, holding that homebuyers themselves are the financial creditors under Section 5(8) of the IBC, not the banks that finance them. Furthermore, Axis Bank had no registered charge on the Corporate Debtor's assets under Section 77 of the Companies Act, 2013, confirming they could not be considered a secured financial creditor of the Corporate Debtor.

case_title: Edelweiss Asset Reconstruction Company Limited vs V Mahesh (IRP of Vasan Health Care Private Limited) & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Edelweiss Asset Reconstruction Company Limited is the Appellant/Financial Creditor. V Mahesh is Respondent No. 1 and the IRP of the Corporate Debtor. Vasan Health Care Pvt. Ltd. is the Corporate Debtor. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: The Corporate Debtor issued a Corporate Guarantee for loans borrowed by its subsidiary, Vasan Dental Hospitals Pvt. Ltd., from IndusInd Bank, which was subsequently assigned to the Appellant. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: The Appellant submitted a total claim of Rs. 507,88,68,502/-, out of which the IRP rejected Rs. 54,97,35,793/- relating to the Corporate Guarantee. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The Appellant filed its initial claim on 04.05.2017 and an updated claim on 17.10.2019 following the revival of CIRP proceedings. The IRP rejected the specific claim on 06.02.2020. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The Appellant shared the Corporate Guarantee dated 11.11.2015 and relevant Board Resolutions via email on 22.01.2020, but the IRP rejected the claim because the guarantee was not reflected as a contingent liability in the Corporate Debtor's books and had not been invoked. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The NCLT upheld the IRP's rejection of the Rs. 54.97 Crore claim on 22.02.2021. The Appellant filed the present appeal challenging this partial rejection of its claim.
legal_issues: Whether a Resolution Professional can reject a creditor's claim based on a corporate guarantee solely because the guarantee is not reflected in the corporate debtor's books of accounts and has not been invoked prior to the insolvency commencement.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The maturity of a claim, default of a debt, or the non-invocation of a guarantee are not valid grounds for a Resolution Professional to reject a claim during the collation process. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 3(6) of the IBC defines a 'claim' as a right to payment whether or not it is matured, fixed, or disputed. Section 25(2)(e) mandates the IRP/RP to collate and maintain an updated list of all claims, irrespective of whether the debt has crystalized or defaulted. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal held that since the Appellant provided the Corporate Guarantee and Board Resolutions before the claim was rejected, the mere fact that the Corporate Debtor failed to reflect it in its books of accounts cannot invalidate the legally executed guarantee. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The IRP and the Adjudicating Authority erred in taking an unsustainable technical stand to reject the claim, as the uninvoked corporate guarantee still constitutes a valid 'claim' under the IBC.
operative_order: The NCLAT allowed the appeal, set aside the NCLT's order rejecting the claim of Rs. 54,97,35,793/-, and directed the RP to verify the corporate guarantee documents and admit the claim.
summary: Edelweiss Asset Reconstruction submitted a claim of over Rs. 507 Crores against the Corporate Debtor, Vasan Health Care Pvt. Ltd.. The IRP rejected a portion of the claim (Rs. 54.97 Crores) arising from a corporate guarantee because it wasn't recorded in the debtor's books and hadn't been invoked, a decision upheld by the NCLT. On appeal, the NCLAT ruled that under Section 3(6) of the IBC, a 'claim' includes unmatured or uninvoked rights to payment. Holding that a corporate debtor's failure to record a guarantee in its books does not invalidate the guarantee itself, the NCLAT set aside the rejection and directed the RP to admit the claim.

case_title: Department of Goods & Service Tax vs Technovaa Plastic Industries Pvt. Ltd. & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant is the Department of Goods & Service Tax. Respondent No. 1 is the Corporate Debtor, Technovaa Plastic Industries Pvt. Ltd.. Respondent No. 2 is Vijay P. Lulla, the Erstwhile Resolution Professional. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: The Appellant's claim pertains to pending statutory dues (GST) owed by the Corporate Debtor for a period of five years. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: The Appellant claimed a total amount of Rs. 82,50,32,950, out of which Rs. 6,12,68,709 was compromised under the Sabka Vishwas Scheme, leaving a balance debt of Rs. 76,37,63,343. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP was initiated on 12.11.2018. The 90-day period for filing claims expired in February 2019. The Appellant filed its claim belatedly on 01.01.2020, which the RP rejected on 03.01.2020. The Resolution Plan was submitted for NCLT approval on 04.10.2019. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The Appellant sought proportionate distribution along with Operational Creditors, but the RP and Successful Resolution Applicant demonstrated that the claim was filed months after the deadline and after the CoC had already approved the resolution plan. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The Adjudicating Authority (NCLT Ahmedabad) approved the Resolution Plan on 04.09.2020 without including the Appellant's belated claim. The Appellant challenged this approval before the NCLAT.
legal_issues: Whether a statutory claim filed by a creditor after the expiration of the 90-day extended time period and after the Committee of Creditors has approved the Resolution Plan can be considered and admitted.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Once a resolution plan is approved by the Adjudicating Authority, all claims that are not part of the resolution plan stand extinguished, and successful resolution applicants must take over the corporate debtor on a 'fresh slate' without facing surprise claims. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 31 of the IBC mandates that an approved resolution plan binds all stakeholders, including government authorities. Regulation 12 of the CIRP Regulations strictly governs the timeline for filing claims, and late claims cannot disrupt an already concluded CoC approval process. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal found that the Appellant filed its claim on 01.01.2020, well after the February 2019 deadline and after the plan was submitted for Adjudicating Authority approval in October 2019, justifying the RP's rejection. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Because the GST department's claim was filed much belatedly and was not part of the approved Resolution Plan, it stood extinguished and could not be accommodated at a later stage.
operative_order: The NCLAT rejected the appeal, stating that the Resolution Plan approved by the Adjudicating Authority did not require any interference, with no order as to costs.
summary: The Department of Goods & Service Tax appealed against an NCLT order that approved the Resolution Plan for Technovaa Plastic Industries without accommodating its statutory GST claim of over Rs. 76 Crores. The NCLAT noted that the CIRP began in November 2018 and the deadline for filing claims expired in February 2019, yet the Appellant filed its claim in January 2020, months after the CoC had submitted the final plan for NCLT approval in October 2019. Relying on the 'fresh slate' doctrine established by the Supreme Court in the Essar Steel and Ghanashyam Mishra cases, the NCLAT held that belated claims not included in the approved plan are extinguished. Consequently, the appeal was rejected.

case_title: Canara Bank vs Manoj Kumar Sharma & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Canara Bank is the Appellant/Financial Creditor. Manoj Kumar Sharma and others are the Respondents, with Respondent No. 1 being a director/personal guarantor of the Corporate Debtor. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: The dispute involves the invocation and recovery of a personal guarantee provided by a director of the Corporate Debtor against the company's loan liabilities. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: The specific default amount and the date of default are not detailed in the brief order. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The Adjudicating Authority passed the contested interim order halting recovery on 26.02.2020. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The Adjudicating Authority's order was a brief, two-sentence directive explicitly stating they were 'not expressing any opinion on merits' but still ordered Canara Bank not to recover the personal guarantee amount. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The NCLT Kolkata Bench, via an order in Misc. A (IB) 338/KB/2020, restrained Canara Bank from recovering the personal guarantee while an appeal regarding the resolution plan was pending. Canara Bank challenged this non-speaking order before the NCLAT.
legal_issues: Whether an Adjudicating Authority can validly issue an interim injunction restraining a financial creditor from invoking a personal guarantee through a non-speaking, unreasoned order.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The recording of reasons is an essential feature of the dispensation of justice, and any judicial or administrative order that lacks reasoning is legally infirm and violates the principles of natural justice. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Relying on Supreme Court precedent, the Tribunal interpreted that judicial pronouncements must explicitly reflect what weighed with the court in granting or declining relief, as reasons are the 'heart' and 'soul' of a speaking order. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Upon reviewing the NCLT's order, the NCLAT applied the test of procedural fairness and found the order entirely bereft of qualitative and quantitative details or any stated rationale for granting the injunction. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT concluded that the NCLT's failure to record reasons caused prejudice to the appellant and hampered the proper administration of justice, necessitating the setting aside of the impugned order.
operative_order: The NCLAT allowed the appeal, set aside the impugned unreasoned order dated 26.02.2020, and remanded the matter to the NCLT Kolkata Bench to decide the application afresh on merits in a fair, just, and reasoned manner.
summary: Canara Bank appealed an interim order by the NCLT Kolkata that restrained the bank from enforcing the personal guarantee of a director of the Corporate Debtor. The NCLAT noted that the NCLT's directive was a non-speaking order devoid of any reasoning or factual analysis. Citing the Supreme Court's ruling in the 'Shukla and Brothers' case, the NCLAT emphasized that recording reasons is the 'heart and soul' of the justice delivery system. Finding the unreasoned injunction legally unsustainable, the NCLAT allowed the appeal, set aside the NCLT order, and remanded the matter for a fresh, reasoned adjudication.

case_title: IDBI Capital Markets & Securities Ltd. vs JBF Petrochemicals Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: IDBI Capital Markets & Securities Ltd. is the Appellant/Operational Creditor. JBF Petrochemicals Ltd. is the Respondent/Corporate Debtor. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: The Corporate Debtor engaged the Operational Creditor to assist in arranging working capital facilities of up to Rs. 2000 Crores (including a Rs. 550 Crore Stand By Letter of Credit) per an 'Offer Letter' dated June 2016. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: The Operational Creditor claimed a default of Rs. 78,00,000/- based on unpaid invoices raised upon achieving specific milestones (First invoice: Rs. 23 Lakhs, Second: Rs. 30 Lakhs, Third: Rs. 45 Lakhs). 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Demand notice under Section 8 of IBC was issued on 21.03.2018. The Corporate Debtor replied on 27.03.2018. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The Corporate Debtor paid Rs. 20 Lakhs towards the first invoice and explicitly signed a 'Statement of Confirmation of Balance' on 30.10.2017 acknowledging the outstanding debt of Rs. 78,00,000/-. However, in reply to the demand notice, it claimed the Operational Creditor failed to disburse the funds or arrange the full sanction. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The NCLT Ahmedabad dismissed the Section 9 application on 21.01.2020, citing a pre-existing dispute regarding deficient services and lack of authority of the signatory. The Operational Creditor appealed to the NCLAT.
legal_issues: Whether a reply to a Section 8 demand notice raising service deficiency constitutes a valid 'pre-existing dispute' when the corporate debtor had previously signed an unconditional 'Confirmation of Balance' acknowledging the exact debt.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A corporate debtor cannot raise a spurious or hypothetical 'pre-existing dispute' regarding service deficiency in response to a demand notice if it has previously, unequivocally acknowledged and confirmed the debt balance in writing. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 8(2) of the IBC requires the corporate debtor to bring to the operational creditor's notice a genuine pre-existing dispute. However, an unambiguous 'Confirmation of Balance' operates as an acknowledgment of liability under Section 18 of the Limitation Act, 1963, legally binding the debtor and negating subsequent, manufactured disputes. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal scrutinized the 'Confirmation of Balance' dated 30.10.2017, signed by the Corporate Debtor's Accounts Executive, and found it to be an unambiguous admission of the Rs. 78 Lakhs debt, which the NCLT had unlawfully ignored. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Because the debt was expressly acknowledged and the dispute raised in the reply to the demand notice was merely an afterthought to evade liability, the NCLT erred in rejecting the application. Furthermore, a company secretary possesses the implied authority to authorize another officer to sign an affidavit for IBC proceedings.
operative_order: The NCLAT allowed the appeal, set aside the NCLT's order dated 21.01.2020, and directed the Adjudicating Authority to restore the Section 9 application, admit it, and proceed in accordance with law.
summary: IDBI Capital filed a Section 9 IBC application against JBF Petrochemicals for unpaid advisory fees regarding the arrangement of working capital. The NCLT rejected the application, observing that IDBI failed to secure the full loan disbursement, constituting a pre-existing dispute, and citing procedural defects regarding the signatory's authority. On appeal, the NCLAT reversed this decision, emphasizing that JBF Petrochemicals had explicitly signed a 'Confirmation of Balance' acknowledging the Rs. 78 Lakhs debt prior to the demand notice. The NCLAT held that this written acknowledgment negated any subsequent claims of deficient service, rendering the dispute spurious, and validated the signatory's delegated authority, thereby directing the admission of the insolvency petition.

case_title: B. Sreekala vs Al Sadiq Sweets & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: B. Sreekala is the Appellant and Promoter/Director of the Corporate Debtor. Al Sadiq Sweets is the 1st Respondent/Operational Creditor. Ms. Baiju P is the 2nd Respondent/IRP. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: The Operational Creditor advanced money to the Corporate Debtor for the export of different grades of Indian Cashew Kernels to Qatar. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: The total claimed default was USD 1,00,000 (advance payment) plus USD 13,500 as interest at 18% p.a.. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: A Section 8 demand notice was issued on 01.08.2020 and received on 10.08.2020. The Section 9 application was filed on 16.09.2020. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The Operational Creditor paid a 70% advance (USD 1,00,000) against a proforma invoice dated 25.11.2019. Due to the COVID-19 lockdown, the export could not be completed, and the contract was terminated around late April 2020. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The Adjudicating Authority (NCLT Kochi) admitted the Section 9 application on 26.02.2021, holding that the default date was 03.01.2020, which was prior to the Section 10A suspension. The Appellant challenged this admission before the NCLAT.
legal_issues: Whether the Section 9 application filed on 16.09.2020 was maintainable given the enhanced threshold limit of Rs. 1 Crore notified under Section 4 of the IBC on 24.03.2020, and whether the default fell within the prohibited period under Section 10A.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The enhanced threshold limit of Rs. 1 Crore applies prospectively to all IBC applications filed on or after 24.03.2020, irrespective of when the default occurred. Additionally, Section 10A strictly bars the initiation of CIRP for any default occurring on or after 25.03.2020. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Notification S.O. 1205(E) dated 24.03.2020 under Section 4 of the IBC dictates the jurisdiction threshold based on the filing date of the application. Section 10A provides an absolute embargo on filing applications for defaults occurring during the specified pandemic period. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal found that the contract was terminated and the debt became payable around 25.04.2020 or 30.04.2020, which squarely falls within the Section 10A period. Furthermore, the claimed default (approx. USD 1,13,500) was well below the Rs. 1 Crore threshold applicable on the filing date (16.09.2020). 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLT erred in admitting the application because it lacked jurisdiction due to the unmet Rs. 1 Crore threshold and the statutory bar under Section 10A of the IBC.
operative_order: The NCLAT allowed the appeal, set aside the NCLT's admission order dated 26.02.2021, dismissed the Section 9 application, and released the Corporate Debtor from the CIRP rigour with immediate effect.
summary: Al Sadiq Sweets filed a Section 9 IBC application against the Corporate Debtor over an unrefunded advance of USD 1,00,000 for a cancelled cashew export contract. The NCLT admitted the application, concluding the default occurred on 03.01.2020, prior to the COVID-19 statutory bars. On appeal, the NCLAT reversed this decision, holding that the application filed on 16.09.2020 was subject to the newly notified Rs. 1 Crore threshold under Section 4, which the claim failed to meet. Additionally, the Tribunal observed the actual default occurred in late April 2020 upon contract termination, falling within the suspended period under Section 10A of the IBC. The appeal was allowed, and the CIRP was quashed.

case_title: M/s. Hasmukh N. Shah & Associates vs M/s. Victoria Entertainment Pvt. Ltd. & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: M/s. Hasmukh N. Shah & Associates is the Appellant. M/s. Victoria Entertainment Pvt. Ltd., M/s. Victoria Enterprises Ltd., M/s. Sanskar Info TV Pvt. Ltd., and M/s. Eastern Ceramics Limited are the Respondents in the respective appeals. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: The appeals arise out of four different Section 9 applications filed by the Appellant. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Specific default amounts and dates are not detailed, as the appeals were dismissed entirely on limitation grounds. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The NCLT passed the impugned orders on 20.07.2018. The Appellant first applied for a certified copy on 21.01.2019, applied again on 27.07.2021, and filed the appeals on 20.09.2021. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The Appellant claimed the appeals were within time because they were never provided a free certified copy of the order as mandated by Rule 50 of the NCLT Rules, and further sought the benefit of the Supreme Court's suo motu extension of limitation due to COVID-19 (from 15.03.2020). 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The Adjudicating Authority (NCLT Mumbai) dismissed the Section 9 applications on 20.07.2018. Over three years later, the Appellant filed these appeals before the NCLAT.
legal_issues: Whether the limitation period for filing an appeal under Section 61 of the IBC is suspended until a free certified copy of the order is provided by the Registry under Rule 50 of the NCLT Rules, 2016.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The limitation period for filing an appeal under the IBC is not suspended while a litigant awaits a free certified copy of the order; aggrieved parties must exercise due diligence and apply for a certified copy proactively. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 61(2) of the IBC consciously omits the phrase 'from the date on which the order is made available' found in Section 421(3) of the Companies Act, indicating the legislature's intent for timely resolutions without waiting for free copies. Rule 50 of the NCLT Rules is a procedural rule that cannot override the strict substantive timelines of the IBC. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal observed that the NCLT order was delivered on 20.07.2018, and the Appellant remained inactive until applying for a certified copy in January 2019 and again in July 2021. The Supreme Court's COVID-19 limitation extension from 15.03.2020 did not cure the unexplained delay from July 2018 to March 2020. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Relying on the Supreme Court's ruling in V. Nagarajan vs. SKS Ispat and Power Ltd., the Tribunal held that a litigant cannot prevent limitation from running by awaiting a free certified copy, rendering the present appeals filed in 2021 barred by time.
operative_order: The NCLAT dismissed all the appeals as barred by time.
summary: M/s Hasmukh N. Shah & Associates appealed four NCLT Mumbai orders dated July 20, 2018, that dismissed its Section 9 IBC applications. The appeals were filed over three years later, on September 20, 2021. The Appellant argued that the limitation period had not commenced because they had not received a free certified copy of the judgment under NCLT Rule 50, and also sought refuge under the Supreme Court's COVID-19 limitation extension. Citing the Supreme Court's judgment in V. Nagarajan, the NCLAT held that the IBC mandates proactive diligence, and limitation under Section 61 is not suspended while awaiting a free copy. Because the delay between July 2018 and March 2020 was unaccounted for, the COVID-19 extension did not apply, and all appeals were dismissed as time-barred.

case_title: Prerna Singh vs Committee of Creditors of M/s Xalta Food and Beverages Pvt. Ltd. & Ors.
appeal_number: Contempt Case (AT) No. 03 of 2020 in Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 104 of 2019
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Prerna Singh is the Applicant/Lessor. The Committee of Creditors (CoC), Naveen Kumar Jain (Resolution Professional/Liquidator), and various lender banks are the Respondents/Contemnors. M/s Xalta Food and Beverages Pvt. Ltd. is the Corporate Debtor. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: The Corporate Debtor leased two warehouses from the Applicant for running its beverage production business at a monthly rent of Rs. 35,73,270/- including GST. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: The Applicant alleged an outstanding rent of Rs. 3,41,94,733/- against total dues of Rs. 4,49,32,020/- during the CIRP period. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The CIRP commenced on 25.07.2018. The Adjudicating Authority passed the liquidation order on 14.06.2019. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The CoC had paid a total of Rs. 3,02,11,464/- towards rent from 01.12.2018 up to the date immediately preceding the liquidation order (13.06.2019), which covered the entire moratorium period as previously directed by the NCLAT. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The Applicant filed a contempt case alleging deliberate disobedience of an earlier NCLAT order dated 31.01.2019, which had directed the CoC to pay rent from 01.12.2018 until the moratorium period ended.
legal_issues: Whether the CoC and RP willfully disobeyed the NCLAT's prior order by ceasing rent payments after a liquidation order was passed, and whether the statutory moratorium (and corresponding CIRP costs) continues after the initiation of liquidation.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A moratorium declared under Section 14 of the IBC ceases to have effect on the date the Adjudicating Authority passes an order for liquidation, ending the liability of the CoC to pay lease rent as a CIRP cost. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Rent qualifies as a CIRP cost under Section 5(13) read with Regulation 31(b) because the lessor's right to recover possession is prejudicially affected by the moratorium. However, under Section 14(4) of the IBC, if a liquidation order is passed under Section 33, the moratorium ceases on the date of that order, and any subsequent claims must be filed before the liquidator. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal verified that the CoC was only mandated to pay rent up to the end of the moratorium (13.06.2019), and evidence showed they had already paid Rs. 3,02,11,464/-, successfully satisfying the rental dues for that exact period. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Because the respondents fully paid the rent for the duration of the moratorium as previously ordered by the Tribunal, there was no willful disobedience or contempt of court.
operative_order: The NCLAT held that no case was made out to punish the Respondents for contempt, and accordingly disposed of the contempt application with no order as to costs.
summary: The Applicant, who leased warehouses to the Corporate Debtor, initiated contempt proceedings against the CoC and RP for allegedly disobeying a prior NCLAT order to pay rent during the CIRP moratorium. The NCLAT evaluated the statutory provisions of Sections 14 and 33 of the IBC, clarifying that the moratorium automatically ceases when a liquidation order is passed. Given that the NCLT ordered liquidation on 14.06.2019, the CoC's liability for rent as a CIRP cost ended on 13.06.2019. Noting that the CoC had already paid over Rs. 3 crores to clear the dues up to that date, the Tribunal found no willful disobedience and disposed of the contempt application.

case_title: Mantena Laboratories Limited vs Edelweiss Asset Reconstruction Company Limited
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Mantena Laboratories Limited is the Appellant/Corporate Debtor. Edelweiss Asset Reconstruction Company Limited is the Respondent/Financial Creditor, having acquired the debt via an assignment agreement from IDBI Bank. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: IDBI Bank sanctioned credit facilities to the Corporate Debtor in 2010, including cash credit and letters of credit, which were later assigned to the Financial Creditor. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: The total outstanding amount claimed in default was Rs. 26,43,25,009.11 as of 31.08.2018. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The account was classified as NPA on 30.06.2012. A Section 13(2) SARFAESI notice was issued on 04.04.2013. A One Time Settlement (OTS) proposal was accepted on 28.02.2018 and revoked on 07.06.2018. The Section 7 application was filed in October 2018. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The Corporate Debtor continuously acknowledged the debt in its financial statements from 2013 to 2018, and entered into an OTS in February 2018, paying Rs. 1 crore but defaulting on the remaining Rs. 9 crores. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The NCLT Hyderabad admitted the Section 7 application on 06.08.2021. The Corporate Debtor appealed, arguing the petition was barred by limitation since the NPA was declared in 2012.
legal_issues: Whether a Section 7 application filed more than three years after the NPA declaration is barred by limitation, or whether continuous balance sheet entries and an accepted One Time Settlement (OTS) proposal constitute valid acknowledgments extending the limitation period under Section 18 of the Limitation Act, 1963 and Section 62 of the Contract Act.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Continuous acknowledgments of debt in a corporate debtor's balance sheets and the execution of a One Time Settlement (OTS) agreement restart the limitation period under Section 18 of the Limitation Act, and a new OTS creates a fresh cause of action under Section 62 of the Contract Act. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 18 of the Limitation Act is attracted when a corporate debtor acknowledges its liability in financial statements signed by its directors/auditors. Furthermore, under Section 62 of the Indian Contract Act, an accepted OTS proposal operates as a novation, substituting the old contract and initiating a new limitation cycle. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal noted that the debt was recorded in the balance sheets up to FY 2017-18 and that the 28.02.2018 OTS agreement—where the debtor paid an upfront amount before defaulting—was an unequivocal admission of a subsisting jural relationship. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Section 7 application filed in October 2018 was well within the limitation period due to the valid extensions provided by the balance sheet entries and the 2018 OTS agreement, rendering the limitation defense meritless.
operative_order: The NCLAT dismissed the appeal, holding that the Adjudicating Authority's order admitting the Section 7 application was free from legal errors, with no order as to costs.
summary: Edelweiss Asset Reconstruction Company filed a Section 7 IBC application against Mantena Laboratories for defaulting on a debt of Rs. 26.43 Crores. The NCLT admitted the application, which the Corporate Debtor appealed, arguing the debt was time-barred because the account was classified as an NPA back in 2012. The NCLAT rejected this defense, observing that the Corporate Debtor had continuously acknowledged the debt in its balance sheets up to FY 2017-18 and had entered into a One Time Settlement (OTS) in February 2018. The Tribunal held that these actions constituted valid acknowledgments under Section 18 of the Limitation Act and provided a fresh cause of action under Section 62 of the Contract Act. Consequently, the appeal was dismissed and the CIRP initiation was upheld.

case_title: Patel Hydro Power Private Limited & Ors. (Appellants)
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Patel Hydro Power Private Limited and five other entities are the Transferor Companies, and Patel Engineering Limited is the Transferee Company (Holding Company). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: The appellants proposed a scheme of merger by absorption of the wholly-owned subsidiary Transferor Companies with their Transferee Company. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: N/A, as this is an amalgamation/merger proceeding under the Companies Act, 2013, not an IBC debt default case. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The NCLT passed the impugned order directing the meetings and procurement of consent affidavits on 15.11.2021. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The merger did not involve the issuance of any new shares, there was no reorganization of the Transferee Company's share capital, and the rights of the Transferee Company's shareholders and creditors remained completely unaffected. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The Appellants filed an application under Sections 230-232 of the Companies Act seeking dispensation of meetings of equity shareholders and creditors. The NCLT directed the Transferee Company to hold the meetings and obtain 90% consent affidavits from Unsecured Creditors, prompting the Appellants to challenge these directions before the NCLAT.
legal_issues: Whether the NCLT erred in refusing to dispense with the meetings of equity shareholders and creditors of a Transferee Company in a scheme of amalgamation involving its wholly-owned subsidiaries where no new shares are being issued and rights are unaffected.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: In a scheme of amalgamation between a holding company and its wholly-owned subsidiaries, the requirement to hold meetings of the transferee company's equity shareholders and creditors can be dispensed with if no new shares are issued and their rights are unaffected. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 232(1) of the Companies Act, 2013 uses the word 'may', conferring discretionary power upon the Tribunal to dispense with the convening of meetings if it is satisfied that the arrangement does not negatively alter or impact the stakeholders' rights. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The NCLAT observed that since the Transferee Company was absorbing its wholly-owned subsidiaries, no new shares were being issued, no dilution in shareholding occurred, and no compromise was offered to the creditors, ensuring zero prejudice to their existing rights. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT concluded that the NCLT's directions mandating meetings and 90% consent affidavits from unsecured creditors were unnecessary under the facts of the case, and therefore set aside those specific directions.
operative_order: The NCLAT allowed the appeal and set aside the Order of the NCLT specifically with respect to the directions regarding the dispensation of meetings of Equity Shareholders and Creditors.
summary: The Appellant companies proposed a scheme of amalgamation under Sections 230-232 of the Companies Act, 2013, to merge several wholly-owned subsidiary Transferor Companies into their holding Transferee Company. They sought to dispense with the meetings of the Transferee Company's shareholders and creditors since no new shares were being issued and no rights were altered. The NCLT directed the holding of these meetings and required 90% consent affidavits from unsecured creditors. On appeal, the NCLAT held that Section 232(1) grants the Tribunal discretion to dispense with such meetings when an amalgamation involves a parent and wholly-owned subsidiaries without affecting the stakeholders' rights or share capital. Consequently, the NCLAT allowed the appeal and set aside the NCLT's directions regarding the meetings and consent affidavits.

case_title: Cotton Casuals (India) Private Limited vs Kanchan Dutta & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Cotton Casuals (India) Private Limited is the Appellant/Purchaser. Kanchan Dutta is the Liquidator of the Corporate Debtor (Respondent No. 1). West Bengal Industrial Development Corporation Limited (WBIDC) is Respondent No. 2. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: The Appellant purchased a leasehold asset of the Corporate Debtor (Enfield Apparels Limited) during the liquidation process. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: WBIDC demanded Rs. 2,96,69,215/- as a transfer fee for the assignment of the sub-lease. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The original e-auction occurred on 11.06.2019. WBIDC demanded the transfer fee on 03.09.2020. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The sub-lease deed dated 06.08.2010 required payment of a 10% transfer fee to WBIDC. The Appellant's own letter dated 26.06.2019 expressly promised to pay the transfer charges to WBIDC if allowed to bid. Furthermore, prior NCLT orders dated 23.06.2020 and 29.07.2020 explicitly directed the Appellant to pay the transfer fee, and these were never challenged. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The NCLT Kolkata directed the Appellant to pay the transfer fee on 02.02.2021. The Appellant challenged this order before the NCLAT.
legal_issues: Whether a sale of a corporate debtor's leasehold asset by a liquidator under the IBC constitutes an 'involuntary transfer' exempt from transfer fees, and whether the purchaser is liable to pay the transfer fee under the sub-lease deed.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A sale of a corporate debtor's assets by a liquidator under the IBC is a transfer on behalf of the corporate debtor and constitutes a voluntary sale, making the purchaser liable for applicable transfer fees as per the lease agreement. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 35(f) and (g) of the IBC empower the liquidator to sell assets and execute documents 'on behalf of the corporate debtor'. Therefore, a liquidator's sale is not an involuntary court sale but an assignment by the company itself. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal relied on the Appellant's express written undertaking to pay the transfer fee, the specific clause in the sub-lease deed mandating the fee, and the Appellant's failure to challenge previous NCLT orders that explicitly directed the payment. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Since the sale by the liquidator was a voluntary assignment on behalf of the Corporate Debtor, and the Appellant had contractually and judicially bound itself to pay the fee, the Appellant could not evade the liability.
operative_order: The NCLAT dismissed the appeal, holding the Appellant liable to pay the transfer fee, and closed the associated contempt case with no order as to costs.
summary: During the liquidation of Enfield Apparels Limited, Cotton Casuals purchased a leasehold asset and was subsequently asked by WBIDC to pay a transfer fee of over Rs. 2.96 Crores as per the sub-lease deed. Cotton Casuals challenged the fee, arguing that a sale by an IBC liquidator is an 'involuntary transfer' exempt from such charges. The NCLAT rejected this argument, citing Supreme Court precedent and Section 35 of the IBC to hold that a liquidator acts on behalf of the Corporate Debtor, making the sale voluntary. Noting that Cotton Casuals had previously provided a written undertaking to pay the fee and had not challenged earlier NCLT orders enforcing it, the NCLAT dismissed the appeal.

case_title: BSE Ltd. vs Asahi Infrastructure & Projects Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: BSE Ltd. (Bombay Stock Exchange) is the Appellant/Operational Creditor. Asahi Infrastructure & Projects Ltd. is the Respondent/Corporate Debtor. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: The Corporate Debtor entered into a Listing Agreement with the Appellant on 30.11.1993, obligating it to pay annual listing fees. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: The Appellant claimed an outstanding default amount of Rs. 8,85,526/- as of 01.04.2017 for Annual Listing Fees (2017-18) and previous arrears. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Invoices demanding the fee were issued on 01.04.2017, leading to a Section 9 application under the IBC. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The Corporate Debtor opposed the application on maintainability, arguing that listing fees are 'regulatory fees' payable under SEBI regulations, not 'operational debt'. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The NCLT Mumbai dismissed the Section 9 application on 11.02.2019, ruling that regulatory fees cannot trigger insolvency. The Appellant appealed the dismissal to the NCLAT.
legal_issues: Whether the annual listing fees and associated arrears payable by a corporate debtor to a recognized stock exchange constitute an 'operational debt' under Section 5(21) of the IBC.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Regulatory dues, such as listing fees owed to a stock exchange, do not fall within the statutory definition of 'operational debt', and the IBC cannot be used as a recovery mechanism for such regulatory fees. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 5(21) of the IBC defines operational debt. The Insolvency Law Committee explicitly deliberated on whether to include regulatory dues within this definition and unanimously concluded they should not be included. Furthermore, Regulation 28 of the Securities Contracts Regulations 2018 classifies a stock exchange's listing department as a 'regulatory department', confirming the fees are regulatory in nature. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal noted that SEBI and stock exchanges possess their own statutory mechanisms and penal provisions under the SEBI Act to recover regulatory dues. Allowing IBC triggers for such dues contravenes the Supreme Court's mandate that the IBC's primary focus is corporate revival, not debt recovery. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Since listing fees are regulatory dues rather than operational debts, the Section 9 application was legally non-maintainable and correctly dismissed by the Adjudicating Authority.
operative_order: The NCLAT dismissed the appeal, holding that the Adjudicating Authority did not commit any error in rejecting the Section 9 application, with no order as to costs.
summary: BSE Ltd. filed a Section 9 IBC application against Asahi Infrastructure for failing to pay annual listing fees and arrears totaling Rs. 8.85 Lakhs. The NCLT rejected the application, holding that listing fees are regulatory dues and not operational debt. BSE appealed, arguing the IBC was applicable as SEBI allegedly lacked an adequate recovery mechanism. Relying on the Insolvency Law Committee Report and the fundamental objective of the IBC—which is corporate revival, not debt recovery—the NCLAT affirmed that regulatory dues do not fall under Section 5(21) of the IBC. Noting that SEBI possesses its own penal provisions for recovery, the NCLAT dismissed the appeal.

case_title: G.S. Buildtech Pvt. Ltd. vs Ardee Infrastructure Venture Pvt. Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: G.S. Buildtech Pvt. Ltd. is the Appellant/Financial Creditor. Ardee Infrastructure Venture Pvt. Ltd. is the Corporate Debtor/Respondent. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: The Appellant disbursed Rs. 1,30,00,000/- to the Corporate Debtor. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: The default amount claimed in the application was Rs. 39 Lakhs. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The Corporate Debtor made its last repayment on 15.03.2016. The Section 7 application was filed on 20.03.2020. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The Appellant relied on the Corporate Debtor's Balance Sheet for FY 2016-17, signed on 01.09.2017, to prove an acknowledgment of the debt extending the limitation period. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The NCLT New Delhi Bench-V rejected the Section 7 application on 28.09.2020, concluding the claim was time-barred and that the Appellant was not a Financial Creditor due to the absence of interest payments. The Appellant challenged this before the NCLAT.
legal_issues: Whether the absence of interest payment precludes a debt from being a 'financial debt' under Section 5(8) of the IBC, and whether an entry in a corporate debtor's balance sheet extends the limitation period under Section 18 of the Limitation Act, 1963.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Payment of interest is not a mandatory prerequisite for a debt to qualify as a financial debt, and an acknowledgment of debt in a balance sheet validly extends the period of limitation under Section 18 of the Limitation Act. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 5(8) of the IBC defines financial debt as a debt 'alongwith interest, if any', where the words 'if any' explicitly indicate that interest is not mandatory. Furthermore, Section 18 of the Limitation Act applies to IBC proceedings, and balance sheets mandatorily prepared under the Companies Act can serve as written acknowledgments. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal noted that the Adjudicating Authority completely failed to examine the FY 2016-17 balance sheet (signed 01.09.2017) to see if it contained an unequivocal acknowledgment of the Rs. 39 Lakh debt, which was essential to resolve the limitation issue. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLT erred in law by imposing a mandatory interest requirement under Section 5(8) and by ignoring critical balance sheet evidence capable of extending the limitation period, necessitating a fresh consideration.
operative_order: The NCLAT allowed the appeal, set aside the Adjudicating Authority's order dated 28.09.2020, and remitted the matter back for fresh consideration of the Section 7 application after issuing fresh notice to the Corporate Debtor.
summary: G.S. Buildtech filed a Section 7 IBC application claiming a default of Rs. 39 Lakhs by Ardee Infrastructure. The NCLT rejected the application, holding it was time-barred since the last payment was in March 2016 and the application was filed in March 2020, and further ruled the applicant wasn't a financial creditor because no interest was charged or paid. On appeal, the NCLAT set aside the dismissal. It clarified that Section 5(8) of the IBC uses the phrase 'interest, if any', meaning interest is not a mandatory ingredient for a financial debt. Moreover, the NCLAT ruled the NCLT erred by ignoring the Corporate Debtor's FY 2016-17 balance sheet (signed September 2017), which could constitute a valid acknowledgment extending the limitation period under Section 18 of the Limitation Act. The NCLAT remanded the matter for fresh adjudication.

case_title: Mr Shankar Sundaram vs M/s Amalgamations Ltd & Ors
appeal_number: IA NO.580/2021 IN TA NO.18/2021 (COMPANY APPEAL (AT) No.325/2019)
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Shankar Sundaram is the Applicant/Appellant. M/s Amalgamations Ltd & Ors are the Respondents. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: The main appeal involves allegations of oppression and mismanagement regarding the distribution of dividends and disproportionate remuneration packages to majority shareholders in profit-making subsidiaries. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: N/A, as this is an oppression and mismanagement dispute under the Companies Act, not an IBC default case. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: N/A. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The Appellant filed an interlocutory application seeking to introduce 'Additional Documents', comprising working sheets for the years 2017-18 to 2020-2021 certified by the Appellant's auditors and certificates of dividends, to prove escalating oppression. The Respondents opposed this, arguing the documents were self-serving, intended to fill lacunae, and that the main appeal could be decided without them. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The Appellant filed IA No. 580/2021 before the NCLAT to admit additional documents at the appellate stage in a pending appeal regarding oppression and mismanagement.
legal_issues: Whether an appellant in an oppression and mismanagement case can introduce additional documentary evidence at the appellate stage to substantiate claims of escalating oppression, when such documents were not before the original Tribunal.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An appellate forum should not allow the introduction of additional documents or evidence if it is intended to fill gaps or lacunae in a party's case, provided the court can pronounce a satisfactory judgment based on the existing materials on record. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Applying the principles analogous to Order XLI Rule 27 of the CPC, additional evidence at the appellate stage is an exception, permitted only when the appellate court requires it to pronounce judgment, and not merely to allow a party to improve their case or raise new points. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal evaluated whether the existing record was sufficient to adjudicate the main appeal. Concluding that the Lis could be determined based on the available materials, it found the introduction of the new working sheets and dividend certificates unnecessary for pronouncing judgment. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Because the Tribunal could decide the main appeal without the newly proposed documents, allowing the application would improperly permit the Appellant to fill lacunae, leading to its dismissal.
operative_order: The NCLAT dismissed IA No. 580/2021 with no order as to costs, declining to take the additional documents on record.
summary: In a pending appeal regarding oppression and mismanagement, the Appellant, Shankar Sundaram, filed an interlocutory application to submit additional documents, including auditor-certified working sheets and dividend certificates from 2017 to 2021, to prove escalating financial oppression by the majority shareholders of M/s Amalgamations Ltd. The Respondents objected, arguing the documents were self-serving and aimed to fill gaps in the Appellant's case. Relying on Supreme Court precedent restricting additional evidence at the appellate stage unless absolutely necessary for pronouncing judgment, the NCLAT held that the main appeal could be decided on the existing record. Consequently, the NCLAT dismissed the application.

case_title: Rajasthan State Road Development & Construction Corporation Ltd vs Vasundhra Gupta
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant/Corporation is Rajasthan State Road Development & Construction Corporation Ltd. Respondent No.1 is Vasundhra Gupta (Suspended Director of Corporate Debtor Aesthetic Stone Arts India Pvt. Ltd.). Respondent No.5 (Sanwarmal Tiwari) was the Operational Creditor who initiated CIRP. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Two work orders were awarded to the Corporate Debtor by the Appellant. Work Order 1 (dated 28.03.2017) was for constructing a building for Rs. 2,99,50,904.12. Work Order 2 (dated 13.03.2019) was for Rs. 11.12 Lacs. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: The Corporate Debtor failed to complete Work Order 1 by the extended deadline of 30.06.2020 (having completed only 76% of work after a 3-year delay). Work Order 2 was also not completed by the 12.05.2019 deadline and remained abandoned for 10 months. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Final notices to complete work were given prior to CIRP and on 30.06.2020. Work Order 1 was terminated on 11.06.2020 and its bank guarantee encashed on 26.06.2020. Work Order 2 was terminated on 04.08.2020. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Evidence included letters of extension (30.03.2020 extending time to 30.06.2020), termination notices, and the Government Order dated 08.06.2020 (granting 6 months extension to non-defaulting contractors, which didn't apply as CD was in default before 19.02.2020). 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Operational Creditor filed Section 9 application admitted on 04.03.2020. CD's suspended director and IRP filed applications under Section 60(5) in July/August 2020, which the NCLT allowed on 07.01.2021 by staying the terminations and invoking Section 14 and 238 IBC. Appellant filed this appeal against that NCLT order.
legal_issues: (i) Whether termination of Work Order 1 violated the provisional extension letter or Government's order. (ii) Whether termination of Work Order 2 violated the Government Order. (iii) Whether termination of the work orders violated Sections 14 & 238 of the IBC. (iv) Whether the invocation of the bank guarantee was illegal.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The Adjudicating Authority's residuary jurisdiction under Section 60(5)(c) of IBC cannot be invoked to entertain contractual disputes arising dehors the insolvency of the corporate debtor, nor can it stay termination of a contract based on grounds unrelated to insolvency. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 14 (Moratorium) does not apply where the appellant is merely availing services of the Corporate Debtor and is not supplying essential goods/services, recovering property, or terminating on grounds of insolvency. Section 238 cannot override a termination done for valid contractual breaches unrelated to insolvency. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal examined the timeline and termination notices, finding that alleged contractual breaches (e.g., failure to complete work over years) were legitimate and not a smokescreen to terminate the agreement merely because of the insolvency resolution process. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT concluded that since the termination of the work orders was due to persistent contractual defaults prior to the CIRP and not motivated by the insolvency of the Corporate Debtor, the NCLT lacked jurisdiction under Section 60(5)(c) to stay the terminations or prevent the encashment of bank guarantees.
operative_order: The Judgment of the Adjudicating Authority is set aside. The Appeal is allowed with no order as to costs.
summary: The appeal involved a dispute over the termination of two work orders and encashment of bank guarantees by Rajasthan State Road Development & Construction Corporation against the Corporate Debtor (Aesthetic Stone Arts India Pvt. Ltd.) after the initiation of CIRP. The NCLT had previously stayed the termination, citing sections 14 and 238 of the IBC. However, the NCLAT, relying on the Supreme Court's ruling in Tata Consultancy Services Ltd., held that the terminations were due to persistent contractual defaults unrelated to the insolvency proceedings. Thus, the NCLT lacked the residuary jurisdiction under Section 60(5)(c) of the IBC to adjudicate this contractual dispute. The appeal was allowed, and the NCLT's order was set aside.

case_title: BSE Limited vs ACIL Cotton Industries Limited
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is BSE Limited (Operational Creditor), a recognized stock exchange. Respondent is ACIL Cotton Industries Limited (Corporate Debtor, formerly Adeshwar Cotton Industries Ltd). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: A Listing agreement was executed on 27.06.1995 for listing Respondent's securities on the Appellant's platform, requiring payment of Annual Listing Fees (ALF) by April 30 every year. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: The claimed operational debt is Rs. 11,33,922/- (Principal: Rs. 10,37,470/- + Interest: Rs. 96,452/-) as of March 2019. The last payment made was Rs. 67,416 on 28.06.2013. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: A Section 8 Demand Notice was issued on 15.03.2019 and dispatched on 19.03.2019 (returned with 'addressee moved', but sent via email). Form 5 stated the debt fell due on 01.04.2015. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The submitted listing agreement had blank pages without remarks, contained initials only on the last page, lacked the seal and signature of the Bombay Stock Exchange, and was entered into with the former name 'Adeshwar Cotton Industries Ltd.' without a new agreement for the changed name. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The Appellant filed a Section 9 petition (C.P. (IB) No. 348/NCLT/AHM/2019) before NCLT Ahmedabad, which dismissed it on 31.12.2020 on grounds of limitation and invalid agreement.
legal_issues: Whether the continuous failure to pay Annual Listing Fees (ALF) constitutes a continuous cause of action saving the Section 9 application from limitation, and whether unpaid listing fees qualify as an 'Operational Debt' under the IBC.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Unpaid regulatory fees, such as listing fees payable to a stock exchange, fall under the ambit of 'Regulatory Dues' and cannot be recovered as 'Operational Debt' under the IBC. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Listing Fees do not constitute 'Operational Dues' for the purpose of initiating CIRP, as SEBI is entitled to recover these regulatory dues per its prescribed regulations. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The NCLAT upheld the NCLT's finding that an agreement lacking full signatures, official seals, and updated corporate entity names cannot be relied upon as a valid contract in the eyes of law to establish debt. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Section 9 application was rightfully dismissed because the listing agreement was legally invalid, the debt fell due on 01.04.2015 making it time-barred, and the listing fees constitute regulatory dues rather than operational debt.
operative_order: The impugned order dated 31.12.2020 passed by the Ld. Adjudicating Authority (NCLT Ahmedabad) is affirmed. The Appeal is dismissed with no order as to costs.
summary: BSE Limited (Appellant) filed an appeal against the NCLT's dismissal of its Section 9 IBC application against ACIL Cotton Industries Limited for an unpaid Annual Listing Fee (ALF) of Rs. 11,33,922. The NCLT had dismissed the petition, ruling that the date of default was 01.04.2015, which made the claim time-barred, and that the submitted listing agreement lacked proper signatures and updated corporate names. The NCLAT affirmed the dismissal, agreeing that the agreement was invalid. Crucially, the NCLAT also established that Listing Fees are considered 'Regulatory Dues' recoverable by SEBI, and therefore do not qualify as 'Operational Debt' under the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code.

case_title: BSE Limited vs KCCL Plastic Limited
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is BSE Limited (Operational Creditor), a recognized stock exchange. Respondent is KCCL Plastic Limited (Corporate Debtor, formerly Kosha Cubidor Containers Limited). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: A Listing Agreement was executed on 10.09.1993 for listing the Respondent's securities on the Appellant's platform, requiring the payment of Annual Listing Fees (ALF) by April 30 every year. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: The claimed operational debt is Rs. 10,66,886/- (Principal: Rs. 10,12,336/- + Interest: Rs. 54,550/-) as of March 2019. The last payment received was Rs. 44,944/- on 31.05.2013. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: A Section 8 demand notice was issued on 15.03.2019 and dispatched via speed post on 19.03.2019, which returned undelivered. Form 5 stated the debt fell due on 01.04.2015. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The submitted listing agreement had blank pages without remarks, contained initials only on the last page, lacked the seal and signature of the Bombay Stock Exchange, and was entered into with the former name 'Kosha Cubidor Containers Ltd.' without a new agreement for the changed name. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The Appellant filed a Section 9 petition (C.P. (IB) No. 349/NCLT/AHM/2019) before NCLT Ahmedabad, which dismissed it on 31.12.2020 on grounds of limitation and the lack of a valid agreement.
