legal_issues: Whether the continuous failure to pay Annual Listing Fees constitutes a continuous cause of action saving the application from limitation, and whether unpaid listing fees qualify as an 'Operational Debt' under the IBC.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Unpaid regulatory fees, such as listing fees payable to a stock exchange, fall under the ambit of 'Regulatory Dues' and cannot be recovered as 'Operational Debt' under the IBC. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Listing Fees are not considered 'Operational Dues' because SEBI is entitled to recover these regulatory dues per its prescribed regulations. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: An agreement lacking full signatures, official seals, and reflecting an outdated corporate entity name without execution of a new agreement cannot be relied upon as a valid contract in the eyes of law. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Section 9 application was rightfully dismissed as the underlying listing agreement was legally invalid, the claim was time-barred (debt fell due on 01.04.2015), and the listing fees constitute regulatory dues rather than operational debt.
operative_order: The impugned order dated 31.12.2020 passed by the Adjudicating Authority (NCLT Ahmedabad) is affirmed. The Appeal is dismissed with no order as to costs.
summary: BSE Limited (Appellant) filed an appeal against the NCLT's dismissal of its Section 9 IBC application against KCCL Plastic Limited for unpaid Annual Listing Fees of Rs. 10,66,886/-. The NCLT had dismissed the petition, ruling that the debt fell due on 01.04.2015 making it time-barred, and that the submitted listing agreement was invalid as it lacked proper signatures and updated corporate names. The NCLAT affirmed the dismissal, agreeing the agreement was unenforceable. Furthermore, the NCLAT ruled that Listing Fees are 'Regulatory Dues' recoverable by SEBI, and therefore do not qualify as 'Operational Debt' under the IBC.

case_title: Solar Industries India Limited vs Kailash Chandra Nuwal
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Solar Industries India Ltd (SIIL). Respondent No. 1 is Kailash Chandra Nuwal (KC Nuwal), a promoter and Vice Chairman. The dispute is between the KC Nuwal Group (minority) and the SN Nuwal Group (majority). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: KC Nuwal acquired 31,76,751 shares in AG Technologies Pvt. Ltd (AGT) on 02.05.2019 and became its director. SIIL subsequently resolved to rent office premises from AGT. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: This is an oppression and mismanagement dispute, not a debt default. The core action was the removal of KC Nuwal as director. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: On 07.11.2019, SIIL held a board meeting (without KC Nuwal) to rent AGT's premises. On 31.07.2020, the Company Secretary emailed KC Nuwal stating he had automatically vacated his office retrospectively from 07.11.2019. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Email evidence showed KC Nuwal informed the Company Secretary of his AGT directorship and shareholding on 03.05.2019 and 28.06.2019. The other directors (SN Nuwal Group) were fully aware and had even funded the acquisition, yet the company cited non-submission of Form MBP-1. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: KC Nuwal filed CP No. 1069/MB/2020 for oppression and mismanagement. On 09.02.2021, NCLT Mumbai granted interim relief staying the 30.07.2020 termination notice. SIIL appealed this interim order to NCLAT.
legal_issues: (i) Whether KC Nuwal contravened Section 184(1) of the Companies Act, 2013 by failing to use the prescribed format, and its consequences. (ii) Whether he contravened Section 184(2). (iii) Whether NCLT effectively ordered a final reinstatement at the interim stage under Section 242(4).
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Substantial compliance in disclosing a director's interest to the company secretary and board suffices to prevent automatic vacation of office, even if the strict prescribed statutory format (Form MBP-1) is not used. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 184(1) is a general disclosure obligation whose technical non-compliance attracts penalties under Section 184(4), but has no link to the automatic vacation clause under Section 167. Section 167(1)(c) and (d) trigger only upon violation of Section 184(2) regarding specific contracts, which didn't apply here as the director was absent from the relevant meeting. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal relied on undisputed email exchanges confirming the board and Company Secretary had actual, documented knowledge of the director's interest, rendering the technical format violation an insufficient ground for retroactive termination. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT concluded that since KC Nuwal had informed the company of his interest, he did not automatically vacate his office. The NCLT's interim injunction against his removal was just, equitable, and within its Section 242(4) powers.
operative_order: The Appeal is dismissed with no order as to costs. The interim order passed previously by the Appellate Tribunal (staying the NCLT's injunction) stands vacated.
summary: Solar Industries India Limited (SIIL) appealed an NCLT interim order that stayed the removal of its Vice Chairman, KC Nuwal. SIIL argued Nuwal automatically vacated his office under Section 167 of the Companies Act because he failed to disclose his interest in a related entity (AGT) using Form MBP-1, per Section 184(1). The NCLAT dismissed the appeal, noting email evidence proved Nuwal had substantially disclosed his interest to the Company Secretary and the board. The NCLAT held that failure to use the prescribed form under Section 184(1) may attract penalties but does not trigger automatic vacation of office under Section 167, making the NCLT's interim protection valid.

case_title: State of West Bengal Through The Principal Secretary 'West Bengal Biotech Development Corporation Limited' vs Keshav Park Private Limited & Anr
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is the State of West Bengal representing the Corporate Debtor, West Bengal Biotech Development Corporation Limited. Respondent No. 1 is Keshav Park Private Limited, the Operational Creditor. Respondent No. 2 is Sashi Kumar Agarwal, the Interim Resolution Professional. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: The Corporate Debtor engaged the Operational Creditor on 22.02.2011 to perform interior decoration and renovation work at a building in Salt Lake City, Kolkata. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: The Operational Creditor raised three bills dated 11.02.2012 amounting to Rs. 35,44,776/-, of which Rs. 6,34,886/- was paid by the Corporate Debtor, leaving the remainder as the alleged default. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The Operational Creditor issued a Section 8 demand notice on 07.11.2017, to which the Corporate Debtor replied on 14.12.2017. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The primary evidence in dispute was the Corporate Debtor's reply letter dated 14.12.2017, which requested a meeting to discuss and settle the claim, and which the NCLT initially interpreted as a promise to pay under Section 25(3) of the Contract Act. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The Operational Creditor filed a Section 9 petition in October 2018. NCLT Kolkata admitted the petition on 28.01.2020, holding the claim was within limitation. The Appellant subsequently challenged this admission before the NCLAT.
legal_issues: Whether the laws of limitation barred the claim of the Operational Creditor, and specifically whether the Corporate Debtor's letter dated 14.12.2017 constituted a valid acknowledgement of debt under Section 18 of the Limitation Act or a promise to pay under Section 25(3) of the Indian Contract Act.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A communication merely inviting a party for discussions to settle a claim does not amount to a legally binding acknowledgement of liability or a promise to pay a time-barred debt. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: For Section 25(3) of the Contract Act to apply, there must be an explicit written promise to pay a time-barred debt; a mere statement showing readiness to 'settle the claim after discussion' is insufficient. Furthermore, under Section 18 of the Limitation Act, an acknowledgement must be made before the expiry of the prescribed period of limitation. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal scrutinized the 14.12.2017 letter and concluded it was solely an invitation to negotiate, finding no specific written promise that could legally revive the time-barred invoices from 2012. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Since the limitation period for the 11.02.2012 invoices expired three years later on 10.02.2015, the 14.12.2017 letter could not extend the limitation period under Section 18, thereby rendering the Section 9 application filed in October 2018 time-barred.
operative_order: The appeal is allowed with no order for costs. The Corporate Debtor is released from the rigors of Section 14 of the IBC, and its management is directed to be immediately handed over to the erstwhile directors.
summary: The State of West Bengal appealed the NCLT Kolkata's admission of a Section 9 IBC petition filed by Keshav Park Private Limited against West Bengal Biotech Development Corporation Limited. The Operational Creditor claimed unpaid dues based on invoices dated 2012, relying on a 2017 letter from the Corporate Debtor that proposed a settlement discussion to bypass the three-year limitation period. The NCLAT overturned the NCLT's decision, ruling that the 2017 letter merely invited negotiation and did not constitute a binding acknowledgement of debt under the Limitation Act or a promise to pay under the Contract Act. Consequently, the claim was declared time-barred, the appeal was allowed, and the CIRP was quashed.

case_title: Mr. T. Prabhakar vs Mr. S Krishnan & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Mr. T. Prabhakar, suspended Director/shareholder of Green Valley Sheltors Pvt Ltd (Corporate Debtor). Respondent No. 1 is S. Krishnan (Resolution Professional). Respondent Nos. 2 & 3 are Nippon Life India AIF Management Ltd and Nippon Life India Asset Management Ltd (Financial Creditors/Debenture Holders). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Under a Mortgage cum Trust Deed dated 01.08.2016, Financial Creditors subscribed via private placement to senior, secured, unrated, unlisted, redeemable NCDs in multiple tranches totaling Rs. 31,75,00,000 to fund housing projects (GVSPL Raksha and GVSPL Green Park). 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default amount claimed was Rs. 36,59,28,316 (Principal: Rs. 25,30,40,154, Interest: Rs. 5,41,45,167, Redemption Premium: Rs. 3,38,37,000, Default Interest: Rs. 2,49,05,995) as of 31.10.2019. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Cheques issued were dishonoured, leading to Section 138 NI Act notices on 26.02.2019. Personal guarantees were invoked on 03.03.2020. The Section 7 application was filed on 18.12.2019. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Evidence of default included Mortgage cum Trust Deed, promissory notes, dishonoured cheques, guarantee deeds, and admitted failure by the Corporate Debtor to meet repayment terms. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Financial Creditors filed IBA/149/2020 under Section 7. NCLT Chennai Division Bench II admitted the application on 12.08.2021. The suspended director appealed the admission before NCLAT Chennai.
legal_issues: (i) Whether debenture holders (comprising 100% of the holders) can initiate Section 7 CIRP without impleading or acting through the Debenture Trustee. (ii) Whether CIRP against a multi-project real estate company must be restricted to specific funded projects (project-wise CIRP) rather than the entity as a whole. (iii) Whether passing the admission order before the deadline for additional written submissions violated natural justice.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Debenture holders qualifying as financial creditors have an independent statutory right under Section 7 of the IBC to initiate CIRP against a corporate debtor without joining or being represented by the Debenture Trustee, unless explicitly barred by contract. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Once existence of a financial debt and default are established under Section 7(4) and 7(5), the Adjudicating Authority must admit the application; directory procedural timelines (e.g., 14-day rule) do not vitiate jurisdiction. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Where debt and default are undisputed on record, technical pleas (such as pending additional written submissions without substantive new defenses, or corporate name changes of creditors) do not show prejudice or bar admission. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Winter Hills project-specific CIRP model was based on specific consent/settlement facts and is not universally applicable to mandate project-wise CIRP where an entity-level default on secured debentures is clearly established.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (CH) (Ins) No. 217 of 2021 is dismissed with no order as to costs, and I.A. No. 437 of 2021 is closed. The order of the Adjudicating Authority admitting the Section 7 petition is upheld.
summary: An appeal was filed by the suspended director of Green Valley Sheltors Pvt Ltd challenging an NCLT Chennai order admitting a Section 7 IBC application filed by debenture holders Nippon Life India entities for a default of Rs. 36.59 Crores. The appellant argued that only the debenture trustee had locus standi, that CIRP should be restricted project-wise to funded developments pursuant to the Winter Hills precedent, and that natural justice was denied regarding written submissions. The NCLAT dismissed the appeal, holding that debenture holders holding 100% debentures possess direct standing as financial creditors, the Winter Hills reverse CIRP was case-specific, and the undisputed financial default justified full admission into CIRP.

case_title: Kedrion Biopharma Inc vs M/S. Wizaman Impex Pvt. Ltd
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Kedrion Biopharma Inc. (Operational Creditor), a Delaware corporation. Respondent is M/S. Wizaman Impex Pvt. Ltd. (Corporate Debtor). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Parties executed a Distribution Agreement on 21.03.2014 for the distribution and sale of plasma pharmaceutical products (Rhogam) in India. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default arose from three unpaid invoices from Dec 2013 to May 2014: USD 25,800, USD 632,100, and USD 604,055.40. The final acknowledged outstanding amount claimed in the demand notice was USD 901,000. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Section 8 demand notices were issued on 25.07.2019 and 07.08.2019. The Section 9 application was filed on 30.06.2020. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Evidence included confirmation letters of debt dated 18.01.2016 and 02.02.2017, a credit memo dated 15.12.2017 offsetting USD 360,000, and settlement offers up to 10.11.2018 proposing USD 99,786.41. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The NCLT New Delhi Bench-V dismissed the Section 9 application on 06.10.2020 as barred by limitation, prompting the present appeal to the NCLAT.
legal_issues: Whether the Section 9 application filed on 30.06.2020 was barred by limitation considering the invoices were from 2013-2014, or whether successive emails acknowledging the debt and offering settlements validly extended the limitation period under Section 18 of the Limitation Act.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Email correspondences acknowledging outstanding dues and offering settlements constitute valid acknowledgments of debt that extend the period of limitation under Section 18 of the Limitation Act. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Applying the Supreme Court's precedent, Section 18 of the Limitation Act applies to IBC proceedings; sequential written acknowledgements of liability before the expiry of the limitation period reset the three-year clock. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal accepted additional electronic evidence (emails) at the appellate stage because it clearly demonstrated the Corporate Debtor's continuous admission of liability and active settlement discussions, proving the claim was kept alive. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Since the corporate debtor offered a revised settlement on 10.11.2018, the limitation period was extended to 09.11.2021; thus, the Section 9 application filed on 30.06.2020 was well within the limitation period and wrongfully dismissed by the Adjudicating Authority.
operative_order: The impugned order dated 06.10.2020 passed by the Adjudicating Authority is set aside, and the Section 9 application filed by the Appellant is allowed. The parties are directed to appear before the NCLT on 18.01.2022 for passing orders regarding the appointment of an IRP and initiation of CIRP under Sections 10, 13, and 14 of the IBC.
summary: Kedrion Biopharma (Operational Creditor) appealed the NCLT's dismissal of its Section 9 IBC application against Wizaman Impex (Corporate Debtor) on limitation grounds. The claim arose from unpaid 2013-2014 invoices for pharmaceutical products. The NCLAT allowed the appellant to introduce additional email evidence demonstrating that the Corporate Debtor had continuously acknowledged the debt and made settlement offers up until November 2018. Relying on Section 18 of the Limitation Act, the NCLAT held that these acknowledgments extended the limitation period to November 2021, rendering the June 2020 application timely. The NCLAT consequently set aside the NCLT's dismissal and allowed the Section 9 application to initiate CIRP.

case_title: Krrish Realtech Private Limited vs Krrish Realtech Private Limited
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant is Krrish Realtech Private Limited, the Corporate Debtor. The Objectors/Interveners are homebuyers (claiming to be unrelated Financial Creditors). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: The Corporate Debtor is a real estate developer that manages projects involving the Objectors, who purchased units/plots, including one objector claiming a consideration of Rs. 33,94,88,869/- for 27 license plots. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: The Corporate Debtor claims to be under a debt of Rs. 673,16,36,869.63/-. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The Corporate Debtor issued an email notice on 30.09.2021 at 3:30 A.M. convening a meeting of Financial Creditors for 5:00 P.M. on the exact same day. The Section 54C application was filed on 08.10.2021. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The objectors presented evidence indicating the mandatory 5-day notice period under Regulation 14 was violated, and alleged that the list of unrelated Financial Creditors fraudulently included related parties to falsely meet the 66% approval threshold. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The Corporate Debtor filed an application for pre-packaged insolvency under Section 54C before NCLT New Delhi. Through orders dated 21.10.2021, 09.11.2021, and 23.11.2021, the NCLT granted the objectors time to file objections. The Corporate Debtor appealed these orders to the NCLAT, claiming the NCLT lacked jurisdiction to hear objectors prior to admission.
legal_issues: Whether the Adjudicating Authority, while considering an application for a pre-packaged insolvency resolution process under Section 54C of the IBC, has the jurisdiction to hear Objectors/Interveners and grant them time to file objections prior to admitting the application.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The Adjudicating Authority possesses the jurisdiction and discretion to adhere to the principles of natural justice by giving objectors an opportunity to be heard prior to admitting a pre-packaged insolvency application, especially to verify statutory compliance. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 424(1) of the Companies Act, 2013 mandates that the Tribunal shall be guided by the principles of natural justice. Chapter III-A of the IBC and its corresponding Regulations do not contain any express provision prohibiting the Adjudicating Authority from hearing objectors or interveners prior to the admission of a Section 54C application. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal noted prima facie procedural breaches—such as holding a meeting on the same day the notice was issued without an agreement for shorter notice by all creditors—justifying the Adjudicating Authority's discretion to hear the objectors' claims of statutory non-compliance. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT concluded that giving time to objectors to highlight statutory non-compliance does not violate the IBC, nor does it create unauthorized procedural remedies. Therefore, the NCLT's interim orders were within its valid jurisdiction.
operative_order: The NCLAT found no error in the orders impugned in the appeal. The appeal is dismissed.
summary: The Corporate Debtor (Appellant) filed an appeal challenging NCLT orders that granted homebuyers (Objectors) time to file replies opposing the admission of a Section 54C Pre-Packaged Insolvency application. The Appellant contended that the IBC does not permit hearing objectors at the pre-admission stage. The NCLAT dismissed the appeal, ruling that Section 424 of the Companies Act mandates adherence to the principles of natural justice, and the IBC does not expressly prohibit hearing objectors. The NCLAT affirmed that the NCLT rightfully exercised its discretion to hear the objectors, particularly given the prima facie procedural irregularities in convening the creditors' meeting.

case_title: Par Formulations Pvt. Ltd. vs Print House (India) Pvt. Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Par Formulations Pvt. Ltd. (Licensee). Respondent No. 1 is Print House (India) Pvt. Ltd. (Corporate Debtor/Licensor). Respondent No. 2 is Manish Baldeva (Former Resolution Professional). Respondent No. 3 is Sify Technologies Limited (Successful Resolution Applicant). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: A Leave and Licence Agreement dated 16.06.2017 was executed for the first floor of a building in MIDC Rabale for 5 years up to 23.08.2022. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: There was no debt default by the Appellant; the dispute pertained to the unilateral termination of the lease by the Successful Resolution Applicant as part of the CIRP. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The Resolution Plan was approved on 23.06.2020. The SRA took over management on 16.10.2020, sent an email seeking vacation on 30.11.2020, and issued a formal termination notice on 26.04.2021. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The Licence Agreement contained Clause 12(a) allowing termination without reason by furnishing a 6-month written notice after the lock-in period. Invoices were paid by the Appellant until the termination dispute arose. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Mumbai approved the resolution plan on 23.06.2020. The Appellant appealed to NCLAT, claiming the plan illegally terminated its lease without hearing or notice.
legal_issues: Whether the approval of a Resolution Plan under Section 31 of the IBC can unilaterally terminate a pre-existing Leave and Licence Agreement in alleged contravention of Section 30(2)(e) of the IBC and Section 62 of the Indian Contract Act.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The termination of an existing lease or license agreement pursuant to an approved Resolution Plan is valid if executed in accordance with the contractual termination clauses of the agreement itself. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: The Tribunal held it was unnecessary to examine whether the Resolution Plan contravened Section 30(2)(e) of the IBC or Section 62 of the Contract Act because the Successful Resolution Applicant effectively terminated the agreement by exercising the contractual 6-month notice provision under Clause 12(a). 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal reviewed the email communications from 30.11.2020 and the formal notice on 26.04.2021, concluding that the 6-month notice period stipulated in the Licence Agreement had been substantially complied with. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT concluded that the Appellant's rights were not unlawfully violated since the termination adhered to the Licence Agreement's terms. The appeal was disposed of by granting the Appellant two months to vacate.
operative_order: The appeal is disposed off with directions. The Appellant is granted two months to shift its operations and vacate the premises, liable to pay utility charges until vacation, upon which the Successful Resolution Applicant shall refund the security deposit.
summary: Par Formulations Pvt. Ltd. (Appellant/Licensee) challenged the NCLT Mumbai's approval of a Resolution Plan submitted by Sify Technologies Ltd. for the Corporate Debtor, Print House (India) Pvt. Ltd. The Appellant argued the plan unlawfully terminated its 5-year Leave and Licence Agreement. The NCLAT noted that the Licence Agreement contained a clause allowing unilateral termination with 6 months' notice. Since the Successful Resolution Applicant had provided adequate notice (via an email in November 2020 and a formal notice in April 2021) in compliance with the agreement's terms, the termination was valid. The NCLAT disposed of the appeal, granting the Appellant two months to vacate the premises and directing the refund of its security deposit upon vacation.

case_title: M/s. Jai International Pvt. Ltd vs M/s. Jaroli Agro Pvt. Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is M/s. Jai International Pvt. Ltd (Operational Creditor). Respondent is M/s. Jaroli Agro Pvt. Ltd (Corporate Debtor). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Appellant advanced money to the Corporate Debtor for rendering consultancy, commission, and brokerage services. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: The outstanding default amount claimed is Rs. 30,75,408.72. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: A Section 8 demand notice was issued on 14.11.2019, to which a reply was sent on 23.11.2019. The Section 9 petition was filed on 06.12.2019. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Evidence included ledger accounts showing transactions till 24.11.2017 signed by the Corporate Debtor's director, and balance sheet/ledger entries acknowledging the Rs. 30 Lakhs closing balance. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Mumbai dismissed the Section 9 petition on 15.07.2021, classifying the advance as a time-barred loan with a pre-existing dispute. The Operational Creditor appealed this dismissal.
legal_issues: Whether an advance given for consultancy services constitutes an 'Operational Debt' under Section 5(21) of the IBC, and whether continuous ledger transactions and balance sheet entries extend the limitation period under Section 18 of the Limitation Act.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An advance payment made towards future services qualifies as an operational debt, and continuous business transactions alongside ledger acknowledgments reset the limitation clock under Section 18 of the Limitation Act. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 5(21) of the IBC covers amounts advanced for the provision of services. Furthermore, financial entries in the corporate debtor's ledgers and the operational creditor's audited balance sheets serve as valid acknowledgments under Section 18 of the Limitation Act. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal relied on continuous debit/credit notes signed by the Corporate Debtor's director up to 2017 and statutory balance sheet entries to override the Adjudicating Authority's finding of a time-barred loan. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT concluded the debt was an operational debt, was within limitation due to Section 18 acknowledgments, and that the alleged dispute involving the director in his individual capacity did not constitute a valid pre-existing dispute for the Corporate Debtor.
operative_order: The impugned order dated 15.07.2021 passed by NCLT Mumbai is set aside. The matter is remanded back to the Adjudicating Authority to initiate CIRP after allowing 30 days for settlement. The appeal is allowed with no order as to costs.
summary: Jai International Pvt. Ltd (Appellant/Operational Creditor) appealed the NCLT Mumbai's dismissal of its Section 9 IBC petition against Jaroli Agro Pvt. Ltd (Corporate Debtor). The NCLT had rejected the Rs. 30.75 lakh claim, viewing it as a time-barred loan entangled in a pre-existing dispute. The NCLAT reversed this decision, holding that the amount advanced for consultancy services constitutes an 'Operational Debt' under Section 5(21). It further ruled that continuous ledger transactions and balance sheet entries validly extended the limitation period under Section 18 of the Limitation Act, and the alleged dispute was unrelated to the Corporate Debtor, thus warranting CIRP admission.

case_title: C Raja John vs Spring Field Shelters Pvt Ltd
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is C. Raja John, Promoter and Suspended Director of the Corporate Debtor, Springfield Shelters Pvt Ltd. Respondent No. 1 is R. Raghavendran, the Resolution Professional, while other Respondents include financial creditors like SBI and Central Bank of India. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: The Corporate Debtor operates in the real estate industry, and the Appellant claimed to have invested Rs. 10.5 Crores and provided collateral security for a loan of Rs. 1.75 Crores. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: The CIRP was initiated, and the Appellant claimed readiness to bring Rs. 45 Crores to settle all liabilities. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The Resolution Professional rejected the Appellant's Expression of Interest on 20.11.2020. The Madras High Court ordered the reactivation of the Appellant's DIN on 08.12.2020. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The Appellant produced a Madras High Court judgment quashing his DIN disqualification and MSME certificates from 28.05.2013 and 19.12.2020 proving the Corporate Debtor's MSME status. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The Resolution Professional rejected the Appellant's Resolution Plan, which the NCLT Chennai upheld on 18.06.2021 by dismissing the Appellant's applications. The Appellant challenged this dismissal before the NCLAT.
legal_issues: Whether the promoter of an MSME Corporate Debtor is eligible to submit a Resolution Plan despite a CoC-prescribed net worth criteria under Section 25(2)(h) and an alleged DIN disqualification under Section 29A(e) of the IBC.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: If a Corporate Debtor is an MSME, its promoters do not need to compete with other Resolution Applicants to regain control, and a High Court order quashing a DIN disqualification removes the ineligibility under Section 29A(e) of the IBC. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 240A of the IBC exempts MSMEs from the strictures of Section 29A(c) and (h) to encourage promoters to regain control. A judicial directive to reactivate a DIN nullifies the disqualification under the Companies Act, rendering Section 29A(e) inapplicable. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Adjudicating Authority erred by ignoring the Madras High Court order reactivating the Appellant's DIN and the valid MSME certificates demonstrating the entity's status as a medium enterprise since 2013. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT concluded that the Appellant did not suffer from disqualification under Section 29A(e) and, as an MSME promoter, should be permitted to submit a Net Worth Certificate and have his Resolution Plan considered by the Resolution Professional.
operative_order: The NCLAT allowed the appeal, quashed the NCLT's order dated 18.06.2021 and the Resolution Professional's rejection order dated 20.11.2020, and directed the RP to consider the Appellant's Resolution Plan.
summary: C. Raja John, promoter of Springfield Shelters Pvt Ltd, appealed the NCLT Chennai's dismissal of his application to submit a Resolution Plan. The Resolution Professional had rejected his plan citing a failure to meet the CoC's Rs. 2 Crore net worth criteria and a DIN disqualification under Section 29A(e) of the IBC. The NCLAT reversed the decision, noting that the Madras High Court had already quashed the DIN disqualification, and relying on Section 240A, held that MSME promoters are not required to compete with other applicants. The NCLAT directed the RP to accept the Appellant's Net Worth Certificate and consider his Resolution Plan.

case_title: Ketan Anant Raj vs Dhanshyam Kantilal Patel
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellants are Ketan Anant Raj and Raajul Ketan Raj, erstwhile directors of the Corporate Debtor (Krishnai Hospital Private Limited). Respondent No. 1 is Dhanshyam Kantilal Patel, the Liquidator of the Corporate Debtor. Respondent No. 2 is Rajkot Nagrik Sahakari Bank, and Respondent No. 3 is Novateur Electrical & Digital System Pvt. Ltd. 2. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The NCLT Mumbai passed the impugned liquidation order on 13.12.2019. The Appellants initially filed a Writ Petition before the Bombay High Court, which denied ad-interim relief on 20.12.2019. The Appellants then filed this appeal before the NCLAT on 19.03.2020. 3. DELAY METRICS: The appeal was filed with a delay of 89 days. The Appellants sought condonation under Section 14 of the Limitation Act, 1963, claiming the time was spent pursuing the Writ Petition in good faith due to the NCLAT's winter vacation. 4. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: A letter dated 19.12.2019 from the Appellant to the Liquidator falsely stated an appeal had already been preferred before the NCLAT, proving the Appellants knew the correct forum. Furthermore, the NCLAT's 2019 calendar showed the tribunal remained open for more than 7 days after the 13.12.2019 order before the winter vacation started on 21.12.2019, contradicting the Appellants' excuse.
legal_issues: Whether the Appellants acted with 'due diligence' and 'in good faith' as required under Section 14 of the Limitation Act, 1963, to warrant the exclusion of the 89 days spent pursuing a Writ Petition before the High Court, thereby condoning the delay in filing the appeal under Section 61 of the IBC.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: To claim the benefit of Section 14 of the Limitation Act, a party must prove they prosecuted the alternative civil proceeding with due diligence and in good faith before a court lacking jurisdiction. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 14 of the Limitation Act cannot be invoked to exclude time if the party had actual knowledge of the correct appellate forum (under Section 61 of the IBC) but deliberately chose to pursue a remedy elsewhere to delay proceedings. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal relied on the Appellant's own letter dated 19.12.2019, which falsely claimed an NCLAT appeal was already filed, establishing that the Appellant knew the correct forum but chose the High Court with deceitful intent. Additionally, the official court calendar proved the NCLAT was open and accessible before the winter vacation, negating the Appellant's primary excuse for not filing in time. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Because the Appellants had knowledge of the correct forum and sufficient time to file the appeal before the NCLAT's winter vacation, their pursuit of the Writ Petition was not in good faith. Consequently, the delay of 89 days could not be condoned under Section 14, rendering the appeal time-barred.
operative_order: Interlocutory Application No. 1590 of 2020 for condonation of delay is dismissed. Consequently, the appeal is dismissed without costs, and all pending I.A.s are also dismissed.
summary: Ketan Anant Raj and Raajul Ketan Raj (erstwhile directors of the Corporate Debtor) appealed the NCLT Mumbai's liquidation order dated 13.12.2019. The appeal was filed on 19.03.2020 with an 89-day delay. The Appellants sought condonation under Section 14 of the Limitation Act, claiming the time was spent pursuing a Writ Petition in the Bombay High Court because the NCLAT was closed for winter vacation. The NCLAT rejected this, citing a letter dated 19.12.2019 wherein the Appellants falsely claimed to have already filed an NCLAT appeal, proving they knew the correct forum all along. Furthermore, the NCLAT calendar showed the tribunal was open for over a week after the impugned order. Finding a lack of good faith and due diligence, the NCLAT dismissed the condonation application and the appeal.

case_title: M/S Indian Potash Limited vs Naresh Kumar Verma & Ors
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is M/s Indian Potash Limited, the Unsuccessful Resolution Applicant. Respondent No. 1 is Naresh Kumar Verma, Resolution Professional for the Corporate Debtor, Bohra Industries Limited. Respondent No. 2 is State Bank of India, the sole CoC member with 100% voting rights. Respondent No. 3 is Sri Krishna Agarwal, Lead Member of the Consortium and the Successful Resolution Applicant. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Submission of competitive resolution plans for the Corporate Debtor during the CIRP process. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: The dispute centered on the value of the resolution plans, with the Successful Applicant offering Rs. 26.31 Crores against the Appellant's offer of Rs. 21.25 Crores. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP initiated on 09.08.2019. Form-G was published on 21.10.2019. Final revised plans were submitted before 19.09.2020, and the NCLT approved the plan on 13.10.2021. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The CoC minutes demonstrated that multiple opportunities to revise the plans were given in the 10th to 13th meetings. The evaluation matrix scored Respondent No. 3 at 51.49 marks and the Appellant at 48.51 marks. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The CoC approved Respondent No. 3's plan with 100% voting and rejected the Appellant's plan. NCLT Jaipur approved the CoC's decision on 13.10.2021, prompting this appeal by the Appellant.
legal_issues: Whether the Adjudicating Authority erred in approving the Resolution Plan of Respondent No. 3, specifically whether the CoC failed to follow the evaluation matrix under Regulation 39(3) and wrongfully denied the Appellant an opportunity to revise its plan.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The commercial wisdom of the Committee of Creditors in evaluating and selecting a resolution plan based on a scoring matrix is paramount and non-justiciable by the Adjudicating Authority. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 61(3) of the IBC strictly limits the grounds for appealing an approved resolution plan. Regulation 39(3) of the CIRP Regulations requires the CoC to evaluate plans strictly as per the evaluation matrix, which is satisfied when the objectively higher-scoring plan is chosen. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal verified from the CoC minutes that multiple revision opportunities were afforded to both applicants, and the chosen plan objectively scored higher (51.49 vs 48.51) and offered greater value (Rs. 26.31 Crores vs Rs. 21.25 Crores). 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT concluded that the CoC complied with the evaluation matrix and properly exercised its commercial wisdom. Therefore, there was no material irregularity or contravention of law in the NCLT's approval of the plan.
operative_order: The NCLAT found no error in the impugned order passed by the Adjudicating Authority and dismissed the appeal with no order as to costs.
summary: M/s Indian Potash Limited (Unsuccessful Resolution Applicant) appealed against the NCLT Jaipur's order approving the resolution plan of a competing consortium (Respondent No. 3) for the Corporate Debtor, Bohra Industries Limited. The Appellant alleged that its plan offered a higher upfront payment, the evaluation matrix was ignored, and it was denied an opportunity to revise its bid. The NCLAT dismissed the appeal, noting that the CoC (represented solely by SBI) provided multiple revision opportunities, and Respondent No. 3's plan objectively scored higher on the matrix (51.49 vs 48.51) with a greater overall value (Rs. 26.31 Crores vs Rs. 21.25 Crores). Relying on the supremacy of the CoC's commercial wisdom, the NCLAT upheld the approval.

case_title: Avneesh Kumar Singh vs Indian Delco Private Limited
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Avneesh Kumar Singh (Suspended Director of Corporate Debtor S N Jee Build Well Pvt. Ltd.). Respondent is Indian Delco Private Limited (Financial Creditor). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Respondent extended a loan facility of INR 5,50,00,000 to the Corporate Debtor under a Loan Agreement dated 02.08.2013, with interest at 12% per annum, out of which INR 3,59,24,490 was disbursed. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: The outstanding amount confirmed as of 01.04.2019 was Rs. 5,42,67,796. The 6-year loan period expired on 03.08.2019, after which the Corporate Debtor failed to clear the dues. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: A legal demand notice was issued on 25.10.2019. The Section 7 application was filed on 07.12.2019. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The debt was acknowledged through a balance confirmation dated 01.04.2019, the audited balance sheet of FY 2015-16, cheques issued for interest payments in 2016, and a Forensic Audit Report admitting the receipt and utilization of the funds. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The Respondent filed a Section 7 application which was admitted by NCLT New Delhi Bench-V on 07.01.2021. The Appellant subsequently filed this appeal against the admission order.
legal_issues: Whether the Section 7 application was maintainable, given the Appellant's contention that the loan agreement was unauthorized under Section 180 of the Companies Act, 2013, and allegedly collusive.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An acknowledged debt supported by consistent financial documentation, including audited balance sheets and partial interest payments, irrefutably establishes a financial debt and default, justifying CIRP admission. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Under Section 7 of the IBC, the Adjudicating Authority must only ascertain the existence of a default. Internal corporate authorization disputes do not negate the financial debt when independent evidence like balance confirmations and forensic audits prove the receipt and utilization of the funds. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal relied on the Corporate Debtor's own audited balance sheets, balance confirmation letters, interest payment cheques, and a forensic audit report, rejecting the Appellant's claim that the loan was a sham. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Since the debt and default were clearly admitted and established through multiple documents, the NCLT correctly admitted the Section 7 application.
operative_order: The impugned order dated 07.01.2021 passed by the Adjudicating Authority is affirmed. The appeal is dismissed.
summary: Avneesh Kumar Singh (Appellant), suspended director of the Corporate Debtor, challenged the NCLT's admission of a Section 7 IBC application filed by Indian Delco Private Limited. The Appellant argued the underlying loan agreement was unauthorized and a sham. The NCLAT dismissed the appeal, holding that the debt and default were clearly established through the Corporate Debtor's audited balance sheets, balance confirmation letters, interest payment cheques, and a forensic audit report showing the funds were actually utilized by the company. Consequently, the NCLT's order initiating CIRP was affirmed.

case_title: Apya Capital Services Private Limited vs Guardian Homes Private Limited
appeal_number: I.A. No. 2068 of 2021 IN Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 412 of 2020
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Apya Capital Services Private Limited (Operational Creditor). Respondent/Applicant is Guardian Homes Private Limited (Corporate Debtor). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Debt for service rendered, where Corporate Debtor made partial payments but later disputed the quality of service. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: An unpaid balance amount of Rs. 2,05,00,000/- remained after a part payment of Rs. 75 Lakhs. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The original NCLAT judgment was passed on 08.12.2020. The Supreme Court dismissed the appeal against this judgment on 01.07.2021. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The Respondent filed IA 2068/2021 arguing an ex-facie error in the 08.12.2020 order, specifically that NCLAT incorrectly treated the Appellant as a Financial Creditor under Section 7 rather than an Operational Creditor under Section 9. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLAT had earlier set aside the Adjudicating Authority's order and directed the admission of the insolvency application on 08.12.2020. The Supreme Court dismissed the subsequent Civil Appeal (No. 1813 of 2021). The Respondent then filed the present Interlocutory Application seeking a recall of the NCLAT's 08.12.2020 order.
legal_issues: Whether the NCLAT has the inherent power under Rule 11 of the NCLAT Rules, 2016 or Section 424(1) of the Companies Act, 2013 to recall its own judgment, especially after the said judgment has been affirmed by and merged with an order of the Supreme Court.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An appellate tribunal does not possess the inherent power to recall its own substantive judgment under the IBC, particularly after the judgment has merged with a higher court's order. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Neither Section 424(1) of the Companies Act (which guides procedure by natural justice) nor Rule 11 of the NCLAT Rules (inherent powers) confers jurisdiction to recall a finalized judgment, as the power of recall/review must be explicitly granted by statute, which is absent in the IBC framework. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal relied on the Supreme Court's order dated 01.07.2021 which dismissed Civil Appeal No. 1813 of 2021 against the very same 08.12.2020 order, applying the doctrine of merger. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Because the 08.12.2020 judgment merged with the Supreme Court's dismissal and the IBC contains no provision for recalling judgments, the interlocutory application for recall is legally not maintainable.
operative_order: The I.A. No. 2068 of 2021 filed by the Respondent/Applicant seeking recall of the judgment dated 08.12.2020 is dismissed as not maintainable.
summary: Guardian Homes Pvt. Ltd. filed an Interlocutory Application to recall an NCLAT order dated 08.12.2020, arguing the Tribunal committed a facial error by admitting the insolvency petition under Section 7 instead of Section 9. The NCLAT dismissed the application as not maintainable. It reasoned that its prior judgment had already been challenged before the Supreme Court, which dismissed the appeal on 01.07.2021, thus merging the NCLAT's order with the Supreme Court's decree. Furthermore, the NCLAT clarified that neither Section 424(1) of the Companies Act nor its inherent powers under Rule 11 allow it to recall a substantive judgment under the IBC framework.

case_title: The Assistant Commissioner vs Pravin Charan Dwary Irp/Rp M/S. Swastik Ceracon
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is The Assistant Commissioner, Central GST, Division Mehsana. Respondent is Mr. Pravin Charan Dwary, IRP/RP of M/s. Swastik Ceracon, the Corporate Debtor. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: The Corporate Debtor had outstanding government tax dues. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: The total tax claim filed by the Appellant in Form-B amounted to Rs. 25,82,25,560/-. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Central GST attached the finished goods of the Corporate Debtor on 31.01.2018. The CIRP was initiated and a moratorium was declared on 15.01.2019. The Appellant filed an application to auction the goods on 12.07.2019. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: A Panchanama dated 31.01.2018 evidenced the attachment of the finished goods, and the NCLT order dated 15.01.2019 evidenced the declaration of the moratorium. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The Appellant filed I.A. 463/AHM/2019 before NCLT Ahmedabad seeking permission to auction the attached goods. The NCLT rejected the application on 08.03.2021 due to the ongoing CIRP, prompting the Appellant to file this appeal before the NCLAT.
legal_issues: Whether a government authority can auction goods of a Corporate Debtor that were attached prior to the commencement of CIRP, while the moratorium under Section 14 of the IBC is in effect.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Once the Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process (CIRP) commences and a moratorium is declared, no authority can proceed to auction the assets of the Corporate Debtor, even if those assets were attached prior to the initiation of the CIRP. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 14 of the IBC mandates a strict prohibition on the continuation of proceedings or execution of orders against the Corporate Debtor's assets during the moratorium period, which supersedes prior attachment actions. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal noted that the NCLT order explicitly declared a moratorium on 15.01.2019, making any subsequent request to auction the assets legally barred. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Relying on the Supreme Court's ruling in Anand Rao Korada, the NCLAT concluded that the Adjudicating Authority was entirely justified in refusing the auction request because the moratorium was already operative, meaning the Appellant's remedy lay in filing a claim, which it had already done.
operative_order: There is no merit in this Appeal. The Appeal is dismissed.
summary: The Assistant Commissioner of Central GST (Appellant) challenged the NCLT Ahmedabad's order rejecting its application to auction attached goods of M/s. Swastik Ceracon (Corporate Debtor). The goods had been attached in 2018 for tax dues exceeding Rs. 25 Crores, prior to the initiation of CIRP in 2019. The NCLAT dismissed the appeal, holding that Section 14 of the IBC prohibits the auction or recovery of the Corporate Debtor's assets once a moratorium is declared. The Tribunal affirmed the NCLT's decision, noting the Appellant had already correctly filed its claim in Form-B and could not bypass the CIRP.

case_title: Vasundhra Gupta vs Mr. Sandeep Mathur & Anr.
appeal_number: Contempt Case (AT) No. 16 of 2021 In Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 131 of 2021
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Applicant is Vasundhra Gupta, the Suspended Director of the Corporate Debtor (Aesthetic Stone Arts India Pvt. Ltd.). Respondents are Mr. Sandeep Mathur (Managing Director) and Rajasthan State Road Development & Construction Corporation Ltd. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: The underlying dispute involves the termination of two construction work orders awarded to the Corporate Debtor by the Respondent Corporation. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: This is not a debt default proceeding; it is a contempt application alleging the violation of a court order. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: On 07.01.2021, the NCLT stayed the termination of the work orders. On 25.02.2021, the NCLAT passed an order directing that the status quo be maintained. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The Applicant relied on running bills raised by a new contractor (Mr. Amit Jain) on 10.11.2020 and 15.02.2021, and payments made on 26.02.2021, to claim that civil work continued after the status quo order. The Respondents countered via affidavit that the work was largely completed by 14.01.2021 and no new civil work was executed after 25.02.2021. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The Applicant filed a contempt application under Section 425 of the Companies Act and Section 12 of the Contempt of Courts Act, alleging willful disobedience of the NCLAT's 25.02.2021 status quo order.
legal_issues: Whether the Respondents committed willful disobedience of the NCLAT's status quo order dated 25.02.2021 by allegedly carrying out pending project work and executing civil work at the site.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: To succeed in a contempt application, the applicant must conclusively prove willful disobedience of a specific court directive. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Proceedings under Section 12 of the Contempt of Courts Act require clear evidence of a breach; processing payments for work substantially completed prior to a status quo order does not inherently establish that new prohibited work was executed in defiance of the order. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal evaluated the photographic evidence, pleadings, and running bills, determining that the new contractor had almost completed the work by 14.01.2021, well before the 25.02.2021 status quo order, and the Applicant failed to supply documentary proof of new civil work post-dating the order. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT concluded that the Applicant failed to establish a case of willful disobedience, as there was no concrete evidence that the Respondents continued prohibited civil work after the status quo order was issued.
operative_order: The Contempt Case is closed, and the Respondents are discharged from the Contempt Case.
summary: Vasundhra Gupta, the suspended director of the Corporate Debtor, filed a contempt application against the Managing Director of Rajasthan State Road Development & Construction Corporation Ltd., alleging willful disobedience of the NCLAT's status quo order dated 25.02.2021. The Applicant claimed the Corporation continued civil work through a newly appointed contractor after the order was passed. The NCLAT reviewed the evidence, including running bills and the Respondent's affidavit, and noted that the new contractor had substantially completed the work by January 2021, prior to the status quo order. Finding no evidence that any prohibited civil work was executed after 25.02.2021, the NCLAT held there was no willful disobedience and discharged the Respondents, closing the contempt case.

case_title: Rizwan Khaleel vs Spicejet Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Rizwan Khaleel, a former employee (Operational Creditor). Respondent is Spicejet Ltd., the Corporate Debtor. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Employment contract; the Appellant resigned on 01.07.2016, with the resignation effective from 01.01.2017. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: The Appellant claimed unpaid salary for the months of November and December 2016, along with other benefits. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: In Part IV of the application, the Appellant himself averred the date of default as 31.12.2016. The Section 9 application was filed on 16.03.2020. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The Appellant relied on emails dated 21.11.2019 to argue the claim was still being processed and not denied until 09.01.2020, but the Tribunal found these emails did not provide any extension of limitation. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The Appellant filed a Section 9 application on 16.03.2020 before NCLT New Delhi Bench-V. The NCLT dismissed it on 08.10.2021 as time-barred. The Appellant subsequently filed this appeal to the NCLAT.
legal_issues: Whether the cause of action and right to sue for unpaid salary accrues when the salary becomes due, or whether it only accrues upon an explicit denial of payment by the employer.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The right to sue for an unpaid operational debt, such as salary, accrues immediately upon the default of payment when it becomes due, not when the debtor subsequently issues an explicit denial. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: For the purpose of limitation under the IBC, time begins to run from the date of default (in this case, the date the salary was due but not paid). An email stating a claim is 'being processed' does not constitute an acknowledgment of debt extending limitation unless explicitly satisfying the legal requirements for acknowledgment. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal noted that the Appellant explicitly declared the date of default as 31.12.2016 in his own application. Since the 3-year limitation period expired on 31.12.2019, the application filed on 16.03.2020 was barred by time. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT concluded that the infringement of the Appellant's right occurred in December 2016 and January 2017 when the salaries were not paid, triggering the limitation period immediately. Consequently, the Section 9 application was filed beyond the three-year limit and was correctly dismissed by the Adjudicating Authority.
operative_order: There is no merit in the Appeal. The appeal is dismissed.
summary: Rizwan Khaleel (Appellant/Operational Creditor) filed an appeal against the NCLT New Delhi's dismissal of his Section 9 IBC application against Spicejet Ltd. (Corporate Debtor). The Appellant sought unpaid salary for November and December 2016. He argued that the limitation period should start from 09.01.2020, the date the company explicitly denied payment, rather than the date of default. The NCLAT rejected this argument, holding that the right to sue accrues immediately when the salary becomes due and is not paid, which the Appellant himself stated was 31.12.2016. Since the application was filed on 16.03.2020, beyond the three-year limitation period, the NCLAT affirmed the dismissal of the application as time-barred.

case_title: Sanjay Ramakant Kudapkar vs Syndicate Bank & Anr
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Sanjay Ramakant Kudapkar, Ex-Director of the Corporate Debtor. Respondent No. 1 is Syndicate Bank, the Financial Creditor. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: The Financial Creditor provided a loan facility to the Corporate Debtor which went into default. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: The total default amount claimed by the Financial Creditor was Rs. 11,65,41,666.41/-, with the date of default mentioned as 31.03.2013. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The Corporate Debtor submitted a One Time Settlement (OTS) offer on 30.03.2016 and sent another letter seeking a 3-month extension on 17.08.2016. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The primary evidence consisted of the OTS offer letters dated 30.03.2016 (offering Rs. 3,33,39,801/-) and 17.08.2016, which were used to demonstrate an acknowledgment of debt. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Mumbai admitted the Section 7 application and initiated CIRP on 16.09.2021. The Ex-Director appealed to the NCLAT contending the application was time-barred.
legal_issues: Whether a One Time Settlement (OTS) offer submitted by the Corporate Debtor constitutes a valid acknowledgment of debt to extend the limitation period under Section 18 of the Limitation Act, 1963 for an application under Section 7 of the IBC.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An offer for a One Time Settlement (OTS) constitutes a valid acknowledgment of debt under Section 18 of the Limitation Act, thereby providing a fresh period of limitation. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 18 of the Limitation Act applies to insolvency proceedings, and a written OTS proposal submitted before the expiration of the original limitation period resets the clock for filing a Section 7 application. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal relied on the OTS offer dated 30.03.2016 and the extension letter dated 17.08.2016, noting that these communications were made within three years of the default date (31.03.2013), successfully extending the limitation period. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Applying the Supreme Court's ruling in Dena Bank vs. C. Shivakumar Reddy, the NCLAT concluded that the OTS offers extended the limitation period, and thus the NCLT correctly admitted the Section 7 application.
operative_order: The NCLAT found no merit in the appeal and dismissed it, upholding the NCLT's order initiating the CIRP.
summary: Sanjay Ramakant Kudapkar (Appellant), Ex-Director of the Corporate Debtor, appealed against the NCLT Mumbai's order admitting a Section 7 IBC application filed by Syndicate Bank (Financial Creditor) for a default of over Rs. 11.65 Crores. The Appellant argued the application was barred by time since the default date was 31.03.2013. The NCLAT dismissed the appeal, observing that the Corporate Debtor had submitted a One Time Settlement (OTS) offer on 30.03.2016 and a subsequent extension letter on 17.08.2016. Relying on Supreme Court precedent, the NCLAT held that these OTS proposals served as a valid acknowledgment of debt under Section 18 of the Limitation Act, effectively extending the limitation period and making the Section 7 application maintainable.

case_title: Prokash Datta vs Indian Bank (Erstwhile Allahabad Bank) & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Prokash Datta, Suspended Managing Director of the Corporate Debtor. Respondent No. 1 is Indian Bank (Erstwhile Allahabad Bank), the Financial Creditor. Respondent No. 2 is the Resolution Professional. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: The Financial Creditor granted financial debt comprising Term Loan-I, Term Loan-II, Term Loan-III, and a Cash Credit Loan to the Corporate Debtor. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: The total amount of debt, including disbursements made under Term Loan-III on various dates, was claimed in a Section 7 application. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The Adjudicating Authority (NCLT Guwahati) rejected the Appellant's I.A. No. 36 of 2021 on 26.08.2021. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The Appellant submitted a handwriting expert's report claiming his signature on the Term Loan-III Agreement was forged. However, the Appellant did not deny receiving the disbursed loan amounts. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The Appellant filed I.A. No. 36 of 2021 before NCLT Guwahati Bench under CrPC and IPC provisions seeking directions against the Financial Creditor for the alleged forgery. The NCLT rejected the I.A., and the Appellant appealed to the NCLAT.
legal_issues: Whether the Adjudicating Authority erred in rejecting the Appellant's application under Section 340 of the CrPC alleging forgery of the Term Loan-III agreement when the actual receipt of the disbursed loan amount was undisputed.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: In proceedings under the IBC, allegations of forgery regarding loan documents do not invalidate the proceedings if the actual disbursement and receipt of the financial debt remain undisputed by the Corporate Debtor. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: For a Section 7 IBC application, the primary consideration is the existence of a financial debt and default; procedural or criminal allegations regarding document signatures are secondary if the debt is otherwise established by the receipt of funds. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal observed that despite the Appellant's reliance on a handwriting expert's report to dispute his signature on the loan agreement, he completely failed to contest or deny the actual receipt of the disbursed funds, thereby establishing the debt. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Since the Appellant did not deny receiving the loan amount, the NCLAT concluded the Adjudicating Authority correctly rejected the interlocutory application alleging forgery, finding no merit in the appeal.
operative_order: The NCLAT found no merit in the appeal and dismissed it.
summary: Prokash Datta, Suspended Managing Director of the Corporate Debtor, appealed against the NCLT Guwahati's rejection of his interlocutory application. The application sought criminal proceedings against Indian Bank under Section 340 of the CrPC, alleging that his signature on the Term Loan-III agreement was forged, which he supported with a handwriting expert's report. The NCLAT dismissed the appeal, holding that while the Appellant disputed his signature on the document, he did not deny the actual disbursement and receipt of the loan amount. Since the existence and receipt of the financial debt were not contested, the NCLT correctly rejected the application.

case_title: Alchemist Asset Reconstruction Company Ltd. vs. Chandra Prakash Resolution Professional Dignity Buildcon Pvt. Ltd. & Ors.
appeal_number: Comp. App. (AT) (Ins.) No. 1026 of 2021 with Comp. App. (AT) (Ins.) No. 1062 of 2021
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant/Financial Creditor is Alchemist Asset Reconstruction Company Ltd. Corporate Debtor is Dignity Buildcon Pvt. Ltd. Respondent is Chandra Prakash, Resolution Professional. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process (CIRP) of the Corporate Debtor to resolve its insolvency. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: The specific default amount and date are not detailed in the appellate order as the dispute concerns the resolution plan voting phase. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP was initiated on 24-04-2019. The 330-day CIRP period (including extensions) ended on 09-03-2021. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Voting records showed that in three rounds, no Resolution Plan secured the requisite 66% vote because the Appellant (holding 35.36% voting share) dissented. Sattva and M3M withdrew their Bid Bond Guarantees of INR 20 Crores. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The Adjudicating Authority (NCLT New Delhi) passed an order on 01-10-2021 directing the CoC to reconsider pending plans, and later on 25-11-2021, directed voting on two plans that had received 64.64% votes. These appeals challenge the 25-11-2021 order.
legal_issues: Whether the Adjudicating Authority correctly directed voting only on the two resolution plans that had previously secured 64.64% votes, excluding other prospective resolution applicants, despite the withdrawal of one of the top bidders and the CoC's prior decision to invite all four original resolution applicants to submit revised plans.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: In the interest of maximizing the value of the corporate debtor and avoiding liquidation, all prospective resolution applicants who participated in the process should be given a final opportunity to submit revised plans if no plan achieves the requisite statutory majority in initial voting rounds and before a liquidation order is passed. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: The statutory intent of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code is the resolution of the corporate debtor; therefore, procedural directives by the Adjudicating Authority should facilitate the consideration of all viable plans by the Committee of Creditors (CoC) to achieve a resolution. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal evaluated the CoC's commercial wisdom and prior meeting minutes (dated 07.10.2021) which showed a collective decision to seek confirmation from all four Resolution Applicants. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The bench concluded that since no plan secured the requisite 66% votes and the CoC had resolved to approach all four resolution applicants, the NCLT's restrictive order of 25.11.2021 was modified to allow all four applicants to submit revised plans and bid bond guarantees, providing one final opportunity for resolution before considering liquidation.
operative_order: The Appeals were disposed of with directions modifying the NCLT's orders dated 25.11.2021 and 01.10.2021. All four Resolution Applicants were granted 15 days to submit their revised plans and reinstate their Bid Bond Guarantees of INR 20 Crores (if withdrawn). The CoC was directed to deliberate and vote on the received plans within 30 days thereafter to make a serious effort to save the Corporate Debtor from liquidation. No order as to costs.
summary: In the CIRP of Dignity Buildcon Pvt. Ltd., the CoC failed to approve any resolution plan across three rounds of voting as no plan secured the required 66% majority, primarily due to the dissenting vote of Alchemist Asset Reconstruction Company Ltd. (holding 35.36%). The NCLT directed voting on only two specific plans. Alchemist and Madhav Dhir appealed. The NCLAT observed that the primary object of the IBC is resolution, not liquidation. Noting that the CoC had previously decided to approach all four original resolution applicants, the NCLAT modified the NCLT's order. It directed that all four applicants be given a final 15-day opportunity to submit revised plans and Bid Bond Guarantees, followed by CoC voting within 30 days.

case_title: PJ Networks Pvt. Ltd. vs. Mr. Pardeep Kumar Lakhani
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is PJ Networks Pvt. Ltd., claiming to provide IT firewall services. Corporate Debtor is M/s. Dion Global Solutions Ltd. Respondent is Mr. Pardeep Kumar Lakhani, the Resolution Professional. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: The Appellant supplied IT services based on a purchase order dated 11.08.2020, providing services from 15.08.2020 to 16.08.2021. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: This is not a default dispute; the issue concerns an unauthorized post-CIRP payment of Rs. 1,26,522 out of a total Rs. 17,89,767 paid to various vendors. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The NCLT admitted the Corporate Debtor into CIRP on 18.08.2020. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: HDFC Bank statements proved that employees of the Corporate Debtor transferred funds to the Appellant on 19.08.2020 (post-CIRP commencement) before the RP received his appointment communication on 24.08.2020 and took charge on 27.08.2020. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The RP filed an application under Section 60(5) to reverse the transactions as non-est in law. The NCLT New Delhi allowed the application on 18.03.2021, directing the Appellant to refund Rs. 1,26,522. The Appellant challenged this refund order.
legal_issues: Whether a payment made to a vendor post-CIRP commencement violates the Section 14 moratorium, and whether the vendor could retain the payment by claiming to supply 'essential services' under Section 14(2) read with Regulation 32 of the CIRP Regulations.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Any payments or transfer of assets made by a Corporate Debtor after the commencement of CIRP and imposition of a moratorium are non-est in law and liable to be refunded to the Resolution Professional. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: The exception for 'essential services' under Section 14(2) of the IBC and Regulation 32 of the CIRP Regulations applies to Information Technology Services only to the extent they are not a direct input to the output produced or supplied by the Corporate Debtor. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal noted that the Appellant failed to raise the Section 14(2) defense before the Adjudicating Authority to prove the nature of its services, and the evidentiary record indisputably showed the payments were executed after the 18.08.2020 CIRP admission order. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Since the payment was made after CIRP had commenced and the moratorium had taken effect, the NCLT committed no illegality in ordering the refund, thereby rendering the appeal meritless.
operative_order: The NCLAT affirmed the order dated 18.03.2021 passed by the Adjudicating Authority and dismissed the appeal, holding that the Appellant must refund the amount.
summary: The case involves an appeal by PJ Networks Pvt. Ltd. challenging an NCLT order that directed the refund of Rs. 1,26,522 to the Resolution Professional of M/s. Dion Global Solutions Ltd. The Corporate Debtor was admitted into CIRP on 18.08.2020, triggering a moratorium. However, on 19.08.2020, before the RP took control, employees transferred funds to the Appellant for IT services. The Appellant argued these were 'essential services' exempted under Section 14(2) of the IBC. The NCLAT upheld the NCLT's refund order, concluding that the payments made post-CIRP violated the moratorium and that the Appellant had failed to plead the essential services exemption before the Adjudicating Authority. The appeal was consequently dismissed.

case_title: Zillion Infrastructure Pvt. Ltd. vs. The Indure Private Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant/Operational Creditor is Zillion Infraprojects Pvt. Ltd. Respondent/Corporate Debtor is The Indure Private Ltd. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: The Corporate Debtor awarded three work orders to the Appellant between 2009 and 2012 for erection, fabrication, commissioning, and painting work at a Thermal Power Plant in Chhabra, Rajasthan. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: The claimed default amount was Rs. 8,34,18,876/- as principal and Rs. 2,41,38,406/- as accumulated interest based on Running Account Bills. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The Appellant issued a Demand Notice under Section 8 of the IBC on 13.09.2017. The Corporate Debtor replied on 23.09.2017 raising disputes. A fresh Demand Notice was issued on 16.11.2017, and the Section 9 Application was filed on 06.12.2017. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The Corporate Debtor produced emails and letters from 2013-2014 pointing out breaches and delays, and a contract termination letter dated 20.11.2014. The Appellant relied on a completion certificate dated 16.04.2015 issued by Rajasthan Rajya Vidyut Utpadan Nigam Ltd. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The Adjudicating Authority (NCLT, New Delhi Bench-II) rejected the Section 9 Application on 03.05.2021 due to a pre-existing dispute. The Appellant challenged this rejection.
legal_issues: Whether the Adjudicating Authority erred in rejecting the Section 9 Application on the ground of a pre-existing dispute despite the operational creditor holding a successful completion certificate from the ultimate project owner.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An application for initiating the Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process by an operational creditor is not maintainable and must be rejected if there is overwhelming documentary evidence demonstrating a genuine pre-existing dispute prior to the issuance of the statutory demand notice. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: The term 'dispute' under Section 5(6) read with Section 8(2) of the IBC encompasses pre-existing correspondence raising substantive issues regarding the quality of service, delays, and the consequent termination of the contract. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal evaluated the correspondence (emails, breach notices, and the termination letter dated 20.11.2014) as valid evidence of a dispute, ruling that a third-party completion certificate does not override or wipe out the inter-se contractual disputes between the main contractor and its sub-contractor. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The bench concluded that since the Corporate Debtor had raised substantial disputes regarding delays, recoveries, and contract termination well before the demand notice, the NCLT committed no error in rejecting the Section 9 application on the ground of a pre-existing dispute.
operative_order: The NCLAT dismissed the appeal, holding that there was no error in the Adjudicating Authority's order. The Tribunal clarified that the rejection of the Section 9 application does not preclude the Appellant from raising its claim for payment of bills in accordance with the terms of the work order in an appropriate forum. There was no order as to costs.
summary: In Zillion Infrastructure Pvt. Ltd. v. The Indure Private Ltd., the Appellant challenged the NCLT's rejection of its Section 9 IBC application for unpaid dues of over Rs. 10 crores relating to thermal power plant works. The Corporate Debtor argued that it had terminated the contract in 2014 due to delays and breaches, explicitly raising these issues in its reply to the Section 8 demand notice. The NCLAT affirmed the NCLT's decision, determining that the termination letter and prior correspondence constituted overwhelming evidence of a pre-existing dispute. It further noted that a third-party completion certificate did not negate these inter-se contractual disputes. Consequently, the appeal was dismissed.

case_title: Go Airlines (India) Limited vs. Sovika Aviation Services Pvt. Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant/Operational Creditor is Go Airlines (India) Limited. Respondent/Corporate Debtor is Sovika Aviation Services Pvt. Ltd. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: The parties entered into a Cargo Agreement dated 09.07.2016 where the Appellant agreed to provide cargo belly space in its aircraft to the Respondent for specific considerations including a signing amount and monthly charges. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: The Appellant issued a demand notice claiming an unpaid operational debt of Rs. 17,60,80,625/- based on multiple outstanding invoices. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The Corporate Debtor replied to the demand notice on 28.12.2017 raising pre-existing disputes including loss of revenue and non-availability of space. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Evidence showed a strained relationship from June 2017, debit notes of Rs. 27.74 Crore raised by the Respondent (and returned by the Appellant), and the Appellant's invocation of a bank guarantee worth Rs. 39.91 Crore on 27.06.2017. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The Appellant filed a Section 9 petition which the NCLT Mumbai dismissed on 26.08.2019 due to the pre-existence of a dispute, leading to this appeal.
legal_issues: Whether the Adjudicating Authority was justified in dismissing the Section 9 application on the ground of a pre-existing dispute regarding the provision of cargo belly space and the invocation of bank guarantees prior to the demand notice.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code is not intended to be a substitute for a recovery forum, nor is it meant to settle contentious civil disputes erupting among parties. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 9 IBC applications are not maintainable when there is an undisputed pre-existence of a real and contentious dispute before the issuance of the demand notice. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal evaluated the prior exchange of debit notes, emails showing operational issues regarding belly space availability, and the invocation of a heavy bank guarantee as clear evidence of a genuine dispute requiring civil adjudication. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The bench concluded that since there was a genuine and serious pre-existing dispute regarding cargo space and cross-claims, the NCLT correctly dismissed the Section 9 petition.
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed, and any interim order stands vacated, with no order as to costs.
summary: Go Airlines (India) Ltd. appealed the NCLT Mumbai's dismissal of its Section 9 application against Sovika Aviation Services Pvt. Ltd. The dispute arose from a 2016 Cargo Agreement where Go Airlines claimed Rs. 17.60 crores as unpaid operational debt for cargo belly space. The Corporate Debtor contested this, citing a severe lack of cargo space, resultant operational losses, and raised cross-claims of Rs. 27.74 crores via debit notes prior to the demand notice. Furthermore, Go Airlines had already invoked a bank guarantee of Rs. 39.91 crores. The NCLAT affirmed the NCLT's finding of a genuine, pre-existing civil dispute, reiterating that the IBC is not a recovery forum. The appeal was consequently dismissed.

case_title: Himachal Pradesh State Electricity Board Limited vs. Suraj Fabrics Industries Limited
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Himachal Pradesh State Electricity Board Limited. Respondent is Suraj Fabrics Industries Limited (Corporate Debtor). The Resolution Professional was Mr. Santosh Choraria, and the Resolution Applicant was M/s Sponge Sales (India) Private Limited. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: The matter relates to the approval of a Resolution Plan for the Corporate Debtor that was passed by the CoC with a 100% vote. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Specific default amounts are not detailed, but the Appellant's admitted claim was settled, and resolution proceeds were disbursed to their account. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The NCLT approved the plan on 12.08.2020. The Resolution Professional informed the Appellant of this via email on 17.08.2020 and confirmed disbursement on 03.09.2020. The appeal was filed on 03.08.2021. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The Respondent produced emails dated 17.08.2020 and 03.09.2020 proving the Appellant received a copy of the impugned order and intimation of the disbursed resolution proceeds. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The Appellant filed the appeal against the 12.08.2020 NCLT Kolkata order along with I.A. No. 1657 of 2021 seeking condonation of an alleged 102-day delay, which the Respondent contested was actually over 356 days.
legal_issues: Whether sufficient cause was shown to condone the substantial delay in filing the appeal when the Appellant claimed lack of knowledge of the impugned order but documentary evidence showed otherwise.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An application for condonation of delay in filing an appeal cannot be allowed on the basis of vague claims of departmental processing delays or false claims of ignorance, especially when there is documentary proof of actual prior knowledge. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Strict adherence to limitation periods under the IBC is required, and a bland statement regarding sending files to various authorities and the Law Department does not constitute sufficient explanation for condonation. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal relied on the emails dated 17.08.2020 and 03.09.2020 as conclusive evidence that the Appellant had complete knowledge of the NCLT's approval order and had already received the resolution amount. 4.
