case_title: Central Board of Indirect Taxes and Customs vs Sundaresh Bhatt, Liquidator of ABG Shipyard
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant is the Central Board of Indirect Taxes and Customs. The Respondent is Sundaresh Bhatt, Liquidator of the Corporate Debtor, ABG Shipyard. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: The Corporate Debtor imported materials/containers between 2012 and 2015 and kept them in Customs Bonded Warehouses to build ships under the Export Promotion Capital Goods (EPCG) Scheme. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: The Corporate Debtor failed to submit an Export Obligation Discharge Certificate and defaulted on customs duties amounting to approximately Rs. 769 crores. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The CIRP was initiated on August 1, 2017, and the liquidation order was passed on April 25, 2019. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The Corporate Debtor never cleared bills of entry for home consumption for years. The Appellant issued notices under Section 72 of the Customs Act and submitted a 'Form C' claim identifying 2531 bills of entries to the Liquidator. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The Liquidator filed IA No. 474/2019 in NCLT Ahmedabad seeking release of the goods. On February 25, 2020, NCLT allowed the application, directing Customs to release the goods without duty payment, prompting this appeal.
legal_issues: Whether uncleared imported goods lying in customs bonded warehouses for years form part of the Corporate Debtor's liquidation estate, and whether the Liquidator can claim them without paying customs duty by relying on the overriding effect of the IBC.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Goods imported but abandoned in a customs warehouse without clearance for home consumption or payment of duty do not belong to the importing entity, as title is deemed relinquished by implication of law. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Sections 48 and 72 of the Customs Act empower authorities to sell uncleared goods to recover dues; Section 238 of the IBC does not override this because such abandoned goods do not qualify as the Corporate Debtor's assets under the IBC. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The tribunal assessed whether the importer took affirmative steps to clear the goods or pay duties prior to CIRP; failing to do so for years established relinquishment of title. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Liquidator cannot take possession of the warehoused goods without upfront payment of customs duty, and the Appellant filing a claim with the Liquidator does not strip the Customs Authority of its statutory right to dispose of the goods.
operative_order: The Appeal is allowed with no order as to costs. The NCLT's impugned order dated February 25, 2020, is modified to the extent that the goods can be released or disposed of as per the applicable provisions of the Customs Act by the Proper Officer.
summary: In a conflict between the Customs Authority and the Liquidator of ABG Shipyard, the NCLAT determined whether uncleared imported goods in customs warehouses formed part of the liquidation estate. The Corporate Debtor imported materials between 2012-2015 but abandoned them without paying duty. NCLT Ahmedabad had ordered the release of these goods to the Liquidator without duty payment, citing IBC's overriding effect. The NCLAT overturned this, holding that under Sections 48 and 72 of the Customs Act, the importer deemed to have relinquished title by failing to clear the goods. Consequently, the goods were not the Corporate Debtor's assets, and the Liquidator could not take possession without paying customs duty. The appeal was allowed.

case_title: Shailendra Singh vs Nisha Malpani & Anr
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant, Shailendra Singh, is an Advocate appointed by the erstwhile Interim Resolution Professional. The 1st Respondent, Nisha Malpani, is the current Resolution Professional for the Corporate Debtor. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: The Appellant was engaged to provide legal services for the Corporate Debtor at a fixed fee of Rs. 33,000 per appearance plus expenses. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Unpaid legal fees amounting to Rs. 2,42,000 for bills raised between August 9, 2018, and September 4, 2018. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The NCLT had initially ordered payment of the arrears within two days on November 7, 2019, which remained unpaid months later. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The core evidence was the NCLT's November 7, 2019 order recording an undertaking by the RP's counsel to clear the arrears, which was allegedly willfully breached. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The Appellant filed a contempt application before the NCLT; on September 23, 2020, NCLT dismissed it on the ground that the IBC lacks contempt jurisdiction, leading to the present appeal.
legal_issues: Whether the Adjudicating Authority (NCLT) has the jurisdiction and power to punish for contempt under Section 425 of the Companies Act, 2013, while adjudicating matters under the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Tribunals possess inherent jurisdiction to punish for contempt to uphold the majesty of law and ensure the enforcement of their orders, preventing their mandate from being rendered ineffective. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: A conjoined reading of Section 408 and Section 425 of the Companies Act, 2013, establishes that the contempt powers vested in the NCLT are not confined exclusively to Companies Act proceedings but extend to its role as the Adjudicating Authority under Section 5(1) of the IBC. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The tribunal employed a purposeful construction of the statute, reasoning that denying contempt jurisdiction would leave the IBC without 'teeth to bite' and render its orders unenforceable. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLT's conclusion that it lacked contempt jurisdiction under the IBC is legally unsustainable; the NCLT possesses full authority to initiate contempt proceedings for willful disobedience of its orders in insolvency matters.
operative_order: The appeal is allowed with no costs. The impugned order dated September 23, 2020, is set aside, and the Adjudicating Authority is directed to restore the Contempt Application to its file and dispose of it on merits after providing due opportunity to both sides.
summary: The case involved an advocate seeking unpaid legal fees of Rs. 2,42,000 from the Resolution Professional of a Corporate Debtor. After the RP allegedly breached a recorded undertaking given to the NCLT to clear the dues within two days, the Appellant filed a contempt application. The NCLT dismissed this application, ruling that it lacked contempt jurisdiction under the IBC. On appeal, the NCLAT overturned this decision, holding that Section 425 read with Section 408 of the Companies Act, 2013, empowers the NCLT with contempt jurisdiction across all matters it adjudicates, including IBC proceedings. Restricting this power would render IBC orders unenforceable. The NCLAT remanded the matter back to the NCLT for adjudication.

case_title: Hemanshu Jamnadas Domadia vs Central Bank Of India
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant is the ex-director and shareholder of the Corporate Debtor, M/s Silver Proteins Pvt Ltd. The 1st Respondent is the Financial Creditor, Central Bank of India. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: The Corporate Debtor availed credit facilities worth Rs. 19,12,50,000 from the Respondent Bank, which was last renewed on March 1, 2015. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: The Corporate Debtor defaulted, leading to the account being classified as a Non-Performing Asset (NPA) on July 1, 2015. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The NPA date was July 1, 2015, and the Section 7 petition was filed by the bank on October 22, 2018. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Evidence included a credit entry of Rs. 5,99,760 in the Corporate Debtor's account on December 30, 2015, and signed balance sheets for the years ending March 31, 2017, March 31, 2018, and March 31, 2019, which recorded the long-term and short-term borrowings payable to the bank. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The NCLT Ahmedabad admitted the Section 7 petition on June 29, 2020. The Appellant challenged this on grounds of limitation and improper authorization.
legal_issues: Whether a Section 7 application filed by a Power of Attorney holder is maintainable, and whether the application was barred by limitation despite part payments and acknowledgments in balance sheets.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An officer authorized by a General Power of Attorney is competent to file an insolvency application on behalf of a financial creditor, and entries in balance sheets constitute valid acknowledgment of debt to extend limitation. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 18 of the Limitation Act applies to IBC proceedings; an acknowledgment of debt in a balance sheet before the expiry of the limitation period starts a fresh period of limitation. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The tribunal rejected the unsupported claim that a part payment was made by an unrelated party and held that signed balance sheets explicitly recording secured borrowings serve as a clear jural acknowledgment of liability. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Section 7 application was duly authorized and filed within limitation due to the extensions provided by the part payment and balance sheet acknowledgments, justifying the NCLT's admission order.
operative_order: The Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 623 of 2020 fails and is dismissed with no order as to costs.
summary: The NCLAT dismissed the appeal filed by the suspended director of M/s Silver Proteins Pvt Ltd against the NCLT's order admitting Central Bank of India's Section 7 insolvency petition. The Appellant argued the petition was time-barred since the NPA date was July 1, 2015, and the petition was filed in October 2018, and that the bank officer lacked proper authorization. The NCLAT held the bank's Assistant General Manager was duly authorized via a General Power of Attorney. Additionally, the limitation period was validly extended under Section 18 of the Limitation Act due to a part payment in December 2015 and acknowledgments of debt in the Corporate Debtor's signed balance sheets for 2017, 2018, and 2019.

case_title: Punjab National Bank vs Eva Agro Feeds Pvt. Ltd. & Anr
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant is Punjab National Bank, a Secured Financial Creditor. Respondent No. 1 is EVA Agro Feeds Pvt. Ltd., the highest bidder. Respondent No. 2 is Sunil Mohan Acharya, Liquidator of the Corporate Debtor, Amrit Feeds Ltd. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: An e-auction for the liquidation sale of the Corporate Debtor's 'Mirzapur Asset'. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: The reserve price for the asset was set at Rs. 10 Crores. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The auction notice was issued on June 28, 2021, and the sole bid was placed on July 20, 2021. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Respondent No. 1 placed a single bid exactly at the reserve price. The Liquidator cancelled the auction relying on Clause 3(k) of the sale notice, observing that another asset (Lucknow Asset) with a lower book value yielded much higher than its reserve price, thus aiming for value maximization. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The NCLT Kolkata allowed Respondent No. 1's IA No. 663/KB/2021 on August 12, 2021, directing the Liquidator to conclude the sale. The Financial Creditor appealed to the NCLAT against this direction.
legal_issues: Whether the highest bidder in a liquidation e-auction acquires a vested right to demand acceptance of their bid, and whether the Liquidator possesses the absolute authority to cancel the auction under the IBBI (Liquidation Process) Regulations to maximize asset value.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The highest bidder in a public auction does not acquire any vested legal right to compel the completion of the sale until the bid is formally accepted and full payment is made. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Clause 12 of Schedule 1 of the Liquidation Process Regulations must be read conjointly with Clauses 11 and 13; Clause 11 specifically empowers the Liquidator to conduct multiple rounds of auctions to maximize realization, affirming the Liquidator's discretion to reject bids. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal verified whether the auction's terms (Clause 3(k) of the sale notice) expressly granted the Liquidator the right to cancel the auction without assigning reasons; exercising this for value maximization is a valid administrative action. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLT erred in directing the sale's completion; the Liquidator validly exercised his discretion to cancel the auction to fetch a better price, and such cancellation does not violate the Liquidation Regulations.
operative_order: The Company Appeal is allowed, and the impugned order of the NCLT Kolkata dated August 12, 2021, is set aside. The Liquidator is directed to initiate a fresh auction process in accordance with the IBC and IBBI Regulations. No order as to costs.
summary: The case involves a dispute over the liquidation e-auction of Amrit Feeds Ltd.'s 'Mirzapur Asset'. Eva Agro Feeds placed a sole bid exactly at the reserve price of Rs. 10 Crores. The Liquidator cancelled the auction to maximize value, but NCLT Kolkata ordered the sale's completion. Punjab National Bank appealed this NCLT order. The NCLAT overturned the NCLT's decision, establishing that a highest bidder possesses no vested legal right to compel a sale until formal conclusion and full payment are achieved. Interpreting Schedule 1 of the IBBI Liquidation Regulations, the Tribunal affirmed the Liquidator's absolute discretion to cancel an auction and conduct multiple rounds to maximize realization for creditors. The NCLAT allowed the appeal and directed a fresh auction.

case_title: Bhatpara Municipality vs Nicco Eastern Private Limited & Anr
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant is Bhatpara Municipality. Respondent No. 1 is Nicco Eastern Pvt. Ltd., the auction purchaser. Respondent No. 2 is Nicco Corporation Limited (Corporate Debtor in liquidation), represented by its Liquidator. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Sale of the Shyamnagar Cable Manufacturing Unit by the Liquidator through an e-auction on an 'As is Where is' and 'No Recourse' basis. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Pending property tax dues amounting to Rs. 68,09,123.61 for the period from the 1st quarter of 2015-16 to the 4th quarter of 2020-21. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The e-auction concluded on October 5, 2020, and possession was handed over on October 9, 2020. The Appellant issued the disputed demand notice for taxes on February 1, 2021. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The sale terms explicitly stated 'No Recourse Basis', yet the municipality demanded past taxes from the new purchaser and withheld the mutation and trade license. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Kolkata passed an order on July 13, 2021, quashing the municipality's demand notice and absolving the purchaser of past liabilities, which the municipality then appealed.
legal_issues: Whether the Adjudicating Authority has the jurisdiction to quash a municipal tax demand notice issued to an auction purchaser, and whether the purchaser is liable for property tax dues that accrued prior to the liquidation sale confirmation.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Outstanding municipal tax dues relating to a period prior to a liquidation sale confirmation do not attach to the property in the hands of the auction purchaser. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 55(1)(g) of the Transfer of Property Act binds the seller to discharge public charges accrued up to the sale date. Under Section 53 of the IBC, past municipal taxes are akin to claims of an unsecured creditor and must be claimed in the liquidation waterfall, not from the successful buyer. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal noted that the demand was made over four months after the auction sale was completed and possession delivered; therefore, the pre-sale tax liabilities belonged solely to the Corporate Debtor's estate. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The auction purchaser cannot be held liable for property tax dues preceding the sale confirmation, and the Adjudicating Authority rightly exercised its jurisdiction to quash the demand notice.
operative_order: The demand notice dated 01.02.2021 is quashed, the appeal fails, and the Impugned Order is upheld. The auction-purchaser is held to be not liable to pay the demanded amount. No order as to costs.
summary: In a liquidation sale dispute, the NCLAT examined whether the auction purchaser, Nicco Eastern Pvt. Ltd., was liable for Rs. 68 lakhs in past property taxes demanded by Bhatpara Municipality. The NCLT had previously quashed the municipality's demand notice. The NCLAT upheld the NCLT's decision, ruling that pre-sale municipal tax dues are akin to unsecured claims governed by Section 53 of the IBC and must be collected from the liquidation estate, not the auction purchaser. Consequently, the auction purchaser was absolved from liability for taxes accrued prior to the sale confirmation, and the appeal was dismissed.

case_title: Assistant Commissioner Of Commercial Taxes vs Right Engineers & Equipment India Pvt. Ltd & Anr
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant is the Assistant Commissioner of Commercial Taxes (Audit), Bangalore. Respondent No. 1 is Right Engineers & Equipment India Pvt. Ltd (Corporate Debtor in liquidation), and Respondent No. 2 is its Liquidator, Mr. Addanki Haresh. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: The claim arises from statutory tax obligations under the KVAT and CST Acts for the assessment year 2016-17. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: The Corporate Debtor owed tax, interest, and penalties totaling INR 75,82,617 (KVAT: INR 36,46,908 and CST: INR 39,35,709). 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The liquidation order was passed on December 2, 2020, and the public announcement set the last date for claim submission as January 11, 2021. The Appellant filed its claim belatedly on March 4, 2021, resulting in a 52-day delay. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The Liquidator rejected the claim on March 17, 2021, solely because it was submitted past the deadline specified in the public announcement. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The Appellant filed IA No. 106 of 2021 before NCLT Bengaluru to condone the delay, which was dismissed on April 5, 2021, leading to this appeal.
legal_issues: Whether a delay of 52 days in submitting a claim to the liquidator by a statutory tax authority can be condoned solely on the ground that the authority was unaware of the Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process and liquidation proceedings.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The limitation period for submitting claims in a time-bound liquidation process cannot be routinely relaxed, and ignorance of public announcements does not constitute sufficient cause for condonation. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Under Regulation 16(1) of the IBBI (Liquidation Process) Regulations, 2016, a stakeholder must submit their claim on or before the last date in the public announcement; any delay requires demonstration of sufficient cause absent of negligence or inaction. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal tests for 'sufficient cause' by evaluating whether there was any inaction, want of bona fide, or negligence by the litigant. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Appellant's claim of being unaware of the CIRP and liquidation process is unworthy of acceptance, as the department failed to take appropriate independent action at the right time to recover the tax, thereby failing to prove sufficient cause for the 52-day delay.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (CH) (Insolvency) No. 255 of 2021 is dismissed with no costs.
summary: The Assistant Commissioner of Commercial Taxes appealed against the NCLT Bengaluru's order dismissing its application to condone a 52-day delay in submitting a tax claim of INR 75,82,617 to the Liquidator of Right Engineers & Equipment India Pvt. Ltd. The public announcement had set the claim deadline as January 11, 2021, but the Appellant filed on March 4, 2021, claiming unawareness of the liquidation. The NCLAT upheld the NCLT's dismissal, ruling that the liquidation process is strictly time-bound. Ignorance of the public announcement and failure to take independent action to recover taxes demonstrated negligence, meaning there was no 'sufficient cause' to condone the delay. The appeal was dismissed.

case_title: Ananta Charan Nayak vs State Bank Of India & Ors
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant is Ananta Charan Nayak, a shareholder, promoter, and suspended Director of the Corporate Debtor, M/s. Nayak Infrastructure Private Limited. The 1st Respondent is the Financial Creditor, State Bank of India. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: The Corporate Debtor is engaged in the engineering, procurement, and construction business and had a business relationship with the Financial Creditor for over 30 years involving loan facilities. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: The loan account was declared a Non-Performing Asset (NPA) on January 28, 2020. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: A notice was issued by State Bank of India on January 30, 2020, and the NCLT admitted the Section 7 application on August 26, 2021. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The Appellant submitted a One Time Settlement (OTS) proposal to the Financial Creditor which remained pending. State Bank of India filed an affidavit on August 4, 2021, to cure a defect in its application by deleting the names of the personal guarantors erroneously included as respondents. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The NCLT Guwahati Bench admitted the Section 7 petition via order dated August 26, 2021. The Appellant appealed to the NCLAT claiming the application was defective and should not have been admitted while an OTS was pending.
legal_issues: Whether a Section 7 application under the IBC can be admitted when a One Time Settlement (OTS) proposal is pending with the Financial Creditor, and whether the initial erroneous inclusion of personal guarantors renders the application fatally defective.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The pendency of a settlement proposal does not legally bar the Adjudicating Authority from admitting an insolvency petition, as the IBC does not provide for keeping proceedings in abeyance for settlement negotiations. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 7 of the IBC mandates a time-bound admission process; if a settlement is reached after admission, the parties have the recourse to withdraw under Section 12A of the IBC. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal reviewed the record and confirmed that the procedural defect of improperly joining personal guarantors was validly cured when the Financial Creditor filed an affidavit deleting those names. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Since the defects in the application were cured and the pending OTS proposal does not impede the statutory timeline for admission, the Adjudicating Authority correctly admitted the Section 7 application.
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed at the stage of admission with no order as to costs, upholding the NCLT Guwahati Bench's order initiating the Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process.
summary: The suspended director of M/s Nayak Infrastructure Pvt Ltd appealed against the NCLT Guwahati's admission of State Bank of India's Section 7 insolvency application. The Appellant argued the application was defective for wrongfully including personal guarantors and that an OTS proposal was pending. The NCLAT dismissed the appeal, noting that SBI had already filed an affidavit curing the defect by deleting the personal guarantors. Furthermore, the tribunal held that a pending settlement proposal does not warrant keeping IBC proceedings in abeyance, as the code prescribes a strict timeframe for admission, leaving Section 12A available if a settlement is eventually reached.

case_title: SP Probuild LLP vs Rabinder Kumar Mintri
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant is SP Probuild LLP, a claimant alleging ownership of 41 flats. The Respondent is Rabinder Kumar Mintri, the Resolution Professional (RP) for the Corporate Debtor, Today Homes Noida India Ltd. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: The Appellant claimed to have paid full consideration to the Corporate Debtor for the purchase of 41 flats. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: The Appellant sought recognition of its ownership and claim over the 41 flats. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The IRP issued a publication inviting claims until September 3, 2019. The Committee of Creditors (CoC) approved the Resolution Plan on March 4, 2020. The Appellant filed its claim belatedly with the RP on June 16, 2020. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The undisputed procedural timeline showed that the Appellant submitted its claim months after the CoC had already approved the Resolution Plan. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The RP rejected the belated claim, prompting the Appellant to file IA No. 3213/2021 on April 19, 2021. The NCLT New Delhi dismissed the application on September 21, 2021, observing it had become infructuous, leading to the present appeal.
legal_issues: Whether a claim filed by a stakeholder can be entertained and relief granted if it is submitted after the Committee of Creditors has already approved the Resolution Plan.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A belated claim filed after the Committee of Creditors has already approved the Resolution Plan cannot be entertained, and no relief can be granted to the claimant at that advanced stage. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: The strict timelines of the Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process (CIRP) under the IBC preclude the consideration of new claims that would disrupt a Resolution Plan already finalized and approved by the CoC. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal evaluated the chronological milestones, specifically noting that the claim submission (June 2020) post-dated the CoC's approval of the plan (March 2020), making it legally impossible to grant the requested relief. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT concluded that no order could be passed in the Appellant's favor due to the late stage at which the application was filed, and dismissed the appeal in limine.
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed in limine.
summary: The Appellant, SP Probuild LLP, appealed the NCLT's dismissal of its application seeking recognition of its claim for 41 flats, for which it allegedly paid full consideration to the Corporate Debtor. The IRP's deadline for claims was September 3, 2019, and the CoC approved the Resolution Plan on March 4, 2020. The Appellant filed its claim belatedly on June 16, 2020, which the RP rejected. The NCLAT upheld the NCLT's dismissal, ruling that no relief could be granted because the claim was filed well after the CoC had already approved the Resolution Plan. The appeal was dismissed in limine.

case_title: Committee of Creditors of M/s. Vasan Health Care Pvt. Ltd. vs Mr. S. Rajendran
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant is the Committee of Creditors of M/s. Vasan Health Care Pvt. Ltd. (Corporate Debtor), and the Respondent is Mr. S. Rajendran, Resolution Professional. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: The Corporate Debtor operates in the healthcare industry, specifically as a chain of eye hospitals with centers spread across Southern States. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: The underlying debt amounts and default dates are not detailed as the dispute solely concerns the extension of the CIRP timelines. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The CIRP was initiated on 21.04.2017, stayed by the High Court on 04.05.2017, and revived on 03.10.2019. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Following a fresh Expression of Interest, 8 bidders expressed interest and 7 prospective resolution applicants were shortlisted. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The NCLT Chennai extended the CIRP period only up to 22.08.2021 in IA/510/CHE/2021; the CoC filed this appeal to extend the period to 30.11.2021.
legal_issues: Whether the Appellants have made out a case showing exceptional circumstances to seek an extension of time for the completion of the Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process (CIRP) beyond the statutory limit of 330 days.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The statutory outer limit of 330 days for completing a Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process can be extended in exceptional circumstances to avoid pushing the corporate debtor into liquidation. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Following the Supreme Court's decision in Essar Steel, the word 'mandatorily' in Section 12(3) of the IBC is struck down, granting tribunals discretion to extend time beyond 330 days. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal assessed whether 'exceptional circumstances' existed, concluding that nationwide COVID-19 lockdowns, pending judicial proceedings, change of the RP, and the active participation of multiple resolution applicants justified an extension. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The bench concluded that to comply with the IBC's objective of value maximization and to treat liquidation only as a last resort, the CIRP time must be extended.
operative_order: The NCLAT set aside the Adjudicating Authority's order dated 03.08.2021, allowed the relief sought in IA/510/CHE/2021, extended the CIRP time till 30.11.2021, and excluded the time spent filing the appeals (18.08.2021 to 25.11.2021).
summary: The Committee of Creditors of M/s. Vasan Health Care Pvt. Ltd. appealed an NCLT Chennai order that restricted the Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process (CIRP) extension to August 22, 2021. The NCLAT examined whether the CIRP timeline could be extended beyond the 330-day limit. Finding exceptional circumstances—namely COVID-19 lockdowns, judicial delays, and active bids from seven shortlisted resolution applicants—the Tribunal granted the extension until November 30, 2021. Relying on Supreme Court precedents like Swiss Ribbons and Essar Steel, the NCLAT emphasized that liquidation must remain a last resort and extending the timeline would fulfill the Code's objective of maximizing the corporate debtor's asset value.

case_title: Manmohan Singh Jain vs State Bank of India
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Financial Creditor is State Bank of India (Consortium Leader), Corporate Debtor is Kiran Global Chems Limited, and Appellant is Manmohan Singh Jain (Suspended Director/Shareholder). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Working Capital credit facilities were availed under a Working Capital Arrangement Consortium Agreement. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default amount claimed is Rs. 52,28,93,796/- and SBI's declared NPA/default date is 27.11.2018. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Legal notice calling advances issued on 21.05.2019; Section 7 application filed on 19.12.2019. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: An acknowledgment of debt under Section 18 of the Limitation Act was executed on 16.08.2018, and a SARFAESI notice under Section 13(2) was issued on 28.01.2019. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Chennai admitted the Section 7 application on 27.04.2021 in IBA/45/2020 despite the missing date of default in Part IV of Form-1; the suspended director appealed this admission.
legal_issues: Whether the omission of the exact date of default in Part IV of Form-1 is a fatal defect rendering the Section 7 application incomplete, and whether the claim was barred by limitation due to a consortium member's earlier NPA date.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The omission to mention the exact date of default in a specific column of Form-1 is not a fatal defect if the date is evident from the pleadings and attached documentary evidence. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 7(5) of the IBC is directory in nature regarding curable defects, and Section 18 of the Limitation Act applies to extend the limitation period upon valid acknowledgment of debt. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Adjudicating Authority must rely on the totality of enclosed documents under Part V of Form-1, such as SARFAESI notices and balance confirmations, to ascertain the existence of debt and the date of default. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The bench concluded that SBI proved its default date independently, the acknowledgment of debt extended limitation, and the technical omission in Form-1 did not invalidate the application.
operative_order: The Tribunal found the appeal devoid of merits and dismissed it with no orders as to cost, thereby upholding the Adjudicating Authority's admission of the CIRP.
summary: Manmohan Singh Jain appealed the NCLT's admission of a Section 7 CIRP petition filed by State Bank of India against Kiran Global Chems Limited. The appellant argued the petition was defective for omitting the default date in Form-1 and time-barred based on a consortium member's earlier NPA date. The NCLAT held that the omission in Form-1 was not fatal as the default date (27.11.2018) was clear from accompanying documents. Furthermore, an acknowledgment of debt on 16.08.2018 legally extended the limitation period. Consequently, the NCLAT dismissed the appeal.

case_title: M/s. Invent Assets Securitisation & Reconstruction Pvt. Ltd. vs. M/s. Girnar Fibres Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Financial Creditor (Assignee) M/s. Invent Assets Securitisation & Reconstruction Pvt. Ltd. (assignee of State Bank of India) vs. Corporate Debtor M/s. Girnar Fibres Ltd. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: State Bank of India granted credit facilities to the Corporate Debtor, which were restructured under the Corporate Debt Restructuring (CDR) Scheme in May 2005. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Account was declared NPA on February 28, 2002; SARFAESI demand notice dated November 7, 2011 claimed a default amount of Rs. 49,78,54,187.32. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Demand notice under SARFAESI Section 13(2) issued on November 7, 2011; possession taken under SARFAESI Section 13(4) on October 3, 2012; BIFR reference registered in 2004, declared sick on April 25, 2006, and reference dismissed on May 4, 2016. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Unsigned extracts of balance sheets for FY 2015-16 and 2016-17, assignment deeds dated March 31, 2010 and September 22, 2011. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Section 7 IBC application filed on October 1, 2018; dismissed by NCLT Chandigarh Bench on March 3, 2020 (CA No. 882/2019 in CP (IB) No. 347/Chd/Pb/2018) as barred by limitation.
legal_issues: Whether the application under Section 7 of the IBC is barred by limitation and whether the period during BIFR reference under SICA or unauthenticated balance sheet entries extend the limitation period under Section 18 of the Limitation Act, 1963.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An application under Section 7 of the IBC is governed by Article 137 of the Limitation Act, 1963 and must be filed within three years from the date of default unless a valid acknowledgment of debt in writing signed by the debtor extends the limitation prior to its expiry. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 22(5) of SICA cannot exclude time for limitation if the 3-year limitation period had already expired prior to the BIFR reference or if the reference stood abated under Section 41 of SARFAESI Act due to Section 13(4) actions. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: An acknowledgment under Section 18 of the Limitation Act or Section 25(3) of the Indian Contract Act requires a written and duly signed statement; unauthenticated and unsigned balance sheet extracts fail to satisfy this standard. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Right to sue accrued on the date of NPA (28.02.2002), and in the absence of valid acknowledgment or applicable SICA exclusion, the Section 7 petition filed in 2018 was barred by limitation.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 556 of 2020 is dismissed. Impugned Order dated March 3, 2020 passed by NCLT Chandigarh Bench is upheld. No order as to costs.
summary: M/s. Invent Assets Securitisation & Reconstruction Pvt. Ltd. appealed an NCLT Chandigarh order dismissing its Section 7 IBC petition against M/s. Girnar Fibres Ltd. as time-barred. The Corporate Debtor's account was declared NPA in February 2002. The Appellant sought exclusion of time under SICA BIFR references and Section 18 of the Limitation Act based on balance sheet entries. The NCLAT held that the limitation period expired three years post-NPA. SICA exclusions were inapplicable as SARFAESI possession in 2012 abated the reference, and unsigned balance sheet extracts failed to constitute valid acknowledgments. The NCLAT affirmed the dismissal of the appeal.

case_title: Nakul Bharana Erstwhile Director Of Dehradun Highway Projects Limited vs. Anil Kohli Appointed IRP For The Corporate Debtor & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Financial Creditor is ICICI Bank Ltd; Corporate Debtor is Dehradun Highway Projects Limited (DHPL), a subsidiary of Era Infra Engineering Limited; Appellant is Nakul Bharana, Ex-Director. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: ICICI Bank granted a term loan of Rs. 2,700 million and an external commercial borrowing of USD 60 million for a BOT annuity project on NH-58 and NH-72. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default amounted to INR 493.43 Crore as of November 30, 2018, later updated to Rs. 565.47 Crore as of February 27, 2020; NPA declared on September 30, 2016. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Demand notice issued on March 27, 2017; Notice of Acceleration issued on December 7, 2018. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Acknowledgment of debt in the Corporate Debtor's 2018 Balance Sheet, Tripartite Agreement dated April 26, 2018, and the Corporate Debtor's own Section 10 filing admitting default. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Section 7 petition CP(IB) 725(ND)/2020 was admitted by NCLT New Delhi Bench-V on September 18, 2020; Appellant appealed seeking to consolidate the CIRP with the parent company's CIRP.
legal_issues: Whether the NCLT's order admitting the Section 7 petition against the subsidiary Corporate Debtor should be set aside on the grounds of a pending group consolidation application, and whether the Financial Creditor's withdrawal of its claim from the parent company's CIRP precludes it from initiating independent insolvency proceedings against the subsidiary.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The pendency of an application for consolidating the CIRP of a subsidiary with its parent company does not bar the Adjudicating Authority from admitting a validly instituted Section 7 application against the subsidiary, nor does a creditor's withdrawal of a claim from the parent's CIRP preclude independent action against the subsidiary. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 18 of the Limitation Act applies to IBC proceedings, establishing that balance sheet entries validly extend the limitation period; Section 65 of the IBC requires explicit proof of fraudulent or malicious intent to annul proceedings, which cannot be presumed merely from a creditor pursuing independent remedies. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The establishment of debt and default via financial statements and parallel admissions (such as filing under Section 10) conclusively satisfies the threshold for admission under Section 7. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Because debt and default were independently established and not barred by limitation, the Section 7 admission was valid and unaffected by the parent company's consolidation proceedings.
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed, and the NCLT's impugned order dated September 18, 2020, is upheld. Any interim order stands vacated, with no order as to costs.
summary: Nakul Bharana, ex-director of Dehradun Highway Projects Ltd, appealed against the NCLT's admission of ICICI Bank's Section 7 insolvency petition. The appellant argued for consolidating the CIRP with its parent company, Era Infra Engineering Ltd, and accused the bank of malicious double-claiming. The NCLAT upheld the admission, observing that the debt and default were undisputed and acknowledged in the corporate debtor's balance sheets and its own Section 10 application. The Tribunal ruled that withdrawing a claim from a parent company's CIRP does not prevent a creditor from initiating independent proceedings against the subsidiary, thereby dismissing the appeal.

case_title: Rajmee Power Construction Limited vs. M/s. Jharkhand Urja Sancharan Nigam Limited
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Operational Creditor (Appellant) is Rajmee Power Construction Limited; Corporate Debtor (Respondent) is M/s. Jharkhand Urja Sancharan Nigam Limited. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: The transaction arises from an Arbitral Award passed in favor of the Appellant on February 14, 2008, which was initially implemented by the Corporate Debtor's predecessor, JSEB. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: An uncommunicated deduction of Rs. 11 Crores was made from the Appellant's dues, leading to a short payment where only Rs. 2,47,16,999 was paid, and the default knowledge accrued on August 6, 2016. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Arbitral Award dated February 14, 2008; part payment cheque dated March 31, 2016; RTI knowledge received on August 6, 2016; challenge to Arbitral Award dismissed on October 6, 2018; Section 8 demand notice sent on May 7, 2019. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: RTI reply dated August 6, 2016, exposing internal board notings to deduct Rs. 11 Crores, and a part payment cheque dated March 31, 2016. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Section 9 application filed on June 4, 2019, was dismissed by NCLT Kolkata Bench on March 18, 2020, solely on the ground of being barred by limitation.
legal_issues: Whether the Section 9 application filed on June 4, 2019, was barred by limitation considering the original arbitral award was from 2008, but knowledge of the short payment deduction was obtained in 2016 and the challenge to the award was dismissed in 2018.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The limitation period for filing an insolvency application is extended by the date of actual knowledge of a concealed default, the date of part payment under Section 19 of the Limitation Act, or the final dismissal of a challenge to an underlying arbitral award. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Article 137 of the Limitation Act triggers the right to sue from the date of default, which shifts forward upon part payment (Section 19) or when a fresh cause of action arises after a recovery certificate or dismissal of an award challenge. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Internal, uncommunicated board decisions regarding deductions do not trigger the limitation clock; the trigger occurs when the creditor officially discovers the deduction (e.g., via RTI) and receives the adjusted payment. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The part payment on March 31, 2016, the knowledge acquired on August 6, 2016, and the award challenge dismissal on October 6, 2018, provided a fresh cause of action, rendering the 2019 Section 9 application within the three-year limitation period.
operative_order: The appeal is allowed, the NCLT Kolkata's impugned order is set aside, and the Adjudicating Authority is directed to proceed in accordance with law.
summary: Rajmee Power Construction Limited appealed the NCLT Kolkata's dismissal of its Section 9 IBC petition against Jharkhand Urja Sancharan Nigam Limited as time-barred. The dispute stemmed from a 2008 arbitral award. The debtor made a part payment in 2016 after internal, uncommunicated deductions, which the appellant discovered via RTI in August 2016. The NCLAT held that the limitation period was renewed by the 2016 part payment, the discovery of the default, and the 2018 dismissal of the debtor's challenge to the arbitral award. Consequently, the 2019 petition was filed within the limitation period, and the appeal was allowed.

case_title: CFM Asset Reconstruction Pvt Ltd vs Vishram Narayan Panchpor Resolution Professional
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Financial Creditor (Assignor) is Janata Sahakari Bank Ltd. Financial Creditor (Assignee/Appellant) is CFM Asset Reconstruction Pvt Ltd. Corporate Debtor is Oaisis Alcohol Ltd. Resolution Professional is Vishram Narayan Panchpor. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: The original loan and underlying security interest were assigned by the original Financial Creditor to the Appellant via a Deed of Assignment. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: The specific default amount and date of default are not detailed, as the dispute revolves around CIRP withdrawal procedures. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP was admitted on 04.08.2020. The Assignment Deed was executed on 21.08.2020. The Assignee submitted withdrawal intention on 25.08.2020. The RP constituted the CoC on 27.08.2020. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The Appellant produced the Assignment Deed dated 21.08.2020, Form FA for withdrawal, and a Demand Draft of Rs. 3 Lakhs towards estimated CIRP costs submitted before the CoC constitution. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Mumbai admitted the Section 7 petition on 04.08.2020. The Appellant filed IA 1198/2020 for withdrawal, which NCLT dismissed on 16.12.2020, stating the RP never filed the withdrawal application and the CoC was already constituted.
legal_issues: Whether an assignee of a Financial Creditor qualifies as an 'Applicant' entitled to file a withdrawal application under Regulation 30A(1)(a) before the constitution of the Committee of Creditors, and whether the RP can reject such application to constitute the CoC.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An assignee of a financial creditor steps into the shoes of the assignor and is legally recognized as an 'Applicant' competent to seek withdrawal of the CIRP prior to the constitution of the Committee of Creditors. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 5(7) of the IBC includes a person to whom a debt is legally assigned as a 'Financial Creditor'. Consequently, under CIRP Regulation 30A(1)(a) and Section 12A, the assignee has the right to withdraw the application. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal found that the assignee timely submitted Form FA and the requisite CIRP costs before the mandatory deadline for CoC formation, proving the RP thwarted the pre-CoC withdrawal process. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The bench concluded that the Adjudicating Authority erred in rejecting the withdrawal application, as the assignee was well within its rights to invoke Regulation 30A(1)(a) before the CoC was formed.
operative_order: The NCLAT allowed the appeal, set aside the impugned NCLT Mumbai order dated 16.12.2020, and directed the Adjudicating Authority to restore IA No. 1198/2020 to its file to pass fresh orders on merits.
summary: CFM Asset Reconstruction Pvt Ltd (Assignee) appealed against an NCLT Mumbai order that dismissed its application to withdraw the CIRP against Oaisis Alcohol Ltd. The Appellant had acquired the debt from the original applicant and submitted Form FA for withdrawal before the Committee of Creditors (CoC) was constituted. The Resolution Professional unlawfully rejected the form and formed the CoC. The NCLAT held that an assignee is a valid 'Applicant' under the IBC and is entitled to seek a pre-CoC withdrawal under Regulation 30A(1)(a). Consequently, the NCLAT set aside the NCLT's order and remanded the matter for fresh adjudication.

case_title: Vishnoo Mittal & Anr Suspended Board Of Director/Shareholder/Resolution Applicant of M/s Xalta Food and Beverages Pvt Ltd vs. Mr Naveen Kumar Jain Resolution Professional
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellants are Vishnoo Mittal and Heavent Malhotra, the Suspended Board of Directors of Corporate Debtor M/s Xalta Food and Beverages Pvt Ltd; Respondent is Naveen Kumar Jain, the Resolution Professional. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process (CIRP) where no resolution plan was initially approved within the statutory 270 days. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: N/A; the dispute centers on procedural irregularities during the CIRP and liquidation initiation rather than initial debt default amounts. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Initial ex-parte liquidation order passed on June 14, 2019; deferred on July 4, 2019; impugned NCLT order passed on June 11, 2021. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Orders dated June 14, 2019, and July 4, 2019, demonstrating the Adjudicating Authority's contradictory directions regarding the continuation of liquidation versus hearing pending applications. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: IA No. 2034/2021 was dismissed by NCLT New Delhi Bench II on June 11, 2021, and the Appellants filed an appeal arguing the NCLT impermissibly reviewed its own July 4, 2019 order.
legal_issues: Whether the Adjudicating Authority (NCLT) possesses the inherent power to review its own previous orders under the IBC, and whether it exceeded its jurisdiction by effectively reviewing its July 4, 2019 order.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An Adjudicating Authority under the IBC does not have the inherent power to review its own orders; it only possesses the statutory power to rectify mistakes apparent from the record or recall ex-parte orders. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 420(2) of the Companies Act, 2013 and Rule 154 of the NCLT Rules allow for the rectification of clerical or arithmetical mistakes but do not confer substantive review jurisdiction. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal found that the NCLT's July 4, 2019 order explicitly deferred liquidation pending the disposal of other applications, meaning the June 11, 2021 order substantively altered this without proper jurisdiction. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLT's impugned order was passed without jurisdiction as it amounted to an impermissible review of its prior procedural directions.
operative_order: The appeal is allowed, and the impugned order dated June 11, 2021, is set aside. The NCLT New Delhi II is directed to restore IA No. 2034/2021 and pass fresh orders on merits.
summary: The Appellants, suspended directors of M/s Xalta Food and Beverages Pvt Ltd, challenged an NCLT order that dismissed their IA and effectively reviewed a prior procedural order deferring the company's liquidation. The NCLT had originally passed an ex-parte liquidation order but later deferred it pending the resolution of other applications. The NCLAT ruled that the NCLT lacks the inherent power to review its own orders under the IBC and the Companies Act, 2013. Consequently, the NCLAT allowed the appeal, set aside the NCLT's impugned order for lacking jurisdiction, and remanded the matter for fresh determination on the merits.

case_title: Thupili Raveendra Babu vs The Competition Commission Of India & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant/Informant is Thupili Raveendra Babu; the Respondents are the Competition Commission of India (CCI), the Bar Council of India (BCI), and various officials of the BCI. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: This dispute does not involve a commercial transaction; rather, it challenges Clause 28 of the BCI's Rules of Legal Education, 2008, which caps the maximum age for admission into legal education at 30 years for general candidates. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Not applicable, as this is a Competition Act dispute concerning age restrictions for legal education, not a financial or operational debt default. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The Appellant appeared for the APLAWCET entrance examination on 01.10.2020; the CCI passed its impugned order dismissing the information on 20.01.2021. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The primary basis of the dispute was Clause 28 of Schedule III, Rule 11 to Part IV of the BCI Rules, which the Appellant alleged was an abuse of dominant position creating indirect barriers to entry into the legal profession. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The Appellant filed information before the CCI under Section 4 of the Competition Act; the CCI closed the case on 20.01.2021 under Section 26(2) stating BCI is not an 'enterprise', which led to the present appeal under Section 53-B before the NCLAT.
legal_issues: Whether the Bar Council of India (BCI) qualifies as an 'enterprise' under Section 2(h) of the Competition Act, 2002, thereby making it subject to scrutiny for alleged abuse of dominant position under Section 4 of the Act regarding its rules on legal education.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A statutory body discharging purely regulatory and standard-setting functions, devoid of any economic or commercial activity, does not fall within the definition of an 'enterprise' under competition law. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: The Tribunal interpreted Section 2(h) of the Competition Act, 2002, concluding that the term 'activity' necessarily implies operations of an economic and commercial character. It simultaneously interpreted Sections 7(1) and 49 of the Advocates Act, 1961, recognizing that the BCI's mandate to prescribe legal education standards is strictly a regulatory function. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal evaluated the nature of the BCI's activities (setting age limits and educational standards) and found that they do not involve the production, distribution, or provision of commercial goods or services. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT conclusively held that the BCI is not an 'enterprise' under Section 2(h) of the Competition Act, 2002; consequently, Section 4 (abuse of dominant position) cannot be attracted, and the CCI correctly dismissed the case.
operative_order: The NCLAT dismissed the Competition Appeal (AT) No. 09 of 2021 with no orders as to costs, upholding the CCI's decision that no prima facie case existed.
summary: Thupili Raveendra Babu challenged the Bar Council of India's (BCI) rule restricting the maximum age for legal education to 30 years, alleging an abuse of dominant position under Section 4 of the Competition Act, 2002. The Competition Commission of India (CCI) dismissed the information, leading to an appeal before the NCLAT. The NCLAT analyzed whether BCI constitutes an 'enterprise' under Section 2(h) of the Act. The Tribunal upheld the CCI's ruling, clarifying that BCI acts as a statutory regulatory body governing legal education standards under the Advocates Act, 1961, and does not engage in economic or commercial activities. Therefore, BCI is not an 'enterprise', and the appeal was dismissed.

case_title: L. Ramalakshmamma & L. Madhusudan Rao vs State Bank of India
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Financial Creditor is State Bank of India (SBI); the Personal Guarantors (Debtors/Appellants) are L. Ramalakshmamma and L. Madhusudan Rao; the Corporate Debtor is Lanco Infratech Ltd. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: SBI initiated insolvency proceedings against the Appellants as personal guarantors for defaults by Lanco Infratech Ltd, which went into liquidation on August 27, 2018. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Proceedings were initiated under Section 95 of the IBC in 2021 following the earlier CIRP/liquidation of the Corporate Debtor; specific debt amounts are unstated. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The Adjudicating Authority (NCLT Hyderabad) passed impugned orders appointing an IRP on July 23, 2021. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The Adjudicating Authority selected Mr. Anil Kohli as IRP from an IBBI panel without waiting for a specific, separate confirmation from IBBI regarding disciplinary proceedings. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: SBI filed Section 95 applications against the Appellants; the NCLT appointed Mr. Anil Kohli as IRP on July 23, 2021; the Appellants appealed, claiming a violation of mandatory pre-conditions under Section 97(1) and 97(2).
legal_issues: Whether the provisions of Sections 97(1) and 97(2) of the IBC, requiring the Adjudicating Authority to seek IBBI confirmation regarding pending disciplinary proceedings before appointing a Resolution Professional, are mandatory or directory.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The use of the word 'shall' in a statute is not always mandatory and must be interpreted based on the object, purpose, and practical implementation of the provision. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: The word 'shall' in Section 97(1) of the IBC is directory, not mandatory, when read in conjunction with Rule 8(1) of the 2019 Personal Guarantors Rules, which allows the NCLT to pick an IRP directly from a pre-approved panel shared by IBBI. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: If the Adjudicating Authority appoints an IRP from the pre-approved IBBI database/panel, the legislative intent of ensuring a qualified, discipline-free professional is satisfied without requiring a fresh, time-consuming individual confirmation. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Adjudicating Authority validly exercised its judicial discretion by appointing the IRP directly from the IBBI panel, and non-compliance with the strict sequential confirmation process of Sections 97(1) and 97(2) does not vitiate the appointment.
operative_order: The appeals (Company Appeal (AT) (CH) (Insolvency) Nos. 220 & 221 of 2021) are dismissed with no costs, upholding the NCLT's appointment of the IRP.
summary: The Appellants, personal guarantors to Lanco Infratech Ltd, challenged the NCLT's appointment of an Interim Resolution Professional (IRP) in insolvency proceedings initiated by State Bank of India. They argued that the NCLT violated Sections 97(1) and 97(2) of the IBC by not explicitly seeking IBBI confirmation regarding disciplinary proceedings before the appointment. The NCLAT held that the word 'shall' in Section 97(1) is directory, not mandatory, and that the NCLT can validly appoint an IRP from a pre-approved IBBI panel to ensure time-bound processes. Consequently, the appeals were dismissed.

case_title: Mr. S. Rajendran vs Committee of Creditors of M/s. Vasan Healthcare Pvt. Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant is Mr. S. Rajendran, the Resolution Professional of the Corporate Debtor, M/s. Vasan Health Care Pvt. Ltd., and the Respondent is the Committee of Creditors. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: The Corporate Debtor is engaged in the Healthcare Industry, operating eye-care hospitals and centers across several Southern States. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: The specific default amount and date of default are not detailed, as the appeal solely addresses the extension of the CIRP timeline. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The CIRP was initiated on 21.04.2017, stayed by the Madras High Court on 04.05.2017, and revived on 03.10.2019. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Following a second round of Expression of Interest, 7 prospective Resolution Applicants were shortlisted, and the Corporate Debtor was gradually reviving, generating a monthly revenue of Rs. 20 Crore. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The RP filed IA/510/CHE/2021 seeking an extension of the CIRP period to 30.11.2021, but the NCLT Chennai, via an order dated 03.08.2021, extended it only up to 22.08.2021, prompting this appeal.
legal_issues: Whether exceptional circumstances exist to justify extending the timeline for completing the Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process (CIRP) beyond the statutory limit of 330 days, thereby preventing the liquidation of the Corporate Debtor.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The statutory outer limit of 330 days for completing a Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process is not strictly mandatory and can be extended in exceptional circumstances to avoid pushing the corporate debtor into liquidation. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Relying on the Supreme Court's ruling in Essar Steel, the word 'mandatorily' in Section 12(3) of the IBC is struck down, granting tribunals the discretion to extend the timeline beyond 330 days. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal evaluated the disruptions caused by nationwide COVID-19 lockdowns, ongoing judicial proceedings, and the active participation of seven shortlisted resolution applicants, determining these constituted 'exceptional circumstances'. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The bench concluded that to adhere to the IBC's primary objective of maximizing asset value and ensuring liquidation remains a last resort, extending the CIRP period was legally justified and necessary.
operative_order: The NCLAT allowed the appeal, set aside the Adjudicating Authority's order dated 03.08.2021, extended the CIRP period till 30.11.2021, and excluded the time spent filing the appeals (18.08.2021 to 25.11.2021).
summary: Mr. S. Rajendran, the Resolution Professional for M/s. Vasan Health Care Pvt. Ltd., appealed an NCLT Chennai order that restricted the CIRP extension to August 22, 2021. The RP sought an extension until November 30, 2021, citing delays from COVID-19 lockdowns, litigation, and the evaluation of seven prospective resolution plans. The NCLAT examined whether the CIRP timeline could be extended beyond the 330-day statutory limit. Relying on Supreme Court precedents like Swiss Ribbons and Essar Steel, the NCLAT emphasized that the 330-day limit is not strictly mandatory in exceptional cases and that liquidation must be a last resort. Finding exceptional circumstances, the Tribunal allowed the appeal and extended the CIRP period to maximize the corporate debtor's value.

case_title: Manoj Kumar Agarwal vs M/s. Mehndipur Balaji Infra Developers Pvt. Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Financial Creditor (Appellant) is Manoj Kumar Agarwal, a Promoter/Director; Corporate Debtor (Respondent) is M/s. Mehndipur Balaji Infra Developers Pvt. Ltd. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: The Appellant, along with other promoters, infused funds amounting to Rs.4,69,66,293/- between September 2014 and April 2016 to purchase real estate property in Kanpur/Lucknow for business development, without any written loan agreement. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: The Appellant claimed a default of Rs.4,69,66,293/-, but there was no fixed date of repayment or evidence of when the amount actually became due and payable. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: A Demand Notice was issued by the Appellant on January 4, 2018, and a Settlement Agreement was allegedly made on February 6, 2019. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The claim was supported by a Balance Sheet as on March 31, 2016, showing accumulated loan in the books, and the Demand Notice dated January 4, 2018, but lacked a written loan agreement fixing repayment dates. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The Section 7 petition was filed and subsequently rejected by the NCLT Allahabad Bench on April 5, 2018, due to the Appellant's inability to justify the existence of default and the lack of a fixed repayment date.
legal_issues: Whether an unsecured loan infused by a promoter without a written agreement and a fixed date of repayment can constitute a default under Section 7 of the IBC upon the mere issuance of a demand notice, or if the conflict merely amounts to an internal dispute of oppression and mismanagement.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The mere issuance of a demand notice for internal funds infused by a promoter without a fixed repayment timeline does not automatically trigger a default for initiating CIRP; internal shareholder disputes must be resolved under the Companies Act rather than the IBC. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 7 of the IBC requires clear substantiation of the existence of default and a specific date when the debt became due and payable, which cannot be unilaterally fabricated by a demand notice when the original understanding lacked a repayment date. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: To establish default under Section 7, there must be concrete evidence proving when the debt became due and payable; in the absence of a written agreement or fixed term, balance sheet entries alone do not satisfy the criteria for a defaulted debt. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Because the Appellant failed to substantiate the existence of a default and a due date for repayment, the debt was not due and payable, rendering the Section 7 application unmaintainable as an apparent misuse of the IBC for internal disputes.
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed, the impugned order of the Adjudicating Authority is upheld, and any interim order stands vacated with no order as to costs.
summary: Manoj Kumar Agarwal, a promoter and director, filed a Section 7 IBC petition against M/s. Mehndipur Balaji Infra Developers Pvt. Ltd., claiming default on an unsecured loan of Rs.4.69 Crores. The NCLT Allahabad rejected the petition, finding no fixed repayment date or evidence of default. The NCLAT upheld the rejection, noting that the funds were infused by promoters for real estate development without a repayment agreement. The Tribunal ruled that a unilateral demand notice cannot establish default, classifying the conflict as an internal dispute concerning oppression and mismanagement under the Companies Act, thus dismissing the appeal.

case_title: Bimalesh Bhardwaj & Ors vs Value Infratech Private Limited & Ors
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellants are homebuyers in the 'SKYWALK RNE' project; Respondents include the Corporate Debtor (Value Infratech India Pvt Ltd), sister companies (Value Infracon, Value Infrabuild), and Capri Global Capital Ltd (Financial Creditor). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Capri Global sanctioned a common loan of Rs. 37.50 crores to the three sister companies on 17.09.2014, out of which Rs. 6.65 crores was specifically disbursed to the Corporate Debtor. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: The Resolution Professional (RP) accepted an aggregated claim of Rs. 149.09 crores from Capri Global encompassing all three sister entities rather than isolating the Corporate Debtor's actual debt. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP was initiated on 03.01.2020, and the CoC hastily decided on liquidation on 12.12.2020. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The RP assigned a 96.77% voting share to Capri Global based on the aggregated loan amount, suppressing the homebuyers' vote share to a mere 3.23%. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT New Delhi passed a liquidation order on 04.01.2021; the homebuyers appealed against the fraudulent constitution of the CoC and the hasty liquidation decision.
legal_issues: Whether the Committee of Creditors (CoC) was validly constituted by clubbing loan claims across multiple companies, and whether the subsequent decision to liquidate the Corporate Debtor violated IBC provisions.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A financial creditor's voting share in a specific Corporate Debtor's CoC must be strictly proportionate to the debt actually disbursed to and owed by that specific Corporate Debtor, even if a common loan agreement exists among multiple co-borrowers. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Under Sections 25 and 29 of the IBC, the Resolution Professional is statutorily bound to prepare an accurate Information Memorandum to facilitate resolution; bypassing this to rush into liquidation vitiates the entire process. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Relying on a prior NCLAT finding, the Tribunal held that disbursal to the Corporate Debtor was limited to Rs. 6.65 crores, rendering the 96.77% vote share allocation (based on Rs. 149.09 crores) legally unsustainable. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The constitution of the CoC was quashed for being improperly and maliciously weighted in favor of one creditor, rendering the liquidation resolution null and void.
operative_order: The NCLAT quashed the constitution of the CoC, remanded the matter to the Adjudicating Authority, directed the immediate replacement of the Resolution Professional, and recommended an investigation into the RP's conduct by the IBBI.
summary: Homebuyers of Value Infratech India Pvt. Ltd. appealed an NCLT order directing the corporate debtor's liquidation. They alleged the Resolution Professional improperly clubbed a financial creditor's (Capri Global) claims across three sister companies, unfairly inflating its CoC voting share to 96.77%. The NCLAT found that Capri Global's claim against the corporate debtor must be strictly limited to the Rs. 6.65 crores actually disbursed to it. Consequently, the CoC was illegally constituted, rendering the hasty liquidation decision invalid. The Tribunal quashed the CoC's constitution, ordered the RP's replacement, and remanded the case.

case_title: Pioneer Engineered Facility Management Services Pvt. Ltd. vs. Medeor Hospital Limited
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Operational Creditor (Appellant) is Pioneer Engineered Facility Management Services Pvt. Ltd.; Corporate Debtor (Respondent) is Medeor Hospital Limited (Previously VPS Rockland Hospital Ltd.). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Agreements dated September 1, 2016, and October 18, 2016, for providing general duty assessment and housekeeping services to the Corporate Debtor's hospital units. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Claimed outstanding dues of Rs. 1,44,27,230/- for the period from October 1, 2018, to May 31, 2019. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Demand notice sent on May 17, 2019; acknowledged by Respondent via email on June 8, 2019. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Correspondence/emails showing pre-existing disputes over service deficiencies, non-submission of labor law compliance documents, inflated invoices, and direct payment of Rs. 18,00,595/- by the Respondent to the Appellant's striking employees. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT New Delhi dismissed the Section 9 application (CP (IB) No. 1759/ND/2019) on March 3, 2020, citing pre-existing disputes.
legal_issues: Whether the NCLT correctly dismissed the Section 9 IBC application on the grounds of a pre-existing dispute regarding service deficiencies and labor law non-compliance, despite the Corporate Debtor deducting TDS on the raised invoices.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Under the IBC, an operational creditor's insolvency application must be rejected if the corporate debtor establishes the existence of a genuine, pre-existing dispute prior to the demand notice. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 9(5)(ii)(d) mandates rejection when a dispute is evidenced; mere deduction of TDS under the Income Tax Act does not constitute an absolute acknowledgment of debt overriding a documented dispute. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Applying the Mobilox Innovations standard, the adjudicating authority only needs to find a plausible dispute that is not spurious, hypothetical, or illusory, without examining the merits of whether the defense will succeed. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Evidentiary emails proving service shortages, labor strikes, and the corporate debtor's forced direct payment of wages established a clear pre-existing dispute, rendering the Section 9 application unmaintainable.
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed, upholding the Adjudicating Authority's order. No order as to costs.
summary: Pioneer Engineered Facility Management Services Pvt. Ltd. appealed the NCLT New Delhi's dismissal of its Section 9 IBC application against Medeor Hospital Limited. The Appellant claimed Rs. 1.44 Crores in unpaid dues for housekeeping services. The NCLAT affirmed the dismissal, finding clear evidence of a pre-existing dispute regarding service deficiencies, non-compliance with labor laws, and instances where the hospital had to directly pay striking staff. Applying the Mobilox standard, the Tribunal concluded that such genuine pre-existing disputes preclude the initiation of CIRP.

case_title: M/S Emaar Hills Township Private Limited vs. Mr. Srinivas Manthena & Mrs. Padmaja Manthena
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Financial Creditors/Allottees are Mr. Srinivas Manthena and Mrs. Padmaja Manthena; the Corporate Debtor (Appellant) is M/s Emaar Hills Township Private Limited. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: The Appellant was developing a township spanning 285 acres at Manikonda Village, Hyderabad, for which the Respondents were real estate allottees. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: The specific default amount is unstated; the core dispute centers on the procedural validity and maintainability of the Section 7 petition. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The NCLT reserved orders on March 4, 2021, and passed the impugned clubbing order on June 18, 2021. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The Respondents and other allottees attempted to club their individual Section 7 applications by filing affidavits instead of formally modifying their petitions to meet the newly amended minimum threshold of 100 allottees or 10%. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Hyderabad directed its registry to club the pending single-allottee applications on June 18, 2021; the Corporate Debtor appealed, arguing this violated the 3rd Proviso to Section 7 of the amended IBC.
legal_issues: Whether pending individual Section 7 applications filed by real estate allottees prior to the 2020 IBC amendment can be clubbed together via affidavits to meet the minimum threshold, or if they must be formally modified and jointly filed to satisfy the statutory requirements.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Single allottee applications filed prior to the IBC amendment cannot merely be clubbed together by the registry; they must be formally modified to comply with the threshold of 100 allottees or 10%. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: The 3rd Proviso to Section 7 of the IBC explicitly requires pending non-admitted applications to be modified to conform to the new threshold within 30 days, failing which they are deemed withdrawn. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Filing a mere affidavit requesting the clubbing of petitions does not satisfy the statutory requirement of filing a modified 'joint' application under Rule 4(1) of the Adjudicating Authority Rules. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Adjudicating Authority erred in passing a blanket order to club the pending applications without directing the allottees to amend their applications to meet the strict threshold requirements of the amended Section 7.
operative_order: The appeal is allowed, and the impugned order dated June 18, 2021, is set aside. The matter is remitted back to the Adjudicating Authority for passing de novo orders on maintainability in accordance with the law.
summary: Emaar Hills Township Pvt Ltd appealed an NCLT Hyderabad order that allowed the clubbing of individual Section 7 insolvency applications filed by real estate allottees. The NCLAT held that under the amended Section 7 of the IBC and the Supreme Court's ruling in Manish Kumar vs. Union of India, pending single-allottee petitions cannot be merely clubbed by the registry via affidavits. Allottees must formally modify their applications to meet the joint threshold of 100 allottees or 10%. The NCLAT allowed the appeal, set aside the clubbing order, and remanded the matter for fresh consideration on maintainability.

case_title: Medsynaptic Private Limited And Ors vs. Dr. Prashant K Lahane
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellants are Medsynaptic Pvt. Ltd., Dr. Ashish Prakash Dhawad, Mr. Sanjay Sukhdeaorao Gorde, and Mrs. Preeti Dhawad; Respondent is Dr. Prashant K Lahane, a 40% shareholder and founder director. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Incorporation of Medsynaptic Private Limited on August 27, 2003, structured on a quasi-partnership basis with a 60:40 shareholding and management split between Appellant No. 2 and the Respondent. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: N/A; dispute arises from internal management deadlocks, removal of the Respondent as a director via an EOGM on May 31, 2021, and challenges to board meeting resolutions. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Board meetings held on March 12, March 31, May 6, and May 31, 2021; EOGM held on May 31, 2021; Company Petition filed on June 9, 2021; NCLT interim order passed on July 19, 2021. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Articles of Association (Articles 25 and 26) designating Appellant No. 2 and the Respondent as non-retiring 'First Directors' holding office until resignation, death, incapacitation, or disqualification. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Mumbai Bench-IV issued an interim stay on July 19, 2021, staying the EOGM resolution removing the Respondent and staying board resolutions from March and May 2021, prompting the Appellants to appeal.
legal_issues: Whether the NCLT erred in granting an interim stay on the implementation of board and EOGM resolutions regarding the removal of a founder director whose office is protected under the Articles of Association as a 'First Director'.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An appellate tribunal will not interfere with a discretionary interim order passed by an adjudicating authority to preserve the status quo and protect the rights of parties pending final adjudication of a company petition under Sections 241-242. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Articles of Association provisions designating 'First Directors' who are not liable to retire except under specific conditions create a prima facie case against arbitrary removal during a corporate dispute. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Where a prima facie case of quasi-partnership disruption and ultra vires removal of a founder director is established, the balance of convenience warrants maintaining interim protection until the main petition is heard on merits. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLT committed no illegality in granting interim stays on the removal resolutions, as complex legal questions regarding whether statutory provisions override the Articles of Association must be decided during the final hearing of the main petition.
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed, and the interim order dated July 19, 2021, passed by the NCLT Mumbai Bench-IV is affirmed, with a request to the NCLT to expedite the main company petition.
summary: Medsynaptic Pvt. Ltd. and its other directors appealed an interim order by NCLT Mumbai that stayed the EOGM resolution removing Dr. Prashant K Lahane as director and halted several board resolutions. The NCLAT held that the NCLT committed no error or illegality, noting that the Respondent, as a founder and 'First Director' under the Articles of Association, had made a strong prima facie case regarding his protected tenure. Finding that deep contentions regarding statutory override over the Articles should be resolved during the final adjudication of the main oppression and mismanagement petition, the NCLAT dismissed the appeal.

case_title: Drip Capital Inc vs Concord Creations (India) Pvt. Ltd
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant/Financial Creditor is Drip Capital Inc., and the Respondent/Corporate Debtor is Concord Creations (India) Pvt. Ltd. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: The transaction was an export finance facility based on a Receivables Purchase Factoring Agreement (RPA) dated 12.12.2018, an Irrevocable Undertaking for Recourse, and a Demand Promissory Note. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: The Financial Creditor paid USD 36,532 to the Corporate Debtor for assigned invoices. Upon dispute by the buyer, the default amount claimed as of 30.11.2019 was USD 38,213.38 (approx. INR 27,39,899.33), with the initial default date being 17.10.2019. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The buyer disputed the invoices on 12.09.2019, and the Financial Creditor issued a Demand Notice on 14.10.2019. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The Financial Creditor submitted the RPA, the Undertaking, the Promissory Note, the buyer's dispute email, and the Demand Notice. The Corporate Debtor did not file a reply or objections before the NCLT. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The NCLT Bengaluru disposed of CP No. (IB) 61/BB/2020 on 28.05.2021 by giving the Corporate Debtor six months to pay, reasoning it was a solvent company. The Financial Creditor appealed this order.
legal_issues: Whether the Adjudicating Authority has the jurisdiction under Section 7 of the IBC to evaluate the financial health or solvency of a Corporate Debtor and defer the initiation of CIRP when the existence of a financial debt and its default are established and undisputed.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Under Section 7 of the IBC, the Adjudicating Authority's jurisdiction is limited to verifying the existence of a default and the completeness of the application; it cannot evaluate the solvency of the corporate debtor to defer or reject CIRP initiation. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 5(8)(e) explicitly includes receivables sold on a with-recourse basis within the definition of 'financial debt'. The Adjudicating Authority is not a recovery forum and must admit the application upon subjective satisfaction of default, as held in Innoventive Industries. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal noted that the documentary evidence (RPA, Undertaking, Demand Note) proved the debt and default, and the Corporate Debtor offered no defense. The NCLT erred by suo motu assessing the debtor's balance sheet to establish solvency. 4.
