DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT concluded that the NCLT exceeded its jurisdiction by granting the Corporate Debtor six months to repay based on its perceived financial health, thereby acting contrary to the mandate of Section 7 of the IBC.
operative_order: The NCLAT allowed the appeal, set aside the NCLT Bengaluru's order dated 28.05.2021, and directed the Adjudicating Authority to restore the petition to its file, admit the same, and proceed further in accordance with the law.
summary: Drip Capital Inc. appealed against an NCLT Bengaluru order that deferred the admission of its Section 7 IBC application against Concord Creations (India) Pvt. Ltd. The NCLT had granted the corporate debtor six months to repay the debt, citing that the company was active, profitable, and not 'insolvent'. The NCLAT held that under Section 7, the Adjudicating Authority only needs to ascertain the existence of debt and default; it has no jurisdiction to evaluate a company's financial health or defer CIRP based on solvency. Since the financial debt (arising from a factoring agreement with recourse) and the default were undisputed, the NCLAT set aside the NCLT's order and directed it to admit the insolvency petition.

case_title: S. Sudeep vs Dhanlakshmi Bank Ltd & Anr
appeal_number: T.A. No. 39 of 2021 / Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 427 of 2020
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant is S. Sudeep (Director of the Corporate Debtor). Respondent No. 1 is Dhanlakshmi Bank Ltd (Financial Creditor). Respondent No. 2 is Trivandrum International Health Services Ltd (Corporate Debtor). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: The Corporate Debtor availed credit facilities for a Multi-Specialties Cancer Block project, executing a Master Credit Agreement, Term Loan Agreement, and Overdraft Cash Credit on 31.03.2015. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: The total claimed default was Rs. 14,24,90,488/- with the date of default fixed as 30.06.2019 based on settlement timelines. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The account was classified as an NPA on 30.05.2016, and the Section 7 application was filed on 10.12.2019. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The Corporate Debtor submitted One Time Settlement (OTS) proposals on 06.12.2018, 12.12.2018, and 11.01.2019 (specifically offering Rs. 8.15 Crores as full and final settlement), which the Bank approved. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The NCLT Kochi Bench admitted the Section 7 application on 07.02.2020 in IBA/51/KOB/19. The Appellant challenged this admission.
legal_issues: Whether the Section 7 application was barred by limitation given the NPA date of 30.05.2016, or if the Corporate Debtor's One Time Settlement (OTS) proposals constituted a valid acknowledgment of debt extending the limitation period under Section 18 of the Limitation Act.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An offer of a One Time Settlement (OTS) made within the original limitation period constitutes a valid acknowledgment of debt in writing, triggering a fresh period of limitation under Section 18 of the Limitation Act. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 18 of the Limitation Act applies to IBC proceedings; an acknowledgment of a subsisting liability creates a new limitation period starting from the date of the acknowledgment. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal evaluated the OTS letters, specifically the one dated 11.01.2019 offering Rs. 8.15 Crores, and determined it explicitly admitted a subsisting jural relation and existing liability before the expiry of the three-year limitation period from the NPA date. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Because the OTS acknowledgment occurred within three years of the NPA date, it provided a fresh limitation period. Therefore, the Section 7 application filed on 10.12.2019 was well within legal time limits.
operative_order: The NCLAT dismissed the appeal (T.A. No. 39 of 2021 / Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 427 of 2020) without costs, thereby upholding the Adjudicating Authority's order initiating the CIRP.
summary: S. Sudeep, a Director of the Corporate Debtor, appealed the NCLT Kochi's admission of a Section 7 insolvency application filed by Dhanlakshmi Bank. The Appellant argued the petition was time-barred since the debt became a Non-Performing Asset (NPA) on 30.05.2016, and the application was filed over three years later on 10.12.2019. However, the NCLAT found that the Corporate Debtor had submitted multiple One Time Settlement (OTS) proposals, notably on 11.01.2019, explicitly acknowledging the debt. The Tribunal held that under Section 18 of the Limitation Act, this OTS proposal served as a valid written acknowledgment of a subsisting liability, triggering a fresh limitation period. Consequently, the NCLAT concluded the application was not time-barred and dismissed the appeal.

case_title: Unigold Systems vs. Fortune Spirits Limited
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Operational Creditor (Appellant) is Unigold Systems (a proprietorship concern through its Proprietor Rajesh Kumar Gupta); Corporate Debtor (Respondent) is Fortune Spirits Limited. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Supply of mono cartons and labels pursuant to purchase orders between 2015 and 2016 involving 17 invoices. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: 17 invoices totaling Rs. 36,29,968/-, with an outstanding principal sum of Rs. 33,27,709/- after part payments. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Invoices dated between May 19, 2015, and December 9, 2016; part payments made on March 16, 2017, and May 17, 2017; email acknowledgment sent on May 10, 2018; Section 8 demand notice issued on February 25, 2019; Section 9 application filed on November 18, 2019. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Ledger accounts for April 1, 2015, to March 31, 2018, showing continuous transactions and part payments, and an email dated May 10, 2018, with an appended statement of account. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Section 9 application was dismissed by the NCLT Cuttack Bench on March 2, 2021, on the ground of being barred by limitation.
legal_issues: Whether a proprietorship concern has locus standi to initiate CIRP under Section 2(f) of the IBC, and whether the Section 9 application was barred by limitation considering part payments and email acknowledgments under Sections 18 and 19 of the Limitation Act.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Proprietorship firms are explicitly covered under Section 2(f) of the IBC and possess the locus standi to initiate corporate insolvency resolution proceedings. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Sections 18 and 19 of the Limitation Act provide that part payments and written email acknowledgments of a debt made within the original limitation period extend the limitation window by computing a fresh period from the date of such payment or acknowledgment. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Continuous transactions, part payments recorded in ledger accounts, and subsequent email communications transmitting statements of account serve as valid evidence of acknowledgment and a running account. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Because part payment was made on May 17, 2017, and a written acknowledgment via email occurred on May 10, 2018, the application filed in November 2019 fell well within the extended limitation period.
operative_order: The appeal is allowed, and the NCLT Cuttack Bench's order dated March 2, 2021, is set aside, with directions to the Adjudicating Authority to proceed in accordance with law.
summary: Unigold Systems, a proprietorship concern, appealed the NCLT Cuttack's dismissal of its Section 9 IBC petition against Fortune Spirits Ltd. on limitation grounds. The NCLAT held that proprietorship firms have the locus standi to file petitions under Section 2(f) of the IBC. Furthermore, the appellate tribunal ruled that part payments made in May 2017 and a written debt acknowledgment via email in May 2018 validly extended the limitation period under Sections 18 and 19 of the Limitation Act. Consequently, the petition filed in November 2019 was within limitation, prompting the NCLAT to allow the appeal.

case_title: Jitender Arora (Resolution Professional of M/s. Premia Projects Ltd.) vs Tek Chand & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant is Jitender Arora, the Resolution Professional of the Corporate Debtor (M/s Premia Projects Ltd). Respondent No. 2 is M/s Solitaire Infomedia Pvt. Ltd., the landowning company. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: The Corporate Debtor (developer) entered into a Collaboration Agreement on 01.10.2012 with Respondent No. 2 (landowner) to develop a housing project on the latter's land, and executed Memoranda of Understanding (MoUs) with homebuyers to collect booking amounts. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: The specific default amounts are not detailed, but it involves substantial funds collected from homebuyers that were allegedly siphoned off, leaving the Corporate Debtor without tangible assets to satisfy creditors. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The Section 7 application against the Corporate Debtor was originally admitted on 30.05.2018. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Evidence showed that Tarun Sheinh was a common director who effectively controlled both the Corporate Debtor and the landowning company. The Corporate Debtor held a controlling 51% (later expanding to almost total control) share in the landowning company. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The RP filed IA No. 4132 of 2020 seeking to initiate a joint CIRP of the Corporate Debtor and its subsidiary (Respondent No. 2). The NCLT rejected this on 29.10.2020, stating there was no provision in the IBC for such relief, prompting this appeal.
legal_issues: Whether the corporate veil between a corporate debtor (developer) and its subsidiary (landowning company) can be pierced to consolidate their assets, and whether a joint Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process (CIRP) can be ordered when their businesses and assets are intricately intertwined to defraud creditors.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The corporate veil between intertwined group companies can be pierced, and substantive consolidation of CIRP can be ordered, when their assets and liabilities are comingled to execute a fraudulent scheme that deprives creditors of meaningful resolution. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Broadly interpreting 'property', 'transaction', and 'transfer' under Sections 3(27), 3(33), and 3(34) of the IBC alongside Section 29, the Tribunal held that assets intimately connected to the corporate debtor's business (like the subsidiary's land) must be included in the Information Memorandum to fulfill the IBC's objective of value maximization. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal applied a 14-point test for consolidation, finding common control, common directors, inter-lacing of finance, pooling of resources, and a fraudulent stratagem to collect funds via the developer while shielding the land asset in the subsidiary. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT concluded that to ensure a fair resolution for the defrauded homebuyers, the assets of both companies must be consolidated. However, since the subsidiary was not yet under CIRP, a formal admission application against it was necessary first.
operative_order: The NCLAT remanded the matter to the Adjudicating Authority with a direction to consider an admission application for the landowning company (Respondent No. 2) and subsequently consider a consolidation of CIRP, completing the process preferably within two months. No order as to costs was made.
summary: The Resolution Professional of M/s Premia Projects Ltd. (Corporate Debtor) appealed an NCLT order that rejected his plea for a joint CIRP involving the Corporate Debtor and its subsidiary landowning company, M/s Solitaire Infomedia Pvt. Ltd. Both companies were controlled by a common director who used a Collaboration Agreement to collect funds from homebuyers through the Corporate Debtor while keeping the project land secure under the subsidiary, later siphoning off the funds. The NCLAT held that the corporate veil must be pierced because the assets and operations of the two companies were inextricably intertwined to defraud creditors. The Tribunal ruled that substantive consolidation of their assets is necessary for a meaningful insolvency resolution and remanded the case to the NCLT to initiate CIRP against the subsidiary and proceed with a joint resolution.

case_title: Navalkumar D Bhoot vs. UCO Bank & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Financial Creditor is UCO Bank; Corporate Debtor is Narendra Solvex Pvt. Ltd.; Appellant is Navalkumar D Bhoot, a stakeholder/shareholder. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Credit facilities totaling Rs. 47,44,31,630.68/- were granted to the Corporate Debtor by UCO Bank between 2005 and 2013. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default amount claimed was Rs. 47,44,31,630.68/- as of the default date on September 30, 2014. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: SARFAESI notice under Section 13(2) issued on January 27, 2015; DRT Recovery Certificate issued on February 12, 2019; Section 7 application filed on August 26, 2019. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: DRT Recovery Certificate dated February 12, 2019, in O.A. No. 196 of 2015, and loan recall notice dated August 27, 2018. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Mumbai Bench-IV allowed UCO Bank's Section 7 application on September 16, 2021, which was challenged by the Appellant in this appeal.
legal_issues: Whether the Section 7 application was barred by limitation given that the default occurred in 2014 while the petition was filed in 2019, whether the power of attorney holder was competent to file the petition, and whether there was any violation of natural justice regarding the corporate debtor's representation.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The issuance of a Recovery Certificate by the Debt Recovery Tribunal (DRT) provides a fresh cause of action and a fresh period of limitation to institute a petition under Section 7 of the IBC. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 7 applications are well within limitation if filed within three years from the issuance of a DRT Recovery Certificate, in line with the principles laid down by the Supreme Court in Dena Bank v. C. Shivakumar Reddy. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: A Chief Manager authorized via a valid power of attorney and accompanying authorization letter possesses full legal competence to institute an insolvency application on behalf of a financial creditor bank. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Because the DRT Recovery Certificate was issued on February 12, 2019, making the August 2019 filing timely, and because the corporate debtor failed to file a valid contest through proper management, the Section 7 admission was legally sound.
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed, upholding the Adjudicating Authority's order dated September 16, 2021.
summary: Navalkumar D Bhoot appealed against an NCLT Mumbai order admitting UCO Bank's Section 7 application against Narendra Solvex Pvt. Ltd. The appellant argued that the petition was time-barred since the default dated back to September 2014 and that the authorized representative lacked competence. The NCLAT dismissed the appeal, holding that the issuance of a DRT Recovery Certificate in February 2019 created a fresh cause of action and renewed the limitation period under the framework established by the Supreme Court in Dena Bank. Furthermore, the Tribunal found no merit in the contentions regarding unauthorized filing or violation of natural justice.

case_title: Sudip Dutta @ Sudip Bijoy Dutta vs. Deepika Bhugra Prasad & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Sudip Dutta @ Sudip Bijoy Dutta (promoter and ex-Director of the Corporate Debtor); Respondent No. 1 is Deepika Bhugra Prasad (Resolution Professional/Liquidator); Respondent No. 2 is State Bank of India (Financial Creditor). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: CIRP was initiated against the Corporate Debtor on an application filed by State Bank of India under Section 7 of the IBC. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Unstated financial debt defaults that triggered the CIRP admission on February 14, 2020. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP initiated on February 14, 2020; single resolution plan withdrawn by the applicant on October 29, 2020; CoC decided to move for liquidation on June 16, 2021; liquidation order passed by NCLT Kolkata on October 8, 2021. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Series of rejected One Time Settlement (OTS) proposals submitted by the Appellant between December 2020 and July 9, 2021, and CoC meeting minutes from the 13th meeting dated June 16, 2021. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Kolkata passed liquidation orders on October 8, 2021, following an application under Section 33 filed by the RP upon CoC recommendation, which the ex-director appealed before the NCLAT.
legal_issues: Whether the CoC's commercial decision to recommend liquidation of the Corporate Debtor upon the failure of a resolution plan is open to judicial interference, and whether the promoter was denied natural justice during the liquidation proceedings.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The commercial wisdom of the Committee of Creditors (CoC) to approve liquidation or reject settlement plans is not open to judicial review unless it suffers from a patent legal infirmity. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 33 of the IBC mandates that if no resolution plan is approved or if the CoC decides to liquidate during CIRP, the Adjudicating Authority has no option but to order liquidation. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: In the absence of a formal Section 12A application or an accepted OTS proposal, prolonged insolvency proceedings cannot be entertained to the detriment of asset values. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Because the CoC exercised its commercial wisdom in a timely and lawful manner to recommend liquidation after 16 months of failed resolution attempts, the liquidation order was fully sustainable.
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed at the stage of admission with no order as to costs, upholding the Adjudicating Authority's liquidation order.
summary: Sudip Dutta, the promoter and ex-director of the Corporate Debtor, appealed against the NCLT Kolkata's liquidation order. The appellant argued that his revised OTS proposals offered better returns than liquidation and that he was denied an effective hearing. The NCLAT dismissed the appeal, holding that the CoC's commercial decision to reject settlement proposals and opt for liquidation under Section 33 is sacrosanct and immune to judicial interference, especially when no formal Section 12A application was on record.

case_title: Mr. Harrish Khurana vs. M/s. One World Realtech Private Limited
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Operational Creditor (Appellant) is Mr. Harrish Khurana (M/s Harrish Khurana & Associates); Corporate Debtor (Respondent) is M/s One World Realtech Private Limited. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: The Appellant claimed he rendered professional services relating to the Companies Act, XBRL conversion, and Delhi Stamp Act pursuant to four invoices totaling Rs. 1,81,000/- raised between May 11, 2017, and January 5, 2018. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Total claimed default amount of Rs. 1,81,000/- for unpaid professional bills. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Invoices raised from May 11, 2017, to January 5, 2018; Section 8 demand notice served; Section 9 application dismissed by NCLT New Delhi on September 6, 2019. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: An e-mail dated April 21, 2018, sent by the Appellant, and an affidavit by Mr. Arun Kishore (Statutory Auditor) stating that the Appellant was engaged by him in his personal capacity as principal rather than directly by the Corporate Debtor. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT New Delhi dismissed the Section 9 application on September 6, 2019, finding no privity of contract, which led to the present appeal.
legal_issues: Whether a professional engaged directly by the statutory auditor rather than the corporate debtor can maintain an application as an operational creditor under Section 9 of the IBC in the absence of privity of contract.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: To qualify as an operational creditor under the IBC, the operational debt must be owed directly by the corporate debtor pursuant to a valid contract or provision of services for the corporate debtor. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Sections 5(20) and 5(21) of the IBC require a direct jural relationship of operational debt and creditor; an engagement by a third party like a statutory auditor does not create a direct operational debt against the corporate debtor. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Clear affidavit evidence from the statutory auditor establishing that he engaged the service provider in his personal capacity negates the existence of privity of contract between the service provider and the corporate debtor. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Because the Appellant failed to prove any direct engagement or privity of contract with the Corporate Debtor, the claim did not constitute an operational debt under the IBC, rendering the Section 9 application unmaintainable.
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed with no order as to costs, upholding the Adjudicating Authority's order dated September 6, 2019.
summary: Mr. Harrish Khurana appealed an NCLT New Delhi order dismissing his Section 9 IBC petition against M/s One World Realtech Private Limited for unpaid professional fees of Rs. 1,81,000/-. The NCLAT affirmed the dismissal, holding that there was no privity of contract between the Appellant and the Corporate Debtor. Based on the statutory auditor's affidavit, the Tribunal found that the Appellant was engaged personally by the auditor rather than by the company, meaning no valid operational debt was owed by the Corporate Debtor. Consequently, the appeal was dismissed.

case_title: Vaibhav Goel & Anr. vs Deputy Commissioner of Income Tax & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellants Vaibhav Goel and Madhu Goel are the Joint Resolution Applicants; Respondent No. 1 is the Deputy Commissioner of Income Tax; Respondent No. 2 is the Monitoring Professional. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: The dispute does not involve a standard commercial default but pertains to the survival and enforcement of statutory tax dues following the approval of a Resolution Plan. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: The Income Tax Department raised assessment demands for AY 2012-13 (Rs. 9,46,80,622), AY 2013-14 (Rs. 25,55,43,350), and AY 2014-15 (Rs. 16,85,79,469) based on excise evasion findings. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP commenced on 31.05.2018; the Resolution Plan was approved on 21.05.2019. Post-approval, the IT Department issued assessment orders in December 2019 raising the fresh demands. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The approved Resolution Plan explicitly stated that waivers of statutory dues would be decided by the respective government departments, and the Appellants had undertaken to pay the liability upon crystallization. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The Appellants filed IA No. 3412/ND/2020 to declare the tax demands invalid, which the NCLT New Delhi dismissed with a cost of Rs. 1,00,000 on 17.09.2020.
legal_issues: Whether the successful Resolution Applicants can challenge fresh tax demands raised post-approval of the Resolution Plan before the Adjudicating Authority, when the approved Plan explicitly directed that the grant of statutory waivers be sought from the respective government departments.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A successful resolution applicant cannot retrospectively challenge or seek modification of an approved Resolution Plan's terms regarding statutory dues via an interlocutory application if they did not appeal the original approval order. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Once a Resolution Plan is approved under Section 31 of the IBC with explicit directions that waivers of statutory dues must be sought from the respective departments, the Adjudicating Authority cannot subsequently issue declaratory relief invalidating tax demands under the guise of plan implementation. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal relied on the text of the NCLT's approval order dated 21.05.2019, which expressly denied blanket statutory waivers and mandated that issues of pre-deposit, interest, or penalties be decided by the relevant government departments. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Because the Appellants accepted the Resolution Plan without challenging the NCLT's refusal to grant blanket statutory waivers, they were precluded from subsequently filing an application to invalidate the Income Tax Department's legitimate demands.
operative_order: The NCLAT dismissed the appeal without costs, affirming the Adjudicating Authority's order dated 17.09.2020 that rejected the Appellants' application and imposed a cost of Rs. 1,00,000 for wasting judicial time.
summary: The Joint Resolution Applicants appealed an NCLT order that dismissed their interlocutory application seeking to invalidate fresh tax demands raised by the Income Tax Department after the approval of their Resolution Plan. The CIRP was initiated in May 2018, and the Plan was approved in May 2019 with a specific clause that waivers of statutory dues must be sought directly from the concerned government departments. Post-approval, the IT Department issued assessment orders demanding significant tax dues for previous assessment years. The NCLAT held that since the Appellants never challenged the original plan approval order—which explicitly delegated statutory waivers to the respective authorities—they could not subsequently use the Adjudicating Authority to invalidate the tax demands. Consequently, the appeal was dismissed.

case_title: Maan Aluminium Ltd. vs. Nitya Electrocontrols Pvt. Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Operational Creditor (Appellant) is Maan Aluminium Ltd.; Corporate Debtor (Respondent) is Nitya Electrocontrols Pvt. Ltd.. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Supply of Aluminium Bus Bars pursuant to a Purchase Order dated February 14, 2017. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Claimed default of Rs. 19,65,818/- based on two invoices dated April 12, 2017 (Rs. 4,81,043/-) and April 13, 2017 (Rs. 14,84,775/-). 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Cheques issued on May 24, 2017, dishonoured on June 20 and June 22, 2017; debit notes issued by the Corporate Debtor in July 2017. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Debit notes issued by the Corporate Debtor on July 13, 2017 (for Rs. 14,84,775/-) and July 17, 2017, pointing out inferior quality of goods, along with courier receipts and stopped-payment post-dated cheques. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Section 9 application filed by the Appellant was dismissed by NCLT New Delhi Bench-VI on February 20, 2020 (CP (IB) No. 456 (ND)/2019), leading to the present appeal.
legal_issues: Whether the NCLT correctly dismissed the Section 9 IBC application on the grounds of a pre-existing dispute regarding the quality of goods supplied, evidenced by debit notes and stopped-payment cheques.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Under Sections 8 and 9 of the IBC, if a corporate debtor raises a pre-existing dispute regarding the quality of goods supported by contemporaneous debit notes before the receipt of a demand notice, the insolvency application must be rejected. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Stopping payment on cheques due to quality defects rather than mere fund insufficiency substantiates a pre-existing dispute under Section 8(2) of the IBC. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Contemporaneous debit notes delivered via courier bearing recipient stamps, together with emails concerning material rejections and commercial breaches, sufficiently establish a genuine pre-existing dispute. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Because a genuine pre-existing dispute regarding inferior goods existed prior to the demand notice, the Section 9 application was rightly rejected as IBC proceedings cannot be used as a substitute for civil recovery.
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed, and the Adjudicating Authority's order dated February 20, 2020, is upheld, with no order as to costs.
summary: Maan Aluminium Ltd appealed against the NCLT New Delhi order dismissing its Section 9 IBC petition against Nitya Electrocontrols Pvt. Ltd. The Appellant sought to recover Rs. 19.65 lakhs for aluminium bus bars supplied in April 2017. The NCLAT affirmed the dismissal, holding that the Corporate Debtor had successfully demonstrated a pre-existing dispute through contemporaneous debit notes for inferior quality goods and stopped-payment cheques. The Tribunal reiterated that IBC is not a recovery forum and cannot be invoked when real commercial disputes exist, thereby dismissing the appeal.

case_title: Smt. Suman Dhir & Ors vs M/S. Gyan Ganga Educational Institute
appeal_number: Contempt Case (AT) No. 27 of 2020 IN Company Appeal (AT) No. 44 of 2018
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Applicants are Smt. Suman Dhir and Shri Sarvesh Dhir; the Respondents/Contemnors are M/s Gyan Ganga Educational Institute Pvt. Ltd. and its Directors. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Unsecured loans provided by the Applicants to the Respondent company. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Applicants claimed Rs. 20,349,111 calculating interest at 15% compounded annually from 01.04.1999, whereas Respondents offered payment at a 10% rate. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The original NCLAT judgment directing repayment was passed on 20.08.2019; legal notice for payment was sent on 25.02.2020. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The Respondents relied on a resolution from the 7th AGM dated 25.09.1998, which reduced the interest rate on unsecured loans from 15% to 10% effective 01.10.1998, and had dispatched checks based on this calculation in September 2019. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Following the 2019 NCLAT order to repay the loan at the 'agreed rate', the Applicants filed a Contempt Case alleging wilful disobedience because the Respondents refused to pay 15% interest post-1999.
legal_issues: Whether the Respondents' calculation and offer of payment at 10% interest instead of 15% constituted wilful disobedience and contempt of the NCLAT's prior order directing repayment at the 'agreed rate'.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: When an order is ambiguous and reasonably capable of more than one interpretation, a proceeding for contempt is not maintainable. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: The phrase 'with interest at agreed rate' in the prior NCLAT order was subject to interpretation; it did not explicitly mandate a 15% rate post-1999. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal reviewed the unchallenged AGM resolution of 25.09.1998 which lowered the rate to 10%, determining that the Respondents' reliance on this resolution was valid and demonstrated an intent to comply rather than wilful disobedience. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT concluded that there was no wilful disobedience, as the Respondents had actively attempted to execute the judgment based on a reasonable and documented interpretation of the 'agreed rate'.
operative_order: The NCLAT disposed of the contempt application and directed the Respondents to deposit the loan amount calculated at 15% interest till 30.09.1998 and 10% compounded annually thereafter with the Executing Court within one month.
summary: Smt. Suman Dhir and others initiated contempt proceedings against M/s Gyan Ganga Educational Institute, alleging wilful disobedience of a 2019 NCLAT order that directed the repayment of an unsecured loan at the 'agreed rate'. The Applicants demanded 15% compound interest, while the Respondents calculated the dues at 10% based on an unchallenged 1998 AGM resolution. The NCLAT, relying on Supreme Court precedent, held that contempt proceedings are not maintainable for ambiguous orders capable of multiple interpretations. Finding no wilful disobedience—as the Respondents' 10% calculation was a valid interpretation of 'agreed rate'—the Tribunal disposed of the contempt case and directed the deposit of the dues accordingly.

case_title: Mayank Dhamania & N.P. Dhamania vs M/S ANS Apartments Pvt. Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellants are N.P. Dhamania and Mayank Dhamania (prospective homebuyers). The Respondent/Corporate Debtor is M/s ANS Apartments Pvt. Ltd. (ANS). Rajput Properties & Developers Pvt. Ltd. (RPD) is a third-party contractor/developer. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: ANS entered into an MOU with RPD on 03.12.2012 to complete construction on ANS's residential project 'Alstonia'. The Appellants booked flats under a self-finance scheme offered by RPD. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Each Appellant deposited Rs. 30,05,659/- with RPD for the booking of flats. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The MOU between ANS and RPD was terminated on 23.08.2013. The Appellants filed their claims with the IRP on 28.01.2020. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Clause 42 of the MOU explicitly stated that no agency or partnership was created between ANS and RPD. RPD collected the booking amounts and deposited them into its own account, rather than the designated joint account as required by the MOU. ANS never issued credit notes or allotment letters to the Appellants. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The IRP rejected the Appellants' claims. The Adjudicating Authority dismissed their subsequent applications (I.A. No. 4885 of 2020 & 4564 of 2020) on 17.11.2020, concluding there was no jural relationship between the Appellants and ANS.
legal_issues: Whether a third-party developer (RPD) acted as an agent of the Corporate Debtor (ANS) when collecting booking amounts from homebuyers, and whether a jural relationship existed between the homebuyers and the Corporate Debtor making the latter liable for the claims under the IBC.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An explicit contractual clause negating the creation of an agency or partnership is determinative of the parties' relationship; a principal is not liable for funds collected by an independent contractor who fails to follow the agreed-upon deposit mechanism, barring direct privity of contract with the end consumer. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: While 'claim' under Section 3(6) of the IBC is interpreted broadly, it fundamentally requires a jural relationship establishing liability or an obligation to pay on the part of the Corporate Debtor. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal relied on the express terms of the MOU (Clause 42), which denied an agency relationship, and documentary evidence showing RPD kept the collected funds in its own account rather than transferring them to the joint account or securing allotment letters from ANS. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT concluded that RPD did not act as an agent of ANS when it collected the Appellants' funds, and because ANS never issued allotment letters or received the funds, no jural relationship or debt existed between the Appellants and the Corporate Debtor.
operative_order: The NCLAT dismissed both appeals (Company Appeal (AT) (Ins.) No. 124 & 125 of 2021) without costs, thereby upholding the Adjudicating Authority's order dated 17.11.2020 which rejected the Appellants' claims.
summary: Mayank Dhamania and N.P. Dhamania (Appellants) appealed an NCLT order that rejected their claims as financial creditors against M/s ANS Apartments Pvt. Ltd. (Corporate Debtor). The Appellants had paid booking amounts to a third-party developer, RPD, which had an MOU to construct towers on the Corporate Debtor's land. The Appellants argued RPD acted as an agent for the Corporate Debtor. The NCLAT examined the MOU and found it explicitly denied any agency or partnership. Furthermore, RPD deposited the homebuyers' funds into its own account instead of the designated joint account, and the Corporate Debtor never issued allotment letters. Consequently, the NCLAT held that no jural relationship existed between the Appellants and the Corporate Debtor, and dismissed the appeals.

case_title: Bharat Bhushan Kumar vs. Spaze Towers Pvt. Ltd. & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant is Bharat Bhushan Kumar and the Respondents include Spaze Towers Pvt. Ltd. (Corporate Debtor/R-1), Resolution Professional, and other allottees/respondents (R-2 to R-41). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: The underlying dispute arose from real estate transactions/allotment involving Spaze Towers Pvt. Ltd. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: The source text does not mention the exact claimed default amount or the specific date of default. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: No specific dates of Section 8 demand notices or loan recall notices are mentioned in the text. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The parties settled the matter amicably out of court, and the Supreme Court subsequently annulled the underlying proceedings. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The original petition was filed as CP No. IB 889/ND/2020 before the lower authority, which led to the initiation of proceedings later challenged through Company Appeal (AT) Insolvency No. 899 of 2021 before the NCLAT.
legal_issues: Whether the appeal should be permitted to be withdrawn in light of the amicable settlement between the parties and the subsequent order passed by the Hon'ble Supreme Court annulling the underlying company petition proceedings.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An appellate tribunal will permit the withdrawal of an appeal when the underlying dispute has been settled amicably by the parties and the core proceedings have been annulled by a superior court. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: The bench interpreted withdrawal provisions and procedural rules under the IBC appellate framework to allow dismissal of an appeal upon the appellant's request following an out-of-court settlement. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Verification of the Hon'ble Supreme Court's order placed on record and the joint submission regarding amicable settlement by counsel. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The appeal along with the interlocutory application is dismissed as withdrawn since the underlying proceedings in CP No. IB 889/ND/2020 stand annulled by the Supreme Court.
operative_order: Permission to withdraw the appeal along with I.A. No. 2506 of 2021 is accorded, and the Appeal is dismissed as withdrawn.
summary: Bharat Bhushan Kumar filed an appeal against Spaze Towers Pvt. Ltd. and others before the NCLAT Principal Bench, New Delhi, registered as Company Appeal (AT) Insolvency No. 899 of 2021, alongside I.A. No. 2506 of 2021 seeking withdrawal due to an amicable settlement. During the hearing, the Appellant's counsel presented the Supreme Court of India's order dated November 18, 2021, in Civil Appeal No. 6798 of 2021, which annulled the underlying proceedings in CP No. IB 889/ND/2020. Consequently, the NCLAT bench comprising Justice Anant Bijay Singh and Ms. Shreesha Merla permitted the withdrawal and dismissed the appeal as withdrawn.

case_title: Innovative Construventures Private Ltd & Anr. vs Brainer Trade and Fin-Tech Private Ltd & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Financial Creditors (CoC) are Pune Peoples Co-Operative Bank Limited and Janaseva Sahakari Bank Limited. Corporate Debtor is Brainer Trade and Fin-Tech Private Ltd. Resolution Applicants/Appellants are Innovative Construventures Private Ltd and Innovative Agro Estates Private Ltd. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: The Appellants were debtors to the Corporate Debtor owing roughly Rs 21 crores. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: The CIRP was initiated voluntarily by the Corporate Debtor under Section 10; specific default amounts are not detailed. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP admitted on 25 July 2018. Form G published on 28 September 2018, extended to 31 October 2018, and further to 15 November 2018. Appellants submitted a complete EOI on 5 January 2019. 180-day period expired 21 January 2019. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The CoC evaluated the Appellants' EOI and rejected it because they failed to provide MSME registration proof, failed to reply to queries regarding Section 29A compliance, and were debtors owing Rs 21 crores to the Corporate Debtor. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Mumbai admitted the CIRP under Section 10 on 25 July 2018. On 21 January 2019, NCLT dismissed the Appellants' application (MA 114/2019) to consider their plan because the CoC rejected their EOI. On 22 February 2019, NCLT allowed the RP's application for liquidation. Appellants challenged both orders before NCLAT.
legal_issues: Whether the Committee of Creditors can summarily reject an Expression of Interest without allowing formal plan submission, and whether the CoC has the authority to resolve to liquidate the Corporate Debtor before the expiry of the statutory 180-day CIRP period.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A resolution applicant has no vested right to have its resolution plan considered or approved. The Committee of Creditors exercises supreme commercial wisdom in deciding the viability of prospective applicants and the resolution of the corporate debtor. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 33(2) of the IBC and its Explanation explicitly empower the CoC to take a decision to liquidate the corporate debtor at any time after its constitution and before the confirmation of a resolution plan, regardless of whether the maximum statutory CIRP period has expired. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal reviewed the CoC's decision-making process and concluded that excluding an applicant who failed to meet documentation requirements and was a substantial debtor to the Corporate Debtor was a valid exercise of commercial wisdom, not subject to judicial interference. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The bench held that the CoC did not act prematurely by opting for liquidation prior to the expiration of 180 days, and the Adjudicating Authority correctly ordered liquidation. The Appellants' appeals were entirely devoid of merit.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 470 & 486 of 2019 are dismissed. No Order as to Costs.
summary: The Appellants challenged the NCLT orders that dismissed their application for the consideration of their resolution plan and ordered the liquidation of Brainer Trade and Fin-Tech Private Ltd. The NCLAT affirmed that an applicant has no vested right for their plan to be considered. Under Section 33(2) of the IBC, the Committee of Creditors is fully empowered to decide to liquidate a Corporate Debtor at any time prior to the approval of a resolution plan without waiting for the 180-day CIRP limit to end. Consequently, both appeals were dismissed.

case_title: Oriental Iron Casting Ltd. vs. Registrar of Companies & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant is Oriental Iron Casting Ltd., and the Respondents are the Registrar of Companies (ROC, R-1) and the Income Tax Department (R-2). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: The underlying dispute involves the striking off of the company's name from the Register of Companies under provisions of the Companies Act, 2013, despite the company holding investments and maintaining financial assets. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: No specific debt default amount or default date is applicable, as the action arose from the striking off of the company name due to alleged non-commencement of business operations. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The ROC issued a notice under Section 248(1) & (4) on 27.04.2017, and subsequently passed an order striking off the company name on 30.06.2017. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The Appellant produced balance sheets for the financial years ending 31.03.2017 and 31.03.2018 showing active investments running into several lakhs, along with details of assets and liabilities. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The Appellant filed an appeal under Section 252 of the Companies Act, 2013 before the NCLT, New Delhi, which dismissed the appeal on 21.11.2019 on the ground that the company was not engaged in business as per its object clause, leading to the present appeal before the NCLAT.
legal_issues: Whether the NCLT was justified in dismissing the appeal under Section 252 of the Companies Act, 2013, and upholding the striking off of the company's name by the Registrar of Companies when the company possessed active financial statements, assets, and investments.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A company's name should not be struck off or kept removed from the Register of Companies if it demonstrates continuous business presence, active financial investments, and valid balance sheet records reflecting assets and liabilities. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Interpretation of Section 252 of the Companies Act, 2013 regarding the restoration of a company's name when sufficient cause and active financial status are demonstrated. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Evaluation of balance sheets and financial records (such as investments running into several lakhs for FY ending 31.03.2017 and 31.03.2018) to determine active corporate existence. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Since the financial records and balance sheets establish active investments and the Respondent No.1 cannot support the striking-out order, the appeal is allowed, and the company's name is ordered to be restored.
operative_order: The order passed by NCLT dated 21.11.2019 and the order passed by the Registrar of Companies dated 30.06.2017 are set aside. The name of the Appellant Company is restored in the Register of Companies at its original serial, and the appeal is allowed with cost.
summary: Oriental Iron Casting Ltd. challenged the NCLT order dated November 21, 2019, which had dismissed its appeal against the Registrar of Companies' order striking off its name from the Register of Companies under Section 248 of the Companies Act, 2013. The NCLAT, comprising Chairperson Justice Ashok Bhushan, Justice Jarat Kumar Jain, and Dr. Ashok Kumar Mishra, noted that the company's balance sheets for the financial years ending March 31, 2017, and March 31, 2018, reflected substantial investments, assets, and liabilities. With Respondent No.1 not supporting the striking-off order, the NCLAT allowed the appeal with cost, setting aside the lower tribunal and ROC orders and directing the restoration of the company's name.

case_title: Biogenetic Drugs Private Ltd. vs. Themis Medicare Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant is Biogenetic Drugs Private Ltd. (claiming to be a decree holder and Operational Creditor), and the Respondent is Themis Medicare Ltd. (Corporate Debtor). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: The underlying claim originated from Civil Suit No. 06-NL/1 of 2017, in which a decree was passed by the Additional District Judge on April 10, 2018. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: A total debt amount of Rs. 28,35,880/- was claimed by the Appellant. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The Appellant issued a demand notice under Section 8 on July 21, 2018, which was duly served and replied to by the Respondent. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: An ex-parte decree was passed in favor of the Appellant in the civil suit, which formed the basis of the operational debt claim along with Form 5 application documents. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The Appellant filed an application under Section 9 of the IBC (C.P.(I.B) No. 696/NCLT/AHM/2019) before the NCLT Ahmedabad Bench, which dismissed the application on February 18, 2021, erroneously treating the applicant as a financial creditor and holding that a decree-holder cannot initiate a Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process, leading to the current appeal.
legal_issues: Whether the Adjudicating Authority erred in dismissing an application filed under Section 9 of the IBC by treating the Appellant as a Financial Creditor instead of evaluating it as an Operational Creditor.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: When an application is filed under Section 9 of the IBC by an operational creditor based on a decree or operational debt, the adjudicating authority must evaluate it within the framework of an operational creditor rather than mischaracterizing the claimant as a financial creditor. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 3(10) of the IBC defines a creditor to include a decree-holder, financial creditor, and operational creditor, but the specific nature of the application filed dictates the statutory provisions to be applied. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Scrutiny of the original application format (Form 5) to verify whether the proceeding was initiated in the capacity of an operational creditor rather than a financial creditor. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Because the foundational premise of the Adjudicating Authority's judgment—treating the application as one filed by a Financial Creditor—was entirely incorrect, the impugned order must be set aside and the matter remanded for fresh consideration.
operative_order: The impugned judgment dated February 18, 2021, is set aside, and the application under Section 9 is revived before the Adjudicating Authority to be considered afresh in accordance with law, without expressing any opinion on other issues.
summary: Biogenetic Drugs Private Ltd. appealed against the NCLT Ahmedabad Bench order dated February 18, 2021, which dismissed its Section 9 application under the IBC. The NCLAT bench comprising Chairperson Justice Ashok Bhushan and Technical Member Dr. Alok Srivastava noted that while the Appellant had filed the application in Form 5 as an Operational Creditor, the Adjudicating Authority incorrectly evaluated the case under the lens of a Financial Creditor. Consequently, the NCLAT allowed the appeal, set aside the impugned order, and revived the Section 9 application for a fresh decision by the Adjudicating Authority.

case_title: M/S New Engineering Works vs NTPC GE Power Services Private Limited
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Operational Creditor is M/S New Engineering Works; Corporate Debtor is NTPC GE Power Services Private Limited. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Work orders issued in June 2015 for Electrical and Mechanical Erection Works at GSECL UKAL ESP 2x200 MW, later amended to a total of Rs. 7,65,14,594. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Operational Creditor claimed a balance of Rs. 1,33,40,071 on the original work, plus additional bills of Rs. 1,42,72,787. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Demand notice under Section 8 issued on 08.03.2019. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Pre-notice emails and meeting minutes (August 2018) showed the Corporate Debtor raised issues of liquidated damages (Rs. 1,58,02,918) for delayed completion and disputed the unilateral bills for additional work. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Section 9 petition was rejected by NCLT Principal Bench New Delhi on 24.10.2019 due to a pre-existing dispute, leading to this appeal.
legal_issues: Whether there was a pre-existing dispute regarding the operational debt, including liquidated damages and unapproved additional work, justifying the rejection of the Section 9 application.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An application for corporate insolvency resolution by an operational creditor must be rejected if there is a pre-existing dispute between the parties prior to the issuance of the demand notice. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Relying on the Mobilox judgment, the definition of 'dispute' under Section 5(6) is inclusive and includes correspondences showing a dispute relating to payment of the debt. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal evaluated pre-notice emails, meeting minutes, and letters indicating the corporate debtor's claim for liquidated damages and rejection of unilateral additional work bills as sufficient evidence of a pre-existing dispute. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT affirmed the Adjudicating Authority's finding that a valid pre-existing dispute existed, warranting the dismissal of the Section 9 application.
operative_order: The impugned order dated 24.10.2019 passed by the Ld. Adjudicating Authority is affirmed. The Appeal is hereby dismissed.
summary: M/S New Engineering Works appealed the NCLT's rejection of its Section 9 application against NTPC GE Power Services Private Limited. The claim involved unpaid balances for mechanical erection work and additional unapproved bills. The Corporate Debtor contested the debt citing a pre-existing dispute over liquidated damages for delayed work and unagreed additional charges. Relying on the Supreme Court's Mobilox judgment, the NCLAT held that correspondence exchanged prior to the demand notice clearly established a pre-existing dispute. Consequently, the NCLAT dismissed the appeal and upheld the NCLT's order.

case_title: The Commissioner of Central Taxes Goods & Service Tax vs. C.S. Ashish Singh & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant is the Commissioner of Central Taxes Goods & Service Tax, and the Respondents are C.S. Ashish Singh (Resolution Professional, R-1), along with Respondents No. 2 and 3 (Successful Resolution Applicants) representing the Corporate Debtor, Fourth Dimension Solutions Limited. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: The matter concerns unpaid Goods and Service Tax (GST) statutory dues originating from a Show Cause Notice issued to the Corporate Debtor. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: The source text specifiesGST dues arising from a Show Cause Notice issued on 19.6.2019, but does not state an exact consolidated total default amount figure. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: A Show Cause Notice for GST dues was issued on 19.6.2019; the Adjudicating Authority approved the resolution plan on 25.09.2020. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Pending GST dues appeared in the balance sheet of the Corporate Debtor and were referenced in a Show Cause Notice, but the Appellant failed to file a formal claim before the Resolution Professional in accordance with the prescribed regulations. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The Adjudicating Authority approved the resolution plan submitted by Respondents No. 2 and 3 under Section 31 of the IBC on 25.09.2020 in I.A. No. 2159/ND/2020 (Company Petition No. (IB) 1232(ND)/2019), prompting the Revenue department to file Company Appeal (AT) (Ins) No. 854 of 2021.
legal_issues: Whether statutory tax dues that were not formally filed as a claim before the Resolution Professional can be entertained or considered after the approval and implementation of a resolution plan under Section 31 of the IBC.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Once a resolution plan has been duly approved by the Adjudicating Authority and implemented, no further or undecided claims can be entertained against the corporate debtor, and the successful resolution applicant takes over the business on a fresh slate. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Interpretation of Section 31 of the IBC and Regulations 7 and 8 of the IBBI (Insolvency Resolution Process for Corporate Persons) Regulations, 2016, establishing that creditors must submit formal claims within the stipulated time and format, and cannot rely merely on entries in the corporate debtor's books or records. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Verification of whether the appellant filed any formal claim before the Resolution Professional in the prescribed form and manner during the corporate insolvency resolution process. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Because the Appellant failed to file a formal claim before the Resolution Professional, and the resolution plan has already been approved and implemented, the belated claim cannot be considered, and the appeal is dismissed.
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed at the stage of admission. No orders as to costs.
summary: The Commissioner of Central Taxes (GST) challenged the NCLT New Delhi order dated September 25, 2020, which approved a resolution plan for Fourth Dimension Solutions Limited under Section 31 of the IBC. The Appellant contended that its GST dues, reflected in a June 19, 2019 Show Cause Notice and the company's balance sheet, should have been automatically accounted for by the Resolution Professional. The NCLAT bench, comprising Justice Jarat Kumar Jain and Dr. Alok Srivastava, observed that the Appellant never filed a formal claim as mandated by the regulations. Citing the Supreme Court's ruling in Ghanshyam Mishra and Sons v. Edelweiss Asset Reconstruction Co., the NCLAT held that a successful resolution applicant cannot be ambushed with undecided claims after plan approval, leading to the dismissal of the appeal at the admission stage.

case_title: M/s Prayag Polytech Pvt. Ltd. vs. M/s Prayag Tubes Pvt. Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant is M/s Prayag Polytech Pvt. Ltd. (Operational Creditor), and the Respondent is M/s Prayag Tubes Pvt. Ltd. (Corporate Debtor). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: The Appellant supplied master batches to the Respondent for which total invoices worth Rs. 13,78,404/- were raised, out of which Rs. 6,62,944/- was paid, leaving a balance amount of Rs. 7,15,460/-. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: A claimed balance default amount of Rs. 7,15,460/- (or Rs. 7,15,460.67/-) was stated as due, arising after April to September 2018 supplies. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: A Demand Notice in Form No. 3 was served by the Appellant on 09.08.2019 and replied to by the Respondent on 27.08.2019; the insolvency petition was filed on 24.10.2019. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Letters dated 29.11.2018 and 30.11.2018 signed by Mr. Devender Kumar Aggarwal as Managing Director confirmed that the outstanding dues of Rs. 7,15,460.67/- were adjusted against the outstanding loan repayable by the Appellant to a group company, M/s Prayag Polymers Pvt. Ltd. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The Adjudicating Authority (NCLT, New Delhi Bench) rejected the insolvency application via order dated 04.03.2021 in Company Petition IB No. 2923/ND/2019, finding no default due to the adjustment, which led to the present appeal.
legal_issues: Whether the Adjudicating Authority committed an error in rejecting the Section 9 application on the ground that the debt stood adjusted against the dues of a sister/group company pursuant to a letter issued by the Managing Director.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A Managing Director of a company is fully empowered to carry out day-to-day functions and bind the company in ordinary commercial matters, including adjustments of accounts, without requiring a specific board resolution under Section 179(3) of the Companies Act, 2013. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Interpretation of the powers of a Managing Director in day-to-day management and the scope of corporate default under the IBC where accounts have been mutually adjusted. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Examination of written correspondence and letters dated 30.11.2018 executed by the Managing Director confirming the adjustment of outstanding dues against group company loans. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Since the debt claimed by the Appellant was validly adjusted against the dues of the group company M/s Prayag Polymers Pvt. Ltd. through letters issued by the Managing Director, no default subsists, and the application was rightly rejected.
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed, with the clarification that the orders passed shall have no bearing on the rights of the parties in any other proceedings.
summary: M/s Prayag Polytech Pvt. Ltd. challenged the NCLT New Delhi order dated March 4, 2021, which dismissed its Section 9 application against M/s Prayag Tubes Pvt. Ltd. The Appellant claimed a default of Rs. 7,15,460/- for master batches supplied. The Respondent contended that the amount was adjusted against dues owed by the Appellant to a group company, M/s Prayag Polymers Pvt. Ltd., via letters dated November 30, 2018, signed by Managing Director Mr. Devender Kumar Aggarwal. The NCLAT bench, comprising Chairperson Justice Ashok Bhushan, Justice Jarat Kumar Jain, and Dr. Ashok Kumar Mishra, held that a Managing Director has full authority for day-to-day functions without needing a separate board resolution for such adjustments. Finding no error in the Adjudicating Authority's conclusion that no default existed, the NCLAT dismissed the appeal.

case_title: Greater Noida Industrial Development Authority vs. Mr. Dinesh Chandra Agarwal & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Greater Noida Industrial Development Authority (GNIDA), claiming as a Financial Creditor; Corporate Debtor is M/s. Maple Realcon Private Limited; Operational Creditor is M/s. Bindals Merchandise. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: GNIDA leased land plot No. GH-01 sector adjoining Tech Zone IV, Greater NOIDA to the Corporate Debtor for developing a sports city. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: GNIDA submitted a claim for Rs. 17,31,22,890. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP initiated on 18.07.2018; CoC approved the plan on 08.11.2019; GNIDA gained knowledge of CIRP around 01.11.2019 but delayed filing its claim until 06.02.2020. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The Adjudicating Authority approved the Resolution Plan on 20.02.2020. Over 11 months later, GNIDA filed I.A. No. 525/2021 and I.A. No. 727/2021 to set aside the RP's actions and recall the approval order. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The NCLT New Delhi dismissed GNIDA's applications on 04.06.2021, leading GNIDA to file this appeal under Section 61 of the IBC.
legal_issues: Whether a belated claim by a statutory authority can be considered after the Committee of Creditors has approved the Resolution Plan, and whether the Adjudicating Authority has the legal provision under the IBC to recall its order approving a Resolution Plan.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A Successful Resolution Applicant takes over the business on a 'fresh slate' and cannot be burdened with 'hydra head' undecided claims that pop up after a Resolution Plan has been approved. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: The Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code (IBC) contains no provision empowering the Adjudicating Authority to recall or review its own order approving a Resolution Plan; the proper remedy is filing an appeal within the limitation period. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal noted the undeniable delay in GNIDA's actions, filing its claim after the CoC's approval and attempting to recall the order 11 months post-approval, which barred it from relief. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Relying on the Supreme Court's decisions in 'Essar Steel' and 'Ghanashyam Mishra', the bench concluded that the implemented resolution plan cannot be disturbed by new claims, dismissing the appeal.
operative_order: The appeal is, therefore, dismissed at admission stage. No orders as to cost.
summary: Greater Noida Industrial Development Authority (GNIDA) challenged the NCLT's refusal to recall its order approving the Resolution Plan for M/s. Maple Realcon Private Limited and to consider its claim of Rs. 17,31,22,890. GNIDA filed its claim on 06.02.2020, well after the CoC had already approved the resolution plan in November 2019. The NCLAT, citing Supreme Court precedents like Essar Steel, ruled that allowing belated claims post-approval would disrupt the 'fresh slate' given to the successful resolution applicant. Furthermore, the NCLAT affirmed that the IBC lacks provisions for the Adjudicating Authority to recall its plan approval order, leading to the dismissal of GNIDA's appeal.

case_title: Committee of Creditors of Educomp Solutions Limited vs. Mr. Mahender Kumar Khandelwal
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant is the Committee of Creditors of Educomp Solutions Limited (represented through State Bank of India), the Respondent is Mr. Mahender Kumar Khandelwal (Resolution Professional), and the Resolution Applicant is M/s Ebix Singapore Pte Ltd. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: The corporate insolvency resolution process involved the submission and approval of a resolution plan by the CoC for the Corporate Debtor, Educomp Solutions Limited. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: The source text does not mention an exact claimed monetary default amount or default date. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The plan approval application CA No. 195(PB)/2018 was filed under Section 30(6); the Adjudicating Authority dismissed it as infructuous on 03.01.2020 after allowing the resolution applicant's withdrawal application (I.A. No. 1816 of 2018). 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The Resolution Applicant sought to withdraw its approved resolution plan after more than one year, leading to litigation across the NCLAT and the Hon'ble Supreme Court. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The Adjudicating Authority dismissed the plan approval application as infructuous on 03.01.2020 consequent to allowing the withdrawal application; the CoC challenged this in Company Appeal (AT) Insolvency No. 587 of 2020 following previous appellate and supreme court rulings.
legal_issues: Whether the Adjudicating Authority erred in dismissing the plan approval application under Section 30(6) as infructuous following the withdrawal of the resolution plan by the successful resolution applicant, when such withdrawal order was subsequently set aside by appellate courts.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Once a resolution plan has been approved by the Committee of Creditors and submitted to the Adjudicating Authority, it is binding and irrevocable under the provisions of the IBC, leaving no scope for unilateral withdrawal or modification by the successful resolution applicant. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Interpretation of Sections 30(6) and 31 of the IBC, establishing that a resolution applicant cannot unilaterally withdraw a submitted plan and that the Adjudicating Authority must consider the plan approval application on merits. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Examination of the binding nature of the CoC-approved resolution plan and the final verdict of the Hon'ble Supreme Court in *Ebix Singapore Pvt. Ltd. v. CoC of Educomp Solutions Ltd.* dismissing the resolution applicant's appeal. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Because the underlying withdrawal order was set aside and the Supreme Court affirmed that resolution plans are irrevocable and binding, the impugned order dismissing the plan approval application as infructuous must be set aside and the application restored for a decision on merits.
operative_order: The appeal is allowed and the impugned order is set aside. The Adjudicating Authority is directed to restore CA No. 195(PB)/2018 and proceed to decide the application under Section 30(6) on merits in accordance with law and timeline guidelines.
summary: The Committee of Creditors of Educomp Solutions Limited appealed against the NCLT Principal Bench order dated January 3, 2020, which had dismissed their plan approval application as infructuous because the resolution applicant, Ebix Singapore Pte Ltd., had been permitted to withdraw its plan. Noting that the withdrawal order was previously set aside by the NCLAT and that the Hon'ble Supreme Court in *Ebix Singapore Pvt. Ltd. v. CoC of Educomp Solutions Ltd.* ruled that resolution plans are binding and irrevocable, the NCLAT bench comprising Judicial Member Justice Anant Bijay Singh and Technical Member Ms. Shreesha Merla allowed the appeal. The NCLAT set aside the impugned order and directed the Adjudicating Authority to restore CA No. 195(PB)/2018 and decide the plan approval application on merits.

case_title: Tijaria Polypipes Limited vs Kevadiya Construction Pvt Ltd
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Operational Creditor is Tijaria Polypipes Limited; Corporate Debtor is Kevadiya Construction Pvt Ltd. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: The Corporate Debtor issued a Purchase Order on 9th March 2018 for plastic products (HDPE, PVC pipes). 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Operational Creditor claimed an outstanding principal of Rs. 34,40,672 after adjusting an advance of Rs. 9,65,554 and credit notes for returned goods. Total demand was Rs. 41,21,405 including interest. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Demand notice under Section 8 of IBC was issued on 27th June 2019. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The Corporate Debtor raised quality objections via email on 24th May 2018 and October 13, 2018. The Operational Creditor admitted via email to lifting the 'complete material' due to defects but only lifted a portion. Additionally, the postal tracking receipt did not match the consignment number, leaving notice delivery unproven. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Ahmedabad dismissed the Section 9 petition on 2nd November 2020 due to a pre-existing dispute and non-service of notice, prompting this appeal.
legal_issues: Whether the Section 9 application was maintainable given the mismatch in postal receipts for the Section 8 demand notice and the emails evidencing a dispute regarding the quality of goods prior to the demand notice.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The IBC is not intended to be a substitute for a recovery forum, and provisions cannot be invoked when there is a real, pre-existing dispute between the parties. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 9 of the IBC requires strict compliance with the delivery of a Section 8 demand notice and the definitive absence of a pre-existing dispute regarding the debt. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal relied on pre-notice email correspondence establishing that the goods were defective and substandard, alongside an admission by the Operational Creditor to take back the complete material, satisfying the threshold for a pre-existing dispute. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Because the demand notice delivery was unproven and the record clearly showed a pre-existing dispute about product quality, the appellate tribunal found no infirmity in the Adjudicating Authority's dismissal of the petition.
operative_order: The Appeal deserves to be dismissed and is dismissed and no order as to costs.
summary: Tijaria Polypipes Limited appealed the dismissal of its Section 9 application against Kevadiya Construction Pvt Ltd. The Operational Creditor sought outstanding dues for supplied pipes, but the Corporate Debtor produced emails showing it had rejected the goods as defective before the Section 8 notice was issued, to which the Operational Creditor had agreed to lift the complete material. The NCLAT upheld the NCLT's finding that the Section 8 notice delivery was unproven and that a genuine pre-existing dispute regarding goods quality existed, reiterating that IBC cannot be used merely for debt recovery.

case_title: Invent Assets Securitisation & Reconstruction Pvt. Ltd. & Saraswat Co-operative Bank Ltd. vs Rajmal Labhchand Mogra
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Financial Creditors are Invent Assets Securitisation & Reconstruction Pvt. Ltd. and Saraswat Co-operative Bank Ltd. The Corporate Debtor is Enviro Bulkk Handling Systems Pvt. Ltd. The Interim Resolution Professional (IRP) is Rajmal Labhchand Mogra. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: The underlying transaction is not detailed; the matter arises from a CIRP initiated under Section 9 by Elecon Engineering Co. Ltd. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: The dispute involves a claim of Rs. 40,20,600 by the IRP towards CIRP costs and fees. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The CIRP was admitted on 04.12.2017. The IRP was appointed on 18.06.2018. The first CoC meeting was held on 16.07.2018. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The CoC resolved in its first meeting on 16.07.2018 to replace the IRP. The CoC subsequently objected to a second meeting called by the IRP on 10.08.2018 and adjourned it sine die. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The Adjudicating Authority (NCLT Mumbai) on 26.06.2019 allowed the IRP's application for fees up to 09.10.2018, the date he was formally replaced by a new RP. The Financial Creditors appealed this fee directive to the NCLAT.
legal_issues: Whether an Interim Resolution Professional is entitled to continue functioning and claim fees up to the date of their formal replacement by the Adjudicating Authority, even after the Committee of Creditors has resolved to replace them in its first meeting.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An Interim Resolution Professional cannot claim continuance of service or ongoing fees once the Committee of Creditors resolves to replace them, unless explicitly directed to continue by the Adjudicating Authority. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 22(5) of the IBC provides that if the Board does not confirm a proposed RP within 10 days, the Adjudicating Authority must specifically order the IRP to continue. Regulation 17(3) of the CIRP Regulations is subservient to Section 22(5) and cannot automatically extend the IRP's mandate without such a statutory order. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal noted that after the CoC's resolution on 16.07.2018 to replace the IRP, no substantial work was effectively conducted by the IRP, invalidating his claim for fees up to 09.10.2018. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT held the IRP had no legal right to function or claim fees post the initial 10-day period following the CoC's replacement resolution, setting aside the NCLT's order granting fees until 09.10.2018.
operative_order: The Appeal is allowed. The order passed by the Adjudicating Authority dated 26.06.2019 is set aside to the above extent. The interim payment of Rs. 10 lakh already made sufficiently covers the fees and no further payment is required.
summary: The Financial Creditors appealed against an NCLT order directing them to pay the Interim Resolution Professional (IRP) fees up to 09.10.2018. The Committee of Creditors had already resolved to replace the IRP in its very first meeting on 16.07.2018. The NCLAT ruled that under Section 22(5) of the IBC, an IRP cannot automatically continue to function or accrue fees after the CoC resolves to replace them, absent a specific order from the Adjudicating Authority. It held that Regulation 17(3) cannot override this statutory limitation. Consequently, the NCLAT allowed the appeal, set aside the fee order, and ruled the previously paid interim amount of Rs. 10 lakhs was sufficient.

case_title: Employee's Provident Fund Organisation vs Cyclo Transmission Ltd. & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Employee's Provident Fund Organisation; Corporate Debtor is Cyclo Transmission Ltd. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Statutory provident fund dues owed by the Corporate Debtor to the Appellant. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Appellant alleged a total claim amount of Rs. 2,68,06,704, but only Rs. 58,06,123 was allocated and paid in the plan. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP initiated on 18.12.2018; claims invited by 08.01.2019. Appellant claimed to submit its claim over a year later on 22.01.2020 via email and 04.02.2020 via speed post. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The Resolution Professional recorded that no formal claim was submitted within the timeline, though the Information Memorandum noted pending PF dues of Rs. 29,59,537 (Employees) and Rs. 28,46,586 (Workmen) which were allocated 100% in the plan on an exceptional basis despite no claim. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Mumbai approved the Resolution Plan on 16.07.2021, and the Appellant challenged this approval before the NCLAT.
legal_issues: Whether a statutory creditor can challenge an approved Resolution Plan for insufficient allocation of dues when its claim was submitted well past the public announcement deadline without any condonation from the Adjudicating Authority.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A creditor who fails to submit a claim within the stipulated time allowed in the public announcement cannot successfully challenge a resolution plan's allocation for its unadmitted claim. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: The approval of a Resolution Plan is sound if it fairly addresses known statutory dues as per the Information Memorandum, even when formal claims were not submitted. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal rejected the Appellant's assertion of submitting a ~2.68 crore claim because it was sent via email and speed post over a year after the deadline, with no order from the Adjudicating Authority directing the RP to receive it. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT found no error in the Adjudicating Authority's approval of the Resolution Plan since the plan allocated 100% of the recorded PF dues and the Appellant's belated higher claim was invalid.
operative_order: There is no merit in the Appeal. Appeal is dismissed.
summary: The EPFO appealed against the NCLT Mumbai's order approving the resolution plan for Cyclo Transmission Ltd., claiming its PF dues of Rs. 2.68 crores were ignored. The NCLAT found that the EPFO failed to submit its claim by the 08.01.2019 deadline, instead attempting to submit it in early 2020 without NCLT permission. Despite the lack of a formal claim, the approved resolution plan voluntarily allocated 100% of the known PF dues (amounting to ~Rs. 58 lakhs) based on the Information Memorandum. Consequently, the NCLAT dismissed the appeal finding no error in the plan's approval.

case_title: Shabeena Arshad & Anr. vs Nilesh Sharma Resolution Professional
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellants are Shabeena Arshad & Anr.; Respondent is Nilesh Sharma, Resolution Professional for Dream Procon Pvt. Ltd. (Corporate Debtor). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: The Appellants made payments to the Corporate Debtor, claiming additional cash payments were made to an ex-director, Mr. Rohit. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: The RP admitted a claim of Rs. 15,75,279 (Rs. 15,29,057 principal + 8% interest), rejecting the higher claimed amount. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: NCLT dismissed the Appellants' application on 02.03.2021. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The RP verified the claim based strictly on the Corporate Debtor's books of account which only reflected Rs. 15,29,057. The cash payments made to Mr. Rohit were not supported by entries in the corporate debtor's books, and the Appellants admitted the ex-directors were fraudulent. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The Adjudicating Authority (NCLT New Delhi) dismissed I.A. No. 2771/2020 filed by the Appellants, holding the RP acted correctly. Appellants appealed to NCLAT.
legal_issues: Whether the Resolution Professional is obligated to admit a claim for alleged cash payments made to an ex-director when such payments are not reflected in the corporate debtor's books of account.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A Resolution Professional is required to verify claims strictly in accordance with the accounting entries appearing in the Corporate Debtor's official books of account. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Under Section 18 of the IBC, the IRP/RP's duty is to receive, collate, and verify claims based on the financial position and verifiable books of accounts of the corporate debtor. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal held that unrecorded cash payments made to an ex-director, unsupported by the corporate debtor's accounting records, cannot form the basis of an admitted claim in CIRP. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT concluded that the RP correctly admitted only the amount reflected in the books and rightfully rejected the unsupported cash claims, dismissing the appeal.
operative_order: In fine, the instant CA (AT) (Ins) No. 581 of 2021 is dismissed. No costs. All connected Interlocutory Applications pending, if any are closed.
summary: The Appellants challenged the NCLT order that upheld the Resolution Professional's decision to partially reject their claim. The Appellants alleged they made cash payments to an ex-director of the Corporate Debtor, Dream Procon Pvt. Ltd. The NCLAT affirmed that under Section 18 of the IBC, the RP must verify claims based on the corporate debtor's books of account. Since the alleged cash payments were not recorded in the books and the Appellants themselves admitted the ex-directors were fraudulent, the unrecorded claims could not be admitted. The appeal was dismissed.

case_title: Vijay Infrastructure Technologies Pvt. Ltd. Vs. Kalpataru Properties Pvt. Ltd. & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Vijay Infrastructure Technologies Pvt. Ltd. (VIT); Respondents are Kalpataru Properties Pvt. Ltd. & Ors. VIT is a group/sister company of the Corporate Debtor. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: The underlying matter involves an Arbitral Award that became final up to the Apex Court. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: None specified in the order. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The NCLT passed the impugned order on 08.10.2021. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The Bombay High Court and the Apex Court previously rejected challenges to the Arbitral Award and attempts by the Ex-Directors to intervene, ruling VIT had no right. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Mumbai rejected VIT's intervention application (IA 2107 of 2021 in C.P.(IB) No. 494/MB/2019) stating it was a futile attempt to obstruct proceedings. VIT appealed this dismissal to the NCLAT.
