legal_issues: Whether an intervention application filed by a sister company of the Corporate Debtor to obstruct CIRP is maintainable when its challenges to the underlying Arbitral Award were previously rejected by the High Court and Supreme Court.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Intervention applications in CIRP that are mere futile attempts by related parties or ex-directors to obstruct proceedings, especially where their rights have been conclusively negated by constitutional courts, cannot be entertained. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: The Adjudicating Authority is not required to look into claims or interventions of entities that have been legally determined to possess no rights by higher courts. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal relied on the binding finality of the Bombay High Court and Supreme Court orders that dismissed the appellant's objections to the Arbitral Award. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT concluded the Appellant had no right whatsoever to maintain the appeal and dismissed it at the threshold.
operative_order: We are of the view that the Appellant has no right of whatsoever and at the instance of the Appellant, this appeal need not be entertained. The Appeal is dismissed accordingly.
summary: Vijay Infrastructure Technologies Pvt. Ltd., a sister company of the Corporate Debtor, challenged the NCLT's dismissal of its intervention application. The NCLAT upheld the NCLT's finding that the intervention was a futile attempt by the ex-directors to obstruct proceedings. Since the Bombay High Court and Supreme Court had already rejected all challenges to the underlying Arbitral Award and ruled that the Appellant had no rights, the NCLAT dismissed the appeal at the threshold, holding the Appellant had no locus standi.

case_title: SCG Construction & Developers Pvt. Ltd. & Anr. vs R. Subramanai Kumar
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellants are SCG Construction & Developers Pvt. Ltd. & Anr.; Respondent is R. Subramanai Kumar (Administrator of DHFL). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Loans availed by Appellants from DHFL. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Appellants sought financial restructuring packages for their loans under an RBI circular. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Requisitions made on 22.08.2020. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The Resolution Plan for the corporate debtor (DHFL) was already approved, rendering the restructuring request moot. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Mumbai dismissed I.A. No. 313 of 2021 on 07.06.2021 as infructuous due to plan approval; Appellants appealed.
legal_issues: Whether an application seeking loan restructuring from an Administrator remains maintainable after the approval of the Corporate Debtor's Resolution Plan.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Interlocutory applications seeking reliefs regarding debt restructuring become infructuous upon the approval of a Resolution Plan. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: N/A. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal noted the factual approval of the Resolution Plan rendering the restructuring request practically moot. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT upheld the NCLT's dismissal of the application as infructuous.
operative_order: In fine, the Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 574 of 2021 is dismissed. No costs.
summary: The Appellants appealed against the NCLT's dismissal of their application seeking loan restructuring under an RBI circular. The NCLAT affirmed the Adjudicating Authority's decision that the application became infructuous once the Resolution Plan for DHFL was approved, and dismissed the appeal.

case_title: Neeta Saha vs Shiv Nandan Sharma
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Neeta Saha; Respondent is Shiv Nandan Sharma (Resolution Professional). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Not detailed; related to corporate debtor's information and assets. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: N/A. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Impugned order passed on 02.11.2021. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: NCLT stayed the arrest warrant against the Appellant but directed her to provide the corporate debtor's email password, which she claims not to know. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT New Delhi passed an interim order in I.A. 5004/2021 directing cooperation; Appellant filed this appeal against the password direction.
legal_issues: Whether an appeal should be entertained against an interim NCLT order directing the sharing of email passwords when the application is still pending.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Appellate courts should not interfere with pending interlocutory applications where the appellant can seek modification directly from the lower tribunal. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: N/A. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal noted the NCLT had already stayed the arrest warrant and the main application was still pending. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT declined to entertain the appeal at this stage, giving liberty to approach the Adjudicating Authority for clarification.
operative_order: At this stage, we are not inclined to entertain this Appeal. The appeal is dismissed.
summary: The Appellant challenged an interim NCLT order directing her to provide the Corporate Debtor's email password to the RP. The NCLAT declined to interfere, noting the arrest warrant was stayed and the application was still pending, advising the Appellant to seek modification directly from the NCLT.

case_title: Department of Sales Tax vs Rajat Mukharjee & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Department of Sales Tax; Respondents are Rajat Mukharjee (RP for Ashtavinayak Auto Pvt. Ltd.) and Leadadroit Services Pvt. Ltd. (Successful Resolution Applicant). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Statutory sales tax dues owed by the Corporate Debtor. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: The Appellant claimed statutory dues of over Rs. 5 Crores, but was allocated only Rs. 4 Lakhs in the plan. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Resolution plan approved by NCLT on 05.03.2021. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The plan allocated a fractional amount to statutory dues, similar to a sister concern's approved plan. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Mumbai approved the Resolution Plan under Section 30(6) on 05.03.2021; Appellant appealed to NCLAT.
legal_issues: Whether a Resolution Plan can be approved if it allocates an amount significantly lesser than the total statutory dues owed to the Sales Tax Department.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A resolution plan is not rendered non-compliant with the IBC merely because it allocates an amount lesser than the total claimed statutory dues. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: The IBC and its Regulations do not mandate full payment of statutory dues in a resolution plan. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal relied on precedent involving a sister concern where similar fractional allocations were upheld by the NCLAT. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT found no infirmity in the NCLT's approval of the plan and dismissed the appeal.
operative_order: We do not find any infirmity in the impugned order of the Adjudicating Authority. There is no merit in the Appeal. The Appeal is dismissed.
summary: The Department of Sales Tax appealed the NCLT's approval of a resolution plan for Ashtavinayak Auto Pvt. Ltd., protesting that only Rs. 4 Lakhs was allocated against its Rs. 5 Crore claim. The NCLAT dismissed the appeal, holding that allocating lesser amounts for statutory dues does not violate the IBC, affirming the Adjudicating Authority's order.

case_title: Ashish Arjunkumar Rathi vs Joseph Philip & 2 Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Ashish Arjunkumar Rathi; Respondents are Joseph Philip & 2 Ors. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Not specified; relates to various applications within a CIRP (C.P./665/IB/CB/2017). 3. DEFAULT METRICS: N/A. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Impugned adjournment order dated 10.08.2021. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The applications were part-heard on 27.09.2021 and 29.09.2021 and listed for further hearing on 06.12.2021. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Chennai adjourned the applications; Appellant sought NCLAT directions for early listing and final orders within a month.
legal_issues: Whether the Appellate Tribunal should interfere with the Adjudicating Authority's scheduling of part-heard interlocutory applications.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Appellate tribunals will generally not interfere with the internal scheduling and adjournment of part-heard matters by the Adjudicating Authority. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: N/A. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal noted the matters were already slated for continued arguments on a specific near date. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT declined to interfere with the pending proceedings and dismissed the appeal.
operative_order: In fine, the instant Appeal is dismissed. No costs. Opportunity is granted to the Learned Counsels for the Parties to make a request for early completion of hearing... if they so desire/advised.
summary: The Appellant sought directions to expedite NCLT Chennai's disposal of several pending applications. Observing that the matters were already part-heard and scheduled for a subsequent hearing on 06.12.2021, the NCLAT Chennai Bench refused to interfere with the Adjudicating Authority's scheduling and dismissed the appeal.

case_title: Srigopal Choudhary vs Indiabulls Housing Finance Ltd. & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Srigopal Choudhary (RP of Shree Ram Urban Infrastructures Ltd.); Respondent is Indiabulls Housing Finance Ltd. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate insolvency context. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: N/A. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: NCLT reserved orders on 27.09.2021 and delivered them on 20.10.2021. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The appeal was filed against the order reserving judgment, but the final order was subsequently passed. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Mumbai reserved orders on 27.09.2021. The RP appealed. The NCLT then delivered the final order on 20.10.2021.
legal_issues: Whether an appeal against an order reserving judgment becomes infructuous once the final judgment is delivered.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An appeal challenging an interim order or reservation of judgment becomes infructuous upon the delivery of the final judgment by the lower court. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: N/A. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Acknowledgment by both parties that the final order was already passed. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT dismissed the appeal as infructuous since the final order had been delivered.
operative_order: In view of above, the Appeal is dismissed as infructuous.
summary: The Resolution Professional appealed against an NCLT Mumbai order that reserved judgment on a matter. Since the NCLT subsequently delivered the final order on 20.10.2021, both parties agreed the current appeal was moot. The NCLAT consequently dismissed the appeal as infructuous.

case_title: Sachin Bhandari vs Osaka Pharmaceuticals Pvt. Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Sachin Bhandari (Successful auction bidder); Respondent is Osaka Pharmaceuticals Pvt. Ltd. (Represented by Liquidator Abhishek Nagori). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Auction sale during liquidation. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: N/A. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Impugned NCLT order passed on 21.09.2021. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The NCLT disposed of the bidder's application holding it should be filed by the liquidator. The liquidator then filed a new application (No. 731 of 2021). 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Ahmedabad disposed of IA 156/2021 on 21.09.2021 as not maintainable by the bidder; Appellant appealed but withdrew after the liquidator filed the appropriate application.
legal_issues: Whether an appeal against the dismissal of a successful bidder's application remains necessary when the liquidator files the appropriate substitution application.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An appeal can be dismissed as withdrawn when subsequent procedural steps (such as the authorized party filing the required application) render the appeal unnecessary. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: N/A. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The appellant's own submission to withdraw the appeal based on the liquidator's new filing. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT allowed the withdrawal and dismissed the appeal with liberty to approach at an appropriate stage.
operative_order: The Appeal stands dismissed as above with liberty as noted above. We have no doubt that the 'NCLT' shall proceed to dispose of the application filed by the Liquidator in accordance with law.
summary: The Appellant, a successful auction bidder, challenged the NCLT's dismissal of his application. After learning that the Liquidator subsequently filed the proper application before the NCLT, the Appellant chose not to prosecute the appeal further. The NCLAT dismissed the appeal as withdrawn with liberty to return if needed.

case_title: Amrapali Fincap Ltd. vs Manish Gupta & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Amrapali Fincap Ltd.; Respondents include Mr. Manish Gupta (Resolution Professional) and others. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process involving the consideration of multiple Resolution Plans. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: N/A. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: NCLT order passed on 28.10.2021; re-voting held on 10.11.2021 and 11.11.2021; Letter of Intent issued on 13.11.2021. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Following the NCLT's directive for re-voting, the CoC completed the voting process and issued a Letter of Intent before the appeal was adjudicated. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT New Delhi (Court-IV) directed the RP to put all Resolution Plans to re-voting under Regulation 39(3B). The Appellant appealed this order to NCLAT.
legal_issues: Whether the Appellate Tribunal should entertain an appeal against an order directing re-voting of resolution plans when the re-voting has already concluded and a Letter of Intent has been issued.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An appeal against an interim procedural directive may be dismissed if subsequent events, such as the execution of the directive, render the immediate interference unnecessary, provided the appellant retains the right to challenge the final outcome. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: N/A. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal took judicial notice of the subsequent events—specifically the completion of CoC re-voting and issuance of the Letter of Intent—as grounds for declining to entertain the appeal. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT concluded that due to the subsequent events, the appeal should be dismissed, reserving the Appellant's right to raise objections during the final plan approval stage.
operative_order: The Appeal is dismissed. It shall be open for the Appellant to raise all his submissions when the plan with regard to which Letter of Intent has been issued comes for approval before the Adjudicating Authority.
summary: Amrapali Fincap Ltd. challenged an NCLT order directing the Resolution Professional to conduct a re-voting on all Resolution Plans. By the time the appeal was heard, the CoC had already completed the re-voting and issued a Letter of Intent. Noting these subsequent events, the NCLAT declined to entertain the appeal and dismissed it, granting the Appellant liberty to raise its objections when the final Resolution Plan is submitted to the Adjudicating Authority for approval.

case_title: Department of State Tax vs Trimax IT Infrastructure & Services Ltd. & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Department of State Tax; Corporate Debtor is Trimax IT Infrastructure & Services Ltd. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Statutory dues including Value Added Tax, Central Sales Tax, and GST owed by the Corporate Debtor to the Appellant. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: The Appellant's total claim was Rs. 260,40,09,899 out of which only 4.88% was allocated and paid. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The Resolution Plan was approved on 04.05.2020 and implemented in July 2020. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The Resolution Plan explicitly allocated 4.88% of the Appellant's claim, and the plan was successfully implemented. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Mumbai Bench-I approved the Resolution Plan on 04.05.2020; the Appellant appealed the approval to the NCLAT.
legal_issues: Whether an approved Resolution Plan can be set aside solely on the ground that a statutory authority received a minimal percentage (4.88%) of its total claim.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The mere fact that a creditor receives a small fraction of its claim in an approved resolution plan is not a valid ground to set aside the acceptance of the resolution plan. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: The approval of a Resolution Plan by the Adjudicating Authority remains valid even if statutory dues are settled at a drastically reduced percentage. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal noted the plan had already been successfully implemented in July 2020 and the Adjudicating Authority had considered all aspects before approval. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Finding no error in the Adjudicating Authority's judgment, the NCLAT held the appeal had no merit and dismissed it.
operative_order: We do not find any merit in the Appeal. The Appeal is dismissed.
summary: The Department of State Tax challenged the NCLT Mumbai's approval of a resolution plan for Trimax IT Infrastructure & Services Ltd., objecting that it received only 4.88% of its Rs. 260.40 crore claim for VAT, CST, and GST. The NCLAT observed that the resolution plan was already implemented in July 2020. The Tribunal ruled that receiving a minimal allocation of a claim is not a legally sufficient ground to invalidate an approved resolution plan. Consequently, the NCLAT found no error in the Adjudicating Authority's decision and dismissed the appeal.

case_title: Mr. Vigyan Prakash Arora vs Addinath Rubbers Pvt Ltd
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Mr. Vigyan Prakash Arora (erstwhile Resolution Professional); Respondent is Addinath Rubbers Pvt. Ltd. (represented by Liquidator Mr. Amit Sharma). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Transition from Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process to Liquidation. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: N/A. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The impugned NCLT order was passed on 06.10.2020. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The Adjudicating Authority made adverse observations against the Appellant in paragraphs 8 and 9 of its judgment, leading to the appointment of a new Liquidator. The new Liquidator had already published public announcements, invited claims, and appointed valuers. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The Adjudicating Authority (NCLT) appointed a new Liquidator instead of allowing the Resolution Professional to continue. The Appellant appealed to the NCLAT against this decision and the adverse remarks.
legal_issues: Whether the Adjudicating Authority's decision to appoint a new liquidator instead of the erstwhile Resolution Professional should be interfered with, and whether the adverse observations made against the RP should be expunged.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Appellate tribunals will generally not interfere with the appointment of a new liquidator if the liquidation proceedings have already advanced significantly, though they may protect the erstwhile professional from unwarranted disqualifications. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: N/A. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal weighed the practical progress made by the new Liquidator (claims invited, valuers appointed) against the Appellant's grievance. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT declined to entertain the appeal to replace the liquidator but held that the adverse observations made by the Adjudicating Authority against the Appellant would not act as a disqualification.
operative_order: We, however, observe that observations made against the Appellant in paragraph- 8 and 9 shall not be taken any adverse observations, to attach any disqualification on the Appellant. The appeal is dismissed subject to above.
summary: The erstwhile Resolution Professional appealed against the NCLT's order dated 06.10.2020, which refused his continuation as Liquidator and appointed a new individual based on certain adverse observations. Upon noting that the newly appointed Liquidator had already taken charge, published announcements, and appointed valuers, the NCLAT declined to interfere with the appointment. However, the Tribunal granted partial relief by clarifying that the adverse observations made by the Adjudicating Authority would not operate as a disqualification against the Appellant. Subject to this clarification, the appeal was dismissed.

case_title: Surinder Mehta & Ors. vs Prime Meiden Ltd. & Ors.
appeal_number: Contempt Case (AT) No. 21 of 2018 & Contempt Case (AT) No. 02 of 2019
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Petitioners are Surinder Mehta & Ors.; Respondents/Contemnors are Prime Meiden Ltd. & Ors. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Contempt proceedings arising out of Company Appeal (AT) No. 397-399 of 2017. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: N/A. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The contempt cases were from 2018 and 2019, with the final withdrawal order on 25.11.2021. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The petitioners explicitly sought permission to withdraw the contempt cases. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The petitioners filed Contempt Cases before the NCLAT, which were ultimately withdrawn during the virtual hearing on 25.11.2021.
legal_issues: Whether the petitioners should be granted permission to withdraw the pending contempt cases.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A tribunal may permit the withdrawal of contempt proceedings upon a formal request by the petitioners. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: N/A. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal acted solely on the request for withdrawal made by the learned counsels for the petitioners. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Tribunal acceded to the request and dismissed the contempt cases as withdrawn without costs.
operative_order: Acceding to the said request for withdrawal, the Contempt Case (AT) No. 21 of 2018 and Contempt Case (AT) No. 02 of 2019 are dismissed as withdrawn. No costs. All connected Interlocutory Applications pending if any, are closed.
summary: The petitioners in the contempt proceedings (Contempt Case No. 21 of 2018 and No. 02 of 2019) arising out of Company Appeal No. 397-399 of 2017 sought permission to withdraw their cases against Prime Meiden Ltd. & Ors. The NCLAT accepted the request and dismissed both contempt cases as withdrawn, closing all pending interlocutory applications without any order as to costs.

case_title: Ganga Ram Agarwal, Resolution Professional Pal Infrastructure & Developers Ltd. vs Rameshwari & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Ganga Ram Agarwal, Resolution Professional for Pal Infrastructure & Developers Ltd.; Respondents are Rameshwari & Ors. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process of Pal Infrastructure & Developers Ltd. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: N/A. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Impugned NCLT orders dated 15.12.2020 (staying CIRP) and 04.10.2021. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Applications I.A 5285/2020, I.A 5233/2020, and Ivn. P-14 were pending before the NCLT. Both parties consented to requesting an expedited hearing. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The NCLT New Delhi passed an interim order staying the CIRP and fixed the matter for 17.11.2021. The RP appealed to the NCLAT solely seeking a direction for the expeditious disposal of the pending applications.
legal_issues: Whether the Adjudicating Authority should be directed to expeditiously dispose of the pending interlocutory applications and the main matter instead of adjourning.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Appellate tribunals may dispose of appeals by directing the lower adjudicating authority to expedite the hearing of pending applications when both parties consent, rather than interfering with interim scheduling orders. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: N/A. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal noted the consensus of both the Appellant and the Respondent requesting an early decision on the pending applications. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT declined to interfere with the merits of the interim stay but directed the Adjudicating Authority to endeavor to dispose of the pending applications and the entire matter expeditiously.
operative_order: With these observations, we dispose off the Appeal.
summary: The Resolution Professional appealed against NCLT orders that stayed the CIRP and scheduled further hearings, pressing only for a direction for an expedited decision on pending applications. Since both parties agreed to request an early disposal, the NCLAT disposed of the appeal with a direction to the Adjudicating Authority to expeditiously decide the pending applications (I.A 5285/2020, I.A 5233/2020, and Ivn. P-14) and the main matter without interfering with the interim stay.

case_title: Bank of Baroda vs JBF Industries Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Bank of Baroda, substituted by its assignee CFM Asset Reconstruction Pvt. Ltd.; Respondent is JBF Industries Ltd. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Debt assignment and settlement. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: N/A. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The order was passed on 12.11.2021. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: CFM Asset Reconstruction Pvt. Ltd., the assignee, submitted an application to substitute its name in place of Bank of Baroda and simultaneously stated it did not wish to continue the proceedings as the matter was settled. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The Appellant filed I.A. No. 2192 of 2021 for substitution, which was allowed, and subsequently requested to withdraw the appeal due to settlement.
legal_issues: Whether the appeal should be disposed of without entering into the merits following a settlement and a request for withdrawal by the substituted assignee.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An appeal may be disposed of without entering into the merits if the parties reach a settlement and the appellant requests withdrawal. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: N/A. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal relied on the mutual consent of the assignee not to proceed and the respondent having no objection. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Tribunal allowed the substitution of the assignee and disposed of the appeal based on the settlement.
operative_order: Let the Applicant name be substituted in place of 'Bank of Baroda' as Appellant on the Appeal. I.A. No. 2192 of 2021 stands disposed of. In view of the above, since the 'Assignee' does not want to continue the proceeding, the Appeal is disposed of accordingly.
summary: CFM Asset Reconstruction Pvt. Ltd., the assignee of the original appellant Bank of Baroda, filed an application to be substituted in the appeal against JBF Industries Ltd. After the substitution was allowed, the assignee informed the NCLAT that the matter had been settled and they did not wish to pursue the appeal. With the respondent having no objection, the NCLAT disposed of the appeal without entering into the merits.

case_title: Rita Dixit vs Mr. Dhirendra Nath & Ors
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Rita Dixit; Respondents include Mr. Dhirendra Nath & Ors. and Mr. Manish Gupta (IRP). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process (CIRP). 3. DEFAULT METRICS: N/A. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Order issued on 22.11.2021. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The Appellant participated in the CIRP proceedings and was declared the Successful Resolution Applicant. The Appellant therefore voluntarily chose not to press the appeal as it became infructuous. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The Appellant filed the present appeal before the NCLAT but withdrew it upon becoming the successful resolution applicant.
legal_issues: Whether the appeal should be dismissed as withdrawn after the appellant was declared the successful resolution applicant, thereby rendering the appeal infructuous.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An appeal can be dismissed as withdrawn when the appellant no longer wishes to press it due to subsequent events rendering it infructuous. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: N/A. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal acted on the explicit submission of the Appellant's counsel to withdraw the appeal. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT allowed the withdrawal and dismissed the appeal as not pressed.
operative_order: Further, Learned Counsel for the Appellant submits that he does not propose to press this Appeal as it has become infructuous, so this Appeal is dismissed as withdrawn not pressed.
summary: Rita Dixit filed an appeal against Mr. Dhirendra Nath & Ors. During the proceedings, her counsel informed the NCLAT that she had participated in the CIRP and was declared the Successful Resolution Applicant. Consequently, since the matter had become infructuous, the Appellant decided not to press the appeal. The NCLAT therefore dismissed the appeal as withdrawn.

case_title: Prem Prakash vs The Principal Secretary, Madhya Pradesh PWD & Ors.
appeal_number: TA (AT) (Competition) No. 05 of 2017 (Old Appeal No. 17 of 2017)
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Prem Prakash; Respondents are The Principal Secretary, Madhya Pradesh PWD & Ors. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Competition matter; specific transaction not detailed in the order. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: N/A. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Order passed on 15.11.2021. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The Appellant appeared in person via virtual mode and explicitly stated he was not pursuing the appeal, seeking permission to withdraw it. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The Appellant filed the appeal before the NCLAT but subsequently sought to withdraw it during the hearing.
legal_issues: Whether the Appellant should be permitted to withdraw the pending competition appeal.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An appellate tribunal may dismiss an appeal as withdrawn upon the voluntary and explicit request of the appellant. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: N/A. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal relied entirely on the oral submission made by the appellant appearing in person to withdraw the case. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT acceded to the appellant's request and dismissed the appeal as withdrawn.
operative_order: Acceding to his said request, the instant TA (AT) Competition No. 05 of 2017 (Old Appeal No. 17 of 2017) is dismissed as withdrawn. No order as to costs.
summary: The Appellant, Prem Prakash, appeared in person during a virtual hearing and requested to withdraw his competition appeal against the Principal Secretary, Madhya Pradesh PWD & Ors. case_title: Puneet Brijmohan Chopra vs Admiral Logistics Zambia Ltd & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Puneet Brijmohan Chopra; Respondent is Admiral Logistics Zambia Ltd. & Ors. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Not specified. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: N/A. 4. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The Appellant filed the appeal before the NCLAT but requested withdrawal during the hearing.
legal_issues: Whether the Appellant should be permitted to withdraw the pending appeal.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An appellate tribunal may dismiss an appeal as withdrawn upon the voluntary request of the appellant. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: N/A. 3. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT acceded to the appellant's request and dismissed the appeal as withdrawn.

case_title: State Bank of India vs Prathyusha Resources and P Ltd
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is State Bank of India; Respondent is Prathyusha Resources and P Ltd. 2. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The Appellant's counsel explicitly informed the Tribunal that the bank was not interested in pursuing the appeal and requested to withdraw it. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The Appellant filed the appeal before the NCLAT but requested withdrawal during the virtual hearing.
legal_issues: Whether the Appellant should be permitted to withdraw the pending insolvency appeal.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An appellate tribunal may dismiss an appeal as withdrawn upon the voluntary request of the appellant's counsel. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: N/A. 3. case_title: Department of State Tax vs. Cyclo Transmissions Ltd. & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant is the Department of State Tax (Operational/Statutory Creditor). The First Respondent is Cyclo Transmissions Ltd. (Corporate Debtor), and the Second Respondent is the Resolution Professional. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: The Appellant's claim stems from unpaid statutory dues owed by the Corporate Debtor to the State Tax Department. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: The total statutory claim submitted by the Appellant was Rs. 7,06,34,158. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The Resolution Plan was approved by the Adjudicating Authority (NCLT, Mumbai Bench) on July 16, 2021. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Under the approved Resolution Plan, the Appellant was allocated and paid only 1.07% of its total admitted claim. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The Resolution Professional filed an application for approval of the Resolution Plan before NCLT Mumbai, which was allowed on July 16, 2021. The Appellant appealed against this approval, arguing the allocation of merely 1.07% of its statutory claim was unjustified.
legal_issues: Whether a Resolution Plan can be rejected or set aside solely on the ground that a statutory operational creditor is allocated only a negligible percentage (1.07%) of its total claim.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The commercial wisdom of the Committee of Creditors in allocating funds under a Resolution Plan cannot be challenged merely because an operational or statutory creditor receives a significantly diminished payout, provided the plan meets all statutory requirements. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: The NCLAT impliedly interpreted Section 30(2) and Section 31 of the IBC to mean that a marginal percentage allocation to an operational/statutory creditor does not constitute an 'error' or illegality in the resolution plan's approval process. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The court applied the test of statutory compliance, ruling that a 1.07% allocation amount alone does not violate the minimum payout thresholds established for operational creditors under the Code. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The bench conclusively held that the mere fact that the Appellant received only 1.07% of its claim is not a legally valid ground to interfere with or set aside the NCLT's approval of the Resolution Plan.
operative_order: The NCLAT found no merit in the appeal and dismissed it, upholding the Adjudicating Authority's order approving the Resolution Plan.
summary: The Department of State Tax challenged the NCLT Mumbai's approval of a Resolution Plan for Cyclo Transmissions Ltd., aggrieved by receiving only 1.07% of its Rs. 7.06 crore statutory claim. The NCLAT, Principal Bench, held that a negligible payout to a statutory creditor is not a valid legal ground to set aside an otherwise compliant Resolution Plan. Consequently, the appellate tribunal found no error in the Adjudicating Authority's judgment, refused to interfere with the approved allocation, and dismissed the appeal on merits.

case_title: Devas Multimedia Private Limited vs Antrix Corporation Limited
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: 1st Respondent/Petitioner is Antrix Corporation Limited. Appellant/1st Respondent is Devas Multimedia Private Limited. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Devas and Antrix entered into an agreement dated 28.01.2005 for leasing of S-band spectrum for providing SDMB Services. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Antrix sought winding up of Devas on grounds of fraud and unlawful purposes. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The winding up petition was filed on 18.01.2021 after termination of the agreement in February 2011 and an ICC Award against Antrix in 2015. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: CBI charge sheets, PMLA proceedings, and evidence of lack of technology and fraudulent diversion of FDI investments for non-ISP purposes were produced. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Bengaluru allowed the winding up petition on 25.05.2021 and appointed a Liquidator. Devas appealed.
legal_issues: Whether the NCLT was justified in ordering the winding up of the corporate debtor under Section 271(c) of the Companies Act, 2013 on grounds that the company was formed for a fraudulent and unlawful purpose and its affairs were conducted in a fraudulent manner.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A company formed for a fraudulent and unlawful purpose or conducting its affairs fraudulently is liable to be wound up. Fraud vitiates all solemn acts and agreements. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 271(c) of the Companies Act, 2013 allows winding up if the Tribunal is of the opinion that the company was formed for fraudulent/unlawful purposes, regardless of ongoing arbitral awards or pending criminal trials. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal evaluated the circumstantial evidence of suppression of material facts, diversion of FDI funds, and non-existence of proprietary technology to deduce fraudulent intent from inception. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT held that the corporate debtor was formed for a fraudulent purpose, its agreement was deceitful, and investments were illegally diverted, justifying the NCLT's winding up order.
operative_order: The Company Appeals (AT) (CH) No. 17 of 2021 & 24 of 2021 are dismissed. The NCLT's order of winding up is upheld.
summary: Antrix Corporation filed a petition to wind up Devas Multimedia on grounds of fraud. The NCLT allowed the petition. On appeal, the NCLAT dismissed the appeal, holding that Devas was incorporated for a fraudulent purpose, secured the 2005 agreement deceitfully, and diverted FDI funds illegally, thus justifying its winding up under Section 271(c) of the Companies Act, 2013.

case_title: Dinesh Gupta vs Vikram Bajaj
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Dinesh Gupta (Suspended Director). Respondent is Vikram Bajaj (Liquidator of Best Foods Ltd.). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate Debtor underwent CIRP. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default led to admission of Section 9 petition on 02.02.2018. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The extended CIRP period expired on 15.11.2019 without an approved resolution plan. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The CoC rejected the resolution plan on 15.11.2019. SBI later sent an email on 07.02.2020 conveying conditional approval, but the Resolution Applicant withdrew its plan on 19.03.2020. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Chandigarh passed a liquidation order on 01.03.2021 under Section 33(1)(a) since no resolution plan was approved within the CIRP period. The suspended director appealed.
legal_issues: Whether the Adjudicating Authority erred in ordering liquidation when a major financial creditor had communicated conditional approval of the resolution plan after the expiry of the CIRP period and the resolution applicant subsequently withdrew the plan.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: If no resolution plan is approved by the CoC with the requisite majority within the statutorily mandated CIRP period, the Adjudicating Authority must order liquidation. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 33(1)(a) of the IBC mandates liquidation if no plan is received or approved before the CIRP expiry. Conditional approval by a creditor post-CIRP expiry does not constitute a valid CoC approval under Section 30(4). 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal noted that the CIRP period lapsed on 15.11.2019, the CoC became functus officio, and the resolution applicant formally withdrew its plan. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT held the liquidation order was legally sound as no valid resolution plan existed or was approved by the CoC prior to the expiry of the CIRP timeframe.
operative_order: The Company Appeal is dismissed. The NCLT's liquidation order is upheld. The Liquidator was suggested to explore selling the company as a going concern.
summary: The Appellant challenged the liquidation order of Best Foods Ltd., arguing that a major creditor had approved the resolution plan via email after the CIRP period expired. The NCLAT dismissed the appeal, holding that the CIRP period had lapsed without a CoC-approved plan and the resolution applicant had withdrawn its offer, making the liquidation order under Section 33(1)(a) inevitable.

case_title: Telangana State Trade Promotion Corporation vs A.P. Gems & Jewellery Park Private Limited & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Telangana State Trade Promotion Corporation. First Respondent is Corporate Debtor. Second Respondent is Financial Creditor. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: The Corporate Debtor is a joint venture in which the Appellant held equity/preference shares. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: N/A. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: N/A. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The Articles of Association gave the Appellant the right to nominate two directors and required an affirmative vote from at least one of its nominee directors for significant policy decisions. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Hyderabad directed the RP to reconstitute the CoC by treating the Appellant as a 'related party' thus denying it voting rights. The Appellant challenged this order.
legal_issues: Whether a shareholder entity having nominee directors with affirmative voting rights on policy decisions under the Articles of Association qualifies as a 'related party' under Section 5(24) of the IBC.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An entity that exercises significant influence over the policy-making processes of a corporate debtor through nominee directors and affirmative voting rights is a related party. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 5(24)(m) and (l) of the IBC covers persons associated on account of participation in policy-making or controlling the board's composition. 'Control' includes de facto control of actual management or policy decisions. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal examined the Articles of Association which mandated that crucial business decisions required the affirmative vote of the Appellant's nominee director, establishing pervasive influence. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT upheld the Adjudicating Authority's finding that the Appellant was a related party and was rightly excluded from voting in the CoC.
operative_order: The Company Appeal is dismissed. The NCLT's order directing the RP to reconstitute the CoC and treat the Appellant as a related party is upheld.
summary: The Appellant challenged its classification as a related party in the CoC. The NCLAT dismissed the appeal, holding that the Appellant's right to nominate directors and its affirmative voting rights over critical policy decisions under the Corporate Debtor's Articles of Association amounted to significant influence and control, squarely placing it within the definition of a related party under Section 5(24) of the IBC.

case_title: V.S. Suresh vs Ask Investment Managers Pvt. Ltd. & Ors
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellants are homebuyers and a suspended director. Respondent No.1 is ASK Investment Managers Pvt Ltd. Corporate Debtor is Ambojini Property Developers Pvt. Ltd. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: ASK invested Rs. 50 Crores (equity and debentures) in the Corporate Debtor under a Subscription and Shareholders Agreement (SSHA). 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default led to CIRP initiation. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: N/A. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: SSHA granted ASK 50% board representation, joint signatory rights on bank accounts, and affirmative voting rights on business plans and budgets. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Chennai directed the RP to include ASK in the CoC with voting rights, finding the 2nd proviso to Section 21(2) exempted it. The Appellants appealed.
legal_issues: Whether an investor holding debentures and exercising significant control via board representation and affirmative voting rights is a 'related party' and excluded from the CoC under Section 21(2) of the IBC.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A financial creditor that acts as an insider with substantial control over the corporate debtor's operations and policy-making is a related party and cannot participate in the CoC. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 5(24) identifies related parties based on participation in policy-making and board control. The 2nd proviso to Section 21(2) exempts regulated financial service providers only if they became related parties solely due to debt-to-equity conversion prior to insolvency. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal noted ASK's extensive rights under the SSHA, including 50% board seats, joint control over bank accounts, and veto powers, proving it had significant influence independent of any debt conversion. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT held ASK was a related party due to its inherent structural control over the corporate debtor, and the 2nd proviso exception did not apply. Thus, ASK is ineligible to be part of the CoC.
operative_order: The appeals are allowed. The NCLT's order is set aside. Respondent No. 1 is declared a related party and excluded from the CoC with voting rights.
summary: Appellants challenged the NCLT order including ASK Investment Managers in the CoC. The NCLAT allowed the appeal, ruling that ASK's extensive rights under the SSHA, such as 50% board nomination and veto powers over policy decisions, made it a related party. It held that the exemption for financial service providers under the 2nd proviso to Section 21(2) did not apply, thereby excluding ASK from the CoC.

case_title: Sree Bhadra Parks and Resorts Ltd. vs Sri Ramani Resorts and hotels Pvt. Ltd
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Sree Bhadra Parks and Resorts Ltd. (Corporate Debtor). Respondent is Sri Ramani Resorts and hotels Pvt. Ltd (Financial Creditor). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: The Respondent paid an advance of Rs. 1 Crore under a Share Purchase Agreement dated 21.11.2012 to acquire 100% shares. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: The Corporate Debtor failed to refund the advance amount of Rs. 1 Crore along with agreed 24% interest. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Subsequent communications and a settlement in 2020 acknowledged the debt. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Addendum agreements and letters (05.09.2014, 17.03.2015) explicitly recorded the Corporate Debtor's promise to refund the advance with 24% interest. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Kochi admitted the Section 7 application on 25.08.2020, later restored it after a settlement failed, and finally admitted the corporate debtor into CIRP on 30.03.2021. The Corporate Debtor appealed.
legal_issues: Whether an advance paid under a share purchase agreement, which was later agreed to be refunded with interest upon the agreement's failure, constitutes a 'financial debt' under Section 5(8) of the IBC.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An advance payment originally made for shares transforms into a financial debt if the parties subsequently agree that the amount is to be refunded with interest due to the failure of the underlying transaction. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 5(8) defines financial debt as a debt disbursed against the consideration for the time value of money. A promised refund carrying an agreed interest rate satisfies this criteria. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal relied on the addendum and subsequent letters where the Corporate Debtor explicitly agreed to refund the advance with 24% interest, showing the time value of money. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT concluded that the advance payment, coupled with the promise to repay with interest, clearly fell within the definition of a financial debt, justifying the initiation of CIRP.
operative_order: The Company Appeal is dismissed. The NCLT's order admitting the Section 7 application and initiating CIRP is upheld.
summary: The Corporate Debtor appealed against the CIRP admission, arguing that a share purchase advance is not a financial debt. The NCLAT dismissed the appeal, noting that documentary evidence showed the Corporate Debtor had explicitly agreed to refund the advance with 24% interest after the share purchase failed. This subsequent agreement satisfied the 'time value of money' requirement, making it a valid financial debt under Section 5(8) of the IBC.

case_title: Ergomaxx India Private Limited vs The Registrar Of National Company Law
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant/Operational Creditor is Ergomaxx (India) Private Limited. 3rd Respondent/Corporate Debtor is Krueger International Furniture Systems Private Limited. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Supply of goods/furniture items where Ergomaxx was the supplier to the Corporate Debtor. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Claimed operational debt of Rs. 50,67,926/-. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: NCLT heard and reserved the matter on 11.12.2020 but passed an order dated 07.12.2020. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Cause lists showed the matter adjourned to 11.12.2020 for hearing/clarification, proving the 07.12.2020 order was never pronounced in open court and was predated. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Section 9 petition was originally disposed of by NCLT Bengaluru advising settlement via the impugned unpronounced order. The Appellant challenged this order before NCLAT for violation of procedural rules.
legal_issues: Whether an order passed by the Adjudicating Authority without formal pronouncement in open court, bearing a date prior to the actual date the matter was heard and reserved for orders, is legally valid or a nullity in the eye of law.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An order or judgment that is never officially pronounced by a Tribunal is a nullity in the eye of law, as pronouncement is an essential judicial act ensuring transparency. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Rules 150 and 151 of the NCLT Rules, 2016 make it mandatory for the Tribunal to pronounce orders. The Tribunal cannot dispense with formal pronouncement, as doing so violates the sanctity of judicial proceedings. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal evaluated the cause lists and order sheets, confirming the matter was listed for clarification on 07.12.2020 and reserved on 11.12.2020, rendering the 07.12.2020 predated order an unpronounced nullity. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT concluded the predated and unpronounced order was a nullity, setting it aside and remitting the matter back for a fresh hearing.
operative_order: The Company Appeal (AT) (CH) (INS) No.133 of 2021 is allowed without costs. The impugned order dated 07.12.2020 is set aside as a nullity, and the matter is remitted back to the NCLT Bengaluru for a fresh hearing on merits.
summary: The Appellant filed a Section 9 petition against the Corporate Debtor for an operational debt of Rs. 50,67,926/-. The NCLT Bengaluru disposed of the petition via an order dated 07.12.2020, which the Appellant discovered online in February 2021. The Appellant challenged the order, arguing it was predated and never formally pronounced, as the matter was actually reserved for orders on 11.12.2020. The NCLAT allowed the appeal, holding that under Rules 150 and 151 of the NCLT Rules 2016, an unpronounced order is a nullity in the eye of law. The NCLAT set aside the impugned order and remanded the case for a fresh hearing.

case_title: Mr. Keshav Agrawal vs Abhijit Guhathakurta
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Mr. Keshav Agrawal, a shareholder of the Corporate Debtor. Respondent No. 1 is Abhijit Guhathakurta, Resolution Professional of Videocon Industries Ltd. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process of a listed company, Videocon Industries Ltd. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: N/A. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: N/A. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: A Resolution Plan was approved by the Adjudicating Authority which extinguished the shareholding of the Corporate Debtor without issuing individual notices to the shareholders. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The NCLT approved the Resolution Plan. The Appellant challenged the approval before the NCLAT, contending it contravened Section 66 of the Companies Act, 2013, and SEBI regulations by extinguishing shares without prior notice.
legal_issues: Whether a Resolution Plan approved by the CoC and Adjudicating Authority can extinguish existing shareholding without complying with Section 66 of the Companies Act, 2013, and SEBI Regulations regarding notice and capital reduction.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Under the IBC, a CoC-approved resolution plan can legally extinguish existing shareholding without prior notice or compliance with capital reduction procedures under the Companies Act or SEBI regulations. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: The Explanation to Section 30(2)(e) of the IBC mandates that any shareholder approval required under the Companies Act or other laws for implementing a resolution plan is deemed to have been given. Furthermore, Section 238 overrides contrary provisions in other laws. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal applied the Supreme Court's ruling in Jaypee Kensington, determining that shareholders have no statutory participation rights in CIRP and cannot challenge the CoC's commercial wisdom regarding equity extinguishment. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT concluded that the objections regarding non-compliance with Section 66 of the Companies Act and SEBI regulations were devoid of merit, thereby dismissing the shareholder's appeal in limine.
operative_order: The Appeal is dismissed in limine without notice to the Respondents. No order as to costs.
summary: The Appellant, a shareholder of Videocon Industries Ltd., challenged the NCLT's approval of a resolution plan on the ground that it extinguished his shares without notice, allegedly violating the Companies Act and SEBI regulations. The NCLAT dismissed the appeal in limine, relying on Supreme Court precedent. It held that the IBC deems shareholder approval for capital reduction as given, and minority shareholders cannot obstruct a CoC-approved resolution plan.

case_title: Peecon Developer Pvt. Ltd. vs Bimal Agrawal
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Peecon Developer Pvt. Ltd. (claiming as Creditor). Respondent is Bimal Agrawal, Resolution Professional of Dagcon (India) Pvt. Ltd. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Appellant paid a principal sum of Rs. 2,08,00,000 to the Corporate Debtor between January and March 2008. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: N/A. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP commenced on 20.11.2019, public announcement on 23.11.2019, and the last date for claims was 04.12.2019. The Appellant submitted the claim on 12.12.2020, with a delay of 374 days. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The Appellant cited the Supreme Court's suo moto limitation extension starting 15.03.2020 to excuse the delay. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT dismissed the Appellant's application under Section 60(5) of IBC seeking a direction to the RP to accept the delayed claim. The Appellant challenged this dismissal.
legal_issues: Whether a creditor can benefit from the Supreme Court's Suo Moto limitation extension order (effective 15.03.2020) for filing a claim when the original deadline for submission expired prior to that date, and whether a 374-day delay in filing a claim should be condoned.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The benefit of the Supreme Court's Suo Moto limitation extension order applies only to limitations expiring between 15.03.2020 and 14.03.2021, and cannot revive a deadline that expired prior to 15.03.2020. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: The IBC mandates a time-bound Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process. Accepting highly belated claims disrupts the timeline and defeats the purpose of the public announcement. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal observed that the deadline expired on 04.12.2019, long before the COVID-19 extension period began, and the CIRP was already nearing its end when the claim was filed. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT affirmed the Adjudicating Authority's dismissal, concluding that entertaining the belated claim would be unfair to other creditors and contrary to the time-bound objectives of the Code.
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed summarily without notice to the other side.
summary: The Appellant submitted its claim to the RP after a delay of 374 days, arguing that the delay should be condoned based on the Supreme Court's suo moto limitation extension. The NCLT rejected the application. The NCLAT dismissed the appeal, holding that the claim deadline (04.12.2019) expired before the Supreme Court's relief period (starting 15.03.2020) began, and accepting such a delayed claim would undermine the time-bound nature of the CIRP.

case_title: Gpr Power Solutions Private Limited vs Mr. Supriyo Chaudhuri
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is GPR Power Solutions Pvt. Ltd. (Operational Creditor). Respondent No. 1 is Mr. Supriyo Chaudhuri (Resolution Professional of Rohit Ferro Tech Ltd.). Respondent No. 3 is Rohit Ferro Tech Ltd. (Corporate Debtor). Respondent No. 4 is TATA Steel Mining Limited (Resolution Applicant). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: The Appellant is an operational creditor. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: N/A. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP commenced on 07.02.2020. Public advertisement inviting claims was issued on 11.02.2020. Last date for filing claims was 21.02.2020. The 90 days period for filing claims under Regulation 12(2) ended in May 2020. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The Appellant filed its claim on 19.12.2020 and learned of its rejection on 14.01.2021. The Appellant claimed the delay was because it only became aware of the CIRP on 27.11.2020, and its 72-year-old CEO was working from home due to COVID-19. The CoC approved the Resolution Plan on 05.06.2021. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Kolkata dismissed the delay condonation application on 09.07.2021. The Appellant appealed the dismissal before the NCLAT.
legal_issues: Whether a highly belated claim submitted by an Operational Creditor can be admitted after the Resolution Plan has already been approved by the Committee of Creditors.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Belated claims filed after the statutorily mandated period cannot be condoned once the Resolution Plan has been approved by the Committee of Creditors, as doing so derails the time-bound resolution process. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Regulation 12(2) of the CIRP Regulations provides a strict 90-day timeline for filing claims. Entertaining claims after the CoC has approved the plan defeats the objective of the Code. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal observed that the CoC approved the Resolution Plan on 05.06.2021. Allowing the claim at this late stage would cause grave prejudice to the completion of the CIRP and be unfair to other creditors who strictly adhered to deadlines. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT found no ground to interfere with the NCLT's order and affirmed the rejection of the delayed claim.
operative_order: The Appeal stands dismissed. There is no ground for interference in the Impugned Order passed by the Adjudicating Authority.
summary: The Appellant, an operational creditor, filed its claim with the RP after a significant delay, citing COVID-19 and lack of prior knowledge of the CIRP. The NCLT dismissed the application to condone the delay, pointing out that the CoC had already approved the Resolution Plan. The NCLAT dismissed the appeal, holding that allowing a belated claim at such a late stage would cause grave prejudice to the completion of the CIRP and be inherently unfair to other creditors.

case_title: National Spot Exchange Limited vs Namdhari Food International Pvt Ltd
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant in Appeal 293 is National Spot Exchange Limited (NSEL, Operational Creditor) and in Appeal 301 is the Deputy Collector (Competent Authority). Respondent is Namdhari Food International Pvt Ltd (Corporate Debtor through Liquidator). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate Debtor was a trading member on NSEL's electronic spot exchange platform. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: The Corporate Debtor defaulted on a principal amount of approximately Rs. 51.02 Crore owed to NSEL/clients. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Section 7 IBC petition was admitted on 30.08.2017. Bank accounts were attached by the Deputy Collector under the MPID Act on 22.10.2018. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The RP filed an application seeking to defreeze the bank accounts attached via the 2018 letter, but the Adjudicating Authority additionally set aside an earlier 31.03.2017 notification that attached the personal properties of the promoters. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Delhi set aside the attachments including the 2017 notification. Both NSEL and the Deputy Collector appealed the order.
legal_issues: Whether attachment of a corporate debtor's bank accounts under the Maharashtra Protection of Interest of Depositors (MPID) Act can continue during CIRP and liquidation, and whether the NCLT exceeded its jurisdiction by setting aside an earlier attachment of the promoters' personal properties.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The provisions of the IBC, specifically the moratorium and liquidation mandate, override inconsistent state laws like the MPID Act regarding the attachment of a corporate debtor's assets. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 238 gives IBC an overriding effect over the MPID Act. Sections 14 and 32A of the IBC protect the corporate debtor's property from attachment proceedings during CIRP and liquidation to ensure value maximization. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal found that the 2018 attachment of bank accounts occurred post-CIRP and was hit by the moratorium. However, the 2017 notification pertained to personal properties of promoters/directors, which were outside the scope of the RP's application and IBC proceedings. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT affirmed the detachment of the corporate debtor's bank accounts but modified the NCLT order to preserve the attachment of the promoters' personal properties.
operative_order: The Appeals are partly allowed. The wording 'read with notification dated 31.03.2017' is expunged from the impugned NCLT order. The rest of the order releasing the Corporate Debtor's bank accounts to the Liquidator is maintained.
summary: The Adjudicating Authority released the corporate debtor's bank accounts and properties attached under the MPID Act. The Appellants challenged this. The NCLAT held that the IBC overrides the MPID Act, meaning the corporate debtor's accounts cannot remain attached during CIRP/Liquidation. However, it partly allowed the appeals by deleting the NCLT's reference to a 2017 notification that attached the promoters' personal properties, as those fell outside the RP's purview.

case_title: Committee of Creditors of Wind World (India) Ltd. vs Suraksha Asset Reconstruction Limited & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is the Committee of Creditors of Wind World (India) Ltd. (and the RP in the connected appeal). Respondent is the Successful Resolution Applicant (SRA) comprising Suraksha Asset Reconstruction Limited, Lakshdeep Investment and Finance Private Limited, and Suraksha Reality Limited. Corporate Debtor is Wind World (India) Ltd. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Submission and approval of a Resolution Plan for resolving the insolvency of the Corporate Debtor. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: N/A. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The CoC initially approved the plan on 16.11.2018 (one day before the 270-day expiry) and the RP filed for approval on 18.11.2018. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The SRA submitted a performance bank guarantee of Rs. 75 Crores. Over 600 days lapsed during the approval process, prompting the SRA to seek withdrawal citing business deterioration and alleged misstatements about O&M contracts. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Ahmedabad allowed the SRA to withdraw its CoC-approved Resolution Plan and ordered the return of the bank guarantee. The CoC and RP appealed against this order.
legal_issues: Whether a Successful Resolution Applicant can unilaterally withdraw or seek modification of a Resolution Plan after it has been approved by the Committee of Creditors but pending final approval by the Adjudicating Authority under Section 31 of the IBC.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The existing insolvency framework provides no scope for effecting modifications or withdrawals of a CoC-approved Resolution Plan at the behest of the successful Resolution Applicant once submitted to the Adjudicating Authority. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Sections 30 and 31 of the IBC strictly circumscribe the Adjudicating Authority's powers, leaving no room to use the residuary powers under Section 60(5)(c) to allow an exit route for the Resolution Applicant. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Relying on the Supreme Court's ruling in 'Ebix Singapore', the Tribunal noted that a submitted Resolution Plan is binding and irrevocable between the CoC and the applicant, and delays or commercial unviability cannot justify withdrawal. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT concluded that the NCLT exceeded its jurisdiction by allowing the SRA to withdraw the plan and ordering the return of the bank guarantee, thereby setting aside the impugned order.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) Nos. 814 and 826 of 2020 are allowed, and the impugned order is quashed and set aside. Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 913 of 2020 filed by the SRA is dismissed. The matter is remitted back to the Adjudicating Authority to decide the application for approval of the Resolution Plan under Section 30/31 of the IBC urgently.
summary: The NCLT permitted the Successful Resolution Applicant to withdraw its CoC-approved Resolution Plan due to delays in the approval process and ordered the return of its performance bank guarantee. The CoC and RP appealed. The NCLAT allowed the appeals, relying on the Supreme Court's decision in 'Ebix Singapore', holding that a CoC-approved Resolution Plan is binding and irrevocable. The IBC does not permit an exit route for the Resolution Applicant, and the Adjudicating Authority lacks jurisdiction under Section 60(5)(c) to permit such a withdrawal.

case_title: Air Travel Enterprises India Ltd vs Union Bank Of India & Ors
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Air Travel Enterprises India Ltd (Promoter/Shareholder of the Corporate Debtor). Respondent No. 1 is Union Bank of India (Financial Creditor). Corporate Debtor is Green Gateway Leisure Limited. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate Debtor availed a term loan of Rs. 25 Crores from UBI for a resort project, which was restructured multiple times up to 12.01.2015. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: The account was classified as NPA on 30.09.2015. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The Section 7 application was filed on 27.12.2019. UBI issued an OTS on 05.11.2019, finalized on 27.11.2019, on which the Corporate Debtor defaulted. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The Tribunal evaluated the various restructuring agreements, part payments, the OTS proposals which functioned as debt acknowledgements, and the pandemic's impact on the Corporate Debtor's travel business. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Kochi admitted the Section 7 application on 15.10.2020. The Appellant challenged this admission before NCLAT on grounds of limitation and unfairness.
legal_issues: Whether the Section 7 application filed by the Financial Creditor was barred by limitation, and whether the CIRP admission should be set aside to allow the Corporate Debtor to settle the dues considering the pandemic's impact on its travel business.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An acknowledgement of debt or a One Time Settlement (OTS) proposal before the expiration of the limitation period constitutes a fresh period of limitation under Section 18 of the Limitation Act. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 18 of the Limitation Act is applicable to IBC proceedings. An OTS agreement with a promise to pay within a timeframe acts as an acknowledgement of the jural relationship of debtor and creditor, renewing the limitation period. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal noted that the OTS agreement dated 05.11.2019 (approved on 27.11.2019) reset the limitation clock, meaning the Section 7 application filed on 27.12.2019 was well within the 3-year period under Article 137. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT held the application was not time-barred. However, exercising equitable jurisdiction due to the pandemic's severe impact on the travel sector and the Corporate Debtor's past bona fide settlement efforts, the NCLAT set aside the CIRP admission and granted 6 months to settle.
operative_order: The admission of the Section 7 application is set aside. The appeal is disposed of with a direction that if the Corporate Debtor fails to settle within 6 months from the date of the order, the Respondent Bank is at liberty to take appropriate steps.
summary: The Appellant challenged the NCLT's admission of a Section 7 application by Union Bank of India. The NCLAT first ruled that the application was not barred by limitation, as an OTS agreement served as a valid acknowledgement of debt under Section 18 of the Limitation Act. However, noting the devastating impact of the COVID-19 pandemic on the Appellant's travel business and its bona fide efforts to settle with lenders, the NCLAT set aside the CIRP admission and granted the Corporate Debtor 6 months to settle the dues.

case_title: Ravindra G. Sapkal vs Samata Nagari Sahkari Patsantha Maryadit
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Ravindra G. Sapkal, erstwhile Chairman/MD of Kalyani Education Pvt. Ltd. (Corporate Debtor). Respondent is Samata Nagari Sahkari Patsantha Maryadit, a Co-operative Credit Society (Financial Creditor). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Working Capital Term Loan of Rs. 5 Crore for expansion of an educational institution. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default occurred on 30.11.2013, with outstanding default amount of Rs. 1,67,82,786.76 as of 25.10.2019. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The Section 7 Application was filed on 22.11.2019. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The Financial Creditor obtained a Recovery Certificate under Section 101 of the Maharashtra Co-operative Societies Act on 21.01.2015 for Rs. 2,16,07,279/-. The Corporate Debtor made several part payments between 2014 and 08.06.2018. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Mumbai admitted the Section 7 Application, holding the debt was within limitation due to the part payments. The Appellant challenged this order claiming limitation and violation of natural justice.
legal_issues: Whether a Section 7 Application filed beyond three years from the date of default is barred by limitation when the creditor holds a valid Recovery Certificate and the debtor has made subsequent part payments extending the limitation period.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The issuance of a Recovery Certificate gives rise to a fresh cause of action, and subsequent part payments by the debtor initiate a fresh period of limitation under Section 19 of the Limitation Act, 1963. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: The provisions of the Limitation Act, specifically Sections 18 and 19, apply mutatis mutandis to IBC proceedings. A Recovery Certificate issued by a competent authority constitutes a fresh right to sue, resetting the limitation clock. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal noted the Recovery Certificate dated 21.01.2015 and undisputed part payments made by the Corporate Debtor up to 08.06.2018, which extended the limitation period well within the 22.11.2019 filing date. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT concluded that the debt was clearly in default and the application was within the limitation period, thereby upholding the NCLT's admission order.
operative_order: The Appeal is dismissed. Interim orders dated 22.03.2021 are vacated.
summary: The Appellant challenged the initiation of CIRP against the Corporate Debtor, arguing the debt was time-barred since the default occurred in 2013 and natural justice was violated. The NCLAT dismissed the appeal, holding that the issuance of a Recovery Certificate in 2015 and subsequent part payments by the Corporate Debtor up to 2018 triggered a fresh limitation period under Section 19 of the Limitation Act, making the 2019 Section 7 application perfectly within time.

case_title: UCO Bank vs Sudip Bhattacharya
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is UCO Bank. Respondent is Sudip Bhattacharya, Resolution Professional of Reliance Naval & Engineering Ltd. (Corporate Debtor). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: UCO Bank furnished a Performance Bank Guarantee (PBG) of Rs. 3,34,90,458/- on behalf of the Corporate Debtor to the Indian Navy for refitting 'INS Savitri'. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: The Corporate Debtor failed to extend the PBG before its expiry. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The PBG was invoked on 22.08.2019. CIRP commenced on 15.01.2020. Indian Navy refunded the amount on 28.09.2020. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The Corporate Debtor did not pay the margin money; UCO Bank paid the invoked amount from its own funds. After the warranty period expired, Indian Navy refunded the amount to UCO Bank, which UCO Bank appropriated. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Ahmedabad directed UCO Bank to refund the amount to the Corporate Debtor's account, classifying it as an asset of the Corporate Debtor hit by the moratorium. UCO Bank appealed.
legal_issues: Whether the refund of money from the reversal of a Performance Bank Guarantee, invoked prior to CIRP and paid from the Bank's own funds (without margin money from the Corporate Debtor), constitutes an asset of the Corporate Debtor subject to the moratorium under Section 14 of the IBC.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Funds refunded from the reversal of a Performance Bank Guarantee do not constitute an asset of the corporate debtor if the guarantee was funded entirely by the issuing bank. A performance guarantee is an independent contract between the bank and the beneficiary. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 3(31) explicitly excludes performance guarantees from the definition of 'security interest'. Section 14(3)(b) exempts a surety in a contract of guarantee from the moratorium. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal noted that UCO Bank paid the invoked guarantee from its own funds because the Corporate Debtor's account lacked margin money. Therefore, the refunded amount belonged to the Bank, not the Corporate Debtor. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT concluded that appropriating the refunded amount by UCO Bank did not violate Section 14 of the IBC, as the funds were not assets of the Corporate Debtor. The NCLT's order was consequently set aside.
operative_order: The Appeal is allowed and the Impugned Order is set aside. No order as to costs.
summary: UCO Bank appealed the NCLT's direction to remit a refunded Performance Bank Guarantee amount into the Corporate Debtor's account. The NCLAT allowed the appeal, holding that the PBG was invoked prior to CIRP and paid entirely from the Bank's own funds without margin money from the Corporate Debtor. Relying on Sections 3(31) and 14(3)(b) of the IBC, the NCLAT ruled that the refunded money was not an asset of the Corporate Debtor and thus not subject to the Section 14 moratorium.

case_title: Deepak Parasuraman And Anr vs Sripriya Kumar Anr
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellants are Deepak Parasuraman and Ingenium Advisory LLP. Respondent No. 1 is Sripriya Kumar (RP). Respondent No. 2 is PR Venkatesh (Promoter MD of Corporate Debtor, Perfect International Fabricators Pvt Ltd). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Appellants claimed to provide business consulting and procurement services to the CD based on agreements dated 12.10.2015 and 16.08.2016. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: The RP challenged transfers totaling Rs. 65 Lacs made to the Appellants. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Payments were made on 19.12.2016, 26.06.2017, and 31.03.2018. RP filed the avoidance application on 04.09.2019. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: No invoices were raised, no service tax was charged, and no TDS was deducted. The 2015 agreement was between R2 personally and Appellant 2. The Appellants shared office space and common directorships in another entity with R2, and Appellant 2's MCA filings showed NIL operational income. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Chennai allowed the RP's application under Sec 43 and 66, declaring the transfers fraudulent and ordering a refund of Rs. 65 Lacs. The Appellants appealed.
legal_issues: Whether the Adjudicating Authority erred in classifying the transfer of Rs. 65 Lacs by the Corporate Debtor to the Appellants as preferential and fraudulent transactions under Sections 43 and 66 of the IBC without a formal forensic audit report.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Transactions lacking basic commercial corroboration (such as invoices, tax deductions, and formal corporate agreements) between interconnected parties can be deemed fraudulent and preferential under the IBC. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Sections 43 and 66 empower the Adjudicating Authority to reverse transactions and order contributions if transfers are found to be fraudulent based on undeniable factual anomalies, even absent a formal transaction audit report. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal evaluated the absence of invoices, non-deduction of TDS, shared office space, common directorships in other entities, and contradictory MCA filings (NIL revenue) to conclude the consultancy agreements were highly suspicious and a sham. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT upheld the NCLT's finding that the transactions were fraudulent and the agreements were suspicious, dismissing the appeal and affirming the direction to refund Rs. 65 Lacs.
operative_order: The impugned order dated 01.02.2020 passed by the Adjudicating Authority is affirmed. The appeal is dismissed with no order as to costs.
summary: The Appellants challenged an NCLT order directing them and the Corporate Debtor's Promoter to refund Rs. 65 Lacs, which were deemed fraudulent and preferential transfers under Sections 43 and 66 of the IBC. The Appellants claimed the payments were bona fide commission for consultancy services based on two agreements. The NCLAT observed that the agreements were highly suspicious because no invoices were raised, no TDS was deducted, no service tax was paid, and the Appellants shared common business interests and office space with the Promoter. Furthermore, the Appellant's financial statements showed NIL operational income for the relevant period. The NCLAT dismissed the appeal, affirming the NCLT's order that the transactions were fraudulent and the funds must be contributed back to the Corporate Debtor.

case_title: Crown Tobacco Company Pvt. Ltd vs Crale Foodlinks Pvt. Ltd
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Crown Tobacco Company Pvt. Ltd. (Operational Creditor). Respondent No. 1 is Crale Foodlinks Pvt. Ltd. (Corporate Debtor). Respondent Nos. 2 and 3 are Directors of the Corporate Debtor. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: The parties entered into a Business Conducting Agreement (BCA) on 29.04.2010 for the Corporate Debtor to operate a restaurant and lounge bar from the Appellant's premises. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: The Appellant claimed outstanding dues of Rs. 35,52,022/- comprising unpaid conducting fees, electricity bills, water bills, and municipal taxes. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The BCA expired on 30.09.2017. Demand Notice under Section 8 of the IBC was sent on 19.02.2018. The Section 9 application was filed on 12.03.2018. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Civil suits (R.A.D. Suit No. 348 of 2017 and Commercial Suit No. 187 of 2018) were pending before the Small Causes Court and Bombay High Court respectively, indicating pre-existing disputes. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Mumbai dismissed the Section 9 petition on 21.09.2020 on the grounds of pre-existing dispute and limitation. The Appellant challenged this dismissal.
legal_issues: Whether the application under Section 9 of the IBC is maintainable when there are pre-existing disputes regarding the underlying agreement and when a portion of the claimed debt is barred by limitation.
ratio_decidendi: 1.
