ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An application for initiating CIRP under Section 9 of the IBC is not maintainable if there is a pre-existing dispute between the parties and if the asserted claims are barred by limitation. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Pending civil suits filed before the issuance of a Section 8 demand notice constitute a valid pre-existing dispute under the IBC. Additionally, operational debt claims are subject to a three-year limitation period, making claims older than three years from the filing date time-barred. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal noted the undisputed existence of pending civil suits in the Bombay High Court and Small Causes Court, establishing a pre-existing dispute. It also calculated that claims prior to 12.03.2015 were time-barred since the petition was filed on 12.03.2018. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT agreed with the NCLT that the claims were partially time-barred and that a clear pre-existing dispute existed, thereby affirming the dismissal of the Section 9 petition.
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed without costs. The NCLT Mumbai's order dated 21.09.2020 dismissing the Section 9 petition is affirmed.
summary: The Appellant (Operational Creditor) challenged the NCLT's dismissal of its Section 9 petition seeking CIRP against the Corporate Debtor for unpaid conducting fees and municipal taxes. The NCLAT dismissed the appeal, holding that there were pre-existing disputes between the parties as evidenced by pending civil suits over tenancy rights. Furthermore, the NCLAT affirmed that claims relating to the period prior to three years before the filing of the petition were time-barred.

case_title: Rama Investment Company Private Limited vs Ankit Mittal
appeal_number: I.A. No. 2440 of 2020 in Company Appeal (AT) No. 238 of 2018
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Applicant is Rama Investment Company Private Limited (Original Respondent No. 9). Respondent is Ankit Mittal (Original Appellant). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Proposed Scheme of Amalgamation and Arrangement involving nine companies (both public and private) merging/demerging into Rama Investment Company Private Limited. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: N/A. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: NCLT Chennai approved the scheme on 12.04.2018. NCLT Mumbai approved it for two companies on 06.12.2017. NCLAT rejected the entire scheme on 29.11.2019. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The Applicant sought modification of the NCLAT judgment under Rule 11 of NCLAT Rules to allow the merger of only the private companies, claiming the Original Appellant only had standing regarding the public companies. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLAT had previously struck down the entire composite scheme due to compromised valuation. The Applicant filed an I.A. seeking partial revival of the scheme for private companies.
legal_issues: Whether the NCLAT can exercise its inherent powers under Rule 11 of the NCLAT Rules, 2016, or Section 231 of the Companies Act, 2013, to modify a final judgment and partially revive a rejected composite scheme of amalgamation for a subset of private companies.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Inherent powers under Rule 11 of the NCLAT Rules cannot be used as a substitute for substantive review or to partially revive a composite scheme that was rejected in its entirety. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 231(1) of the Companies Act, 2013 allows modification only if a scheme is sanctioned under Section 230. Since the scheme was rejected, Section 231 cannot be invoked. Rule 11 cannot be used to reopen and segregate parts of a rejected composite scheme. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal observed that the scheme was presented and evaluated as a single composite arrangement. Clause 21 of the scheme explicitly stated that failure to secure necessary approvals would render the entire scheme void. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT held that partially reviving the scheme would amount to rewriting the rejected arrangement, which falls outside the scope of inherent powers, leading to the rejection of the Application.
operative_order: The Application (I.A. No. 2440 of 2020) is rejected. The Contempt Case record is transferred to the Chennai Bench.
summary: The Applicant sought clarification/modification of an NCLAT order that had rejected a composite Scheme of Amalgamation, requesting that the merger of only the private companies be allowed to proceed. The NCLAT rejected the application, holding that inherent powers under Rule 11 cannot be used to review a final judgment or subdivide a composite scheme that was rejected in its entirety due to compromised valuation.

case_title: Jayesh Sanghrajka vs The Monitoring Agency Nominated By The Committee of Creditors of Ariisto Developers Pvt. Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Jayesh N. Sanghrajka, erstwhile Resolution Professional (RP) of Ariisto Developers Pvt. Ltd. Respondent is the Monitoring Agency of the Corporate Debtor. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Approval of a Resolution Plan and calculation of CIRP costs, specifically the fee of the RP. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: N/A. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP initiated on 20.11.2018; 20th CoC meeting held on 12/13.11.2019. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: During the 20th CoC meeting, just before submitting the plan, the CoC approved a 'success fee' of Rs. 3 Crores for the RP. The RP had already been charging Rs. 8 Lakhs per month. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Mumbai approved the Resolution Plan but disallowed the Rs. 3 Crore success fee, directing it to be distributed among creditors. The RP appealed, arguing the fee fixation was the CoC's commercial wisdom.
legal_issues: Whether the Committee of Creditors has the authority under its 'commercial wisdom' to grant a 'success fee' to the Resolution Professional at the final stage of CIRP, and whether the Adjudicating Authority has the jurisdiction to disallow such a fee.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The fixation of the Resolution Professional's fee is not a business decision protected by the 'commercial wisdom' of the CoC. A 'success fee'—being speculative, contingent, and not directly related to actual expenses incurred—is not permitted under the IBC or its Regulations. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 5(13) and CIRP Regulations require RP fees to be transparent, reasonable, and directly related to the CIRP. The IBBI Circular dated 12.06.2018 emphasizes reasonableness and does not sanction 'success fees'. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal observed that inserting a Rs. 3 Crore success fee at the 11th hour, when the RP was already drawing a high monthly fee, acted more as an unjustified reward that diminished the creditors' payout. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT held that the Adjudicating Authority correctly exercised its jurisdiction to disallow the success fee and redistribute the funds, affirming that RP fees must be reasonable and are subject to judicial scrutiny.
operative_order: The Appeal is dismissed. No order as to costs.
summary: The Appellant (Resolution Professional) challenged the NCLT's decision to disallow a Rs. 3 Crore 'success fee' approved by the CoC at the end of the CIRP. The Appellant argued this was a commercial decision of the CoC. The NCLAT dismissed the appeal, holding that the fixation of an RP's fee is not part of the CoC's 'commercial wisdom' and is justiciable. The NCLAT ruled that the IBC does not contemplate speculative or contingent 'success fees', which act as unjustified rewards at the expense of creditors, thereby upholding the NCLT's order to redistribute the amount among creditors.

case_title: Yogesh Kundra vs SEW & Prasad Joint Venture
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Yogesh Kundra (Suspended Director of Corporate Debtor, Gati Infrastructure Pvt. Ltd.). Respondent No. 1 is SEW & Prasad Joint Venture (Operational Creditor). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Construction contract between SPJV and GIPL. A settlement agreement dated 14.12.2013 was executed involving multiple parties, shifting the debt burden primarily to the holding company, Amrit Jal Ventures Pvt. Ltd. (AJVPL). 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Operational Creditor claimed Rs. 36.01 Crores (Rs. 33.98 Crores under the settlement agreement and Rs. 2.03 Crores withheld for incomplete work). 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The Section 9 application was filed in 2017 based on defaults in 2014-2015. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The 14.12.2013 agreement stipulated GIPL would pay only Rs. 10 Crores, and the remaining Rs. 23.98 Crores was to be paid by AJVPL. GIPL paid the Rs. 10 Crores. Regarding the Rs. 2.03 Crores, correspondence showed GIPL withheld funds citing incomplete work, and a 'Certificate of Merit' issued by GIPL was merely for the Operational Creditor's pre-qualification needs elsewhere, not proof of completion. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Hyderabad admitted the Section 9 application. The Division Bench of NCLAT split, referring the matter to a third member.
legal_issues: Whether a Section 9 application is maintainable when a multiparty settlement agreement transfers the debt liability away from the corporate debtor, and whether a 'Certificate of Merit' negates a pre-existing dispute regarding incomplete work.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An application under Section 9 of the IBC is not maintainable if the alleged debt is legally owed by a third party pursuant to a settlement agreement, breaking the debtor-creditor relationship, or if there is a genuine pre-existing dispute regarding service completion. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 9 requires a clear operational debt owed by the corporate debtor and the absence of a pre-existing dispute. If a settlement agreement explicitly discharges the corporate debtor upon partial payment, no debt remains actionable against it. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The third member analyzed the 14.12.2013 settlement agreement, finding GIPL discharged its liability by paying Rs. 10 Crores. For the Rs. 2.03 Crores, emails proved GIPL consistently raised issues of incomplete work, and the 'Certificate of Merit' was issued merely to assist the creditor with other clients, thereby establishing a pre-existing dispute. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Third Member concluded there was no debtor-creditor relationship for the main claim and a valid pre-existing dispute for the withheld amount, directing the appeal to be allowed.
operative_order: The Third Member recorded an opinion that the appeal deserves to be allowed, agreeing with the Technical Member. The opinion was directed to be placed before the Division Bench for final disposal orders.
summary: The Appellant challenged the initiation of CIRP under Section 9, arguing no debtor-creditor relationship existed due to a 2013 settlement agreement that transferred the debt liability to its holding company, and raising a pre-existing dispute over Rs. 2.03 Crores withheld for incomplete work. Following a split verdict by the NCLAT Division Bench, the Third Member held that the Corporate Debtor had discharged its liability under the settlement agreement and that correspondence clearly evidenced a pre-existing dispute regarding the incomplete work, rendering the Section 9 application unmaintainable.

case_title: Suman Kumar Sharma vs Central Railside Warehouse Company Limited
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Suman Kumar Sharma (Proprietor of Sri Balaji Transport), the Operational Creditor. Respondent is Central Railside Warehouse Company Limited (CRWC), the Corporate Debtor. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Handling and transport of goods at Rail Warehousing Complex (RWC), Hatia. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Operational Creditor claimed Rs. 51,65,270/- as outstanding debt. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Demand Notice under Section 8 sent on 01.02.2018; last payment received on 16.02.2016. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Custody and Indemnity Bond holding the Operational Creditor liable for losses. Letters dated 01.11.2012 and 10.12.2012 from CRWC alleging shortage of 335 MT of boiled rice and holding the Operational Creditor responsible. Settlement Agreement dated 13.08.2014 between FCI and CRWC sharing transit losses 50:50. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT New Delhi dismissed the Section 9 application on 11.07.2019 citing pre-existing dispute. Appellant appealed to NCLAT.
legal_issues: Whether a pre-existing dispute existed between the Operational Creditor and the Corporate Debtor prior to the issuance of the Section 8 Demand Notice, rendering the Section 9 Application non-maintainable.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An application under Section 9 of the IBC must be rejected if there is a plausible pre-existing dispute that is not spurious, hypothetical, or illusory. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 5(6) of the IBC defines dispute. Under Section 9(5)(ii)(d), the Adjudicating Authority must reject the application if notice of dispute has been received or there is a record of dispute. The failure to reply to a Section 8 notice does not preclude raising the defense of a pre-existing dispute before the Adjudicating Authority. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal found the Custody and Indemnity Bond and pre-2018 communications regarding stock shortages and transit losses constituted sufficient evidence of a real, pre-existing dispute. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT affirmed the NCLT's dismissal, holding that the Corporate Debtor established a plausible contention requiring further investigation, which took the matter outside the summary jurisdiction of the IBC.
operative_order: The Appeal is dismissed. The Order of the Adjudicating Authority is confirmed. No order as to costs.
summary: The Appellant (Operational Creditor) filed an appeal against the NCLT's dismissal of its Section 9 application. The Appellant argued it was not liable for storage losses and that the Corporate Debtor failed to reply to the Section 8 notice. The NCLAT dismissed the appeal, holding that documentary evidence, including an Indemnity Bond and prior correspondence regarding stock shortages, clearly established a pre-existing dispute. The failure of the Corporate Debtor to reply to the demand notice did not bar it from raising the defense of a pre-existing dispute during the adjudicatory proceedings.

case_title: The Deputy Commissioner Division-Vii vs Kiran Shah
material_facts:
1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is The Deputy Commissioner Division-Vii, Central GST, Ahmedabad South. Respondent is Mr. Kiran Shah, Resolution Professional of the Corporate Debtor.
2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Claim for statutory tax dues (GST) against the Corporate Debtor during its Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process (CIRP).
3. DEFAULT METRICS: The Appellant submitted a claim of Rs. 13,34,44,050/-.
4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP commenced on 12.03.2020. Public announcement dated 18.03.2020 set the last date for claims as 31.03.2020. Factoring in lockdown and 90-day extension, the absolute deadline was 16.08.2020. The Appellant filed the claim on 04.09.2020, with a 19-day delay.
5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The RP had informed the Appellant of the CIRP via email on 28.07.2020. The RP rejected the claim on 05.09.2020 for being filed beyond the extended deadline. The CoC subsequently approved a Resolution Plan with a 91.02% majority, which was pending Adjudicating Authority approval.
6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The Appellant challenged the RP's rejection before the NCLT Ahmedabad. The NCLT dismissed the application, holding that allowing delayed claims at the final stage of CIRP would derail the process. The Appellant then filed this appeal before the NCLAT.
legal_issues: Whether a statutory creditor can compel a Resolution Professional to collate and admit a claim submitted after the extended deadline under the IBC, especially when a Resolution Plan is already under consideration by the CoC.
ratio_decidendi:
1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The timelines prescribed under the IBC and CIRP Regulations for submission of claims are strictly mandatory. Claims submitted beyond the extended deadline cannot be entertained, as it would disrupt the time-bound resolution process.
2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 15 of the IBC and Regulation 6(2)(c) mandate a last date for submission of claims. Section 18 requires the RP to receive and collate claims submitted pursuant to the public announcement. Section 21(1) cannot be interpreted to force the RP to collate claims received outside the prescribed time limit.
3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal noted that the Appellant was explicitly informed of the CIRP via email on 28.07.2020 but still filed the claim on 04.09.2020, beyond the 16.08.2020 extended deadline. The Tribunal found no lack of knowledge on the Appellant's part and no dereliction of duty by the RP.
4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT concluded that the RP correctly rejected the belated claim, emphasizing that accepting late claims at the advanced stage of CIRP would diminish asset value and hamper successful reorganization, upholding the NCLT's dismissal.
operative_order: The Appeal fails and is accordingly dismissed. No Order as to costs.
summary: The Appellant (Central GST Department) appealed the NCLT's order upholding the Resolution Professional's rejection of its claim for Rs. 13.34 Crores. The claim was filed 19 days after the extended deadline (which included COVID-19 lockdown extensions) had passed. The NCLAT dismissed the appeal, ruling that the IBC mandates strict adherence to timelines. Since the Appellant was informed of the CIRP before the deadline but still filed late, and the CoC was already finalizing a Resolution Plan, the RP was justified in rejecting the belated claim.

case_title: Chand Prakash Mehra vs Praveen Bansal
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Chand Prakash Mehra, Erstwhile Director of Corporate Debtor M/s. Silverton Spinners Ltd. Respondent No. 1 is Praveen Bansal (IRP). Respondent No. 2 is State Bank of India (Financial Creditor). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Consortium lending where Canara Bank was the lead banker, and SBI was a consortium member, granting credit facilities to the Corporate Debtor. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: The debt outstanding was Rs. 151,19,70,185.24 as on 31.12.2017. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The account became NPA on 15.01.2013 (revised date after CDR failure). Section 7 application was filed by SBI on 05.03.2018. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Corporate Debtor sent a letter on 21.05.2015 to Canara Bank acknowledging the debt and executed documents. A subsequent proposal letter on 15.06.2016 explicitly acknowledged the specific debt amounts owed to SBI. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Kolkata admitted the Section 7 petition filed by SBI. The suspended director appealed, claiming SBI lacked standing to sue independently of the consortium lead bank and that the debt was time-barred.
legal_issues: Whether an individual bank in a consortium can file a Section 7 application independently of the Lead Bank, and whether letters acknowledging debt to the Lead Bank or proposing restructuring extend the limitation period under Section 18 of the Limitation Act.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An individual financial creditor in a consortium possesses an independent statutory right under Section 7 of the IBC to initiate CIRP upon default, irrespective of inter-creditor agreements. Written communications acknowledging the debt, even if addressed to a party other than the specific creditor, reset the limitation period. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 238 overrides inter-creditor agreements limiting the right to sue to the Lead Bank. Explanation (a) to Section 18 of the Limitation Act explicitly allows an acknowledgment to be valid even if addressed to a person other than the creditor. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal found the letters dated 21.05.2015 and 15.06.2016 constituted clear, written acknowledgments of the outstanding debt. These acknowledgments extended the limitation period well beyond the 05.03.2018 filing date. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT concluded that SBI had the locus standi to file the application and that the application was well within the limitation period, affirming the NCLT's admission order.
operative_order: The Appeal is dismissed. The interim order staying the constitution of the CoC is vacated, and the period from 29.11.2019 till the date of the order is excluded from the CIRP timeline. No costs.
summary: The Appellant challenged the initiation of CIRP by SBI, arguing that only the Lead Bank (Canara Bank) could sue under their consortium agreement and that the 2013 NPA date made the 2018 petition time-barred. The NCLAT dismissed the appeal, holding that Section 238 of the IBC overrides inter-creditor agreements, granting SBI an independent right to file under Section 7. Furthermore, the NCLAT ruled that written acknowledgments by the Corporate Debtor in 2015 and 2016 validly extended the limitation period under Section 18 of the Limitation Act.

case_title: Ramkrishna Electricals Limited vs Atul Rajwadkar
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Ramkrishna Electricals Ltd (Operational Creditor). Respondent No. 1 is Atul Rajwadkar (Liquidator/RP of the Corporate Debtor, Enestee Engineering Limited). Respondent Nos. 2 and 3 are suspended Directors of the Corporate Debtor. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Appellant supplied transformers and fabrications to the Corporate Debtor. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Outstanding balance for FY 2017-18 was Rs. 2,66,75,764/-. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP commenced on 17.09.2019. Payments were withdrawn by the Appellant between 23.07.2019 and 15.10.2019. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The Appellant withdrew Rs. 2,42,54,481/- from a specific cooperative bank account of the Corporate Debtor after the commencement of CIRP, allegedly in connivance with the suspended directors. No claim was filed by the Appellant with the RP. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Mumbai allowed IA No. 1109 of 2020 under Section 66(1), directing the Appellant to refund the withdrawn money. The Appellant appealed, arguing lack of knowledge of CIRP and denying fraudulent intent.
legal_issues: Whether a creditor can validly withdraw funds from a Corporate Debtor's bank account after the commencement of the Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process (CIRP), and whether such withdrawal violates Section 14 of the IBC, thereby justifying an order for refund under Section 66.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Any withdrawal of funds from the accounts of a corporate debtor after the commencement of the Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process (CIRP) constitutes a violation of the moratorium under Section 14 of the IBC. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 14 prohibits transferring, encumbering, alienating, or disposing of any of the corporate debtor's assets during the moratorium period. Withdrawals orchestrated by suspended directors post-CIRP commencement fall under the purview of Section 66(1) as acts intended to defraud creditors. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal noted that the pattern of immediate cheque clearances following deposits into a newly opened cooperative bank account during the CIRP period indicated a grey area and connivance between the Appellant and suspended directors. The failure of the Appellant to file a formal claim with the RP further supported the illegality of the withdrawals. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT concluded that regardless of the Appellant's claimed ignorance of the CIRP, the withdrawal of funds violated Section 14. Therefore, the Adjudicating Authority's order directing the refund under Section 66 was legally sound.
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed. The order directing the Appellant to refund Rs. 2,42,54,121/- to the Corporate Debtor's account is upheld. The Appellant is granted liberty to file a claim before the Liquidator in accordance with the IBC. Pending IAs are disposed of, and interim orders are vacated. No costs.
summary: The Appellant challenged the NCLT's order under Section 66(1) of the IBC directing it to refund Rs. 2.42 Crores withdrawn from the Corporate Debtor's account post-CIRP commencement. The Appellant argued it was collecting legitimate dues in the ordinary course of business without knowledge of the CIRP. The NCLAT dismissed the appeal, holding that any withdrawal of funds during CIRP strictly violates the moratorium under Section 14 of the IBC. The NCLAT affirmed the refund order, noting the suspicious nature of the transactions facilitated by suspended directors, and advised the Appellant to file a formal claim with the Liquidator.

case_title: Suspended Management Of Jay Polypack vs SGV Foils Pvt Ltd
material_facts:
1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Suspended Management Of Jay Polypack Pvt. Ltd. (Corporate Debtor). Respondent No. 1 is SGV Foils Pvt. Ltd. (Operational Creditor). Respondent No. 2 is Pradeep Kabra (Resolution Professional).
2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Claim under Section 9 of IBC by the Operational Creditor against the Corporate Debtor.
3. DEFAULT METRICS: Not explicitly specified in the order, but led to the admission of the Section 9 application.
4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The ex-parte order admitting the Section 9 application was passed on 27.05.2020. The Appellant filed an application to set aside the ex-parte order on 06.11.2020. The Committee of Creditors (CoC) was constituted on 20.11.2020. The impugned order disposing of the application was passed on 23.03.2021.
5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The Appellant claimed non-receipt of notice regarding the Section 9 application and became aware of the ex-parte admission order only on 06.10.2020. The Appellant and Operational Creditor reportedly reached a settlement on 19.11.2020, before the CoC's constitution. However, the IRP proceeded to constitute the CoC on 20.11.2020. The Adjudicating Authority disposed of the set-aside application on 23.03.2021, stating it was unable to use its power under Rule 49 of NCLT Rules belatedly.
6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Ahmedabad admitted the Section 9 application ex-parte. The Corporate Debtor's application to set aside the ex-parte order under Rule 49 of NCLT Rules was disposed of. The Suspended Management appealed this disposal before NCLAT.
legal_issues: Whether the Adjudicating Authority can exercise its powers under Rule 49(2) of the NCLT Rules, 2016, to set aside an ex-parte order initiating the Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process (CIRP) after the Committee of Creditors (CoC) has been constituted.
ratio_decidendi:
1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The Adjudicating Authority cannot set aside an ex-parte admission order initiating CIRP under Rule 49(2) of the NCLT Rules once the Committee of Creditors (CoC) has been constituted.
2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Relying on the Supreme Court's decision in 'Swiss Ribbons Pvt. Ltd. Vs. Union of India', once a petition under Section 7 or 9 is admitted, the proceeding becomes a proceeding in rem. Before the constitution of the CoC, the Adjudicating Authority has the power to allow withdrawal or settlement under Rule 11 of NCLT Rules or set aside an ex-parte order under Rule 49(2) if notice was not served. However, after the CoC is constituted, the Adjudicating Authority loses this power, and the Corporate Debtor's remedy is to file an appeal under Section 61 of the IBC or the Operational Creditor must follow the withdrawal procedure under Section 12A of the IBC read with Regulation 30A.
3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal noted that while the application to set aside the ex-parte order was filed on 06.11.2020 (before the CoC constitution), the Adjudicating Authority passed the impugned order on 23.03.2021, after the CoC had already been constituted on 20.11.2020. Because the CoC was in existence at the time the order was passed, the Adjudicating Authority lacked the power to set aside the admission order under Rule 49(2).
4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT concluded there was no illegality in the Adjudicating Authority's refusal to set aside the ex-parte order because the CoC had been constituted. The proper recourse for settlement after CoC constitution is an application for withdrawal under Section 12A of the IBC.
operative_order: The Appeal is dismissed, with no order as to costs.
summary: The Appellant (Suspended Management) appealed the NCLT's refusal to set aside an ex-parte order admitting a Section 9 CIRP application. The Appellant argued they never received notice and had settled with the Operational Creditor prior to the CoC's constitution. The NCLAT dismissed the appeal, holding that once the Committee of Creditors (CoC) is constituted, the Adjudicating Authority cannot set aside an admission order using its powers under Rule 49(2) of the NCLT Rules. Since the CoC was constituted before the NCLT passed its order on the set-aside application, the only remedy available for the settled dispute is the formal withdrawal procedure under Section 12A of the IBC.

case_title: PLBB Products Pvt. Ltd vs Piyush Periwal
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is PLBB Products Pvt. Ltd. (Successful Resolution Applicant). Respondent No. 1 is Piyush Periwal (Promoter/Erstwhile Director of Corporate Debtor). Respondent No. 2 is Stressed Assets Stabilization Fund (SASF). Respondent No. 3 is Sandeep Khaitan (Resolution Professional of National Plywood Industries Ltd.). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate Debtor (an MSME) acted as a corporate guarantor for a loan originally disbursed to National Boards Ltd. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Original loan amount was Rs. 3.07 crores; SASF claimed Rs. 133,54,94,330/-. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP commenced on 08.11.2019. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Corporate Debtor is an MSME. The CoC approved the Appellant's Resolution Plan with 91.84% voting share. Respondent No. 1 sought to submit a resolution plan belatedly. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Guwahati allowed the suspended management of the Corporate Debtor (an MSME) a chance to submit a resolution plan by 01.03.2021, and directed the CoC to consider it alongside the existing plan. The Successful Resolution Applicant appealed this order.
legal_issues: Whether the Adjudicating Authority erred in granting a belated opportunity to the suspended management of an MSME corporate debtor to submit a resolution plan, after the CoC had already approved the resolution plan of the Successful Resolution Applicant.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The Adjudicating Authority possesses the discretion to grant the suspended management of an MSME corporate debtor a fair opportunity to present a resolution plan, even at a belated stage, to promote entrepreneurship and value maximization in line with the objectives of the IBC. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 240A of the IBC exempts MSMEs from the restrictive provisions of clauses (c) and (h) of Section 29A. This legislative intent encourages MSME promoters to participate in the resolution process to retain control. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal noted the corporate debtor's MSME status and the exorbitant inflation of the claimed debt (from Rs. 3.07 crores to Rs. 133 crores over 20 years). It found no harm in allowing the CoC to evaluate an alternative viable plan from the MSME promoter, as doing so aligns with the Code's goals. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT concluded that the NCLT's order providing an opportunity to the MSME promoter was legally sound and aligned with the legislative intent of Section 240A, thereby dismissing the appeal.
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed. The NCLT's order allowing the suspended management to submit a resolution plan is affirmed. The Adjudicating Authority is requested to decide IA No. 51 of 2020 before finally approving any Resolution Plan. No order as to costs.
summary: The Appellant, whose resolution plan was approved by the CoC, challenged the NCLT's order granting the suspended management of the MSME corporate debtor a belated opportunity to submit a competing resolution plan. The NCLAT dismissed the appeal, holding that Section 240A of the IBC specifically intends to encourage MSME promoters to resolve insolvency and retain control. Therefore, giving the MSME promoter a chance to submit a viable plan for the CoC's consideration aligns with the Code's objective of promoting entrepreneurship and maximizing asset value.

case_title: UCO Bank vs SREI Equipment Finance Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant in Appeal No. 232/2020 is UCO Bank (Creditor). Appellant in Appeal No. 43/2021 is the Reserve Bank of India (Regulator). Respondents are SREI Equipment Finance Ltd. (Transferee Company) and SREI Infrastructure Finance Ltd. (Transferor Company). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Proposed amalgamation/slump exchange between the holding company (Transferor) and its 100% subsidiary (Transferee). 3. DEFAULT METRICS: N/A. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The NCLT ordered creditor meetings to be held on 16.12.2020 and 23.12.2020. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The NCLT issued an interim direction (Para 23(xviii) of the impugned order) prohibiting creditors from taking coercive steps, declaring accounts as NPA, or reporting defaults, citing Section 230 of the Companies Act and Rule 11 of NCLT Rules. The CoC subsequently rejected the scheme. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Kolkata directed the convening of creditor meetings and passed a status quo order preventing creditors from classifying the debts as NPA. UCO Bank and RBI appealed against this status quo direction.
legal_issues: Whether the Adjudicating Authority (NCLT) has the jurisdiction under Section 230 of the Companies Act, 2013, read with Rule 11 of the NCLT Rules, to issue a blanket injunction restraining creditors and statutory regulators (like RBI) from classifying accounts as NPA or taking coercive recovery steps while a scheme of arrangement is pending consideration.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The NCLT cannot use its inherent powers or its jurisdiction under Section 230 of the Companies Act to injunct statutory regulators from enforcing prudential norms (like NPA classification) or to restrain creditors from exercising their contractual and statutory recovery rights pending the approval of a scheme of arrangement. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 230 of the Companies Act, 2013 does not contain a provision analogous to Section 391(6) of the 1956 Act, which allowed for a stay of proceedings. RBI Master Circulars on NPA classification have statutory force and banks are bound to follow them; the NCLT cannot override these regulatory mandates under the guise of protecting a proposed scheme. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal noted that the creditors themselves hold the power to approve or reject the scheme (requiring a 75% majority). If creditors support the scheme, they will naturally refrain from coercive steps. However, a preemptive judicial injunction barring them from declaring accounts as NPA violates RBI regulations and exceeds the NCLT's limited jurisdiction at the first motion stage. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT concluded that the specific direction in paragraph 23(xviii) of the NCLT's order was legally unsustainable and set it aside, while leaving the rest of the order intact.
operative_order: The direction in para 23(xviii) of the impugned order dated 21.10.2020 and para 3 of the daily order sheet dated 21.10.2020 passed by the Tribunal is set aside. Both appeals are disposed of with these observations. No orders as to costs.
summary: UCO Bank and the RBI challenged an NCLT order that, while convening meetings for a scheme of arrangement, directed creditors to maintain status quo and injuncted them from classifying SREI's accounts as NPA. The NCLAT allowed the appeals, ruling that the NCLT lacks the jurisdiction under Section 230 of the Companies Act to pass such sweeping injunctions that interfere with statutory RBI regulations and the creditors' independent recovery rights. The specific direction restraining NPA classification was struck down.

case_title: Kapil Jain vs Registrar Of Companies, Gwalior
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Kapil Jain (claiming to be a Creditor). Respondent No. 1 is Registrar of Companies (ROC), Gwalior. Respondent No. 2 is Rahul Steel Forging Pvt. Ltd. (Struck-off Company). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Appellant claimed to have provided consultancy services to Respondent No. 2 in 2007 for Rs. 6,90,500/-, of which Rs. 6,45,000/- remained unpaid. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Outstanding amount claimed by Appellant is Rs. 6,45,000/-. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The company's name was struck off by the ROC on 17.05.2008 due to non-filing of returns since 31.03.1999. The Appellant filed the restoration application under Section 252(3) later, within the 20-year limitation. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The ROC established that the company had not filed financials since 1999 and was not operational. Respondent No. 2's own reply admitted the Managing Director suffered severe health issues from 2000, halting operations. Yet, letters acknowledging debt in 2007-2019 were allegedly signed by this same individual who was no longer a director and was incapacitated. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Indore dismissed the application for restoration, finding lack of reliable evidence of creditor status and suspecting mala fide intent. The Appellant appealed.
legal_issues: Whether a company struck off by the ROC should be restored under Section 252(3) of the Companies Act, 2013, upon an application by an alleged creditor whose claims of ongoing business and debt acknowledgment are contradicted by the company's non-operational status and the signatory's incapacity.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An application for restoring a struck-off company under Section 252(3) of the Companies Act, 2013, must be rejected if the applicant fails to prove the company was carrying on business or in operation at the time of strike-off, or if the application is filed with mala fide intent to bypass statutory limitation periods. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 252(3) allows a creditor to seek restoration within 20 years if it is 'just' or if the company was operational. However, if the company's directors failed to appeal within the three-year limit under Section 252(1), using a 'creditor' to file under 252(3) as a proxy constitutes a mala fide abuse of process. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal found the Appellant's claim of providing services in 2007 unbelievable, as the company had been non-operational since 2000. Furthermore, the letters acknowledging the debt were signed by an elderly, severely ill former director, rendering the documents highly suspicious. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT concluded that the application was a proxy attempt by the company to revive itself after its own limitation period had expired, and the creditor's claims were factually unsubstantiated. The NCLT's dismissal was upheld.
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed. The impugned order of the NCLT is upheld. No order as to costs.
summary: The Appellant, claiming to be a creditor, challenged the NCLT's refusal to restore the name of Respondent No. 2 company, which was struck off by the ROC in 2008. The NCLAT dismissed the appeal, noting that the company had been non-operational since 2000 and the alleged debt acknowledgements were highly suspicious, having been signed by an incapacitated former director. The Tribunal held that the application was a mala fide attempt by the company's management to use the 'creditor' as a proxy to circumvent the expired three-year limitation period for companies to seek restoration under Section 252(1).

case_title: Pandurang Ramchandra Shinde vs Vijendra Kumar Jain
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Financial Creditor is IDBI Bank Limited, Corporate Debtor is Cyclo Transmissions Limited, Appellant is Pandurang Ramchandra Shinde (Suspended Director/CEO), Respondent is Vijendra Kumar Jain (Resolution Professional). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Appellant extended an unsecured loan of Rs. 1,14,91,955 to the Corporate Debtor. The Corporate Debtor had receivables of Rs. 91,56,687 from three entities (Meltek Infosystems, Micros M Technichems, Maharashtra Shetkari Sugar). 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default details of original CIRP not specified, but preferential transaction involved squaring off Rs. 91,56,687 of unsecured loan against receivables, and unauthorized sale of a car for Rs. 50,000/75,000. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Section 7 application filed on 06-03-2018, admitted on 18-12-2018. Squaring off done on 31-03-2018. Car sold during CIRP on 31-12-2018. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Auditor's report confirming ledger adjustment writing off receivables against Appellant's unsecured loan. Tax invoice and Motor Sale Delivery Receipt proving sale of the Corporate Debtor's car post CIRP commencement. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: RP filed IA No. 1108 of 2020 seeking directions under Section 43, 44, 66, 67, 69, and 70. NCLT Mumbai allowed the application on 07-01-2021, directing Appellant to deposit Rs. 91,56,687 and the car's sale amount. Appellant appealed to NCLAT.
legal_issues: 1. Whether the squaring off of the Corporate Debtor's receivables against the unsecured loan owed to the Appellant after the filing of the Section 7 petition constituted a preferential transaction under Section 43 of the IBC? 2. Whether the sale of the Corporate Debtor's car by the Appellant during the moratorium without RP approval violated Section 14 of the IBC?
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Adjusting a corporate debtor's receivables to pay off an unsecured loan owed to a related party after the initiation of insolvency proceedings gives the related party an undue beneficial position and constitutes a preferential transaction. Further, alienation of corporate assets during the moratorium without RP authorization is strictly prohibited. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 43(2) is attracted when there is a transfer of the corporate debtor's interest for the benefit of a creditor putting them in a beneficial position. Section 14 imposes an absolute bar on transferring assets after CIRP admission. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal relied on audited balance sheets, ledger accounts, and invoices which clearly demonstrated the asset transfers post the relevant statutory dates without RP consent. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT held the squaring off of Rs. 91,56,687 to be a preferential transaction under Section 43, and the sale of the car to be a direct violation of the Section 14 moratorium, upholding the NCLT's order for contribution to the asset pool.
operative_order: The NCLAT upheld the Adjudicating Authority's direction ordering the Appellant to deposit Rs. 91,56,687 for the squared-off amount. The NCLAT further held the car sale invalid, declaring it property of the Corporate Debtor, and directed the RP to take possession of it or claim loss contribution, and directed further legal/criminal action against the Appellant for the unaccounted Rs. 25,000. Appeal disposed with no order as to costs.
summary: The Appellant, a suspended director of Cyclo Transmissions Ltd., challenged an NCLT order directing him to return Rs. 91,56,687 and a car sold during the CIRP moratorium. The NCLAT found that the Appellant had fraudulently squared off his unsecured loan against the company's receivables and illegally sold the company car without the RP's permission. The Tribunal upheld the NCLT's finding of a preferential transaction and violation of Section 14, affirming the order to deposit the funds and directing further action against the Appellant.

case_title: Mr. Sundaresh Bhat (Liquidator of ABG Shipyard Limited) vs Union Of India & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Financial Creditor is ICICI Bank Ltd, Corporate Debtor is ABG Shipyard Limited, Appellant is Sundaresh Bhat (Liquidator). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Sale of the Corporate Debtor's assets through public auction during liquidation. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: N/A (Liquidation process timelines at issue). 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Liquidation order passed on 25-04-2019. Amendment to Clause 12 of Schedule I made on 25-07-2019 extending balance payment time from 15 to 90 days. IBBI Circular issued on 26-08-2019 stating amendment only applies prospectively. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Four consecutive failed auction attempts by the Liquidator due to the short 15-day timeline, prompting the Liquidator to seek application of the 90-day amended timeline. IBBI Circular dated 26-08-2019 restricted application. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Liquidator filed IA 698 of 2020 before NCLT Ahmedabad seeking to apply the amended 90-day timeline. NCLT denied the relief on 02-12-2020 relying on the IBBI Circular. Liquidator appealed to NCLAT.
legal_issues: Whether the amendment to Clause 12 of Schedule I of the IBBI (Liquidation Process) Regulations, 2019 (extending the time for payment of auction balance consideration from 15 to 90 days) applies retrospectively to ongoing liquidation processes, and whether an IBBI Circular can restrict its applicability prospectively.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An administrative circular cannot override, restrict, or interpret the applicability of a subordinate legislation/regulation. A procedural amendment extending timelines to facilitate the objective of value maximization applies retrospectively to ongoing pending processes. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: The NCLAT held that the IBBI's power under Section 196 of the IBC to issue guidelines does not extend to interpreting provisions or modifying the temporal applicability of a gazetted Regulation. Clause 12 is procedural and does not expressly restrict application to prospective liquidations. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal reviewed the IBBI Discussion Paper dated 27-04-2019 and found the intent was to resolve practical difficulties in auction sales, making the 90-day extension a beneficial procedural change. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT held that the amended 90-day timeframe applies to all pending liquidation processes regardless of the date of the liquidation order, declaring the IBBI Circular dated 26-08-2019 legally unenforceable in this regard.
operative_order: The NCLAT modified the NCLT Ahmedabad order and allowed the Appellant-Liquidator to apply and enforce the amended Clause 12 of Schedule I (granting 90 days for balance sale consideration) to the ongoing liquidation process initiated before 25-07-2019. The Appeal was disposed of with no costs.
summary: The Liquidator of ABG Shipyard challenged an NCLT order that denied him the ability to grant a 90-day timeline for auction purchasers to pay the balance consideration, relying on an IBBI Circular which stated the 90-day amendment was only prospective. The NCLAT ruled that the procedural amendment applied to ongoing liquidations to maximize asset value and held that the IBBI Circular could not legally restrict the gazetted Regulation's applicability. The Liquidator was permitted to use the extended 90-day timeline.

case_title: Narendrabhai Shah, Director Pioneer Globex Pvt. Ltd. vs LIM FA PTE Ltd. & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Operational Creditor is LIM FA PTE Ltd (a Singapore company), Corporate Debtor is Pioneer Globex Pvt. Ltd., Appellant is Narendrabhai Shah (Director). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Contract dated 01-03-2016 for the supply of metal scrap through shipment from Poland to Nhava Sheva Port in India. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Unpaid CFR value of USD 2,17,682.10 plus interest. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Demand notice under Section 8 issued on 11-12-2017. Section 9 application filed thereafter. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Sales Contract, Tax Invoice signed by both parties, Bill of Lading (made 'to order') validated by the Corporate Debtor's director on 14-05-2016, and email admissions dated 12-10-2016 offering to pay in parts. Corporate Debtor claimed non-receipt of goods. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Ahmedabad admitted the Section 9 application on 20-01-2020, dismissing the defense of non-delivery. The Corporate Debtor's Director filed an appeal before NCLAT challenging the foreign company's board resolution and alleging non-delivery.
legal_issues: 1. Whether the Section 9 application filed on behalf of a foreign company based on a plain paper Board Resolution without apostille/notarization was valid? 2. Whether the Corporate Debtor's claim of non-receipt of goods constituted a valid pre-existing dispute despite acknowledging the 'to order' Bill of Lading and sending emails offering payment?
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Technical defects in a foreign corporate authorization document (such as lack of apostille) do not invalidate an insolvency application if the authority is otherwise substantively established. A defense of non-receipt of goods is untenable when the debtor has countersigned a negotiable bill of lading and sent contemporaneous emails acknowledging the debt and proposing repayment. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 8(1) demand notice requirements are substantially met even if there are minor formatting deviations, provided the core particulars (invoice, default amount) are delivered. Section 85 of Evidence Act regarding Power of Attorney notarization was held distinguishable from internal corporate board resolutions. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal relied heavily on the 'to order' (negotiable) nature of the Bill of Lading and the Corporate Debtor's express confirmation of shipment quality/quantity, viewing subsequent non-delivery claims as a spurious defense. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT found no pre-existing dispute regarding the delivery of goods, validating the authorization of the Operational Creditor's representative, and upheld the admission of the Section 9 application.
operative_order: The NCLAT dismissed the appeal filed by the suspended Director of the Corporate Debtor, upholding the Adjudicating Authority's order admitting the Section 9 application. No orders as to costs were made.
summary: The Appellant challenged the admission of a Section 9 application filed by a Singapore-based Operational Creditor, arguing that the goods (metal scrap) were never delivered and that the foreign board resolution authorizing the petition lacked proper apostille/notarization. The NCLAT rejected these technical objections, noting the corporate resolution was validly signed by directors. It further dismissed the non-delivery defense because the Corporate Debtor had countersigned the negotiable Bill of Lading and admitted liability in subsequent emails. The appeal was dismissed.

case_title: P.R. Venkatesh vs Sripriya Kumar, RP
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Operational Creditor is M/s Jotun India Pvt. Ltd. Corporate Debtor is Perfect International Fabricators Private Limited. Appellant is PR Venkatesh (Erstwhile Promoter/MD). Respondents are Sripriya Kumar (Resolution Professional), Ingenium Advisory LLP, and Deepak Parasuraman. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Alleged consultancy agreements dated 12.10.2015 and 16.08.2016 for arranging working capital loans and facilitating purchase orders, for which commission fees were allegedly paid. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: The disputed amount is a fraudulent transfer of Rs. 65,00,000/- made to the respondents. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP admitted on 29.04.2019. Payments totaling Rs. 65 lacs were made in tranches on 19.12.2016, 20.06.2017, and 31.03.2018. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: RP discovered the payments were unsupported by valid commercial documentation: no invoices were raised, no service tax/GST was charged, and no TDS was deducted. The RP also proved that Ingenium operated from the Appellant's residence and the parties held cross-shareholdings in a related company (Udveka Engineering Pvt. Ltd.). 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: RP filed MA/987/2019 under Sections 43 and 66 of the IBC. On 01.02.2020, NCLT Chennai allowed the application, declaring the transactions fraudulent and ordering a refund. The Promoter appealed to the NCLAT.
legal_issues: Whether the transfer of Rs. 65 Lacs by the Corporate Debtor to Ingenium Advisory LLP constituted a fraudulent and preferential transaction under Sections 43 and 66 of the IBC.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Payments made by a corporate debtor to a closely connected entity based on unsubstantiated agreements, without standard commercial markers such as invoices or tax deductions, are liable to be classified as fraudulent transactions. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 66 of the IBC is attracted when transactions lack commercial justification and are executed to siphon funds for a fraudulent purpose, which can be inferred from the relationships and absence of statutory tax compliance. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal scrutinized the commercial validity of the transaction by examining standard business practices (raising invoices, deducting TDS) and the proximity of the parties (shared directors, common registered addresses). The absence of standard practices rendered the agreements suspicious and void. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT concluded that the consultancy agreements were created as an afterthought to justify the siphoning of Rs. 65 lakhs, thereby upholding the NCLT's finding of fraud.
operative_order: The NCLAT dismissed the appeal, affirming the Adjudicating Authority's order that directed the Respondents to jointly and severally contribute Rs. 65 Lacs back to the Corporate Debtor. No order as to costs.
summary: The Appellant, erstwhile promoter of Perfect International Fabricators, challenged an NCLT order declaring a Rs. 65 Lacs transfer to Ingenium Advisory LLP as fraudulent under the IBC. The NCLAT found the purported consultancy agreements used to justify the payments were highly suspicious, noting the lack of invoices, no TDS deductions, and the close relationship between the parties (shared office space and cross-directorships). Concluding that the transactions lacked commercial substance, the NCLAT dismissed the appeal and upheld the NCLT's direction to refund the money to the Corporate Debtor.

case_title: K. Srinivas Krishna vs Shyam Arora
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Operational Creditor is PVM Innvensys Pvt. Ltd., Corporate Debtor is C-Tel Infosystems (P) Ltd., Appellant is K. Srinivas Krishna (Suspended Director), Respondents are Shyam Arora (IRP) and State Bank of India (Financial Creditor). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Claim for operational debt. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Original claims of Rs. 50,32,028/- and Rs. 3,67,200/-. The Rs. 3,67,200/- claim was admitted and fully paid. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP initiated on 23-01-2020. CoC constituted on 05-10-2020. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The CoC resolved with 100% voting share to withdraw the Section 9 application after the Corporate Debtor settled the admitted claims of the OC and the sole FC. However, the Operational Creditor refused to sign Form FA because its larger, disputed claim of Rs. 50,32,028/- was rejected. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The IRP filed an application for withdrawal under Section 12A based on the CoC's resolution. NCLT New Delhi dismissed it on 18-02-2021 because it was not signed/filed by the original Applicant (the OC). The Suspended Director appealed to the NCLAT.
legal_issues: Whether a withdrawal application under Section 12A of the IBC can be allowed when the original applicant (Operational Creditor) deliberately refuses to sign Form FA despite full settlement of its admitted claims and 100% CoC approval for withdrawal.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: When an applicant maliciously refuses to sign the withdrawal form despite receiving full payment of its admitted dues and securing 100% CoC approval for withdrawal, the Appellate Tribunal can invoke inherent powers to terminate the insolvency proceedings to prevent an abuse of process. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: While Section 12A of the IBC and Regulation 30A mandate that the withdrawal application be filed by the original applicant, strict adherence to this procedural requirement is not justified if it allows the applicant to extort unverified claims. Rule 11 of the NCLAT Rules, 2016 empowers the Tribunal to override such hyper-technicalities to serve justice. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal noted that the Supreme Court had already dismissed the Operational Creditor's appeal regarding the disputed claim, leaving the creditor with no legitimate ground to block the withdrawal. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT held that the Operational Creditor's refusal to sign Form FA was a blatant misuse of its position and set aside the CIRP admission under its inherent powers.
operative_order: The NCLAT invoked Rule 11 of the NCLAT Rules, 2016, set aside the NCLT's impugned order, and quashed the initiation of the CIRP against the Corporate Debtor. The Corporate Debtor was released from the rigors of CIRP, the IRP was directed to hand over records to the Board of Directors, and the matter was remitted to the NCLT to determine the IRP fees/costs payable by the Corporate Debtor. No costs were awarded.
summary: The Appellant challenged an NCLT order that rejected a Section 12A withdrawal application simply because the Operational Creditor refused to sign Form FA. Despite the Corporate Debtor paying the admitted claims and the CoC approving the withdrawal with 100% voting, the Operational Creditor maliciously held out due to a rejected claim. The NCLAT ruled that the Operational Creditor was misusing the CIRP process as a recovery tool. Invoking its inherent powers under Rule 11, the Tribunal bypassed the technical requirement of the applicant's signature, allowed the appeal, and fully released the Corporate Debtor from insolvency proceedings.

case_title: Precision Hydraulics Private Limited vs Bhairavi Cargo And Logistics Private Limited
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Operational Creditor is Precision Hydraulics Private Limited, Corporate Debtor is Bhairavi Cargo And Logistics Private Limited. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Sale/transfer of MEIS Licenses between July and November 2018. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default of Rs. 1,29,70,574 claimed as of 25.09.2018. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Corporate Debtor issued a legal notice on 26.10.2019. Operational Creditor issued a Section 8 Demand Notice on 26.11.2019. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Corporate Debtor's prior legal notice dated 26.10.2019 acknowledged the sale of certificates but raised disputes regarding payments allegedly made to personal accounts of ex-employees, demanding Rs. 12,02,995 from the Operational Creditor. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Section 9 application dismissed by NCLT Chennai on 04.03.2021 on the ground of a pre-existing dispute.
legal_issues: Whether a pre-existing dispute existed between the parties prior to the issuance of the Section 8 Demand Notice, rendering the Section 9 application non-maintainable?
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An application for initiating CIRP under Section 9 is not maintainable if the Corporate Debtor establishes a plausible pre-existing dispute prior to the issuance of the statutory demand notice. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: 'Pre-existing dispute' under Section 8(2) of the IBC encompasses prior exchanges of legal notices wherein the Corporate Debtor contests the payment mechanics and raises counterclaims. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal relied on the legal notice sent by the Corporate Debtor one month prior to the Section 8 demand notice, which disputed the payment methodology and raised a counterclaim, satisfying the test laid down in Mobilox Innovations. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT affirmed that the exchange of legal notices prior to the Section 8 demand notice clearly established a genuine pre-existing dispute.
operative_order: The NCLAT dismissed the appeal as devoid of merits, upholding the Adjudicating Authority's order rejecting the Section 9 application. No orders as to costs.
summary: The Appellant challenged the NCLT's dismissal of its Section 9 application seeking to initiate CIRP for an unpaid amount of Rs. 1.29 crores relating to the sale of MEIS licenses. The NCLAT affirmed the dismissal, finding that the Corporate Debtor had issued a legal notice a month prior to the Section 8 demand notice, raising genuine disputes over payments routed to personal accounts of employees and asserting a counterclaim. Applying the Mobilox precedent, the Tribunal held that this constituted a valid pre-existing dispute.

case_title: Gay Printers vs Ramesh Kumar Suneja
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Financial Creditor is Gay Printers (Appellant), Corporate Debtor is Pawan Buildwell (Respondent Ramesh Kumar Suneja is the Director). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Claim of financial debt based on an alleged advance in a property deal. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: The disputed amount was treated as a forfeited advance by the Corporate Debtor pursuant to an MOU dated 18.05.2015. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Section 340 Cr.P.C. application dismissed by NCLT on 03.02.2020. The 30-day appeal period expired on 04.03.2020. Appeal filed with a 299-day delay on 29.12.2020. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Corporate Debtor relied on an MOU dated 18.05.2015 to justify forfeiture. Appellant alleged the MOU was forged because the stamp paper was issued on 21.08.2017. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT dismissed the original Section 7 petition for failure to prove financial debt without relying on the MOU. Appellant then filed a Section 340 Cr.P.C. application alleging forgery, which the NCLT dismissed. Appellant appealed to the NCLAT.
legal_issues: 1. Whether the 299-day delay in filing the appeal could be condoned under Section 61 of the IBC in light of the Supreme Court's COVID-19 limitation extension? 2. Whether an application under Section 340 Cr.P.C. is maintainable when the allegedly forged document was not the basis of the Adjudicating Authority's decision?
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An application for prosecution under Section 340 Cr.P.C. is unwarranted if the allegedly fabricated document did not form the basis of the court's adjudication. Furthermore, the statutory power to condone delay is strictly limited and cannot be expanded beyond the prescribed grace period using general limitation extensions if the original limitation expired prior to the relief period. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 340 Cr.P.C. requires it to be 'expedient in the interests of justice' to order an inquiry, a condition not met when the impugned document had no bearing on the final judgement. Under Section 61 of the IBC, delay beyond 15 days cannot be condoned. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal noted that the NCLT dismissed the Section 7 petition because the Appellant failed to prove the debt, completely ignoring the allegedly forged MOU. On limitation, the original 30-day period expired on 04.03.2020, before the Supreme Court's 15.03.2020 COVID-19 relief cutoff. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT held the appeal was hopelessly barred by limitation and inherently lacked merit since the forged document did not influence the NCLT's decision.
operative_order: The NCLAT dismissed the application for condonation of delay and dismissed the appeal both as barred by limitation and on merits. No order as to costs.
summary: The Appellant sought to prosecute the Respondent under Section 340 Cr.P.C., alleging that a forged MOU was submitted during a Section 7 IBC proceeding. The NCLT dismissed the application because the MOU was not relied upon to decide the case. The NCLAT affirmed this decision, noting the forged document did not form the basis of the adjudication. The NCLAT also rejected the Appellant's attempt to use the Supreme Court's COVID-19 limitation extension, holding that the appeal was time-barred by 299 days, as the limitation period expired before the relief took effect.

case_title: Raja Bahadur Welfare Association vs Okay Estate Developers Private Limited
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Raja Bahadur Welfare Association (a tenant welfare association). Respondents are Okay Estate Developers Pvt. Ltd. (Demerged Company) and Grid Infradevelopers Pvt. Ltd. (Resulting Company). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: A Scheme of Arrangement for the Demerger of the Project Division of the Demerged Company into the Resulting Company. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: An outstanding amount of Rs. 1,48,33,407 was shown as payable to the 'erstwhile owner' of Rajabhadur Building in the financial statements. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: NCLT passed orders dispensing with creditors' meetings on 14.05.2020 and ordering publication on 17.07.2020. Appeal filed on 26.02.2021. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The provisional balance sheet of the Demerged Company as of 31.12.2019 reflected the 'Rajabhadur Building payable account' as constituting approximately 15% of the total unsecured creditors. Respondents refused to share the Scheme documents with the Appellants, claiming they were only tenants and not creditors/shareholders. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Mumbai directed the issuance of notices to regulators and publication but did not explicitly secure notice to the Appellants. The Appellants filed an appeal under Section 421 of the Companies Act to obtain the Scheme documents and raise objections.
legal_issues: Whether a welfare association representing tenants/parties whose payable amount constitutes more than 5% of the total unsecured debt has the locus standi to receive notice and object to a Scheme of Arrangement under Section 230(4) of the Companies Act, 2013?
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Any creditor or class of creditors whose debt represents not less than 5% of the total outstanding debt of a company undergoing a Scheme of Arrangement has a statutory right to object to the scheme and must be served with the scheme documents. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 230(4) of the Companies Act, 2013 explicitly grants the right to object to a compromise or arrangement to persons holding not less than 5% of the outstanding debt. The Tribunal also applied the Supreme Court's Suo Motu order to exclude the pandemic period for limitation purposes. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal scrutinized the Respondent company's provisional balance sheet and found that the payable amount linked to the Appellants' building was around 15% of the total unsecured creditors, clearly exceeding the 5% statutory threshold. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT concluded that the Appellants had locus standi to object to the Scheme of Arrangement and were entitled to be served with the scheme documents.
operative_order: The NCLAT allowed the appeal, directing the Respondents to serve the Appellants with the notice, company scheme, and related papers within 30 days. The NCLT was directed to consider the Appellants' objections before the final disposal of the petition.
summary: The Appellant, representing tenants of a building acquired by the Respondent, challenged an NCLT order regarding a Scheme of Demerger, arguing they were denied notice and copies of the Scheme despite being owed a substantial sum. The Respondents contended the Appellants were merely tenants and not creditors. The NCLAT analyzed the financial statements and found that the payable amount associated with the building constituted approximately 15% of the total unsecured debt. Because this exceeded the 5% threshold under Section 230(4) of the Companies Act, the NCLAT granted locus standi to the Appellants and directed the Respondents to serve them with the Scheme documents for filing objections.

case_title: M Sai Eswara Swamy vs Siti Vision Digital Media Pvt. Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Financial Creditors are Vision Infotel India Pvt. Ltd. and Vision Infracon India Pvt. Ltd. Appellant is M Sai Eswara Swamy (50% shareholder and Director of Financial Creditors). Corporate Debtor is Siti Vision Digital Media Pvt. Ltd. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Alleged loan advanced to the Corporate Debtor. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Unpaid loan amount (exact quantum not specified in the order). 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Not explicitly stated. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: There was a deadlock in the Financial Creditor companies. The other 50% shareholder/Director refused to sign a board resolution to sue the Corporate Debtor (in which his wife held a 4% share). Further, no board resolution under Section 186 of the Companies Act was passed for advancing the loan. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The NCLT dismissed the Section 7 petition for lack of a board resolution authorizing the Appellant to file it, and lack of a resolution for advancing the loan. The Appellant appealed, arguing the petition should be maintained under the 'doctrine of derivative action'.
legal_issues: Whether a 50% shareholder and director of a Financial Creditor company can file a Section 7 petition under the IBC on the basis of the 'doctrine of derivative action' despite the absence of a board resolution authorizing such filing.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The doctrine of derivative action cannot be invoked to bypass the explicit statutory requirements for initiating a Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process under the IBC. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Under Section 7(1) of the IBC read with the Central Government Notification dated 27.02.2019 (S.O. 1091(E)), only specific persons, including a person 'duly authorized by the board of directors of a company', are competent to file an application on behalf of a financial creditor. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal noted it was undisputed that there was no board resolution authorizing the Appellant to file the petition, nor was there a board resolution passed to advance the loan as required under Section 186 of the Companies Act. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT held that general corporate doctrines like derivative action do not override the strict procedural mandates of the IBC notification. The lack of a board resolution renders the Section 7 petition non-maintainable.
operative_order: The NCLAT summarily dismissed the appeal without issuing notice to the Respondent, finding no flaw in the Adjudicating Authority's order. No order as to costs.
summary: The Appellant, a 50% shareholder and director of the Financial Creditor, filed a Section 7 petition against the Corporate Debtor without a board resolution due to a corporate deadlock. He relied on the 'doctrine of derivative action' to maintain the petition. The NCLAT upheld the NCLT's dismissal of the petition, ruling that the doctrine of derivative action does not apply to Section 7 of the IBC. A specific MCA notification strictly requires a person to be duly authorized by the board of directors to file on behalf of a company.

case_title: Sardar Ji Di Hatti Departmental Store Pvt. Ltd. vs Sunil Kumar Agrawal
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Operational Creditor/Appellant is M/s Sardar Ji Di Hatti Departmental Store Pvt. Ltd. Corporate Debtor is M/s KPG International Pvt. Ltd. Resolution Professional/Respondent is Sunil Kumar Agrawal. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Outstanding dues owed by the Corporate Debtor to the Operational Creditor. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Operational Creditor claimed an outstanding amount of Rs. 43,45,844/-. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP commenced on 27.01.2020. Public announcement inviting claims was made on 31.01.2020, with a deadline of 12.02.2020. Claim was submitted via speed post on 22.01.2020 (sic, context suggests Dec 2020) and via email on 24.12.2020. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The Appellant admitted missing the public announcement and being unaware of the CIRP until December 2020. The RP rejected the claim on 31.12.2020 and 05.01.2021 because it was filed after a delay and a resolution plan was already pending before the CoC. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Appellant filed I.A. No. 143 of 2021 seeking directions to the RP to admit the delayed claim. NCLT New Delhi dismissed the application on 09.03.2021, holding that under Regulation 12(2), the RP could not be directed to consider the time-barred claim. Appellant appealed to NCLAT.
legal_issues: Whether the Resolution Professional is obligated to admit a claim filed by an Operational Creditor after the expiry of the 90-day statutory period provided under Regulation 12(2) of the IBBI (CIRP) Regulations, especially when a resolution plan is already under consideration by the CoC.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A creditor's claim filed beyond the 90-day period stipulated in Regulation 12(2) of the CIRP Regulations is liable to be rejected, particularly when the creditor had knowledge or means of knowledge of the CIRP and the resolution process is at an advanced stage (e.g., a resolution plan is pending CoC approval). 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: The statutory timeline for filing claims is designed to ensure the time-bound nature of the CIRP. While some NCLT orders have treated Regulation 12(2) as directory, a party that deliberately delays submission despite knowledge of the process cannot bypass the deadline, especially once a plan is pending. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal noted the Appellant's own admissions in its pleadings that it missed the publication and only filed the claim long after the 90-day expiry. The Tribunal found the Appellant had full knowledge and deliberately failed to submit the claim in time. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT held that the RP and Adjudicating Authority acted correctly in rejecting the time-barred claim, as admitting it at an advanced stage would derail the time-bound CIRP.
operative_order: The NCLAT affirmed the order dated 09.03.2021 passed by the Adjudicating Authority (NCLT, New Delhi Bench-V) and dismissed the appeal. No order as to costs.
summary: The Appellant, an Operational Creditor, challenged the NCLT's dismissal of its application seeking admission of a delayed claim. The Appellant had missed the public announcement and filed its claim months after the 90-day deadline under Regulation 12(2) had expired, at which point a resolution plan was already pending before the CoC. The NCLAT upheld the rejection, noting that the CIRP is a time-bound process and the Appellant's own admissions showed it failed to act diligently despite having means of knowledge. The appeal was dismissed.

case_title: Mapletree Leather Goods Pvt Ltd vs Savan Godiawala & Ors
appeal_number: IA NO. 436 OF 2021 in TA No. 91/2021 in Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 314 of 2020
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant/Applicant is Mapletree Leather Goods Pvt Ltd (Resolution Applicant). Corporate Debtor is M/s Falcon Tyres Limited. First Respondent is Savan Godiawala (Resolution Professional). Eighth Respondent is the Liquidator. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Submission of a Resolution Plan for the revival of the Corporate Debtor. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Not explicitly detailed (focus is on liquidation vs resolution plan). 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP initiated on 1.5.2018. Liquidation order passed on 30.12.2019. E-Auction scheduled for 29.09.2021. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The CoC rejected the Appellant's resolution plan due to failure to provide a Performance Bank Guarantee and discrepancies in the revised financial offer (found to be Rs. 100 Crores instead of Rs. 370 Crores). NCLT ordered liquidation. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Bengaluru ordered liquidation on 30.12.2019. Appellant filed an appeal (Comp. App. (AT) (Ins.) No. 314 of 2020) and filed IA 436/2021 seeking to stay the E-Auction scheduled for 29.09.2021.
legal_issues: Whether the Appellant/Resolution Applicant is entitled to an interim stay of the liquidation process and E-Auction pending the final adjudication of its appeal against the liquidation order.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An interim stay of a scheduled liquidation E-Auction will not be granted to a failed Resolution Applicant when doing so would amount to granting the final relief sought in the appeal and scuttle the statutory liquidation process. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: The commercial wisdom of the Committee of Creditors in rejecting a resolution plan (e.g., for lack of a bank guarantee or inadequate financial offer) is paramount and not generally subject to interference by the Adjudicating or Appellate Authority unless there is a clear statutory violation. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal evaluated the 'prima facie' case and 'balance of convenience'. It found that since the liquidation order was passed in 2019 and the liquidator had already taken steps toward auction, staying the auction on the eve of the event would disrupt the process and not serve the balance of convenience. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT concluded that the Appellant failed to establish a prima facie case or that the balance of convenience favoured halting the E-Auction, and therefore denied the interim stay.
operative_order: The NCLAT dismissed I.A. No. 436/2021 seeking a stay on the E-Auction and liquidation proceedings. No costs were awarded.
summary: The Appellant, whose resolution plan was rejected by the CoC, challenged the NCLT's liquidation order and sought an interim stay to halt an E-Auction of the Corporate Debtor's assets scheduled for 29.09.2021. The NCLAT denied the stay, emphasizing that the CoC's commercial wisdom in rejecting the plan (due to lack of a performance bank guarantee and inadequate offer) is paramount. The Tribunal ruled that the balance of convenience did not favour disrupting the advanced liquidation process, and dismissed the interim application.

case_title: BKB Transport Pvt. Ltd. vs NTPC Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Operational Creditor/Appellant is BKB Transport Pvt. Ltd. Corporate Debtor/Respondent is NTPC Ltd. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Contract Agreement dated 30.06.2016 for transportation of coal from Amrapali Mine to Bandag Railway Siding via RCR mode for a bid amount of Rs. 2,11,95,00,000/-. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Operational Creditor claimed Rs. 11,21,44,047.40/- as due and payable. Corporate Debtor alleged short supply and claimed retention of Rs. 78,95,38,277/- as penalties. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Section 8 notice dated 12.04.2020. Corporate Debtor replied on 21.04.2020 disputing the debt and claiming penalties. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The Corporate Debtor sent multiple letters in 2018 alleging short supply of coal and asserting the Operational Creditor's liability for penalties. The Corporate Debtor's reply to the Section 8 notice reiterated this pre-existing dispute regarding penalties for short supply. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Principal Bench dismissed the Section 9 application on 04.01.2021, finding a pre-existing dispute regarding the short supply and penalties. The Appellant appealed, specifically requesting the expunction of certain paragraphs in the NCLT order that commented on the merits of the dispute.
legal_issues: Whether specific observations made by the Adjudicating Authority touching upon the merits of a pre-existing dispute (e.g., confirming the occurrence of short supply and liability for penalty) should be expunged to prevent prejudice in future arbitration proceedings.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: While dismissing a Section 9 application on the ground of a pre-existing dispute, the Adjudicating Authority must not render definitive findings on the merits of that dispute, as such findings could prejudice the parties in subsequent civil or arbitral proceedings. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Under Section 9 of the IBC, the Adjudicating Authority's role is limited to determining the existence of a dispute prior to the demand notice, not adjudicating the dispute itself. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The NCLAT noted that the Adjudicating Authority's paragraphs 29 and 34 definitively concluded that the Operational Creditor failed to supply coal and was liable for penalties. The Respondent conceded these paragraphs touched on the merits. 4.
