DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT ordered the expunction of paragraphs 29 and 34 from the impugned order, without disturbing the underlying dismissal of the Section 9 petition for a pre-existing dispute.
operative_order: The NCLAT disposed of the appeal by ordering the expunction of Paragraphs 29 and 34 from the NCLT's impugned order dated 04.01.2021. The NCLAT clarified it did not go into the merits of the pre-existing dispute.
summary: The Appellant challenged an NCLT order dismissing its Section 9 application against NTPC Ltd. due to a pre-existing dispute over coal supply shortages and penalties. The Appellant did not contest the dismissal itself but requested the removal of specific paragraphs (29 and 34) where the NCLT conclusively ruled on the merits of the short supply and penalty liability, arguing this would prejudice future arbitration. The NCLAT agreed, and with the Respondent's concession, ordered the expunction of those specific paragraphs to preserve the parties' rights in other forums, disposing of the appeal.

case_title: Fipola Retail (India) Private Limited vs M2N Interiors
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant (Corporate Debtor) is Fipola Retail (India) Private Limited, and the Respondent (Operational Creditor) is M2N Interiors, a sole proprietorship represented by its proprietor Mr. M. Murali. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Not explicitly detailed in the provided order, but pertains to an underlying operational debt. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: The specific default amount and dates are not detailed in the appellate order. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: On 25.02.2020, the NCLT initially granted time to amend the cause title. The matter was delayed due to the Covid-19 lockdown, with further time for compliance granted on 17.09.2020. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The Respondent filed a memo on 05.10.2020 citing an NCLAT judgment (Neeta Saha vs Mr. Ram Niwas Gupta) to argue that the application was maintainable without the previously ordered amendment. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Chennai initially directed the Operational Creditor to amend the cause title because the petition was filed in the name of the proprietorship concern. Subsequently, on 01.02.2021, the NCLT accepted the Respondent's memo, took the petition on record, and directed the Corporate Debtor to file a reply. The Corporate Debtor appealed this order, arguing the NCLT improperly reviewed its own prior order.
legal_issues: Whether an application under Section 9 of the IBC filed in the name of a Sole Proprietorship Concern, represented by its Sole Proprietor, is legally maintainable under Section 2 and Section 3(23) of the Code?
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An insolvency application filed by a sole proprietorship firm is legally maintainable under the IBC, provided it is properly represented by its sole proprietor. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 2 of the IBC explicitly states that the provisions of the Code apply to 'proprietorship firms', and the definition of 'person' under Section 3(23) is an inclusive definition that encompasses such entities. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal examined the cause title and found that it reflected both the name of the sole proprietorship concern and its sole proprietor, thereby sufficiently establishing the legal identity required to file the petition. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Relying on the precedent set in 'Neeta Saha vs Mr. Ram Niwas Gupta', the NCLAT concluded that there was no error in the Adjudicating Authority taking the application on record without a formal amendment, thus rejecting the Corporate Debtor's contention.
operative_order: The NCLAT found no illegality in the Common Order passed by the Adjudicating Authority on 01.02.2021. The appeal was declared devoid of merits and accordingly dismissed, with no orders as to costs.
summary: The Appellant challenged an NCLT order that took a Section 9 application filed by a sole proprietorship on record. The Appellant argued that the NCLT improperly reviewed an earlier order directing the Operational Creditor to amend its cause title. The NCLAT dismissed the appeal, ruling that under Section 2 and the inclusive definition of a 'person' in Section 3(23) of the IBC, a petition filed by a proprietorship firm represented by its sole proprietor is perfectly maintainable. Following established precedent, the NCLAT upheld the Adjudicating Authority's decision to proceed with the matter.

case_title: Ind Bharat Power Madras Ltd vs Rohan Varma Constructions Pvt Ltd
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Ashish Arjunkumar Rathi, Liquidator for Ind-Barath Power (Madras) Ltd. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Administration of the liquidation process of the Corporate Debtor. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: N/A. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Liquidation order passed on 22.04.2019. NCLT granted a stay on the liquidation process on 15.11.2019. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The Liquidator filed an application seeking exclusion of the stay period from the calculation of time for asset realization under IBBI Regulations, as the judicial stay prevented the completion of the sale and prejudiced his fee computation under Regulation 4. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Hyderabad dismissed IA No. 28 of 2021 on 22.04.2021, choosing to extend the liquidation period by one year instead of explicitly granting the exclusion of the stay period. The Liquidator appealed to the NCLAT.
legal_issues: Whether the period of a judicially imposed stay on a liquidation process should be explicitly excluded from the statutory timeline for the realization of assets and the calculation of the liquidator's fee under Regulations 4 and 44 of the IBBI (Liquidation Process) Regulations, 2016.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The period during which a judicial stay is operational must be explicitly excluded from the statutory timelines for asset realization and liquidator fee calculation, in accordance with the maxim 'actus curiae neminem gravabit' (the act of the court shall harm no person). 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Regulation 44 read with Regulation 4(3) sets specific timelines that affect the Liquidator's fee brackets. A failure to explicitly exclude a judicial stay unfairly prejudices the Liquidator by pushing them into a lower fee bracket despite the delay being beyond their control. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal noted the indisputable existence of the stay from 15.11.2019, which factually halted the liquidator's ability to conclude the sale. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT concluded that the Adjudicating Authority erred in merely extending the liquidation period rather than formally excluding the stay period, thereby wrongfully prejudicing the Liquidator's rightful fee claim.
operative_order: The NCLAT allowed the appeal and set aside the impugned order, directing the formal exclusion of the stay period (operative since 15.11.2019) from the calculation of the time taken for the realization and distribution of assets under Regulation 44 read with Regulation 4(3). No orders as to costs.
summary: The Liquidator appealed against an NCLT order that refused to formally exclude a judicial stay period from the liquidation timeline, which adversely impacted the Liquidator's fee structure under Regulation 4 of the IBBI Regulations. The NCLAT applied the maxim 'actus curiae neminem gravabit', ruling that the Liquidator should not suffer financial prejudice due to delays caused by court orders. The Tribunal allowed the appeal and directed the explicit exclusion of the stay period from the statutory timelines.

case_title: Mr. Dhananjay Krishnanath Gaikwad vs Mr Gaurav Adukia & Ors
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Dhananjay Krishnanath Gaikwad. Corporate Debtor is Tuljabhavani Cold Storage Pvt. Ltd. (Respondent No. 3). Respondent No. 1 is Gaurav Ashok Adukia (Resolution Professional). Respondent No. 2 is ICICI Bank Ltd. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Not directly applicable; relates to the CIRP process and procedural exclusion of time. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Not detailed; concerns procedural delays during CIRP. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The disputed exclusion period was 146 days from 04.03.2020 to 27.07.2020. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: On 04.03.2020, in CA(AT)(INS) 376/2020, NCLAT recorded the Appellant's intent to settle and stated that if the CoC was not yet constituted, it 'may not be constituted till the next date.' On 23.07.2020, NCLAT directed the RP to constitute the CoC and proceed in accordance with the law. The RP received this order on 27.07.2020 and constituted the CoC on 29.07.2020. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Mumbai granted an exclusion of 146 days (from 04.03.2020 to 27.07.2020) from the CIRP timeline via an order dated 17.03.2021 in I.A. No. 410 of 2021. The Appellant appealed to the NCLAT arguing the 04.03.2020 order did not constitute a formal stay.
legal_issues: Whether a statement in an appellate tribunal order noting that the 'CoC may not be constituted till the next date' functions as a judicial stay on the CIRP timeline, justifying the exclusion of that time period from the statutory CIRP duration.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Time elapsed during which the Resolution Professional is judicially restrained from constituting the Committee of Creditors and advancing the CIRP must be excluded from the statutory timeline of the CIRP. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: The wording 'may not be constituted' in a judicial order functions practically as a stay, suspending the RP's ability to act. A subsequent order explicitly permitting the RP 'to constitute the Committee of Creditors and to proceed further' confirms the existence of the prior stay. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal read the order dated 04.03.2020 contextually with the subsequent order dated 23.07.2020. The explicit permission granted in July to constitute the CoC logically necessitated the conclusion that a stay was operational since March. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT concluded the NCLT correctly interpreted the prior NCLAT orders as having stayed the CIRP, and thus the exclusion of 146 days was proper and legal.
operative_order: The NCLAT dismissed the appeal, upholding the NCLT Mumbai's order dated 17.03.2021 in I.A. No. 410 of 2021 that granted the exclusion of 146 days from the CIRP period. No orders as to costs.
summary: The Appellant challenged an NCLT order that excluded 146 days from the CIRP timeline, arguing that a prior NCLAT order stating the 'CoC may not be constituted' was merely a recording of a statement, not a formal stay. The NCLAT rejected this argument, finding that a subsequent NCLAT order explicitly lifting the restriction and allowing the RP to proceed proved that a stay was indeed in effect. The NCLAT upheld the Adjudicating Authority's decision to exclude the 146-day period, dismissing the appeal.

case_title: Rajnish Gupta vs KG Somani Liquidator Of Delicious Coco Water Pvt. Ltd. & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Rajnish Gupta. Respondents are KG Somani (Liquidator of Delicious Coco Water Pvt. Ltd.) and SIDBI. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Not applicable; relates to liquidation proceedings and settlement offer. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Not explicitly detailed. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Main IA 412/2021 was reserved for orders on 06.08.2021. Appellant filed IA 3710/2021 to introduce new documents, which was rejected on 26.08.2021. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Appellant sought to introduce a letter from SIDBI dated 19.08.2021 accepting a settlement offer but subject to the NCLT's decision. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT New Delhi dismissed IA 3710/2021 on 26.08.2021, refusing to take additional documents on record as the main IA was already reserved.
legal_issues: Whether additional documents can be brought on record through a fresh application after the main application has already been heard and reserved for orders.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An application to place additional documents on record is not maintainable if filed after the main matter has already been heard and reserved for orders. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: The Tribunal affirmed the procedural rule safeguarding the finality of hearings once orders are reserved. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal noted the new application was filed post-reservation, and the document itself did not mandate halting liquidation. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT held that the Adjudicating Authority correctly denied the introduction of new documents post-reservation, finding no merit to admit the appeal.
operative_order: The NCLAT declined to admit the appeal, thereby dismissing it.
summary: The Appellant challenged an NCLT order that denied permission to place a settlement letter from SIDBI on record. The NCLT rejected the request because the main application was already reserved for orders. The NCLAT upheld this procedural dismissal, finding no merit to admit the appeal.

case_title: R. Velu vs. Invent Assets Securitisation & Reconstruction Pvt Ltd
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is R. Velu, the Resolution Professional of the Corporate Debtor (Palm Lagoon Backwater Resorts Pvt Ltd). Respondent is Invent Assets Securitisation & Reconstruction Pvt Ltd, the Successful Resolution Applicant. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: The Respondent submitted a Resolution Plan which was approved by the CoC on 19.08.2020 and by the Adjudicating Authority on 10.09.2020. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: As per the approved plan, the Respondent was required to pay Rs. 50,00,000 (after adjusting EMD/Performance Guarantee of Rs. 25,00,000) within 15 days of the order. The Respondent failed to pay. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: On 23.09.2020, Respondent sought extension. On 23.10.2020, Respondent sought to withdraw the plan citing RBI rejection of UVARC plan. 330 days CIRP limit expired by end of October 2020. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: E-mail communications showed the Respondent's refusal to implement the plan. The Monitoring Committee resolved on 30.10.2020 to seek liquidation. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: RP filed MA No. 186/KOB/2020 for liquidation under Section 33(3). NCLT Kochi by order dated 10.02.2021 dismissed it holding it was functus officio to order liquidation or direct EMD refund.
legal_issues: Whether the Adjudicating Authority has the jurisdiction to order liquidation of a Corporate Debtor under Section 33(3) of the IBC if the Successful Resolution Applicant fails to implement the approved resolution plan after the expiry of the 330-day maximum CIRP period.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: If a Successful Resolution Applicant contravenes the approved resolution plan and the statutory time limit for CIRP expires, the Adjudicating Authority is bound to pass an order for liquidation. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 33(3) of the IBC permits 'any person' whose interests are prejudicially affected to apply for liquidation if the plan is contravened. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Adjudicating Authority must determine objective contravention of the plan's payment terms and the exhaustion of the mandatory 330-day timeline under Section 12(3) of the IBC. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Adjudicating Authority erred in holding itself functus officio; upon contravention of the plan by the Respondent and completion of 330 days, it was mandatory to order liquidation under Sections 33(3) and 33(4).
operative_order: The NCLAT allowed the appeal in part, set aside the NCLT Kochi's impugned order dated 10.02.2021 rejecting the liquidation application, and directed the Adjudicating Authority to pass an order of liquidation under Section 33(3) and 33(4) of the IBC.
summary: The Resolution Professional appealed against NCLT Kochi's refusal to order liquidation after the Successful Resolution Applicant (Respondent) failed to implement the approved plan and sought its withdrawal. The NCLAT held that since the 330-day CIRP period had expired and the Respondent contravened the plan's payment terms, the NCLT was not functus officio but statutorily obligated to order liquidation under Section 33(3) of the IBC. The appeal was allowed.

case_title: Ms. Indrani Brahmachari vs. Mr. Chandra Prakash
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is an allottee/homebuyer. Respondent No. 1 is the RP of the Corporate Debtor (Granite Gate Properties Pvt. Ltd.). Respondent No. 2 is Ms. Arti Saraf (landlady of alternate premises). Respondent No. 3 is Mr. Vidur Bharadwaj (Ex-Director of holding company Three C Infra Pvt. Ltd). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Appellant booked an apartment in 2010. Due to delay, Respondent No. 3 allegedly accommodated Appellant in alternate rented premises owned by Respondent No. 2, undertaking to pay rent. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Respondent No. 2 demanded rent from October 2019 and filed an eviction suit after CIRP was initiated on 10.01.2019. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP initiated 10.01.2019. Appellant filed a claim in Form C on 23.03.2020. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: A Rent Agreement dated 27.11.2018 was executed only between Appellant and Respondent No. 2. A cheque for advance rent was issued by Respondent No. 3. No contractual link existed between the Corporate Debtor and the rent agreement. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Appellant filed IA 2468 of 2020 before NCLT New Delhi seeking protection from eviction and directing the RP to pay rent. NCLT dismissed it on 15.07.2020 holding Corporate Debtor had nothing to do with the rent agreement.
legal_issues: Whether a Corporate Debtor undergoing CIRP can be directed to pay rent for alternate accommodation provided to an allottee by an ex-director of its holding company, based on an arrangement to which the Corporate Debtor was not a party.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An ad-hoc private arrangement providing preferential benefits to one allottee by an ex-director cannot be enforced against the Corporate Debtor in CIRP unless there is a binding prior contract linking the Corporate Debtor to such liability. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Directing the RP to pay rent for one allottee's alternate accommodation would violate the IBC's scheme by according preferential treatment not provided to other similarly situated allottees. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal scrutinized the rent agreement and found the Corporate Debtor was not a signatory, thereby establishing no privity of contract to fasten liability during CIRP. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Even applying the doctrine of lifting the corporate veil, the Corporate Debtor could not be forced to bear the rental costs for the Appellant as it lacked a contractual basis and would disrupt the equitable treatment of allottees under the IBC.
operative_order: The NCLAT disposed of the appeal, declining to grant the relief of restraining eviction or directing the RP to pay rent, while observing the Appellant may take appropriate defense in the civil eviction proceedings initiated by Respondent No. 2. No costs were imposed.
summary: An allottee appealed an NCLT order refusing to restrain her eviction from alternate rented premises or direct the RP of the Corporate Debtor to pay her rent. The NCLAT held that the rent arrangement was a private deal involving an ex-director and the landlady, with no binding contract against the Corporate Debtor. Enforcing it would grant impermissible preferential treatment to the Appellant over other allottees in CIRP. The appeal was dismissed.

case_title: M/s. Dyanamic Engineers Limited vs. M/s. Muhlenbau Equipments Private Limited
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is M/s Dyanamic Engineers Limited (Operational Creditor). Respondent is M/s Muhlenbau Equipments Private Limited (Corporate Debtor). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Respondent issued a Purchase Order on 11.03.2016 for supply and commissioning of automation and control systems for Rs. 33,00,000 plus taxes. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Invoices dated 09.12.2016 aggregated Rs. 37,86,750. Respondent made part payments leaving a principal due of Rs. 8,19,977 (total claim Rs. 12,96,427 with interest). 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Demand Notice under Section 8 issued on 13.11.2019. No reply was sent. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Post filing of the Section 9 petition, Respondent sent an e-mail on 03.11.2020 stating work was unsatisfactory and demanded withdrawal of the case to issue Form-C, establishing the dispute was an afterthought. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Section 9 application CP (IB) No. 119/BB/2020 was filed. NCLT Bengaluru by order dated 24.02.2021 disposed of it, directing Respondent to settle the claim in 3 months instead of admitting the CIRP.
legal_issues: Whether the Adjudicating Authority can dispose of a Section 9 application with a direction to settle the claim when the operational debt and default are established and no pre-existing dispute was raised prior to the statutory demand notice.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Once an operational debt and default are conclusively established and no valid pre-existing dispute is raised prior to the Section 8 demand notice, the Adjudicating Authority must admit the Section 9 application. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 9 admission is mandatory ('shall admit') if the application is complete, unpaid, and undisputed; the Tribunal cannot exercise equitable jurisdiction to substitute admission with a direction to settle. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: A dispute raised via email only after the initiation of insolvency proceedings (demanding withdrawal of the case for issuing statutory forms) is a spurious afterthought and does not constitute a pre-existing dispute. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Adjudicating Authority's order directing settlement was patently illegal and reflected non-application of mind since the statutory thresholds of debt and default under Section 3(12) and 5(21) were fully met.
operative_order: The NCLAT allowed the appeal, set aside the NCLT Bengaluru's order dated 24.02.2021, and directed the Adjudicating Authority to admit the Section 9 application and initiate CIRP against the Corporate Debtor within 15 days.
summary: The Operational Creditor challenged NCLT's refusal to admit its Section 9 application despite undisputed debt and default, where NCLT merely directed the Corporate Debtor to settle the claim in 3 months. The NCLAT held that since the debt and default were proven and the dispute was an afterthought raised post-petition, admission was mandatory. The appeal was allowed, and the NCLT was directed to initiate CIRP.

case_title: Sunil Kumar Agrawal vs. Committee of Creditors, KPG International Pvt. Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Sunil Kumar Agrawal, Resolution Professional of KPG International Pvt. Ltd. Respondent No. 1 is the Committee of Creditors through PNB. Respondent No. 2 is Mrs. Rama Gupta, Resolution Applicant. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: CIRP of KPG International Pvt. Ltd. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: N/A (Dispute pertains to CIRP timeline calculation). 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP commenced on 29.01.2020. 180 days expired on 27.07.2020. Central and State Governments imposed Covid-19 lockdown from 25.03.2020 to 31.10.2020 (221 days). 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: RP filed an application seeking exclusion of 221 days from the CIRP timeline due to the pandemic lockdown to facilitate the approval of a received resolution plan. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT New Delhi vide order dated 01.04.2021 partly allowed the application, excluding only 98 days (25.03.2020 to 30.06.2020). The RP appealed to exclude the full 221 days.
legal_issues: Whether the entire period of the Covid-19 lockdown (221 days) should be excluded from the computation of the statutory CIRP period under the IBC.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The entire duration of government-imposed lockdowns due to the Covid-19 pandemic must be excluded from CIRP timelines to prevent severe prejudice to the resolution process. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: As per IBBI Notification dated 29.03.2020 and Regulation 40C, the lockdown period shall not be counted within the timeline of the resolution process. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal evaluated the timeline and took judicial notice of the lockdown spanning from 25.03.2020 to 31.10.2020. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Adjudicating Authority erred by only excluding 98 days; excluding the full 221 days was necessary to fulfill the legislative intent of the IBC and allow the CoC to approve the pending resolution plan.
operative_order: The NCLAT set aside the impugned order dated 01.04.2021, allowed the appeal, and directed the exclusion of 221 days (from 25.03.2020 to 31.10.2020) as well as the time spent pursuing the appeal from the CIRP period.
summary: The Resolution Professional appealed an NCLT order that excluded only 98 days of the Covid-19 lockdown from the statutory CIRP period. The NCLAT held that based on IBBI notifications, the entire 221-day lockdown period from March to October 2020 must be excluded to allow for a proper resolution process. The appeal was allowed.

case_title: Dhanlaxmi Bank Ltd. vs. Techno Fab Manufacturing Ltd. & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Dhanlaxmi Bank Ltd., a secured creditor. Respondents are Techno Fab Manufacturing Ltd. & Ors.. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: The Appellant held an exclusive first charge over an asset of the Corporate Debtor under Section 52(1)(b) of the IBC. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: N/A (Dispute over realization of security interest during liquidation). 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Liquidation was ordered on 05.09.2018. The physical possession of the asset was handed to the Appellant on 03.09.2019. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Auctions were conducted on 03.09.2019 and 06.01.2021, showing gaps of 15 months and 8 months where no effective steps were taken to successfully realize the security interest. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The Liquidator demanded the asset back. The Appellant sought a 6-month extension to realize the security, which the Adjudicating Authority dismissed, prompting this appeal.
legal_issues: Whether a secured creditor can retain possession of a secured asset indefinitely during liquidation if it fails to realize its security interest within the prescribed statutory timeframe.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A secured creditor must realize its security interest in a time-bound manner; failure to do so mandates relinquishment of the asset to the liquidation estate. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Under Regulation 21-A(2) and Regulation 21(3) of the IBBI (Liquidation Process) Regulations, 2016, a secured creditor must realize the asset and remit excess funds within 180 days; failing this, the asset automatically becomes part of the liquidation estate. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal relied on the undisputed timeline (3 years since liquidation commencement and prolonged inaction) to conclude that the creditor was given ample opportunity but failed to realize the asset. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Adjudicating Authority rightly directed the return of the asset within 7 days as the Appellant failed to comply with the statutory time limits for realization.
operative_order: The NCLAT summarily dismissed the appeal, finding no legal flaw in the Adjudicating Authority's direction for the Appellant to hand over physical possession of the asset back to the liquidator within 7 days.
summary: The Appellant, a secured creditor, took physical possession of a secured asset but failed to successfully auction it for over three years following the liquidation order. After the Adjudicating Authority directed the return of the asset to the liquidation estate, the Appellant appealed, seeking a 6-month extension. The NCLAT upheld the lower court's decision, ruling that under IBBI Liquidation Regulations 21 and 21-A, a secured creditor must realize its security interest in a time-bound manner (180 days), failing which the asset reverts to the liquidation estate.

case_title: Jitendra Mehta & Ors vs Indtext India Pvt. Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Jitendra Mehta & Ors (Appellants/Claimed Financial Creditors), Indtext India Pvt. Ltd. (Respondent/Corporate Debtor). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Claim for consideration of retirement of director Mohit Jitendra Mehta, reimbursement of interest payable for a vehicle loan (Mercedes E Class), and reimbursement of expenses as per MoUs dated 18.03.2017 and 27.11.2017. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Claimed amount of Rs. 1,29,33,381/- with date of default on 30.11.2018. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The Corporate Debtor allegedly issued cheques and acknowledged the debt. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: MoUs dated 18.03.2017 and 27.11.2017 detailing the agreement between retiring director Mohit Jitendra Mehta and continuing director Ravi Avinash Shuthar for repayment of invested amounts and car loan instalments. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: A Section 7 application was dismissed by the Adjudicating Authority via impugned order dated 30.03.2021 on the grounds that the amount claimed was not a financial debt.
legal_issues: Whether the amount claimed by a retiring director as consideration for retirement, vehicle loan reimbursement, and expenses under an MoU constitutes a 'financial debt' under Section 5(8) of the IBC, and whether the appellant qualifies as a 'Financial Creditor' under Section 5(7).
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Amounts agreed to be paid to a retiring director by another director for return of investment and personal vehicle loan reimbursements under a mutual understanding do not constitute a financial debt. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: The bench interpreted 'financial debt' under Section 5(8) of the IBC, finding that personal agreements between directors for retirement consideration and vehicle expenses lack the commercial effect of a borrowing by the corporate debtor. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal examined the MoUs and found they reflected an inter-se arrangement between the retiring director and the continuing director to repay investments, rather than a debt disbursed against the consideration for the time value of money to the company. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The bench definitively upheld the Adjudicating Authority's ruling that the claimed amount is not a financial debt under Section 5(8) and the appellants are not Financial Creditors under Section 5(7), dismissing the appeal.
operative_order: The Appeal is dismissed summarily without notice to the other side.
summary: Jitendra Mehta & Ors filed a Section 7 application against Indtext India Pvt. Ltd. claiming Rs. 1,29,33,381/- arising from MoUs regarding retirement consideration and vehicle loan reimbursements. The Adjudicating Authority dismissed the petition, ruling the claim was not a financial debt. The NCLAT upheld the dismissal, concluding that the MoUs reflected a personal arrangement between directors rather than a borrowing by the Corporate Debtor, thereby not qualifying as a financial debt under Section 5(8) of the IBC.

case_title: Jatin Bachani vs Manish Kumar Gupta
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Jatin Bachani (Appellant/Allottee and Financial Creditor), Shri Manish Kumar Gupta (Respondent No. 1/Resolution Professional of M/s Three C Project Pvt. Ltd.). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: The Appellant is an allottee and Financial Creditor of the Corporate Debtor undergoing CIRP. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: N/A (The dispute pertains to procedural delays in replacing the RP, not an initial monetary default). 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The Appellant filed an application before the Adjudicating Authority on 19.07.2021 to direct the RP to bring an agenda for the removal/replacement of the RP before the CoC. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The impugned order dated 11.08.2021 was a simple one-line scheduling order: 'List the matter for hearing on 22.09.2021'. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Aggrieved by the lack of a decision after over a month and the mere adjournment of the matter, the Appellant filed the present appeal before the NCLAT challenging the 11.08.2021 scheduling order.
legal_issues: Whether an appeal is maintainable under Section 61 of the IBC against a mere adjournment or scheduling order where no adverse findings have been passed against the appellant.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A party cannot appeal a simple scheduling or adjournment order because such an order does not adversely affect their legal rights. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: The Tribunal interpreted Section 61 of the IBC, holding that the right to appeal is restricted to an 'aggrieved person,' which necessitates that an adverse order must have been passed against the appellant by the Adjudicating Authority. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal reviewed the impugned order and observed it was strictly administrative ('List the matter for hearing...'), containing no substantive determination or adverse action against the appellant. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The bench conclusively ruled that since no adverse order was passed, the appellant did not qualify as an aggrieved person under Section 61, rendering the appeal not maintainable.
operative_order: The Appeal is dismissed as not maintainable, with a request to the Adjudicating Authority to decide the Appellant's pending application at the earliest.
summary: Jatin Bachani, a financial creditor, filed an application before the NCLT seeking a CoC vote on removing the Resolution Professional. Aggrieved by a one-line NCLT order adjourning the hearing to a future date, the appellant approached the NCLAT. The NCLAT dismissed the appeal, establishing that a mere adjournment order does not constitute an adverse ruling. Consequently, the appellant could not be considered an 'aggrieved person' under Section 61 of the IBC, making the appeal legally unmaintainable.

case_title: State Bank of India vs Chanchal Dua
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: State Bank of India (Appellant/Financial Creditor), Chanchal Dua (Respondent/Resolution Professional for KK Milk Fresh India Ltd.). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: The Appellant is a Financial Creditor exercising 39.75% voting rights in the Committee of Creditors of the Corporate Debtor. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: N/A (The appeal pertains to procedural delays in deciding a liquidation application). 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: An application (I.A. No. 210 of 2020) for liquidation under Section 33(1) of the IBC was filed on 29.08.2020 and remained pending for over a year. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The Adjudicating Authority passed an order on 24.08.2021 stating: 'As jointly prayed, put up in the week commencing 15th September, 2021 for arguments before the Regular Court/through Video Conferencing.' 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Aggrieved by the long pendency and the adjournment order dated 24.08.2021, the Appellant filed the present appeal before the NCLAT seeking directions to the Adjudicating Authority to decide the application expeditiously.
legal_issues: Whether an appeal under Section 61 of the IBC is maintainable against a mere adjournment or scheduling order that does not record any adverse findings against the appellant.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An appeal cannot be maintained against a simple scheduling order that does not adversely affect the legal rights or interests of the appellant. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: The Tribunal evaluated Section 61 of the IBC, concluding that the right to appeal requires a party to be aggrieved by an adverse order; a routine adjournment does not fulfill this criterion. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal reviewed the impugned order dated 24.08.2021 and found it was strictly administrative, passed on a joint prayer, and contained no substantive determination or adverse action against the appellant. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The bench conclusively ruled that because there was nothing against the appellant in the impugned scheduling order, the appeal was not maintainable under Section 61 of the IBC.
operative_order: The Appeal is dismissed as not maintainable, with a request to the Adjudicating Authority to decide the pending I.A No. 210 of 2020 at the earliest as per law.
summary: State Bank of India, a financial creditor, filed an appeal against an NCLT order that merely adjourned the hearing of a long-pending liquidation application under Section 33(1) of the IBC. The NCLAT evaluated the impugned scheduling order and noted it was passed on a joint prayer without any adverse findings against the appellant. Consequently, the Tribunal established that a mere adjournment order does not constitute an adverse ruling, rendering the appeal legally unmaintainable under Section 61 of the IBC, and dismissed the appeal while requesting the NCLT to expedite the matter.

case_title: Ankit A Verma vs Navin Srichand Kanjwani
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Ankit A Verma (Appellant/Member of Suspended Management), Navin Srichand Kanjwani (Respondent/Resolution Professional of BD Overseas and Fiscal Services Ltd.). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: N/A (The appeal pertains to CIRP procedural compliance). 3. DEFAULT METRICS: N/A. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The NCLT passed the impugned interim order on 20.07.2021 rejecting the appellant's application. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The appellant alleged non-supply of the Resolution Plan prior to CoC approval, claiming a violation of Section 24 of the IBC and Regulation 21 of the CIRP Regulations. The RP submitted that the plan had not been approved and parties were directed to file objections. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The Adjudicating Authority (NCLT Ahmedabad) rejected the appellant's interlocutory application. Aggrieved by the interim order, the appellant filed an appeal under Section 61 while the Resolution Plan was still pending approval before the NCLT.
legal_issues: Whether the appellate tribunal should interfere in the CIRP process on the ground of alleged non-supply of a resolution plan to suspended management when the plan is still pending consideration and approval before the Adjudicating Authority.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An appellate tribunal will decline to interfere in an ongoing CIRP when the underlying resolution plan is still pending final consideration before the Adjudicating Authority. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: The tribunal interpreted its appellate jurisdiction as warranting restraint from premature interference in matters currently sub-judice before the NCLT to respect the time limits fixed by the IBC. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The bench noted the undisputed fact that the Resolution Plan had not yet been approved and the NCLT was actively considering objections. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The bench conclusively ruled that since the resolution plan's approval was still pending before the Adjudicating Authority, there was no merit in interfering at this interim stage, and dismissed the appeal.
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed.
summary: Ankit A Verma, a suspended management member, appealed against an NCLT interim order that rejected his plea regarding the non-supply of the Resolution Plan before CoC approval. The appellant alleged violations of Section 24 of the IBC. The NCLAT observed that the Resolution Plan was still pending approval before the Adjudicating Authority, which had already allowed parties to file objections. Consequently, the NCLAT found no merit to interfere prematurely in the CIRP process and dismissed the appeal.

case_title: Mr. Ravi Ajit Kulkarni vs. State Bank of India
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant Ravi Ajit Kulkarni is the Personal Guarantor of Corporate Debtor Pratibha Industries Limited. Respondent is State Bank of India acting through Resolution Professional Ram Ratan Kanoongo. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: A personal guarantee was executed on 10.03.2017 for credit facilities granted to the Corporate Debtor. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: The debt allegedly became due on 01.02.2016 and default occurred on 07.04.2016. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The Section 95 application was filed on 25.01.2021 after serving demand notices on the guarantor. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The RP submitted Form C application with demand notices but the Adjudicating Authority proceeded to hold there was 'default' at the pre-admission stage itself. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The NCLT Mumbai admitted the application under Section 95 on 12.03.2021, commencing interim moratorium and confirming the appointment of the RP while prematurely recording a finding of default without giving hearing to the guarantor.
legal_issues: Whether the Adjudicating Authority can record a conclusive finding of 'default' while appointing the Resolution Professional under Section 97 before receiving the RP's report under Section 99, and whether the Personal Guarantor is entitled to a hearing before the appointment of the RP.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The Adjudicating Authority's role at the stage of Sections 95-97 of the IBC is limited to appointing the Resolution Professional and declaring the interim moratorium, leaving the determination of default for Section 100. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 97 involves no adjudicatory function. The phrase 'allowing' the application or establishing 'default' relates to Section 100 after the RP evaluates evidence under Section 99. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: At the pre-appointment stage, limited notice is required to ensure natural justice by informing the guarantor of the interim moratorium, but full merits and defenses on debt/default must wait for the Section 99 report. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLT erred by concluding that default had occurred prior to the RP's examination, rendering the subsequent RP report a mere formality; hence, the premature findings were set aside.
operative_order: The appeal is partly allowed. The findings of the NCLT regarding 'default' at the preliminary stage and the subsequent RP report are set aside. The appointment of the RP is not disturbed, but the RP is directed to afford a fresh opportunity to the Appellant under Section 99 and submit a new report.
summary: The NCLAT ruled that while adjudicating a Section 95 application against a personal guarantor, the Adjudicating Authority must only appoint the Resolution Professional under Section 97 and cannot prematurely conclude that a 'default' has occurred. Determining default is reserved for Section 100 after the RP submits a report. The NCLT's premature finding of default against the Appellant was set aside, and the RP was directed to issue a fresh report.

case_title: M/S. Mohan Gems & Jewels Private Limited vs. Vijay Verma & Anr
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is the Liquidator of Mohan Gems & Jewels Private Limited (Corporate Debtor). Respondent No. 1 is Vijay Verma (Successful Bidder), and Respondent No. 2 is the IBBI. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Sale of the Corporate Debtor as a going concern during liquidation proceedings. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Not applicable directly, as the case concerns the validity of selling the corporate debtor as a going concern in liquidation for Rs. 4,51,99,713. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The e-auction concluded on 20.11.2019, and the successful bidder deposited the amount between 18.12.2019 and 16.01.2020. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The Liquidator filed an application seeking closure of liquidation without dissolution under Regulation 45(3)(a) of the IBBI Liquidation Process Regulations. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT New Delhi dismissed the Liquidator's application on 16.09.2020, holding that Regulations 39C of CIRP and 32A/45(3) of Liquidation Regulations were inconsistent with Section 54 of the IBC, which mandates dissolution.
legal_issues: Whether the Liquidator is legally authorized to sell the Corporate Debtor as a going concern during liquidation under IBBI Regulations, and whether such regulations permitting closure without dissolution conflict with Section 54 of the IBC.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The sale of a Corporate Debtor as a going concern during liquidation without its legal dissolution is valid, permissible, and aligns with the IBC's primary objective of maximizing asset value and preserving employment. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 54 of the IBC applies when assets are completely liquidated, but Regulation 32(e) and 45(3)(a) validly permit closure of the process if the entity is sold as a going concern, preserving its legal shell. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal noted that delegated legislation framed by IBBI under Section 240 is valid and that NCLT cannot declare validly framed IBBI regulations ultra vires. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLT exceeded its jurisdiction by ruling the IBBI regulations as inconsistent with the Code. The sale as a going concern is a lawful mechanism to avert corporate death.
operative_order: The appeal is allowed, and the NCLT's order dismissing the Liquidator's application for closure of the liquidation process is set aside. The sale of the Corporate Debtor as a going concern is validated.
summary: The Adjudicating Authority had struck down IBBI Regulations permitting the sale of a corporate debtor as a going concern in liquidation without dissolution, terming them ultra vires the IBC. The NCLAT reversed this, ruling that NCLT cannot invalidate IBBI regulations and that selling the corporate entity as a going concern aligns perfectly with the IBC's core objective of value maximization and preventing corporate death.

case_title: Niklesh Tirathdas Nihalani vs. Shah Poddar Nihlani Organisers Pvt Ltd & Ors
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant Niklesh Tirathdas Nihalani (8% shareholder representing Nihalani family). Respondent No. 1 is Shah Poddar Nihlani Organisers Pvt Ltd. Respondents 2-16 are other shareholders/directors and outsiders. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Transfer of company shares by existing family members to outsiders. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: The dispute involves the transfer of 8,535 shares to outsiders during FY 2012-13. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The share transfers were allegedly recorded with RoC on 14.08.2014. The Appellant filed the Section 59 petition on 19.09.2017. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The original Articles of Association (AOA), specifically Article 13, mandated pre-emptive rights to existing shareholders before transferring shares to non-members. During the pendency of the NCLT appeal, the respondents held an EGM on 12.12.2017 and amended the AOA to remove the pre-emptive rights clause. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Ahmedabad dismissed the Section 59 petition on 03.08.2020 as time-barred (applying the 3-year limitation from the RoC filing date) and dismissed the Section 241/242 petition for oppression and mismanagement.
legal_issues: Whether the petition for rectification of the register of members under Section 59 of the Companies Act 2013 was barred by limitation, and whether the transfer of shares and subsequent amendment to the AOA constituted oppression and mismanagement.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Limitation for fraud or suppression of facts begins from the date of the applicant's knowledge. Furthermore, amending a company's AOA during pending litigation to retroactively justify illegal share transfers constitutes gross oppression. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 17 of the Limitation Act pauses the clock until fraud is discovered. The doctrine of indoor management protects a non-executive shareholder who lacked prior knowledge. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Since the respondents did not contradict the appellant's affidavit regarding the date of knowledge, the NCLT erred in relying solely on the date the annual return was filed with the RoC to trigger limitation. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The share transfers explicitly violated the pre-emptive rights in the original AOA and the mid-litigation EGM to alter the AOA demonstrated malafide intent to oppress minority shareholders.
operative_order: The NCLAT set aside the NCLT's judgment. The share transfers made in violation of the original AOA are declared void ab initio and cancelled. Respondent No. 1 Company is directed to rectify the Register of Members within 30 days and refund the share application money. The EGM resolution amending the AOA is declared illegal and shall not be given effect.
summary: The Appellant challenged the clandestine transfer of family company shares to outsiders, bypassing pre-emptive rights mandated by the AOA. While the petition was pending, the respondents altered the AOA to validate the transfers. NCLT dismissed the petition as time-barred. The NCLAT reversed this, ruling that limitation in fraud cases starts from the date of knowledge, the share transfers were void ab initio, and the mid-litigation AOA amendment was an oppressive act.

case_title: Ranjeet Singh vs. M/s Karan Motors Private Limited
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellants are ex-employees (Ranjeet Singh, Shally Sati, Deepa Sati, Hansa Dutt Sati, Asha Devi) acting as Operational Creditors. Respondent is M/s Karan Motors Private Limited (Corporate Debtor). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Claim for unpaid salary arrears spanning 2013, 2014, and 2017, along with gratuity and 18% interest. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Claimed defaults ranged from Rs. 4 Lakh to Rs. 18.91 Lakh per employee. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Resignations occurred between late 2017 and 2018. Section 8 Demand notices were issued by some appellants on 04.10.2017, and Section 9 applications were filed in 2019. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The Corporate Debtor had already paid the admitted principal salary amounts during the NCLT proceedings. The remaining claims pertained strictly to disputed, time-barred salary from 2013-2014, gratuity, and interest, alongside the employer's counterclaims of Rs. 31.33 Lakh for damages due to misconduct and absenteeism. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT New Delhi dismissed the Section 9 applications on 18.02.2020 on the ground that the admitted principal amount had been paid, extinguishing the occurrence of default.
legal_issues: Whether an application under Section 9 of the IBC is maintainable solely for the recovery of disputed interest, gratuity, and time-barred salary arrears after the admitted principal debt has been paid by the Corporate Debtor.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The IBC is not a debt recovery mechanism. Insolvency proceedings cannot be triggered by an operational creditor for disputed, time-barred claims or solely for the recovery of interest when the principal debt has been satisfied. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Operational debt under Section 5(21) includes employment dues, but claims must be undisputed and within limitation. Some appellants failed to issue Section 8 demand notices entirely, rendering their Section 9 applications defective. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal noted that the appellants failed to show any acknowledgment of debt by the Corporate Debtor from 2014 onwards to save limitation, and the Adjudicating Authority possesses no equity jurisdiction to overlook the Limitation Act. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Since the Corporate Debtor paid the admitted dues and the remaining amounts were either time-barred, heavily disputed (with counterclaims for damages), or procedurally defective, the initiation of CIRP was unwarranted.
operative_order: The appeals were dismissed. The NCLAT affirmed the NCLT's orders dismissing the Section 9 applications, holding that there was no merit in the appeals.
summary: Multiple ex-employees filed Section 9 applications against Karan Motors to recover unpaid salaries from 2013/2014, gratuity, and interest. The Corporate Debtor paid the undisputed principal amounts during NCLT proceedings and disputed the rest, citing misconduct and limitation. NCLAT affirmed the NCLT's dismissal of the applications, reiterating that the IBC is not a recovery forum for time-barred, disputed claims or pure interest recovery.

case_title: Mr. Nitin Chandrakant Naik & Anr vs. Sanidhya Industries LLP & Ors
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellants are Promoters/Suspended Directors and Personal Guarantors of the Corporate Debtor (Simrut Foods & Hospitality Pvt. Ltd.). Respondent 1 is Sanidhya Industries LLP (Successful Resolution Applicant), Respondents 4 & 5 are Financial Creditors. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Personal properties of the Appellants were mortgaged to secure credit facilities for the Corporate Debtor. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: The CIRP involved an admitted debt of approximately Rs. 6.88 Crores to Financial Creditors. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The CIRP was initiated on 03.09.2018. The Resolution Plan was approved by NCLT on 13.11.2019. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The Resolution Plan explicitly mandated the transfer of the Appellants' personal mortgaged properties to the Resolution Applicant. The Information Memorandum did not properly list these personal assets as Corporate Debtor assets, nor were they valued during the CIRP. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The NCLT Mumbai approved the resolution plan on 13.11.2019, directing the personal guarantors to execute tripartite agreements to transfer their personal properties to the SRA.
legal_issues: Whether a Resolution Plan in a Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process (CIRP) can legally compel the transfer of personal properties belonging to Personal Guarantors without initiating separate, lawful insolvency proceedings against them under Part III of the IBC or other relevant laws.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The personal properties of a Corporate Debtor's guarantors do not form part of the Corporate Debtor's estate and cannot be forcibly liquidated, transferred, or consumed through a Resolution Plan without proper recourse to statutory proceedings against the guarantors themselves. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 14 (moratorium) protects the Corporate Debtor, but does not drag the personal guarantor's assets into the CIRP asset pool. Section 31 binds the guarantor to the restructured debt terms but does not authorize the direct expropriation of their personal assets within the Corporate Debtor's CIRP. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal noted that the personal assets were never properly valued as corporate assets in the Information Memorandum. Transferring them bypasses the SARFAESI Act, the DRT framework, or Part III of the IBC. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLT committed a material irregularity by approving a plan that confiscated third-party personal assets. The resolution plan was therefore held ultra vires and legally unsustainable.
operative_order: The appeal is allowed. The NCLT's order approving the Resolution Plan is quashed and the Resolution Plan is rejected. Because the CIRP period under Section 12 had already expired, the matter was remitted to the Adjudicating Authority to pass a liquidation order for the Corporate Debtor under Section 33.
summary: The Adjudicating Authority approved a Resolution Plan that forced the Promoters/Personal Guarantors to transfer their personal real estate to the Successful Resolution Applicant to satisfy the Corporate Debtor's debt. The NCLAT struck down the plan, ruling that personal properties of guarantors are not corporate assets and cannot be forcibly transferred under a CIRP resolution plan without due process of law against the guarantors themselves.

case_title: Maitreya Doshi vs. Anand Rathi Global Finance Ltd. & Anr
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant Maitreya Doshi is the Suspended Director of Doshi Holdings Pvt. Ltd. (Corporate Debtor). Respondent No. 1 is Anand Rathi Global Finance Ltd. (Financial Creditor). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Loan-cum-Pledge agreements were signed advancing Rs. 6 Crores jointly to M/s Premier Ltd. and Doshi Holdings Pvt. Ltd. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default of Rs. 8,35,25,398/- occurred on the repayment of the loan. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The Section 7 application was filed in 2020. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The Appellant argued that Doshi Holdings was merely a pledgor of shares, not a borrower, as the funds were directly deposited into Premier Ltd.'s account. However, loan agreements clearly designated Doshi Holdings as 'Borrower 2/Pledgor', and demand promissory notes and receipts were jointly signed by the Appellant on behalf of both entities as co-borrowers. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Mumbai admitted the Section 7 petition against Doshi Holdings on 19.02.2021, despite having already admitted a separate CIRP against Premier Ltd.
legal_issues: Whether an entity that executes loan documents as a 'co-borrower' and pledges shares can be subjected to a Section 7 CIRP as a Corporate Debtor, and whether parallel CIRP proceedings can be maintained against two co-borrowers for the same underlying debt.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A co-borrower who explicitly executes loan agreements and promissory notes assumes joint and several liability for the debt, qualifying as a Corporate Debtor under Section 7, regardless of which co-borrower's bank account actually received the disbursed funds. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Under Sections 5(7) and 5(8), a debt disbursed to co-borrowers against the time value of money establishes a financial debt for both. The NCLAT clarified that the bar on simultaneous applications against principal borrowers and guarantors established in 'Dr. Vishnu Kumar Agarwal' was per incuriam regarding Section 60(2) and (3) and does not prevent action against co-borrowers. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal relied strictly on the contractual language. The 'Loan cum Pledge Agreement' explicitly identified Doshi Holdings as 'Borrower 2', and joint loan receipts/promissory notes were executed. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Doshi Holdings was not merely a third-party pledgor (which would exempt it under the 'Anuj Jain' precedent), but a direct co-borrower. Hence, the initiation of CIRP was legally justified.
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed with no order as to costs. The NCLAT affirmed the NCLT's admission order initiating the CIRP against Doshi Holdings Pvt. Ltd.
summary: The Financial Creditor initiated CIRP against Doshi Holdings for defaulting on a Rs. 6 Crore loan. The Appellant claimed Doshi Holdings only pledged shares and didn't receive the funds, meaning it wasn't a 'Financial Debtor'. NCLAT rejected this, analyzing the loan documents to find that Doshi Holdings explicitly signed as a co-borrower and joint promisor. NCLAT also ruled that parallel CIRP proceedings against co-borrowers for the same debt are legally permissible under the IBC.

case_title: SM Milkose Limited vs. Parvinder Kumar Bhatt
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant No. 1 is SM Milkose Limited (Successful Resolution Applicant). Appellant No. 2 is Applied Electro Magnetics Pvt. Ltd. (Corporate Debtor). Respondent No. 4 is Bank of India (90% CoC voting share). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Implementation of a Resolution Plan and the appropriation of funds generated during the CIRP period. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: The Resolution Plan settled the Bank of India's claim of Rs. 41.50 crores for a final amount of Rs. 9.00 crores. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP initiated on 26.10.2017. Final Resolution Plan approved by CoC on 19.07.2018 and later by the NCLT on 23.12.2020. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: During the first CoC meeting, Bank of India demanded that 25% of the Corporate Debtor's operational receipts during the CIRP be earmarked to its loan accounts. Over Rs. 1.68 crores accrued in a separate bank account. While early drafts of the plan allowed the Bank to keep pre-April 2018 receipts, the final approved plan mandated a flat payout of exactly Rs. 9 crores as full and final settlement. The Bank refused to release Rs. 88,16,071 generated during the CIRP. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT New Delhi passed an order on 23.12.2020 allowing the Bank to retain the CIRP receipts outside the Rs. 9 crore plan envelope.
legal_issues: Whether a Financial Creditor holding majority voting rights in the CoC can unilaterally appropriate operational accruals generated by the Corporate Debtor during the CIRP moratorium to offset its own debt, bypassing the terms of the finally approved Resolution Plan.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Any operational revenues generated by a Corporate Debtor during the CIRP period are assets of the Corporate Debtor. Creditors cannot alienate or appropriate these funds to satisfy their individual claims in violation of the Section 14 moratorium. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 14(1)(b) prohibits the transfer, encumbrance, or disposal of any of the Corporate Debtor's assets during the moratorium. A CoC decision allowing a specific creditor to siphon off CIRP-period revenues violates the Code. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal relied strictly on the commercial wisdom of the CoC as reflected in the final approved Resolution Plan, which fixed the Bank of India's total recovery at Rs. 9 crores without any clause permitting the retention of CIRP-period accruals. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLT erred in allowing the Bank to keep the extra funds. The Bank is bound by the Rs. 9 crore final settlement, and the leftover CIRP accruals belong to the Corporate Debtor/Successful Resolution Applicant.
operative_order: The NCLAT quashed the impugned NCLT order. The Resolution Professional was directed to account for all amounts received by the Corporate Debtor during the CIRP in the Bank of India account and ensure they are applied strictly per the IBC and the approved Resolution Plan. Any balance shall enure to the benefit of the Successful Resolution Applicant.
summary: Bank of India, holding 90% voting power, forced the Corporate Debtor to deposit a portion of its operational earnings during the CIRP into a separate account and attempted to appropriate these funds over and above its Rs. 9 Crore settlement in the approved Resolution Plan. The NCLAT ruled this illegal, stating that CIRP accruals belong to the Corporate Debtor and are protected by the Section 14 moratorium, ordering the Bank to adhere strictly to the final Resolution Plan.

case_title: Ankit Goyat vs. Sunita Agarwal & Anr
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant Ankit Goyat represents the Corporate Debtor (Antriksh Infratech Pvt. Ltd.). Respondent No. 1 is Sunita Agarwal (Real Estate Allottee/Financial Creditor). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: An MoU dated 28.02.2015 whereby the Allottee 'invested' Rs. 25 Lakhs for 24 months with an assured return of 25% per annum. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: The Allottee demanded a refund of Rs. 47,31,164 (principal plus 25% interest) after the 24-month period expired. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Demand notice issued on 01.02.2019. NCLT passed the ex-parte admission order on 17.09.2019. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The MoU explicitly termed the transaction an 'investment', granting the allottee a buy-back option where they could take the money with the 25% assured return without any obligation to take possession of the apartment. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT New Delhi proceeded ex-parte against the Corporate Debtor and admitted the Section 7 petition on 17.09.2019, treating the allottee as a genuine homebuyer Financial Creditor under Section 5(8)(f).
legal_issues: Whether a real estate allottee who enters into a 'buy-back' agreement with a guaranteed 25% annual return qualifies as a genuine 'Financial Creditor' under the IBC or merely a 'speculative investor' attempting to use the IBC as a recovery mechanism.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The IBC is not a recovery mechanism for speculative investors. A real estate allottee executing a lucrative agreement prioritizing massive assured returns and guaranteed buy-backs without genuine intent to take possession falls outside the protective scope intended for genuine homebuyers. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: While the 2018 amendment to Section 5(8)(f) includes homebuyers as Financial Creditors, the Supreme Court's ruling in 'Pioneer Urban Land' clarifies that developers can defend against Section 7 applications by proving the allottee is a speculative investor acting with malicious intent to recover funds in a falling market. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal scrutinized the MoU's terms, particularly Clauses 2(f) and (g), which allowed the allottee to walk away with a 25% return without forfeiting earnest money or taking possession, concluding it was a purely financial, speculative investment disguised as a property purchase. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Allottee was a speculative investor abusing the IBC for debt recovery. The admission of the CIRP was therefore legally flawed.
operative_order: The appeal is allowed. The NCLT's ex-parte admission order under Section 7 is set aside. The Corporate Debtor is released from the rigours of the IBC moratorium and restored to its Board of Directors. The IRP fees are to be borne by the Corporate Debtor.
summary: An individual invested Rs. 25 lakhs in a real estate project under an MoU promising a massive 25% assured annual return and a guaranteed buy-back option. Upon default, she triggered CIRP against the builder. The NCLAT reversed the NCLT's admission order, ruling that the allottee was a 'speculative investor' attempting to use the IBC as a coercive recovery tool for a lucrative financial transaction, which contravenes the Code's objective.

case_title: Rishima SA Investments LLC vs. Sarga Hotel Private Limited
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant Rishima SA Investments LLC is a 35% shareholder/financial creditor. Corporate Debtor is Sarga Hotel Private Limited. Operational Creditor is Universal International Creation Limited (Hong Kong). SIDCL holds 65% of the Corporate Debtor. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Supply of marble slabs by the Operational Creditor between 2014 and 2016. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Claimed principal amount of US$ 324,021.71 (approx. Rs. 2.30 Crores). 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Last valid invoice was dated 23.01.2016. The Section 9 application was filed over four years later on 21.07.2020. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Appellant Rishima recently won an ICC Arbitral Award against the Corporate Debtor and SIDCL. Immediately after, the Hong Kong-based Operational Creditor filed a Section 9 application using un-apostilled documents and unverified ledger entries. The Corporate Debtor suspiciously admitted the debt instantly upon receiving a mere email from the NCLT registry without a formal hearing. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Kolkata admitted the Section 9 application on 12.08.2020 with extraordinary haste based on the Corporate Debtor's admission.
legal_issues: Whether the NCLT erred in admitting the Section 9 application by ignoring the Limitation Act and violating principles of natural justice amidst strong evidence of fraudulent collusion aimed at stalling an arbitral award execution.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An Adjudicating Authority must independently verify the authenticity of documents, the authority of the filer, and the limitation period before initiating CIRP, especially when the Corporate Debtor suspiciously volunteers to admit the debt without mounting a defense. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 9 applications must be filed within the 3-year limitation period from the date of default. Unverified, un-apostilled foreign ledgers and unauthenticated letters cannot be relied upon to extend limitation. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal found the operational creditor's documents (single-page board resolutions, un-apostilled authority letters, foreign language bank statements) entirely unreliable. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Section 9 application was time-barred as the default occurred in 2016 and the 2017 payment ledger was of doubtful origin. The lightning-fast admission process, bypassing a proper hearing, strongly pointed to a malicious, collusive attempt by the Corporate Debtor to use the Section 14 moratorium to dodge the pending arbitral award.
operative_order: The appeal is allowed. The NCLT's impugned order dated 12.08.2020 admitting the CIRP is set aside. The Corporate Debtor is released from the moratorium, and the IRP is directed to hand back control to the Corporate Debtor's management.
summary: After a minority shareholder won a major international arbitral award against the Corporate Debtor, a foreign operational creditor suddenly filed a Section 9 application using highly suspicious, time-barred invoices from 2016. The Corporate Debtor immediately surrendered and admitted the debt, resulting in a hasty NCLT admission order. The NCLAT struck down the order, determining the debt was time-barred and the proceeding was a collusive sham designed to trigger a moratorium and dodge the arbitral award.

case_title: Panch Tatva Promoters Pvt. Ltd. vs. GPT Steel Industries Ltd. & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Panch Tatva Promoters Pvt. Ltd. (Unsuccessful Resolution Applicant). Respondent No. 1 is GPT Steel Industries Ltd. (Corporate Debtor) represented by its Resolution Professional. Respondent No. 2 is the Committee of Creditors (CoC). Respondent No. 3 is GP Global Energy Pvt Ltd (Successful Resolution Applicant). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Submission and consideration of resolution plans for the corporate insolvency resolution of the Corporate Debtor. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Not directly applicable, as the dispute pertains to the procedural evaluation and approval of competing resolution plans during the CIRP. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The 270-day CIRP period expired on 19.02.2020. The CoC approved R-3's resolution plan on 18.02.2020 with an 82.41% voting share. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The Appellant submitted multiple conditional/contingent resolution plans that allowed for a midway exit, which is non-compliant with the IBC. R-3 submitted a compliant plan. The Appellant attempted to disqualify R-3 by alleging R-3 failed to implement a resolution plan in another CIRP (Allied Strips Ltd.). 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The Appellant filed an application before NCLT Ahmedabad to halt the approval of R-3's plan and mandate the consideration of its own revised plan. NCLT dismissed the application on 03.07.2020 as premature and devoid of merit, leading to this appeal.
legal_issues: Whether a prospective resolution applicant has a vested right to have its plan approved, and whether a delay in implementing a resolution plan in another CIRP constitutes a 'failure to implement' rendering the applicant ineligible under Regulation 38(1-B) of the CIRP Regulations read with Section 29A of the IBC.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An unsuccessful resolution applicant has no vested or fundamental right to have its resolution plan approved. The commercial wisdom of the CoC in evaluating and approving a plan is paramount and not subject to judicial interference unless it breaches statutory frameworks. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Delay in implementing a resolution plan in a separate CIRP does not automatically equate to a 'failure to implement' causing ineligibility under Regulation 38(1-B) of the CIRP Regulations, unless the Adjudicating Authority has specifically determined a contravention under Section 33(4) of the IBC. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal noted that the Appellant's plan was inherently conditional and submitted at the eleventh hour after the CoC had already voted to approve R-3's plan. R-3's delays in other matters did not statutorily disqualify them. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The CoC validly exercised its commercial wisdom in approving R-3's plan. The Appellant lacked the locus to stall the pending Section 31 approval proceedings by challenging the CoC's commercial decision.
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed with no order as to costs. The interim stay order dated 29.07.2020 is vacated, and the Adjudicating Authority is requested to urgently decide the pending application for resolution plan approval under Section 31 of the IBC.
summary: The Appellant, an unsuccessful resolution applicant, challenged the CoC's approval of Respondent No. 3's resolution plan, alleging that R-3 was ineligible under CIRP Regulations due to implementation delays in another CIRP. The NCLAT dismissed the appeal, holding that mere delay does not constitute a statutory 'failure to implement' without an explicit NCLT order. Furthermore, the Appellant's own plan was conditional and submitted late. The Tribunal reiterated the settled law that an applicant has no vested right to plan approval, and the CoC's commercial wisdom remains supreme and immune from interference.

case_title: Assistant Commissioner Of Customs vs Ca Kannan Tiruvengadam
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant MSC Meditteranean Shipping and Assistant Commissioner of Customs. Respondent is CA Kannan Tiruvengadam (RP of BRG Iron & Steel Co. Pvt. Ltd.). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Delivery of marine containers containing Alloy and Melting Scrap. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Outstanding customs duty of Rs. 78,84,54,741. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP commenced on 05.03.2019. Goods were auctioned by customs on 26.04.2019. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Customs Department auctioned 256 containers AFTER the CIRP moratorium was imposed. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT directed Customs to remit the sale proceeds to the RP and imposed a penalty on the Customs officer for violating the moratorium.
legal_issues: Whether Customs authorities can legally auction goods belonging to the Corporate Debtor under Section 48 of the Customs Act to recover dues during the CIRP moratorium period.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Assets belonging to the Corporate Debtor cannot be alienated, transferred, or auctioned by any statutory authority during the CIRP moratorium. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 14 of IBC overrides Section 48 of the Customs Act, 1962, due to the non-obstante clause in Section 238 of the IBC. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The goods belonged to the Corporate Debtor (established via LC and bills of lading), bringing them strictly under the control of the RP and the protection of the moratorium. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Customs auction conducted during the moratorium was illegal. Sale proceeds must be transferred to the RP, and Customs must submit its claim as an Operational Creditor.
operative_order: MSC's appeal is dismissed. Customs' appeal is partly allowed; the NCLT's penalty of Rs 1 Lakh is set aside, but the direction to hand over the sale proceeds to the Corporate Debtor and file a claim as an Operational Creditor is confirmed.
summary: The Customs Department auctioned imported goods of the Corporate Debtor to recover statutory dues after the CIRP moratorium had commenced. NCLAT held that Section 14 of the IBC prohibits the alienation of the Corporate Debtor's assets and overrides the Customs Act, 1962. The auction was ruled illegal, and Customs was directed to remit the sale proceeds to the Resolution Professional.

case_title: Mr. D.K. Mohanty vs M/S. Jai Balaji Industries & Anr
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant D.K. Mohanty (MD of Orissa Minerals Development Company Ltd., Corporate Debtor). Respondent No. 1 is Jai Balaji Industries (Operational Creditor). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: MoUs for the supply of Iron Ore. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Operational debt claims based on Arbitral Awards from 2010. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Arbitral Awards passed in 2010. Section 34 appeals dismissed in 2012. Section 37 appeals dismissed for default on 22.11.2019 but later restored on 02.03.2020. Section 8 demand notices were issued on 14.02.2020. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The Operational Creditor issued a Section 8 demand notice while the Corporate Debtor's application to restore the Section 37 appeal was pending. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Kolkata admitted the Section 9 application on 30.09.2020, concluding that no dispute was technically pending on the exact date the demand notice was sent.
legal_issues: Whether an operational debt is subject to a 'pre-existing dispute' under Section 8 of the IBC if a Section 37 appeal against an arbitral award was dismissed for default but subsequently restored.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The restoration of an appeal relates back to its original date of filing, reviving the pre-existing dispute in the eyes of the law. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: The pendency of Section 34 or Section 37 proceedings under the Arbitration Act constitutes a pre-existing dispute under Section 8(2)(a) of the IBC. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Since the restoration application was filed before the demand notice was issued and the appeal was subsequently restored, the dispute remained active and ongoing. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The debt was disputed due to the active challenge against the arbitral awards, rendering the Section 9 application non-maintainable.
operative_order: The appeals are allowed. The NCLT's admission order is set aside, and the Corporate Debtor is released from the CIRP and the rigours of the moratorium.
summary: An Operational Creditor filed a Section 9 application relying on arbitral awards, leveraging the fact that the Corporate Debtor's Section 37 appeals had been dismissed for default. However, the appeals were later restored. NCLAT set aside the CIRP admission, holding that the restoration of the appeals related back to their original filing, thereby sustaining a pre-existing dispute when the demand notice was issued.

case_title: Asset Reconstruction Company India vs Mohammadiya Educational Society
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Asset Reconstruction Company (India) Limited (Financial Creditor). Respondent is Mohammadiya Educational Society (Corporate Debtor). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Loan facility availed by the educational society. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default of a financial debt exceeding Rs. 1 lakh. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Section 7 application was dismissed on 26.03.2019. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The Respondent is a society registered under the Societies Registration Act, 1860, and deemed registered under the AP Societies Registration Act, 2001. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Hyderabad dismissed the Section 7 petition on the ground that a registered society is not a 'corporate person' and therefore the IBC is not applicable.
legal_issues: Whether a society registered under the Societies Registration Act, 1860 (or deemed registered under the AP Societies Registration Act, 2001) qualifies as a 'corporate person' under Section 3(7) of the IBC to be subject to CIRP.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The provisions of the IBC do not apply to societies registered under the Societies Registration Act because they are not incorporated with limited liability. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 2 and Section 3(7) of the IBC explicitly cover companies, LLPs, and entities incorporated with limited liability. A registered society is not incorporated with limited liability, and the Central Government has not notified societies under Section 2(d). 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Although Section 18 of the AP Act renders a society a 'body corporate' for certain functional purposes (suing and holding property), it does not transform it into a company or a limited liability entity for the purposes of the IBC. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: A registered society falls outside the jurisdiction of the Adjudicating Authority under the IBC.
operative_order: The appeals are dismissed with no order as to costs. The NCLT's decision that a society is not subject to the IBC is affirmed.
summary: A Financial Creditor attempted to initiate CIRP against an educational society. The NCLAT affirmed the NCLT's dismissal of the application, ruling that a society registered under the Societies Registration Act is not a 'corporate person' under Section 3(7) of the IBC because it is not incorporated with limited liability.

case_title: Nitin Garg vs State Bank Of India & Ors
