material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant Nitin Garg (Suspended Director of Corporate Debtor M/s Alupan Composite Panels Pvt Ltd). Respondent No. 1 is State Bank of India. Respondent No. 3 is M/s Alucom Panels Pvt Ltd (Auction Purchaser). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Loan facility that was declared NPA on 28.06.2016. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default leading to SARFAESI action. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Property possessed on 27.08.2019. E-auction held 24.10.2019. Sale certificate issued 30.12.2019. CIRP commenced on 24.01.2020. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The sale under the SARFAESI Act was confirmed, and the sale certificate was issued prior to the CIRP moratorium. The certificate was registered post-CIRP on 15.02.2020. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT dismissed the appellant's application seeking cancellation of the SARFAESI sale, holding that title had already legally passed to the purchaser.
legal_issues: Whether a property sold under the SARFAESI Act before the commencement of CIRP forms part of the Corporate Debtor's assets if the sale certificate was registered after the imposition of the Section 14 moratorium.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: In a public auction under the SARFAESI Act, the sale becomes absolute and title vests in the purchaser upon the confirmation of the sale and issuance of the sale certificate, regardless of subsequent registration. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Under Section 17(2)(xii) of the Registration Act, a sale certificate issued by an authorized officer in a public auction does not require compulsory registration to effectuate the transfer of title. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Since the sale certificate was issued on 30.12.2019 and CIRP commenced on 24.01.2020, the property was no longer an asset of the Corporate Debtor when the moratorium was imposed. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Section 14 moratorium does not invalidate a SARFAESI sale concluded prior to the CIRP commencement date.
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed without costs. The NCLT's order refusing to cancel the SARFAESI sale is upheld.
summary: The Suspended Director of the Corporate Debtor sought to invalidate a SARFAESI auction sale of the company's factory, arguing that the sale certificate was registered after the CIRP moratorium began. NCLAT rejected this, ruling that in a public auction under SARFAESI, title transfers upon the issuance of the sale certificate, which occurred before CIRP. Thus, the property was no longer an asset of the Corporate Debtor when the moratorium took effect.

case_title: Safeco Hygiene Films Pvt. Limited vs Loganmoy Ltd. Matheson Trust Co. (BVI) Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellants are Safeco Hygiene Films Pvt. Ltd. and SBPL Polymers LLP (minority shareholders, 34%). Respondent No. 1 is Loganmoy Ltd. Matheson Trust Co. (majority foreign shareholder, 66%). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Joint Venture Agreement for hygiene films manufacturing. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Appellants failed to invest 50% equity as required by the JVA, resulting in R1 holding a 66% stake. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: R1 sent a requisition notice on 20.12.2017 to hold an EGM. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The Appellant group managed the company but refused to amend the Articles of Association to incorporate the JVA and refused to convene the EGM requisitioned by the majority shareholder to appoint directors. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Ahmedabad allowed R1's petition to convene the EGM under Section 100 of the Companies Act and appointed an observer to prevent oppression by the minority management.
legal_issues: Whether minority shareholders managing a company can refuse to convene an EGM requisitioned by the majority shareholders under Section 100 of the Companies Act, and whether NCLT can direct the convening of such EGM.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The Board of Directors cannot alter the agenda or refuse to convene an EGM validly requisitioned by shareholders meeting the statutory threshold under Section 100 of the Companies Act. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 100 guarantees shareholders the right to requisition an EGM. Minority shareholders in control of the Board cannot use their position to thwart the majority's statutory rights. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Since the Appellants failed to honor the JVA's funding terms and deliberately refused to convene the EGM to appoint the majority's directors, their actions constituted mismanagement and oppression. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLT correctly exercised its jurisdiction to allow the majority shareholders to hold the EGM and to appoint an observer to ensure fairness.
operative_order: The appeals are dismissed. The NCLT's order directing the convening of the EGM under an observer's supervision is upheld.
summary: Minority shareholders controlling the Board of a Joint Venture company refused to convene an EGM requisitioned by the majority foreign investor. NCLAT upheld the NCLT's order directing the EGM to be held under an observer's supervision, ruling that the Board cannot suppress the majority shareholders' statutory right to requisition a meeting under Section 100 of the Companies Act.

case_title: Mr. Ravi Sankar Devarakonda vs Mr. Kesava Kolar
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Ravi Sankar Devarakonda (Erstwhile Resolution Professional). Respondent is Kesava Kolar (Managing Director of Corporate Debtor Maxworth Realty India Ltd). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Payment of CIRP expenses and RP professional fees. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Unpaid CIRP fees of Rs. 11,92,828 and Rs. 33,20,592 approved by the CoC. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: NCLT initially ordered payment of fees on 25.07.2018. A contempt petition was filed in 2020. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The Corporate Debtor's ex-management repeatedly failed to pay the RP's fees despite multiple NCLT orders granting extensions. The Respondent completely ignored the contempt proceedings and did not appear before the NCLT. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Bengaluru refused to initiate contempt proceedings, citing ignorance of whether the contemnor was financially solvent, and merely advised the RP to 'persuade' the contemnor to pay.
legal_issues: Whether the Adjudicating Authority erred in declining to exercise its contempt jurisdiction under Section 425 of the Companies Act based on an assumption of the contemnor's possible financial insolvency, despite repeated, deliberate non-compliance with its orders.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The contempt jurisdiction exists to uphold the majesty and dignity of the tribunal. Willful and deliberate disobedience of court orders cannot be ignored or excused based on mere assumptions about the contemnor's financial solvency. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Under Section 425 of the Companies Act, 2013, the NCLT possesses the same jurisdiction as the High Court under the Contempt of Courts Act, 1971, to punish willful disobedience. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The repeated failure to pay court-ordered fees, combined with absolute non-appearance in the contempt proceedings, demonstrated willful and contumacious disobedience. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLT shirked its statutory duty by asking the RP to 'persuade' the contemnor instead of adjudicating the contempt petition on its merits.
operative_order: The appeal is allowed. The NCLT's order dismissing the contempt petition is set aside, and the matter is remitted back to the NCLT for fresh adjudication on merits.
summary: An erstwhile Resolution Professional filed a contempt petition against the Corporate Debtor's Managing Director for willfully failing to pay court-ordered CIRP fees. The NCLT dismissed the petition, citing uncertainty over the MD's financial solvency, and told the RP to 'persuade' him. NCLAT reversed this, ruling that the NCLT abdicated its responsibility under Section 425 of the Companies Act and must adjudicate willful disobedience to uphold the tribunal's majesty.

case_title: Mr. Pralhad Hage & Ors vs Mr. Shyam Sirur
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellants are Pralhad Hage and others (minority shareholders holding Class A and B shares). Respondents are Shyam Sirur and others (majority shareholders of Cotmac Electronics Private Limited). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Disputes over company management and conversion of Class B shares. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: N/A. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Requisition for EGM sent on 04.07.2020. EGM held on 07.08.2020. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The majority shareholders requisitioned an EGM to remove Appellant No. 3 as a Director and subsequently removed Appellant No. 1 from the Managing Director post. The Appellants sought an ad-interim injunction, alleging oppression and loss of livelihood. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Mumbai refused to grant an ad-interim stay on the EGM and board meetings.
legal_issues: Whether an ad-interim injunction should be granted to restrain the holding of an EGM and Board meetings validly requisitioned by majority shareholders to remove directors, pending a final decision on an oppression and mismanagement petition.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Courts should not preemptively interfere with the democratic functioning of a company or injunct validly convened shareholder meetings unless the action is ex-facie illegal, perverse, or causes irreparable harm. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Under company law, majority shareholders have a statutory right to requisition meetings and remove directors. Legitimate expectations of employment cannot override the democratic will of the majority unless oppression is proven at the final hearing. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Appellants failed to establish a prima facie case of illegality in the convening of the meetings, and the balance of convenience did not favor granting a stay. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLT properly exercised its discretion in refusing to injunct the EGM and Board meetings. The appellate tribunal will not substitute its discretion for that of the first instance court absent gross illegality.
operative_order: The appeals are dismissed with no order as to costs.
summary: Minority shareholders sought to injunct an EGM and a Board meeting called by the majority to remove them from executive positions, claiming oppression and loss of livelihood. NCLAT upheld the NCLT's refusal to grant a stay, emphasizing that courts should not preemptively restrain the statutory right of majority shareholders to hold meetings and vote on corporate governance issues.

case_title: Ishita Halder vs Siba Kumar Mohapatra
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant Ishita Halder (Shareholder of Corporate Debtor Mackeil Ispat & Forging Limited). Respondent No. 2 is State Bank of India (Financial Creditor). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Loan facility from a consortium of banks. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Debt declared NPA on 28.01.2014 (SBI) and at various dates in 2013/2014 for other consortium banks. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Section 7 application filed on 01.02.2019. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The Corporate Debtor continuously submitted OTS proposals from 2014 to 2018 and made several upfront part payments in 2018 towards the OTS. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Kolkata admitted the Section 7 petition on 03.02.2020.
legal_issues: Whether OTS proposals constitute an acknowledgment of debt extending the limitation period under Section 18 of the Limitation Act, and whether Section 23 of the Evidence Act renders such OTS offers inadmissible as evidence of acknowledgment.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An offer for a One Time Settlement (OTS) and part payments made towards it constitute a valid acknowledgment of debt, which restarts the limitation period under Sections 18 and 19 of the Limitation Act. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 23 of the Evidence Act (which bars admissions made 'without prejudice' or under condition) does not automatically invalidate OTS proposals as evidence of debt acknowledgment under the IBC unless explicitly proven. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The continuous OTS proposals in 2016, 2017, and 2018, combined with actual upfront payments in 2018, clearly extended the limitation period well before the 3-year expiration. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The debt was not time-barred because the Corporate Debtor actively acknowledged the liability within the limitation window.
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed. There shall be no orders as to costs. The NCLT's order admitting the CIRP is affirmed.
summary: A shareholder of the Corporate Debtor challenged the initiation of CIRP by SBI, arguing the debt from 2014 was time-barred and that OTS proposals could not be used as evidence of acknowledgment due to Section 23 of the Evidence Act. NCLAT rejected this, ruling that repeated OTS offers and part payments made by the Corporate Debtor in 2018 validly extended the limitation period under the Limitation Act, making the Section 7 petition well within time.

case_title: Mohd. Nazim Khan vs Committee of Creditors of M/s International Trenching Private Limited & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Mohd. Nazim Khan is the Interim Resolution Professional (IRP) of the Corporate Debtor M/s International Trenching Pvt. Ltd., HDFC Bank Ltd is the sole Financial Creditor (CoC). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Not discussed in detail, CIRP initiated by Operational Creditor Sonal Anand. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default details not applicable to the main issue. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP initiated on 08.08.2019, 1st CoC meeting on 21.09.2019. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: CoC with 100% voting share resolved to replace IRP with another RP without assigning reasons. IRP refused to step down claiming time limitations. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Original CP (IB)-889(ND)/2019 was admitted; later, NCLT in CA-766/2020 ordered the replacement of IRP on 20.11.2020 based on 87% CoC vote, which the IRP challenged.
legal_issues: Whether the Interim Resolution Professional has any vested legal right to continue as Resolution Professional once the Committee of Creditors resolves to replace him in its commercial wisdom.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An Interim Resolution Professional has no vested legal right to continue on the post once the Committee of Creditors takes a decision to replace him. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 22(2) of the IBC vests paramount status on the commercial wisdom of the CoC to replace the IRP, which is not open to judicial intervention. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: If the replacement is sought with the requisite voting share under Section 22, it is non-justiciable. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The bench upheld the NCLT order confirming the replacement of the IRP, affirming the supremacy of the CoC's commercial wisdom.
operative_order: The impugned order dated 20.11.2020 replacing the IRP is confirmed. The appeal is dismissed with no merit.
summary: The appellant, an IRP of M/s International Trenching Pvt. Ltd., challenged his replacement by the CoC. The NCLT upheld the CoC's resolution. The NCLAT affirmed the NCLT's decision, ruling that an IRP holds no vested right to continue in office and the commercial wisdom of the CoC regarding the replacement of an IRP is paramount and non-justiciable. The appeal was dismissed.

case_title: M/s. Hira Cotton vs Mr. T.V. Balasubramanian
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: M/s. Hira Cotton is the Operational Creditor/Transferee, Sholingur Textiles Limited is the Corporate Debtor, and T.V. Balasubramanian is the Resolution Professional. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Appellant supplied cotton to the CD and was owed a sum. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Operational debt of Rs. 5,95,05,918. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Sale agreement executed on 22.06.2018. CIRP commenced on 04.02.2019. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: CD transferred a non-core piece of land valued at Rs. 88,54,790 to the Operational Creditor to partially settle the antecedent debt. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: RP filed MA/709/2019 to set aside the sale agreement as a preferential transaction. NCLT allowed it on 26.02.2021 and imposed costs of Rs. 50,000, which the Operational Creditor appealed.
legal_issues: Whether the execution of the sale agreement by the Corporate Debtor to partially settle antecedent operational debt within one year of CIRP constituted a preferential transaction under Section 43 of the IBC, and if it fell within the 'ordinary course of business' exception.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A transfer of property to an unrelated creditor for an antecedent debt within one year preceding insolvency that puts the creditor in a more beneficial position than in liquidation is a voidable preferential transaction. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: The transfer was not in the 'ordinary course of business' under Section 43(3)(a) as it was a transfer of a capital asset to settle accumulated dues. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Applying the Supreme Court's test in Anuj Jain, the transaction was between unrelated parties within the one-year look-back period and disturbed the waterfall mechanism of Section 53. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The transaction was preferentially discriminatory to other creditors and rightfully set aside by the NCLT.
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed, upholding the NCLT's order declaring the transaction preferential and void. However, the cost of Rs. 50,000 imposed on the appellant is set aside.
summary: The RP of Sholingur Textiles Ltd challenged a sale agreement where the Corporate Debtor transferred land to an Operational Creditor, M/s. Hira Cotton, to partially settle antecedent debts within one year of insolvency. The NCLAT affirmed that the transfer was not in the ordinary course of business and constituted a preferential transaction under Section 43 of the IBC, as it favored one creditor over others. The appeal was dismissed, though the NCLT's cost penalty was waived.

case_title: M/s. Kushal Traders vs Mr. T.V. Balasubramanian
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: M/s. Kushal Traders is the Operational Creditor/Transferee, Sholingur Textiles Limited is the Corporate Debtor, T.V. Balasubramanian is the Resolution Professional. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Appellant supplied cotton and was owed dues by the CD. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Claimed operational debt of Rs. 1,92,39,541. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Sale deed executed on 04.07.2018. CIRP commenced on 04.02.2019. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: CD conveyed a piece of land to the Operational Creditor for Rs. 1,69,07,250 to settle the operational debt. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: RP filed MA/745/2019 seeking to avoid the sale deed under Section 43. NCLT declared it preferential on 26.02.2021, and the Operational Creditor appealed.
legal_issues: Whether the transfer of land to settle antecedent operational dues within the look-back period constitutes a preferential transaction under Section 43 of the IBC.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Settling antecedent operational debts by transferring the corporate debtor's land to the creditor within the one-year look-back period is a preferential transaction. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Such a transfer does not fall within the 'ordinary course of business' exception under Section 43(3)(a). 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Evaluated using the Anuj Jain framework: it was an unrelated party transfer within one year of insolvency, putting the creditor in a beneficial position over others under the Section 53 waterfall. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLT correctly avoided the transaction as it prejudiced other creditors holding equal or higher precedence.
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed, finding no illegality in the NCLT's order avoiding the preferential transaction. No order as to costs.
summary: The Operational Creditor, M/s. Kushal Traders, appealed an NCLT order that voided a land transfer from the Corporate Debtor meant to settle Rs. 1.69 crores in antecedent operational debt. Applying the Supreme Court's precedents, the NCLAT ruled that conveying real estate to settle trade debts within one year of insolvency is a preferential transaction that violates the IBC's priority of distribution. The appeal was dismissed.

case_title: Mahesh Hardware & Pipes Pvt. Ltd. vs Jains & Alliance Palm Ventures Pvt. Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Mahesh Hardware & Pipes Pvt. Ltd. is the Operational Creditor, Jains & Alliance Palm Ventures Pvt. Ltd. is the Corporate Debtor. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Operational Creditor supplied Supreme Plumber Pipe Products based on purchase orders since 2015. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Total claimed default of Rs. 12,75,316 (Principal Rs. 9,15,107 + Interest) as of 19.06.2019. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Section 8 demand notice issued on 19.06.2019 and served on 28.06.2019. CD replied on 15.07.2019. Section 9 petition filed on 04.11.2019. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: CD claimed it paid Rs. 2,60,594 which was unadjusted, but OC produced ledger entries confirming receipt and adjustment of these payments. CD's reply to demand notice merely stated it would verify bill authenticity but did not raise a specific dispute. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT rejected the petition on 19.06.2020 citing pre-existing dispute, suppression of payments, and the IBC not being a recovery forum, which the OC appealed.
legal_issues: Whether a vague assertion of verifying invoice authenticity constitutes a 'pre-existing dispute', and whether a solvent company can be subjected to CIRP for a valid operational debt.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A pre-existing dispute must be genuine and supported by evidence, not a patently feeble legal argument or an assertion of fact unsupported by evidence. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 8(2) requires a clear notice of dispute; an undertaking to verify bills and pay genuine ones does not constitute a pre-existing dispute. The 1 crore threshold notification dated 24.03.2020 is not retrospective. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Adjudicating Authority must separate the grain from the chaff; since the CD failed to identify any specific non-genuine bills and the OC correctly accounted for part-payments, the defense was spurious. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLT erred in rejecting the application as there was no pre-existing dispute and the debt was clearly due and payable.
operative_order: The impugned order is set aside. The case is remitted to the NCLT with a direction to admit the Section 9 application after giving notice to the Corporate Debtor to enable a pre-admission settlement.
summary: The Operational Creditor appealed the NCLT's dismissal of its Section 9 application, which had been rejected on grounds of a pre-existing dispute and an attempt to use the IBC as a recovery forum. The NCLAT overturned the NCLT, finding that the Corporate Debtor's vague reply promising to verify invoices did not amount to a valid pre-existing dispute. The NCLAT remanded the matter with directions to admit the insolvency petition.

case_title: The Central Board Of Trustees, EPF vs The Liquidator (Sri. Gorur Narasimhamurthy Venkataraman)
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Central Board Of Trustees, EPF (Employees' Provident Fund Organisation) is the Appellant/Creditor, Sri. Gorur Narasimhamurthy Venkataraman is the Liquidator of M/s. Bunt Solar India Pvt. Ltd. (Corporate Debtor). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Statutory dues relating to unremitted employee provident fund contributions. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default in EPF dues amounting to Rs. 2,34,10,240 spanning from 2015 to 2017. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Liquidator issued public announcement on 05.10.2019. Appellant submitted claim on 11.10.2019. CD was dissolved by NCLT on 06.01.2021. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The liquidator requested the Appellant to file a notarized claim in Form C, which was not done properly. The CD had zero/nil assets, rendering the liquidation estate empty except for minor fixed deposits. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT passed a dissolution order on 06.01.2021. The Appellant challenged the dissolution, demanding priority payment of EPF dues.
legal_issues: Whether directions for priority payment of EPF dues under Section 36(4)(a)(iii) can be passed against a liquidator when the Corporate Debtor has nil assets and has already been dissolved.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: While provident fund dues are excluded from the liquidation estate and hold priority, no recovery can be enforced if the corporate debtor's assets are nil and the entity is legally dissolved. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 36(4)(a)(iii) exempts EPF dues from the liquidation estate, meaning they must be paid in full outside the Section 53 waterfall, provided funds exist. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The court observed that the liquidation estate possessed nil value and the company ceased to exist, rendering any payment directives factually impossible to execute. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Since the Corporate Debtor was dissolved and had no assets, no effective relief could be granted against the non-existent entity.
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed as devoid of merits. No orders as to cost, as no directions can be passed against a non-existent entity with nil value.
summary: The EPFO appealed against the NCLT's dissolution order of M/s Bunt Solar India Pvt. Ltd., seeking priority payment of Rs. 2.34 crores in EPF dues. While the NCLAT agreed that EPF dues fall outside the liquidation estate and supersede the IBC's waterfall mechanism, it dismissed the appeal because the Corporate Debtor had absolutely no assets and had already been dissolved. The tribunal concluded it could not issue financial directives against a non-existent entity with nil value.

case_title: M/s. Sri Ganapathi Financiers vs M/s. Srirangam Priya Promoters Private Limited
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: M/s. Sri Ganapathi Financiers is the Financial Creditor, M/s. Srirangam Priya Promoters Pvt. Ltd. is the Corporate Debtor, and Mr. A. Francis is the Managing Director. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Loan of Rs. 1 Crore allegedly given to the CD for business and real estate development. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Claimed outstanding of Rs. 76,53,969 including a principal of Rs. 50,00,000 as of 16.12.2019. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Mortgage deed executed 20.10.2015. MoU executed on 05.07.2019 undertaking to repay within 45 days. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Bank statements showed the loan was transferred to the personal RTGS account of the MD, Mr. A. Francis, not the CD. The MD mortgaged his personal property. The MoU was unregistered and lacked signatures of all lenders on every page. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The NCLT dismissed the Section 7 petition on 23.02.2021 due to lack of privity and because the MoU was unregistered, which the creditor appealed.
legal_issues: Whether an unregistered MoU can be relied upon as a 'financial contract' to initiate Section 7 proceedings against a Corporate Debtor when the actual loan was disbursed to the personal account of its Managing Director.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A Section 7 application cannot be maintained against a corporate debtor if the financial disbursement was made to a director in their personal capacity and there is no privity of contract with the corporate debtor. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: An unregistered MoU purporting to create rights over immovable property is inadmissible in evidence under Section 49(C) of the Registration Act and does not constitute a valid financial contract under IBC Rules if its genuineness is in severe doubt. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal noted the bank statements proved disbursement to the MD's personal account, and the suspicious, unregistered MoU lacking signatures of all lenders could not establish corporate liability. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLT correctly rejected the application as there was no enforceable financial debt owed by the Corporate Debtor.
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed as devoid of merits. No orders as to costs, granting the appellant liberty to avail alternate legal remedies.
summary: The appellant financial institution challenged the NCLT's dismissal of its Section 7 petition against a real estate company. The NCLAT affirmed the dismissal, finding that the loan was actually disbursed to the personal bank account of the company's Managing Director, who mortgaged his personal property. The tribunal rejected the creditor's reliance on a suspicious, unregistered Memorandum of Understanding, ruling that there was no privity of contract with the Corporate Debtor.

case_title: Dr. Joe Verghese & Ors vs M/s Omega Hospitals Pvt Ltd & Ors
appeal_number: I.A. No. 2313 of 2020 in Company Appeal (AT) No. 77 of 2019
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Dr. Joe Verghese, Dr. R.L. Kamath, and Dr. P. Subramanya Bhat are Appellants/Applicants (minority shareholders). M/s. Omega Hospitals Pvt. Ltd. is the Company (Respondent No. 1), and Dr. K. Mukund is the contesting Respondent. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Management and operation of a multi-specialty hospital. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Not applicable; pertains to oppression and mismanagement. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The original NCLT order was passed on 24.01.2019. The IA was filed in 2020. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Applicants alleged massive financial fraud, dual invoicing of patients, siphoning of hospital revenue to a private entity (Mangalore Heart Scan Foundation), and production of two conflicting audited balance sheets for FY 2017-18. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT disposed of the original company petitions without going into the allegations of mismanagement. During the pendency of the appeal, the appellants filed this IA seeking a forensic audit.
legal_issues: Whether a forensic audit should be ordered during the pendency of an appeal concerning oppression and mismanagement to ascertain allegations of severe financial fraud and siphoning of funds.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The Tribunal possesses the inherent power to order a forensic audit during appellate proceedings to unearth truth regarding allegations of fraud and siphoning of corporate funds, aiding the final determination of oppression and mismanagement claims. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Such an audit is necessary in the larger interest of the company under Sections 241/242 to ascertain the veracity of financial discrepancies before final disposal. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The presence of conflicting financial statements, absence of statutory audits for recent years, and serious allegations backed by shareholders holding 49.4% equity justified the appointment of an auditor. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The bench allowed the application, mandating a forensic audit to assist the Tribunal in deciding the main appeal, without expressing an opinion on the final merits.
operative_order: I.A. No. 2313 of 2020 is allowed. The Independent Chairperson is directed to appoint a Forensic Accountant to audit the financial years 2017-18 to 2020-21, with the report to be submitted in a sealed cover within three months.
summary: During a pending appeal concerning oppression and mismanagement in Omega Hospitals, the minority shareholders filed an interlocutory application seeking a forensic audit. They alleged severe financial irregularities, including dual invoicing and siphoning of funds to a rival entity. The NCLAT allowed the application and directed an independent chairperson to appoint a forensic auditor to investigate the accounts from 2017 to 2021 to aid the tribunal in adjudicating the main appeal.

case_title: Gangar Opticians Pvt. Ltd. vs Jayantilal Bhimshi Gangar & Ors
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Gangar Opticians Pvt. Ltd. is the Appellant Company. Jayantilal Bhimshi Gangar and Pragnesh Jayantilal Gangar are the Respondents (ousted directors/shareholders holding 16.25% and 5% respectively). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Close-knit family business running over 60 optician retail stores. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Not applicable (Oppression and Mismanagement). 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: NCLT passed interim orders maintaining status quo on 26.09.2019 and 15.10.2019, and the impugned order appointing a valuer on 16.12.2020. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The Respondents alleged illegal removal from the board and restriction from offices. The Appellant alleged the Respondents stole confidential data, misused emails, and froze company bank accounts. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: In CP 4065/2019, the NCLT passed an interim order on 16.12.2020 appointing an independent valuer to value the company's assets, which the Company appealed.
legal_issues: Whether the NCLT can order the valuation of a company's assets as an interim relief in a Section 241/242 petition without first establishing the factual merits of the oppression and mismanagement claims.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Appointing an independent valuer at the interim stage of an oppression and mismanagement petition is improper and premature without first establishing the factual basis of the dispute. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 242 provides various methodologies to arrest internal disputes; ordering a valuation implicitly signals a buy-out remedy, which should only follow a substantive finding of oppression. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal noted that exposing a flagship commercial company to a valuation process during a bitter internal dispute severely degrades its commercial image and value. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLT erred in ordering valuation at the initial interim stage, as such a measure is a final relief mechanism.
operative_order: The appeals are disposed of. The NCLT's impugned order dated 16.12.2020 appointing an independent valuer is set aside, while the previous status quo orders remain undisturbed.
summary: In a bitter family dispute over the control of Gangar Opticians, the ousted minority shareholders filed an oppression and mismanagement petition. The NCLT passed an interim order appointing an independent valuer. The NCLAT set aside this order, ruling that appointing a valuer is a final relief mechanism (often leading to a buyout) and is highly improper at the interim stage, as it can damage the flagship company's commercial reputation before the facts are established.

case_title: Mr. Kishore Bachuram Kapdi vs Bank of Maharashtra & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Kishore Bachuram Kapdi is the Promoter/Director of M/s Afcan Impex Pvt. Ltd. (Corporate Debtor), Bank of Maharashtra is the Financial Creditor. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Financial credit facilities extended by the Bank. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default amount of Rs. 8,44,15,488. Date of NPA was 28.10.2016. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CD executed balance confirmations on 30.09.2016 and 15.07.2019. Section 7 application filed on 28.07.2020. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The bank relied on balance confirmation letters explicitly acknowledging the debt to extend limitation under Section 18 of the Limitation Act. The Appellant claimed he missed NCLT hearings because he was quarantined with COVID-19 after a Europe trip. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT admitted the Section 7 application ex-parte on 17.02.2021 after the CD failed to appear despite notices, which the promoter appealed.
legal_issues: Whether the Section 7 application was time-barred when the NPA date was in 2016, and whether the NCLT violated natural justice by proceeding ex-parte.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Balance confirmation letters signed by the corporate debtor constitute valid acknowledgments of debt under Section 18 of the Limitation Act, renewing the three-year limitation period. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 18 applies to IBC proceedings; an acknowledgment before the expiration of the limitation period extends it. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Since the CD acknowledged the debt on 15.07.2019, the filing on 28.07.2020 was well within three years. Furthermore, natural justice was not violated as the CD's claim that a single director's COVID quarantine prevented any appearance was untenable for a corporate entity. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLT correctly admitted the application as the debt was within limitation and the CD willfully ignored the notices.
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed as having no substance, affirming the NCLT's ex-parte admission of the insolvency application. No cost.
summary: The promoter of Afcan Impex challenged the NCLT's ex-parte admission of a Section 7 insolvency petition filed by the Bank of Maharashtra, claiming the debt was time-barred (NPA in 2016) and that COVID-19 prevented his appearance. The NCLAT dismissed the appeal, ruling that balance confirmation letters signed in 2019 validly extended the limitation period under Section 18 of the Limitation Act. The tribunal also found the company's failure to appear before the NCLT unjustified.

case_title: Mohd. Nazim Khan vs HDFC Bank Limited & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Mohd. Nazim Khan is the Interim Resolution Professional (IRP) of the Corporate Debtor M/s International Trenching Pvt. Ltd. HDFC Bank Limited is the sole Financial Creditor. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Not discussed in detail; CIRP initiated against the CD. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Not applicable. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP 180 days expired on 04.02.2020. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The CoC had resolved to replace the IRP. Later, CoC resolved to initiate liquidation. The IRP challenged the NCLT order directing him to convene a CoC meeting for CIRP extension. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The NCLT directed the IRP to convene a CoC meeting on 13.10.2020. The IRP appealed, arguing the application was filed by the financial creditor without authorization.
legal_issues: Whether the NCLT's direction to convene a CoC meeting to consider CIRP extension can be challenged by the IRP when the CoC subsequently resolves for liquidation and the IRP's prior appeal regarding his replacement has been dismissed.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An appeal by an IRP against procedural directions of the NCLT becomes infructuous and stale if the CoC subsequently resolves to liquidate the Corporate Debtor and the IRP's primary appeal against replacement is dismissed. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: The commercial wisdom of the CoC is paramount. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Since the connected appeal was dismissed and CIRP moved to liquidation, the current appeal had no surviving cause of action. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The appeal was dismissed as stale and lacking merit.
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed with no order as to costs.
summary: The IRP challenged an NCLT order directing him to convene a CoC meeting for a CIRP extension. The NCLAT dismissed the appeal, noting that the CoC had already resolved to liquidate the Corporate Debtor and the appellant's connected appeal regarding his replacement had been dismissed, rendering the present appeal stale and infructuous.

case_title: Shapoorji Pallonji and Company Private Limited vs M/S. Shore Dwellings Pvt. Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Shapoorji Pallonji and Company Private Limited is the Operational Creditor. M/S. Shore Dwellings Pvt. Ltd (formerly Mantri Dwellings Pvt. Ltd.) is the Corporate Debtor. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Construction contract dated 14.01.2011 for Mantri Pinnacle High Rise Residential Project. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Acknowledged debt of Rs. 6,98,47,408. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Final bill issued on 09.05.2019. Section 8 demand notice issued on 05.08.2020. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The parties executed a settlement recording the debt payable in installments, which the CD defaulted on. CD requested a revised payment schedule in Jan 2020 but still failed to pay. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT rejected the Section 9 application on 18.12.2020, citing ongoing negotiations and COVID-19 economic scenarios, which the OC appealed.
legal_issues: Whether the Adjudicating Authority can reject a Section 9 application on equitable grounds, such as pending settlement negotiations or economic hardship, when debt and default are clearly admitted and there is no pre-existing dispute.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The Adjudicating Authority is not a court of equity; if the criteria under Section 9 are fulfilled (admitted debt, default, and no pre-existing dispute), the application must be admitted. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 9 leaves no room to reject an application merely because negotiations are ongoing or economic conditions are bleak, provided the statutory threshold is met. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The NCLT erred by substituting the statutory requirements with its own equitable considerations of the COVID-19 scenario. The CD clearly admitted the debt in meetings and failed to honor revised payment schedules. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLT's order was illegal per se as it ignored the undisputed debt and default.
operative_order: The impugned order is set aside. The Adjudicating Authority is directed to admit the Section 9 application in accordance with the law, after affording an opportunity to the parties.
summary: The NCLT had rejected a Section 9 application filed by a construction company despite admitted debt and default, citing ongoing negotiations and economic hardships due to COVID-19. The NCLAT overturned the decision, emphasizing that the NCLT is not a court of equity and must strictly evaluate whether the statutory criteria of debt, default, and lack of pre-existing dispute are met. The matter was remanded for admission.

case_title: M/s. Unicon Buildtech vs Aishwarya Mohan Gahrana
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: M/s. Unicon Buildtech is the Prospective Resolution Applicant. Aishwarya Mohan Gahrana is the Resolution Professional of the Corporate Debtor, Durha Vitrak Private Limited. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Submission of a resolution plan for the Corporate Debtor. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Not applicable. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The 6th CoC meeting was held on 28.01.2021. Liquidation ordered on 31.05.2021. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The Appellant requested a postponement of its presentation to the CoC due to internet issues caused by farmer protests. The CoC proceeded to consider and reject the plan on merits, citing its conditional nature, lack of upfront payment, and lack of experience. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Following the CoC's rejection, the NCLT ordered liquidation on 31.05.2021. The Appellant challenged this, arguing its pending application to present its plan was ignored.
legal_issues: Whether a prospective resolution applicant has a vested right to demand the CoC consider its plan or grant an adjournment for presentation, thereby halting liquidation proceedings.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A prospective resolution applicant has no vested right to have its resolution plan approved or to dictate the timelines of the CoC's commercial decision-making process. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 33(2) empowers the CoC to recommend liquidation. The decision to reject a plan is a non-justiciable commercial decision. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The CoC had evaluated the plan clause by clause and rejected it on valid commercial grounds (e.g., conditional model, no upfront payment). The NCLAT cannot second-guess this commercial wisdom. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLT's liquidation order was valid, and the rejection of the resolution plan by the CoC cannot be interfered with.
operative_order: The NCLAT declined to entertain the appeal, and it was disposed of accordingly.
summary: A prospective resolution applicant challenged the NCLT's liquidation order, arguing that the CoC arbitrarily rejected its plan after it requested an adjournment due to internet issues. The NCLAT dismissed the appeal, relying on the Supreme Court's ruling in Arcelormittal that resolution applicants have no vested right to plan approval. The CoC's rejection was based on sound commercial wisdom, which the NCLAT refused to interfere with.

case_title: M/s. Hira International Ltd. vs M/s. Girdharilal Sugar & Allied Industries Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: M/s. Hira International Ltd. is the Operational Creditor. M/s. Girdharilal Sugar & Allied Industries Ltd. is the Corporate Debtor. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Supply of Soya Bean by the Operational Creditor to the Corporate Debtor. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Outstanding operational dues of Rs. 59,75,055. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Last bill dated 28.07.2015. RTGS part-payment made on 24.11.2017. Section 9 application filed on 17.07.2019. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: ICICI Bank statement showed a payment of Rs. 2 Lakhs on 24.11.2017 from 'Premier Nutritions', which was the registered trade name of the Corporate Debtor for GST purposes. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT dismissed the application on 08.12.2020 on the grounds of limitation (ignoring the part-payment as a 'paltry' sum from a different entity) and raising doubts over invoice dates.
legal_issues: Whether a part-payment made by a Corporate Debtor under its registered trade name extends the limitation period under Section 19 of the Limitation Act, irrespective of the payment's quantum.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Any part-payment of a debt extends the limitation period under Section 19 of the Limitation Act, and the statute creates no distinction based on the quantum (e.g., 'paltry') of the payment. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 19 of the Limitation Act restarts the limitation period from the date of part-payment. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The GST certificate confirmed that the entity making the payment was merely the trade name of the Corporate Debtor. Hence, the payment was validly from the CD, extending the limitation period to November 2020, making the July 2019 filing timely. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLT erred in dismissing the application on limitation and incorrectly cast doubt on undisputed invoices.
operative_order: The impugned order is quashed and set aside. The matter is remitted back to the Adjudicating Authority with a direction to admit the application and pass consequential orders.
summary: The NCLT had dismissed a Section 9 application on limitation grounds, disregarding a part-payment because it was small and made under a trade name. The NCLAT reversed this, holding that Section 19 of the Limitation Act does not distinguish based on the quantum of payment, and GST records proved the trade name belonged to the Corporate Debtor. The debt was therefore within limitation, and the NCLT was directed to admit the petition.

case_title: Vijisan Jewels Pvt. Ltd vs Cimme Jewels Limited & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Vijisan Jewels Pvt. Ltd is the Appellant/Tenant. Cimme Jewels Limited is the Corporate Debtor in liquidation, and Mr. Naren Sheth is the Liquidator. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Leave and license agreement for factory premises measuring 1019.81 sq meters in MIDC, Mumbai. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Unpaid rental dues by the tenant since January 2020. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Lease expired on 31.03.2019. Liquidation order passed on 25.03.2019. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The Appellant refused to vacate the premises after the lease expired and sought to buy the property directly from the Liquidator outside the e-auction process, offering Rs. 10.5 Crore. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The Liquidator filed an application for vacant possession. NCLT directed the Appellant to vacate, pay arrears, and participate in the e-auction. The Appellant challenged this order.
legal_issues: Whether a tenant/licensee of a Corporate Debtor in liquidation has the locus standi to demand a private sale of the leased property by the Liquidator outside the statutory e-auction process.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Being a tenant does not confer any locus standi to seek directions against a Liquidator or to bypass the statutory e-auction mechanism for the realization of assets. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Chapter VI of the IBBI (Liquidation Process) Regulations, 2016 mandates specific procedures for the realization of assets (e.g., e-auctions), which cannot be subverted by a tenant forcing a private sale. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Appellant was an illegal occupant post-lease expiration and failed to pay rent. Such frivolous actions disrupt the time-bound liquidation process. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLT's direction for the tenant to vacate, pay arrears, and participate fairly in the e-auction suffered from no legal infirmity.
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed as frivolous and not maintainable. Interim orders are vacated with no orders as to costs.
summary: An illegal occupant whose lease with the Corporate Debtor had expired sought to bypass the e-auction process and compel the Liquidator to sell the factory premises directly to it. The NCLAT upheld the NCLT's order directing eviction and payment of rent arrears, holding that a tenant has no locus standi to dictate the liquidation asset realization process and must participate in the standard e-auction.

case_title: Department of Sales Tax vs Rajat Mukharjee & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Department of Sales Tax (Maharashtra) is the Appellant/Operational Creditor. Rajat Mukharjee is the Resolution Professional of M/s AVK Automall Pvt. Ltd. (Corporate Debtor). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Statutory sales tax dues owed to the government. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: The Appellant filed a claim for Rs. 14,84,33,763. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Resolution plan was approved by the NCLT on 05.03.2021. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The CoC (with 94.60% voting share) approved a Resolution Plan submitted by M/s Leadadroit Services Pvt. Ltd. that allocated only Rs. 14.50 Lakhs toward operational creditors including statutory authorities, effectively imposing a 99% haircut on the Sales Tax dues. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT approved the Resolution Plan via order dated 05.03.2021. The Sales Tax Department appealed, questioning the massive haircut.
legal_issues: Whether a Resolution Plan providing a 99% haircut to statutory dues of the Sales Tax Department can be set aside when it has been duly approved by the Committee of Creditors in its commercial wisdom.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Once a Resolution Plan is approved by the Adjudicating Authority, it becomes binding on all stakeholders, and any statutory dues not fully accommodated within the plan stand extinguished. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 31 of the IBC binds the Central/State Governments and local authorities to the approved Resolution Plan, extinguishing unprovided claims (following the Supreme Court's decision in Ghanshyam Mishra). 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The CoC approved the distribution pattern, including the payout to statutory authorities, utilizing its non-justiciable commercial wisdom. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT declined to interfere, affirming that operational creditors (including tax authorities) must accept the haircuts determined by the CoC.
operative_order: The appeal is disposed of at the stage of admission as the tribunal declined to admit it. No orders as to costs.
summary: The Maharashtra Department of Sales Tax appealed against an NCLT order approving a Resolution Plan that imposed a 99% haircut on its tax claims. Relying on the Supreme Court's ruling in Ghanshyam Mishra, the NCLAT dismissed the appeal, holding that statutory dues are bound by the CoC's commercial wisdom and stand extinguished to the extent they are not provided for in the approved Resolution Plan.

case_title: Mr. Ashutosh Jain vs Morpheus Developers Pvt. Ltd.
appeal_number: Contempt Case (AT) No. 18 of 2020 in Company Appeal (AT) (Ins.) No. 1155 of 2019
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Ashutosh Jain (Erstwhile IRP) and Sandeep Kumar Bhatt (Erstwhile RP) are the Applicants. Morpheus Developers Pvt. Ltd. (Corporate Debtor) and its Directors are the Respondents/Contemnors. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Payment of IRP/RP fees and CIRP costs following a settlement between the Corporate Debtor and allottees. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Unpaid CIRP costs of Rs. 6,90,310 to the IRP and a balance of Rs. 13,90,000 to the RP. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: NCLT directed payment on 18.09.2019. NCLAT ordered payment by 02.12.2019. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The Corporate Debtor withdrew its appeal by promising to pay the CIRP costs by 02.12.2019 but failed to pay the full amounts, ignoring multiple opportunities to reply to the contempt applications. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The Applicants filed contempt applications before the NCLAT. The Respondents failed to appear or file a reply, demonstrating deliberate avoidance.
legal_issues: Whether the Corporate Debtor and its Directors committed contempt of court by deliberately avoiding the payment of CIRP costs and fees directed by the Adjudicating Authority and affirmed by the NCLAT.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Deliberate failure by corporate debtor management to pay statutorily mandated CIRP costs and professional fees, despite clear judicial directives and undertakings, warrants the initiation of contempt proceedings. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 425 of the Companies Act, 2013 empowers the Tribunal to punish for contempt. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The blatant disregard for the payment deadline (02.12.2019) and failure to appear or file replies established deliberate non-compliance by the contemnors. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT concluded that the Respondents willfully disobeyed the orders and directed the Adjudicating Authority to formally register and proceed with a contempt case.
operative_order: The NCLAT directed the Adjudicating Authority (NCLT, Principal Bench) to register a Contempt Case against Respondent Nos. 1 to 3 and proceed as per law. Parties were directed to appear before the NCLT on 01.09.2021.
summary: The erstwhile IRP and RP filed contempt applications against the Corporate Debtor and its directors for failing to pay CIRP costs and fees as directed by the NCLT and promised before the NCLAT. Noting the respondents' deliberate evasion and failure to appear or reply, the NCLAT found willful disobedience and directed the NCLT to register a formal contempt case against the management.

case_title: West Bengal Financial Corporation vs Bijoy Murmuria & Ors
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Financial Creditor/Appellant (West Bengal Financial Corporation), Corporate Debtor (Dimension Steel & Alloys Pvt. Ltd.), RP (Bijoy Murmuria), Resolution Applicant (C. P. Ispat Pvt. Ltd.). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process (CIRP) initiated in 2019. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Not explicitly detailed in this appeal (CIRP already ongoing). 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP extended till 22.12.2020. CoC decided on liquidation on 04.01.2021. Resolution plan submitted late on 05.02.2021. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Minutes of CoC dated 04.01.2021 recommending liquidation. Adjudicating Authority condoned 43 days delay for RA to submit plan to CoC. CoC extended time further on 25.03.2021. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Adjudicating Authority in IA/426(KB)2021 rejected Appellant's application to order liquidation under Section 33 despite timeline breaches, preferring resolution.
legal_issues: Whether an order for liquidation under Section 33 of the IBC is mandatory when the CIRP timeframe expires, or whether the Adjudicating Authority can exercise discretion to allow consideration of a delayed Resolution Plan to prioritize resolution over liquidation.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The main objective of the IBC is the resolution of the Corporate Debtor, and liquidation should only be ordered as a last resort; strict non-adherence to timelines may be excused if a viable resolution plan is pending approval. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 33 of IBC does not strip the Adjudicating Authority of its discretion to withhold a liquidation order when a resolution plan has already been approved by the CoC, even if timelines under Section 12 were breached. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Evaluated the advanced stage of the CIRP (voting completed, plan approved by CoC) against the delay, concluding the prejudice of liquidation outweighs procedural delays. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The bench upheld the Adjudicating Authority's discretion to decline a liquidation order and consider the approved Resolution Plan on its merits, dismissing the appeal.
operative_order: The appeal was dismissed. The Adjudicating Authority was directed to consider the Resolution Plan as placed before it on its own merits in terms of the provisions of law. No costs.
summary: In a CIRP concerning Dimension Steel & Alloys Pvt. Ltd., the CoC initially recommended liquidation but later considered a delayed resolution plan. West Bengal Financial Corporation appealed against the NCLT's refusal to order immediate liquidation under Section 33 of the IBC. The NCLAT dismissed the appeal, holding that the IBC's primary objective is resolution, and the NCLT correctly exercised its discretion to wait for the CoC's decision on an approved plan rather than forcing liquidation.

case_title: Vinod Sehwag vs Siemens Financial Services Pvt. Ltd. And Ors
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Financial Creditor (Siemens Financial Services Pvt. Ltd.), Corporate Debtor (Xalta Foods & Beverages Pvt. Ltd.), Personal Guarantor (Vinod Sehwag), Resolution Professional (Amit Ojha). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Underlying loan for which Vinod Sehwag stood as a personal guarantor. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default in repayment of the loan along with interest; exact amount/date not detailed in the appellate order. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Orders passed on 22.03.2021 and 09.06.2021. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The Adjudicating Authority prematurely concluded that a default occurred in its initial order appointing the RP, before receiving the Section 99 report. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT New Delhi admitted the Section 95 application ex-parte on 22.03.2021, appointed an RP, and declared a default. On 09.06.2021, it rejected the Guarantor's recall application. The Guarantor appealed to NCLAT.
legal_issues: Whether the Adjudicating Authority can record a finding of 'default' at the stage of appointing a Resolution Professional under Section 97 of the IBC, and whether a limited notice must be given to the Personal Guarantor before such appointment.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: At the stage of acting on an application under Section 95 read with Section 96 of the IBC, the Adjudicating Authority cannot pre-judge or record a finding of 'default', as this preempts the Resolution Professional's statutory report. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 97 does not involve adjudication of default; the stage for considering default arrives only under Section 100 after the RP submits a report under Section 99. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Applied the principles of natural justice and the precedent set in 'Ravi Ajit Kulkarni', determining that failing to issue limited notice to the guarantor and pre-determining default prejudiced the statutory process. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The bench set aside the premature finding of default and the subsequent report, ruling that a limited notice must be issued to the Personal Guarantor merely to secure presence, after which the RP must prepare the Section 99 report objectively.
operative_order: The appeal was partly allowed. The Adjudicating Authority's premature findings of default were set aside. The appointment of the RP was maintained, but the RP's report was set aside. The matter was remitted back for the RP to give the Guarantor an opportunity under Section 99 and file a fresh report.
summary: Siemens Financial Services initiated insolvency against Vinod Sehwag, personal guarantor for Xalta Foods. The NCLT appointed an RP and simultaneously declared a default without issuing notice to Sehwag. Relying on the Ravi Ajit Kulkarni precedent, the NCLAT ruled that recording a default at the Section 97 stage is premature and prejudices the Section 99 report. The NCLAT partly allowed the appeal, setting aside the default findings and the RP's report, and remitted the matter for fresh compliance with principles of natural justice.

case_title: Dnyaneshwar Krishnaji Takalkar & Ors vs B. D. Impex Pvt. Ltd. & Ors
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellants (Dnyaneshwar Krishnaji Takalkar, Praveen Dnyaneshwar Takalkar, Sachin Dnyaneshwar Takalkar - Suspended Directors), Respondent No. 1 / Operational Creditor (B. D. Impex Pvt. Ltd.), Corporate Debtor (Kohinoor Precision Component Ltd.). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Underlying operational debt leading to CP No. 2323/I&B/2018. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Not explicitly detailed in the appellate order as the appeal was dismissed on limitation. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Impugned NCLT order passed on 02.01.2020. Certified copy issued on 07.01.2020. Maximum condonable appeal period (30+15 days) expired on 21.02.2020. Appeal filed on 10.03.2021. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The appeal was filed more than a year after the expiry of the statutory 45-day outer limit for filing an appeal under Section 61 of the IBC. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The NCLT Mumbai passed an order on 02.01.2020. The suspended directors filed the present appeal on 10.03.2021, falsely claiming in their memo that the appeal was within the 30-day period.
legal_issues: Whether the Appellate Tribunal has the jurisdiction to entertain an appeal filed beyond the absolute statutory limitation period of 45 days (30 days + 15 days condonable) under Section 61 of the IBC.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The Appellate Tribunal has no jurisdiction to entertain an appeal filed beyond the maximum prescribed period of 45 days (30 days regular + 15 days condonable), regardless of the reasons for the delay. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 61(2) of the IBC strictly limits the filing of an appeal to 30 days, with a proviso allowing a maximum extension of 15 days if sufficient cause is shown; this outer limit is mandatory and inflexible. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Calculated the limitation period from the date the certified copy was issued (07.01.2020) and found the appeal date (10.03.2021) to be far beyond the permissible 45-day window. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The bench concluded that since the appeal was filed well beyond the 15-day condonable period after the expiry of the initial 30 days, it was entirely time-barred and beyond the Tribunal's jurisdiction to entertain.
operative_order: The appeal was dismissed as time-barred. No costs were imposed.
summary: Suspended directors of Kohinoor Precision Component Ltd. appealed an NCLT order over a year after it was passed, incorrectly claiming the appeal was within limitation. The NCLAT examined the dates, noting the order was passed on 02.01.2020 and the appeal was filed on 10.03.2021. The Tribunal dismissed the appeal strictly on limitation, ruling that under Section 61 of the IBC, it lacks jurisdiction to condone any delay beyond the maximum permissible period of 45 days (30 days standard + 15 days condonable).

case_title: The Deputy Commissioner of GST and Central Excise vs Vijaykumar V. Iyer
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Operational Creditor/Appellant (Deputy Commissioner of GST and Central Excise), Corporate Debtors (Dishnet Wireless Limited and Aircel Cellular Limited), Resolution Professional (Vijaykumar V. Iyer), Resolution Applicant (UV Asset Reconstruction Company Ltd). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Unpaid statutory dues (GST and Central Excise) owed by the telecom companies. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Alleged total statutory dues amounting to roughly 100 Crores, predating the CIRP. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP initiated in 2018. Resolution plan approved on 09.06.2020. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The Appellant failed to file any claim during the entire CIRP period. The Resolution Plan contained Clause 9.1.4 explicitly preventing the customs/excise board from voiding transactions or imposing successor liability. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Mumbai approved the Resolution Plans for Dishnet and Aircel on 09.06.2020. The GST Department appealed, claiming they had no notice and their dues were ignored despite being in the company's records.
legal_issues: Whether statutory dues owed to the government can be enforced or challenged against a Successful Resolution Applicant if the government department failed to file a claim during the CIRP before the approval of the Resolution Plan.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Claims that are not submitted during the CIRP and are consequently not a part of the approved Resolution Plan stand completely extinguished upon approval of the plan. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 31 of the IBC mandates that a duly approved resolution plan is binding on all stakeholders, including the Central and State Governments regarding statutory dues. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal relied strictly on the Hon'ble Supreme Court's ruling in 'Ghanshyam Mishra', determining that the Appellant's failure to file a claim pre-approval was fatal, rendering any internal records of the Corporate Debtor irrelevant. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Since the Appellant did not file claims during the CIRP, their dues were lawfully extinguished, and the Adjudicating Authority correctly approved the Resolution Plan which shielded the new applicant from past statutory liabilities.
operative_order: The appeals were dismissed. The Appellant was directed to follow the binding precedent of the Supreme Court, extinguishing their claims. No costs were ordered.
summary: The GST and Central Excise Department appealed the NCLT's approval of the resolution plans for Dishnet Wireless and Aircel Cellular, arguing their statutory dues of around 100 crores were ignored despite being in the corporate records. The NCLAT dismissed the appeals, noting the Department failed to file any claims during the CIRP. Applying the Supreme Court's ruling in Ghanshyam Mishra, the NCLAT held that all unfiled statutory claims are permanently extinguished upon approval of a Resolution Plan under Section 31 of the IBC.
